title: Ogunquit couple sues town over fines for rooster statues
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Ogunquit couple sues town over $1,700 in fines for rooster statues
The couple says the rooster statues are a source of comfort for their 6-year-old daughter, who has autism. The town argues the roosters serve as an advertisement for the couple's restaurant.
Ogunquit couple sues town over $1,700 in fines for rooster statues
The couple says the rooster statues are a source of comfort for their 6-year-old daughter, who has autism. The town argues the roosters serve as an advertisement for the couple's restaurant.
An Ogunquit couple that has been fined $1,700 by the town over rooster statues displayed outside of their home has filed a federal lawsuit, claiming that their First Amendment rights have been violated.
Dave and Sara LeBlanc first displayed a 6-foot-tall tin rooster in front of their Main Street home in May 2025 as a show of love and support for their daughter, Pyper, who has autism. The couple said Pyper, who is now 6 years old, loves roosters and that the statue helped her find comfort while she waited for the school bus and when she came home from school each day.
Since their daughter loved the rooster statue so much, Dave and Sara LeBlanc said they acquired about two dozen tin roosters over time but never displayed more than eight at once on their property with the exception of the Christmas holiday season, when they arrange roosters to appear as if they are pulling Santa's sleigh.
The LeBlancs also own The Omelette Factory, a breakfast restaurant that is attached to the family's home. After the roosters on their front lawn became a popular landmark in town, the couple decided to add a rooster to the logo on The Omelette Factory's merchandise, which is sold inside the restaurant. In the lawsuit, Dave and Sara LeBlanc said the rooster became like "a family crest," and that the restaurant's merchandise does not depict the roosters displayed on their lawn.
On or about April 3, 2026, the town sent a letter to the LeBlancs, notifying them that they were in violation of the Zoning Code for "unpermitted signage" and "overage of allowable square footage of signage." In the letter, the town ordered the LeBlancs to immediately remove the unpermitted signage, including but not limited to the rooster statues.
"It's a range of emotions for her because she's like, 'Why can't the town be nice? Like, we're taught to be nice,'" Sara LeBlanc said.
According to the lawsuit, Ogunquit Code Enforcement Officer Tyler McOsker told the couple that the town viewed the tin roosters as signs because the statues are believed to be advertisements for The Omelette Factory.
"Never imagined it getting to the point where it is. But it had to. We had no choice," Dave LeBlanc said. "It's just where it brought us. We have beliefs and we have a job to do to raise her. Do we go along and just get steamrolled, or stand up for what you believe in life?"
The town sent another letter to the LeBlancs on April 6, imposing a $150 fine for illegal signage because of the rooster statues. Ten days later, the town sent another letter imposing an additional $300 fine for failing to remove the decorative roosters.
The LeBlancs appealed their fines to the Zoning Board of Appeals, arguing that the rooster statues are not signs or advertisements but instead "are art, a comfort for their daughter, and a symbol of their love for her," according to the couple's lawsuit. The Zoning Board of Appeals heard the couple's appeal on June 11 and affirmed McOsker's determination that the rooster statues are signs. The board, however, did grant a disability variance, under which the couple could keep two roosters on the residential side of their home on the condition that the roosters be incorporated into a railing affixed to the residence.
In the lawsuit, the LeBlancs said they did not wish to add a railing to their home and instead chained two roosters to the decorative pillars flanking the front door of their house. The couple then gave their remaining rooster statues to friends and neighbors, who have displayed the roosters in front of their homes and businesses as a show of support for Pyper and as a symbol of neurodiversity awareness and acceptance.
On June 24, the town fined the LeBlancs an additional $500 for failing to build a railing for the two roosters. The couple was then fined an additional $750 on Sept. 17 for failing to remove the roosters or affix them to a railing.
The LeBlancs have paid all the fines assessed against them to date, totaling $1,700, under protest. The couple has also removed their decorative roosters from public sight.
The couple's lawsuit states that in July, the LeBlancs filed a public records request under Maine's Freedom of Access Act (FOAA) in an effort to obtain town records showing previous enforcement actions involving artwork, sculptures, lawn ornaments, public art or similar displays that were deemed to be signs under the Ogunquit Zoning Code.
The LeBlancs received all records related to the FOAA request from the town on Sept. 22. According to the couple's lawsuit, the records the LeBlancs received contained no records relating to prior enforcement actions, whether historical or in relation to rooster statues.
In their lawsuit, the couple said that the rooster statues displayed in front of other Ogunquit homes and businesses — some of which belonged to the LeBlancs — have not resulted in any citations or fines against those residents and business owners. The LeBlancs also said in their lawsuit that the records they received from the town indicate Ogunquit does not apply its sign regulations to other decorative objects displayed on residential or commercial properties, such as lobster buoys, nautical art, antique farm equipment or large tiki statues.
The LeBlancs also take issue with the Ogunquit Zoning Code's language. In their lawsuit, the couple said the Zoning Code defines an advertising sign as "a sign which identifies the goods or services available at a business or provides information about those goods and services." The LeBlancs argue that under that definition, whether a display is a regulated advertising sign depends entirely on what the town perceives to be its expressive content.
"Here, the town has decided that the LeBlancs' roosters are signs because the LeBlancs own The Omelette Factory, and town officials have therefore imagined the roosters to say 'eat at The Omelette Factory.' In reality, the roosters mean different things to different people," the lawsuit states. "When the very same roosters stand in front of a neighbor's home, the town treats them as decorations, not signs. The LeBlancs would own and display these roosters regardless of whether they owned a restaurant. Yet, merely because the LeBlancs happen to own an eatery, the town considers their roosters a sign for it."
The couple argues that the town's sign code and policies and practices regarding the enforcement of that code violate their right to free speech as guaranteed by the First Amendment.
"Plaintiffs want to display their tin roosters in front of their home without the threat of fines and code enforcement hanging over their heads," the lawsuit states.
The LeBlancs seek a judgment declaring that the Ogunquit Zoning Code is "unconstitutionally vague," as well as a permanent injunction prohibiting the town from enforcing the code against the decorative roosters. The couple also seeks damages in compensation for the town's enforcement against them, including the $1,700 in fines they paid.
Attorneys from the Institute for Justice, a national nonprofit, public interest law firm, are representing the LeBlancs. Last month, Institute for Justice attorney Daniel Woislaw sent a letter to McOsker and Ogunquit Town Manager Matthew Buttrick, in which he called on the town to rescind the fines it levied against the LeBlancs.
"It is not something that towns have a monopoly on deciding what art is or what art means. These roosters mean a lot of things to a lot of people. To the LeBlancs, they are a comfort for Pyper and a symbol of their life," Woislaw said. "It's not neutral. It's not evenhanded, it's uneven, it's unfair and it's arbitrary. So that's why this is unconstitutional."
Ogunquit town officials did not provide a comment on the lawsuit filed by the LeBlancs.

title: Measles is surging in the US. Here’s how the Trump administration has responded
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — With the U.S. experiencing its worst year for measles in decades, international health experts have decided that the U.S. has lost its status as a country that eliminated the continuous spread of the disease.
The U.S. has racked up more measles cases than in any year since 1991, with confirmed cases surpassing 5,000 in 2026, according to the latest data. Pennsylvania alone has seen more than 1,500 cases.
The Pan American Health Organization ‘s decision underscores a significant public health setback for the United States as the Trump administration reshapes federal vaccine policy.
Experts say that while the Trump administration did not create the underlying vaccination problem — which predates President Donald Trump’s return to office — the Republican administration’s policies and public messaging may have exacerbated it.
In a statement, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Erica Schwartz said it would maintain a focus on stopping outbreaks.
Nationally, 92.4% of kindergartners received their required measles-mumps-rubella shots in the 2025-26 school year, down from 92.5% the previous year and 95.2% in 2019-20, according to data from the CDC. That is below the approximately 95% coverage needed to prevent measles outbreaks, and some communities have substantially lower vaccination rates.
Here’s a look at how the Trump administration has handled the worst year for measles in more than three decades:
Mixed messages from the administration
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has a long record of questioning vaccine safety, has repeatedly promoted claims that vaccines are associated with autism, despite extensive scientific evidence finding no causal relationship.
And he has delivered mixed messaging on measles specifically. He has occasionally endorsed the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine as “effective,” but also continues to raise unfounded safety concerns about the shots. In August, he told CNN: “I believe that the MMR vaccine prevents measles.” In that same interview he questioned the safety of the vaccine.
Trump reinforced those doubts at an event over the summer where he signed an executive order calling for splitting up the MMR vaccine. He said falsely that taken together the shot was “quite lethal.” Doctors say, and years of real-world evidence prove, that the combination MMR vaccine is both safe and effective at protecting children from illness.
Separate vaccines for measles, mumps and rubella are not available in the United States and producing them that way would be a logistical feat for drugmakers.
Josh Michaud, associate director of global and public health policy at healthcare research nonprofit KFF, said past administrations back to the 1990s, when confronted with measles outbreaks, were aggressive in telling the public how important vaccination is against the disease. That’s not happening now, he said.
“What we’re not seeing from the administration is strong communications about the need for vaccinations,” he said.
During the most recent measles outbreak, Kennedy promoted vitamin A as a possible treatment, which created concern among medical professionals that the administration was giving undue attention to alternatives rather than emphasizing vaccination.
Questioning measles deaths
Throughout the surge of measles cases, Kennedy has repeatedly challenged health officials’ accounts of deaths from the disease.
In August, Pennsylvania officials reported two measles-related deaths. The county coroner later said they involved infants too young to be vaccinated, with the virus itself causing one of the deaths.
After Gov. Josh Shapiro stressed that vaccinations could have averted the deaths, Kennedy said the deaths “may even have been altogether fabricated.” He later acknowledged that one of the deaths was due to measles.
The remark echoed similar statements he made after last year, when three measles-related deaths were recorded. Kennedy questioned whether one of the children who died was killed by measles.
Medical experts said the political quarreling over the deaths diverted focus from an exploding public health threat.
The overhaul of vaccine policy
As health secretary, Kennedy has spearheaded an overhaul of the nation’s vaccine policy. Last year, he fired all 17 members of a key vaccine advisory committee and hired vaccine critics among the replacements. In January, his department downsized the childhood immunization schedule. The moves were temporarily halted by a judge earlier this year.
Kennedy also acknowledged personally directing the CDC to update its website late last year to contradict its longtime guidance that vaccines don’t cause autism.
Critics say the overhaul and the administration’s overt questioning of immunization safety have fueled skepticism about vaccines.
Surveys indicate growing public wavering over support for the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine. An August 2025 Annenberg survey found that 82% would be “very” or “somewhat” likely to recommend that an eligible child in their household get the MMR vaccine, compared to 90% in November 2024.
Kennedy has defended his upending of federal health policy by saying the changes will restore trust in America’s public health agencies. Doctors counter that the false and unverified information he promotes and the vaccine policy changes undermine confidence in vaccination and leave more people vulnerable to preventable disease.
Along with freezing and canceling billions in research under Kennedy’s leadership at the start of the Trump administration, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services laid off more than 10,000 workers and shut down entire offices and programs. Experts say those cuts may have impacted state and local health departments’ ability to adequately respond to outbreaks.
Measles designation won’t change federal response, CDC chief says
PAHO officials expect the U.S., along with Bolivia and Mexico which also lost their elimination status, to each submit a plan “in the coming weeks” for how they will go about trying to stop transmission for at least a year and regain measles elimination status, said Dr. Daniel Salas, PAHO’s executive manager for immunizations.
A decision to strip the U.S. of its measles elimination status will not change how federal health officials are addressing outbreaks, Schwartz said.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans,” she said. “Vaccination does.”
She said federal officials have invested $100 million to help state and local health departments to reach communities with measles outbreaks. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.”
Michaud said the designation change is “a marker for how we backtracked on public health, particularly related to measles prevention, and particularly related to vaccines.”
“It encapsulates this idea that the United States is more vulnerable than ever to infectious diseases,” he said.

title: Trump's pick for Navy secretary acknowledges the Iran war is straining military resources
text:
Trump's pick for Navy secretary acknowledges the Iran war is straining military resources
President Donald Trump's pick to lead the U.S. Navy acknowledged the strain of the Iran war as senators from both political parties pressed him at his confirmation hearing Tuesday about the impact of long ship deployments on sailors, drawdowns to stockpiles of advanced weapons and resources being shifted away from countering China.
Video above: What is a dirty bomb and is the US a target?
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, a Trump loyalist and combat veteran, is seeking the permanent top civilian job during a particularly volatile time in Washington. He also faces the extra hurdle of needing a waiver from Congress, because he left active-duty service less than seven years ago.
“This war, again, I know it’s a strain on our Navy,” Cao told the Senate Armed Services Committee, but he insisted that “it’s really set China back on their heels” to see all the military services work together.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, grilled Cao on the costs of the Iran war, noting that independent estimates or media reports say the naval blockade on Iranian shipping costs about $32.5 million a day and Iranian strikes on the Navy's regional headquarters in Bahrain did at least $400 million in damage.
Cao confirmed the figure for the blockade but said he could not offer a full damage assessment in Bahrain because “it’s a nonpermissive area for us to go," despite telling a reporter months ago that Iran “blew the hell out of Bahrain."
The hearing offered a rare opportunity to question a top military leader publicly about the Iran war and other issues. It follows recent firings of Navy officials and a failed impeachment attempt in the House against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, partly over his handling of the 8-month-old conflict. Republicans lost the House and Senate in the midterm elections, which were widely seen as a repudiation of the war and will put Democrats in control of Congress in January.
Cao faces questions over living conditions and mental health during long deployments
Cao was asked to address concerns that lawmakers have raised over living conditions aboard warships deployed to the Middle East and sailors' mental health, following reports of crew stress and supply shortages on the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier and other ships. The Lincoln endured a record-breaking deployment supporting the Iran war before returning to its homeport of San Diego in October.
Republican Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi, who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, noted that the “incredibly challenging deployments” take a toll on sailors and their families.
Sen. Mark Kelly, a Democrat from Arizona, said his office had received “reports of not enough food and inadequate basic necessities” from other warships that are now deployed.
“One parent told us that there’s their kid, lost more than 45 pounds in six months because of a lack of food,” Kelly said.
Cao said he was focused on sailors' welfare but argued that sailors going hungry was "like my kids opening up the refrigerator door and saying there’s nothing to eat in here.”
When asked about suicide attempts aboard the ships, Cao told Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, that what he saw "as eight suicide attempts, I see as eight suicide mitigations.”
Cao says the Navy is making progress on munitions
The conflict with Iran has strained U.S. stockpiles of air defense interceptors as well as other missiles such as the Navy's Tomahawk cruise missile, which can be fired offshore by a ship but safely strike targets hundreds of miles inland.
GOP Sen. Deb Fischer of Nebraska pointed to concerns about the dwindling munition stockpiles, while fellow Republican Sen. Joni Ernst of Iowa also noted the strain to Navy resources of maintaining the blockade on Iranian shipping.
Sen. Jack Reed of Rhode Island, the committee’s ranking Democrat, said in his opening remarks that “the munitions expended and damage sustained from Operation Epic Fury alone will take years to recover.”
When lawmakers raised concerns over munitions stocks, Cao said there’s been a boost in production of Tomahawks and other weapons.
“When I was in uniform, we only produced 125 Tomahawks a year. Right now we’re well above 60 every month,” Cao said.
He said efforts are also underway to boost the production of interceptors that are used by Navy ships to shoot down incoming missiles.
However, Cao also conceded that the Navy has taken to using expired munitions, comparing it to adding water to expired bread and putting it in the microwave. He didn't identify the specific munitions involved.
“For some of these munitions, we recoded them. And so we’re able to shoot off the expired munitions,” Cao said.
Democrats press Cao on recent Navy firings
Democratic lawmakers say the Navy failed to inform Congress that it fired the entire leadership team of a nuclear-powered attack submarine after an underwater collision. Separately, the sea service fired the commander of a destroyer deployed to the Middle East.
Cao made the case against the Navy’s traditional policy of publicly announcing the removal of commanders and instead argued that he wants “to make sure that we don’t destroy their careers.”
“We relieve commanding officers for everything from negligence to even just fraternization or, you know, harassment,” Cao said, “and I want to make sure that we’re protecting their livelihood afterwards as well.”
Trump nominated Cao for the permanent job in September. Cao has been serving as acting Navy secretary since April after John Phelan’s departure, which came with little public explanation. Before that, Cao was serving as Navy undersecretary and had run an unsuccessful Republican bid in 2024 to unseat Virginia Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine.
Cao fled Vietnam with his family as a child in the 1970s before attending the U.S. Naval Academy. He was commissioned as a special operations officer and went on to serve with SEAL teams and special forces in Iraq, Afghanistan and Somalia, according to his Senate campaign biography.
Cao left active duty in 2021. To take the secretary post, he needs a waiver from a law that prohibits military officers from serving as a service secretary until they have been retired for at least seven years.
A similar law, which has been on the books since the end of World War II, exists for the secretary of defense and is designed to ensure truly civilian control of the military. Congress has only granted exceptions three times for that post — twice in the past decade, for retired Marine Gen. James Mattis during the first Trump administration and retired Army Gen. Lloyd Austin under President Joe Biden.
In each case, Republican and Democratic lawmakers expressed an aversion to waiving the requirement and setting precedent for future exceptions. They raised concerns about further erosion of the already precarious concept of civilian control of the military.

title: Fewer students traveling from abroad to study at US universities
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Fewer students traveling from abroad to study at US universities
Fewer international students are studying at U.S. universities as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education, data released Monday shows.
Related video above: Judge dismisses case of deported Babson College student
Overall, U.S. campuses saw a 9% decrease in international enrollment this fall compared with last year, according to a survey from the Institute of International Education. And the number of new students entering the United States for the first time fell by 15%.
“No one aspires to send their kids to get educated in the U.S.,” said Veena Dubal, general counsel for the American Association of University Professors, whose father traveled from India to attend Tuskegee University, then the Tuskegee Institute, in the late 1960s on a student visa.
“It feels like an unsafe place. That’s the message that the Trump administration has been sending to families all over the world, and they’re listening.”
Last year, the enrollment decreases were partially offset by large numbers of students who stayed in the U.S. for temporary work after graduating. But after months of speculation, the Department of Homeland Security proposed requiring schools to pay a $70,000 fee for every student who participates in the optional practice training program.
Although the rule hasn't been finalized, participation in the program, known as OPT for short, dropped 6% this fall, according to the survey.
International students facing political headwinds
The proposed rule, which is expected to face legal challenges, is part of wider DHS efforts that include terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, along with detaining and deporting many of them.
And this summer, the administration finalized a rule that will prevent international students from staying in the U.S. for more than four years without approval from the federal government, although a judge has temporarily blocked it.
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the changes were intended to crack down on loopholes that international students were exploiting by extending their studies.
Although the U.S. remains the top destination for international students globally, the changes are having an effect, college leaders told the IIE.
Among more than 800 U.S. colleges and universities surveyed this fall, 88% blamed the visa application process and 70% blamed travel restrictions for the enrollment drops. And if OPT options are limited, 95% of schools predicted that international students would likely look to another country, according to the survey, which offers an early look at trends before full data is released next year.
Politics aren't the only reason students are looking elsewhere, said Mirka Martel, head of research, evaluation and learning for the institute. Its survey found more global competition for international students and the rising cost of a U.S. degree also contributed.
Fanta Aw, the executive director and CEO of NAFSA, an association that represents international education, said students also are worried about research funding. Last year, the Trump administration began dismantling the federal grant-giving process and attempting to exert more political influence over what projects get funded.
“They’re saying to themselves, ‘Too much uncertainty in the United States. It’s too difficult, and you know, more importantly, we have many more choices today than we did 10 years ago. Why subject ourselves to this?’” Aw said, noting that students are going to places like China.
NAFSA, in partnership with the international education technology company JB International, found that amid the enrollment decline, international students’ contributions to the U.S. economy dropped by $2.4 billion this fall.
Colleges see budgets squeezed
American colleges and universities heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue. So the drops have punched big holes in tuition revenue at some schools.
At Cleveland State University, international enrollment has dropped by 46% in two years, from 1,542 in fall 2025 to 828 this fall. And fewer than 50 new international students started this fall, said Provost Nigamanth Sridhar, who estimated that the budgetary impact ranges from $2 million to $4 million.
Decades ago, he arrived in the U.S. on an F1 student visa and participated in OPT. Eventually, he went through the process to become a naturalized citizen.
“I am here in this position, in this job, because I had the opportunity to come to the United States as an international graduate student and then decided to stay here and build a career,” said Sridhar, who is from India. “So international education is personal to me.”
The biggest drops were at the graduate level. This fall's data shows a 15% drop in international graduate enrollment, compared to a 3% decrease at the undergraduate level. The report also found declines in international students from India, which sends more students to the U.S. to study than any other country.
Midterms raise questions about the future
Sarah Spreitzer, vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents, said substantial immigration bills are unlikely while Trump remains president. But she said congressional oversight might halt new policies targeted at international students.
“Those types of things could provide more certainty for our international students that there’s not just going to be these sudden or unexplainable changes,” Spreitzer said.

title: How to watch out for snakes and other dangerous critters
text:
SCOTTSDALE, Az. (InvestigateTV) — Under decks, inside sheds or even in outdoor equipment, snakes can hide around your yard and in parks.
They’re vital to our ecosystem for hunting insects and rodents, but a bite can mean life or death.
The rattlesnake, which is found in a majority of the U.S. and more common in the southwest, is one species that people should be aware of.
An Arizona grandfather recovered after being bitten by a diamondback rattlesnake during an evening walk near his home.
Gary Takacs, 66, was walking in his neighborhood when he accidentally stepped on a rattlesnake.
“It literally — I just put my left foot down and it responded back with a bite to my ankle. I was wearing running shoes with short socks, no ankle protection, no hiking boots or anything,” Takacs said.
He said the bite felt like a charge of electricity running through his leg.
“Extreme pain, felt the fangs, could feel it and then instantly felt the pain from the bite,” Takacs said.
He was able to walk home a few blocks away, and his wife called 911. Takacs was given a dose of anti-venom and spent the night in a hospital ICU. He is expected to make a full recovery.
“I’m giving my grandkids stories to tell, so maybe they’ll embellish it, make it greater down the road. I just count myself very blessed, very fortunate,” he said.
Takacs, a frequent runner and hiker, wants to share his story and let others know the importance of taking extra precautions this time of year and keeping an eye out for rattlesnakes.
Aries Clark with the Phoenix Herpetological Sanctuary said when the weather heats up, rattlesnakes can pop up anywhere — not just on hiking trails.
Snake experts recommend that if you see or hear a rattler, step away very slowly.
Takacs said he will be paying more attention from now on.
“I have a head lamp that has LED lamp that lights everything up. If I am going to be up before sunrise or after sunset, I will have lighting, just going to be more aware,” he said.
How to watch out for animals
Giving a snake space applies to all creatures, as many states have more than one type of venomous animal.
Wildlife experts say the best way to tell if a snake is venomous is to learn about the specific species in your area.
“It’s obviously going to be their patterns and their markings and also their habitat,” said Elizabeth Kimble, an Arkansas wildlife expert. “Their head shape and their eye shape is not a 100% definite way to tell if it’s a venomous snake or non-venomous snake and if you’re that close your too close if you don’t know what kind of snake it is.”
Kimble said snakes generally avoid confrontation and usually only strike if provoked.
The reptile is most likely to be found near water in the early morning or late evening.
When you’re in more wooded areas, hiking or working in your garden you should wear closed-toed shoes. Experts suggest keeping yards trimmed low and be cautious around wood or leaf piles.
Experts say to have a professional remove any snakes and in some states it is illegal to kill snakes.

title: 2-year-old’s heart and lungs to save other young children in need through organ donation
text:
LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT/Gray News) - A Kentucky family is preparing for an honor walk for their 2-year-old son ahead of an organ donation at UK Hospital.
Abel Beckler was declared brain dead last Saturday after his parents said he had a seizure and went into cardiac arrest.
“I wish I could hold and hug my little boy just one more time,” Haley Hurt, Abel’s mother, said.
Abel would have turned 3 at the end of the month. His parents said they want to turn their tragedy into miracles for other families through organ donation.
The hospital has matched Abel’s heart and lungs to other young children. Hurt said his liver possibly will go to a 9-month-old baby.
“His liver is possibly going to go to a 9-month-old baby that could get out and see the whole entire world that my little boy didn’t get to finish seeing,” Hurt said.
Abel’s father, Logan Beckler, said Abel had a heart of gold and loved babies. He said the donations give him a small sense of peace.
“The Lord’s work meant for us to be here to make that boy bigger than just how tall he was, and that does fill my heart up some, although it may not fill it all. I believe that was his mission,” Beckler said.
Abel’s parents said the process is opening their eyes to the need for child organ donation. They want parents to know it is an option if they ever deal with the death of a child.
“Through this, we have learned that it is not common, especially here at UK, for a kid to donate organs,” Amber Duerson, Abel’s stepmother, said.
The family said that because of organ donation, this is only the beginning of Abel’s story.
“To be able to wake up every day and know that something of my son is still living and has many years to live,” Hurt said.
The family said funeral arrangements depend on the organ donation process.
On Friday in Estill County, the family will host an Abel-Strong fundraiser to bring family and friends together to honor him, with donations going to the Ronald McDonald House.

title: USPS proposes shipping rate increases. Here’s when they would start

(CNN) - After the holidays, it could cost you more to ship packages with the U.S. Postal Service.
The Postal Service wants to raise the prices of shipping services starting Jan. 17.
The cost for domestic shipping would go up roughly 6%.
That includes Priority Mail, Priority Mail Express, Ground Advantage and Parcel Select.
International shipping rates would be raised roughly 8%.
There will also be a permanent 8% domestic fuel surcharge.
The USPS Board of Governors believes these new rates will keep the service competitive while providing the agency with much-needed revenue as it continues to struggle with financial issues.
The proposed increases still need to be reviewed by the Postal Regulatory Commission before they take effect.
The cost of stamps will not change.

title: California bans Waymo autonomous vehicles from state freeways, saying they pose an 'imminent hazard'
text:
California banned Waymo’s autonomous vehicles from state freeways, saying they pose an “imminent hazard” after recent traffic incidents, including one where three of the driverless cars drove into a construction zone.
The California Department of Motor Vehicles issued the ban last Wednesday after two incidents on California freeways, said Jonathan Groveman, a department spokesperson.
A Waymo spokesperson said in a statement that the company has “temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance.” The company did not provide more detail. Waymo’s autonomous vehicles have expanded onto freeways in San Francisco, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Miami and Austin, according to the company.
The construction zone incident occurred on Nov. 5 and the second incident, which involved California Highway Patrol vehicles, occurred the next day on a highway in San Francisco, according to Groveman.
Video of the Nov. 6 incident circulated widely on social media last week. In the footage, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to bypass California Highway Patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break.
“The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present,” Groveman said.
Groveman added that “similar incidents” previously occurred on May 18.
The Waymo spokesperson said the “recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California” did not “involve any injuries or collisions.”
Waymo continues to operate the vehicles as normal on California surface streets, according to the company.
California’s restrictions bar Waymo from both operating and testing its driverless vehicles on California freeways, according to Groveman. He said the restrictions will remain in effect until “Waymo demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions.”
___
Kelety reported from Phoenix.

title: How often are Maine animals being impacted by lead poisoning?
text:
How often are Maine animals being impacted by lead poisoning?
The bald eagle that was rescued last week by Ogunquit firefighters and police officers is making positive steps toward recovery and even potentially returning to the wild following a diagnosis of lead poisoning.
According to The Center for Wildlife, where the eagle was sent, it is now flying, eating and standing.
"His numbers registered as it would be more humane, probably to euthanize, because even if they rally and recover a little bit, they can end up with long-term lung and heart issues if their body is in a state of emaciation," said Executive Director Kristen Lamb.
Despite that, the workers stayed hopeful, and now the eagle is headed to chelation therapy. According to Lamb, it's therapy that wouldn't have been possible when the eagle first came in. However, now, the eagle is one step closer to recovery and being returned to the wild, which Lamb said isn't guaranteed, but is certainly the goal.
According to Lamb, the condition of the eagle wasn't a rarity.
"Most of the raptors and loons and some of the other water birds that we treat every year have some level of lead," said Lamb.
She said that the higher levels of lead seen in birds typically happen in three ways. One of those is hunters using lead ammo to hunt waterfowl, and the other is through lead sinkers. The use of fishing equipment including lead and using lead ammo to hunt waterfowl are both illegal in Maine.
"It's likely non-hunters, maybe, or people that aren't using ethical hunting, that are leaving that behind," commented Lamb.
Lamb added that the use of gut piles as bait could also lead to the ingestion by animals — or later by people — of lead.
"It's also a neurotoxin for humans. So eating prey or food that hunters have shot with lead shot is not great for our families," said Lamb. "And it's also not great to be handling lead all the time."
Lamb stated that she does not disapprove of hunting and fishing in Maine, but when there are so many lead alternatives available, it should be less of an issue.

title: Pope Leo says there is no change to agenda or priorities after his lung cancer surgery
text:
Pope Leo says there is no change to agenda or priorities after his lung cancer surgery
Pope Leo XIV said his recent lung cancer surgery has not altered his agenda, outlook or even sense of mortality, as he projected a long pontificate focused on unity and healing within the church.
Leo seemed full of health, energy and jokes during an airborne news conference on Monday while returning to Rome from Peru. The grueling, 12-day trip through three South American countries left several members of the travelling Vatican delegation and press corps sick.
Related video: Pope Leo XIV flies on helicopter while on Latin America trip
“I’m not 100% but I’m pretty good,” Leo said of his surgical recovery. “Endurance is one of the gifts the Lord gave me.”
Leo, 71, had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Oct. 13 because of a cancerous tumor. He said it was discovered by chance during an annual checkup and appeared at first as a shadow on his lung.
“The first news was a surprise. There were no symptoms. I felt fine,” he said. Once the cancer was confirmed, he decided to proceed immediately to have it removed, and said he hoped his experience would help others not fear having checkups or pursue preventive care.
Leo saw no need for the provisional letter of resignation
Prior to going into surgery, Leo said he saw no need to make provisions for the leadership of the Catholic Church if he were left medically impaired and unable to govern.
He said he hadn’t written any instructions, as his predecessors had done, outlining the criteria under which he would resign, which some legal experts believe is necessary if a pope were to end up in an irreversible coma and unable to articulate his resignation.
“Eventually I will do it, I think, but I don’t see the need now,” Leo said, adding that he never doubted he would be in good enough shape afterward to make the South America trip. He credited good doctors, prayer and what he described as a strong sense of determination to recover.
Leo also showed himself in no hurry to appoint new cardinals who will eventually elect his successor, another sign that he is planning to be around for a while. “I will eventually get around to that,” he said.
The pontiff also seemed in no hurry to get things done, saying he still doesn’t know what trips he’ll be taking next year — aside from his previously confirmed trip to South Korea to attend World Youth Day in August.
Unity above all else, Leo says
Leo made it very clear that his No. 1 priority was “unity” and healing in the church, a reference to the polarization that has always existed but in some ways deepened during Pope Francis’ sometimes turbulent pontificate.
Leo was asked, for example, whether he would consider ordaining married men to ease the priest shortage in the Amazon, where remote Indigenous communities can go months or longer without a priest to celebrate the sacraments. Amazonian bishops had asked Francis to allow for such a change but he declined.
Leo said he had no plans to go down that path, either, saying the issue was too divisive.
While ordaining married men is one solution to the priest shortage, Leo said “it’s a solution which in certain areas of the church can cause division because there is not universal, if you will, acceptance.”
“One of my priorities is first to promote unity and communion among us as members in the church,” he said.
“It may be in the future that some things will change. However for right now, for what I believe, an important part of my ministry of the church is to heal, bring people together,” he added.
He similarly said he had no plans to change one of Francis’ most divisive decisions restricting the celebration of the old Latin Mass. Traditionalist Catholics had hoped Leo would be more sympathetic to their cause and would reverse Francis’ crackdown.
But Leo said Francis’ decision already allowed for exceptions and that his decision stands.
Spiritual abuse requires canonical change
Where Leo did hint at some change was on the thorny issue of clergy abuse.
He met with abuse survivors in Argentina and in Peru, and said he recognized that the issue of “spiritual abuse” was a problem in the church that needed to be addressed.
For over two years, a Vatican working group has been studying “spiritual abuse,” given the increasing number of cases of people — often adult women — who accuse priests of using their spiritual authority to psychologically, physically or sexually abuse them.
While the Catholic Church has laws punishing priests who sexually abuse minors, priests who use their spiritual authority to take advantage of people under their care rarely are sanctioned since there are no explicit laws criminalizing the practice.
Leo, a canon lawyer, said he was aware of the loophole in the church’s canon law.
“Spiritual abuse is a very serious topic in the church,” and needs to be addressed canonically, Leo said. “In order to exercise justice, you have to have a codification or a juridical expression of how to apply that, and that’s a very vague concept still,” he said.
At the same time, he conceded that “we all probably could describe either specific cases or kinds of instances where that has happened.”
One recent case of alleged spiritual abuse is expected to land soon on Leo’s desk. A Vatican-appointed tribunal is deciding the fate of the Rev. Marko Rupnik, a once-famous Jesuit mosaic artist accused by two dozen women of spiritual, psychological and sexual abuse.
The women began complaining about his behavior in the 1990s, but nothing was ever done until the victims went public, amid suspicions he was protected by his Jesuit superiors, up to and including Francis.

title: Maine’s Hannah Pingree to join other incoming governors at seminar in Utah

Maine Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree will end her week at a forum in Utah where she will join more than a dozen other incoming governors.

title: Man charged in killing of a Black woman found hanging from a Mississippi tree is due in court
text:
JACKSON, Miss. (AP) — One of three men charged in the death of a Black woman whose body was found hanging from a Jackson, Mississippi, tree last summer is due in court on Tuesday.
Earnest Lloyd Jr., 25, is expected to appear for the preliminary hearing on a charge of murder.
The positioning of Tasia Fortune’s body when it was found on Aug. 3 stoked fears that the 29-year-old was targeted because of her race and conjured memories of the state’s long and painful history of lynching. However, all three suspects in Fortune’s death are Black. Authorities say that the three staged the scene after a drug dispute.
Some officials had called for a federal civil rights investigation, but Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney said that props were left at the scene “as part of the staging” of Fortune’s death.
Over the past two years, about a half-dozen Black women and men have been found hanged across the South. None of the deaths has been found to be criminal, though in some cases critics said that law enforcement appeared to move quickly to label them suicides before having sufficient evidence to rule out foul play.
Like Lloyd, 45-year-old Eric Clark and 51-year-old Jarques Ratliff are being held on murder charges. Police have said that Ratliff had an “association” with Fortune.
Judge Jeffery Reynolds, who set bond at $5 million for Clark following his arrest in late September, called Fortune’s killing “heinous.”
“People justifiably didn’t know if we had a killer on the loose who might hang people for racial reasons,” Reynolds said.
Brackney said that the fear that the image of Fortune’s hanging body evoked has damaged the community.
“We know we have a very sordid history around lynchings and racial terror across this nation and particularly around the South. That is still a very current narrative. It is still a very raw narrative,” she said.
Prior to any of the arrests, Fortune’s mother, Christy Spivey, told The Associated Press that she didn’t believe race had anything to do with her daughter’s death. Spivey is white. She said that Fortune’s father is Black.
“I think this is something very personal, very personal,” Spivey said, insisting that someone who was acquainted with Fortune was involved.
Spivey said that following a hearing for Ratliff earlier in September, Clark hugged her at the courthouse.
“He never said he did it, but he said he was there to turn himself in for murder,” Spivey told reporters following Clark’s own hearing later that month.

title: Obituary: David Allen Johnston
text:
FORT MYERS, Fla. – David Allen Johnston, beloved husband, father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, passed away peacefully on Oct. 28, 2026, in Fort Myers, Fla. Born Jan. 31, 1937, in Boston, Mass., David made his home in Cape Elizabeth, Maine, and cherished his time in SW Florida, where he enjoyed the sunshine, golf, and the friendships he made along the way.
David shared a beautiful life with his late wife, Esther Stirling Johnston. Their love story began when he married his girlfriend, turning a young romance into a lasting partnership filled with love, family, and shared memories.
For many years, David and Esther owned and operated Guilian’s Floor Covering in Portland, Maine, building a business and a life together in the community they called home. David took pride in his work and the life he built with his family.
David had a lifelong love of sports and was a proud Florida State University football player. His time at Florida State remained a special part of his story, reflecting his competitive spirit and love of the game.
David and Esther made their home in Cape Elizabeth, where they enjoyed the beauty of coastal Maine. When winter arrived, David headed south to Naples and the Fort Myers area, embracing the warmth and sunshine of Florida. An avid golfer, he was a loyal member of Purpoodock Golf Club in Cape Elizabeth, and Quail Creek Village in Naples where he enjoyed the game and the camaraderie of fellow golfers.
Above all, David treasured his family. He is survived by his sons, Jeffrey and his wife Kelly of Scarborough, Maine and Fort Myers, and Jon and his wife Claudine of Fort Myers. His legacy continues through his five grandchildren and three greatgrandchildren.
David will be remembered for his love of family, his years in business, his passion for football and golf, and the two places he called home. From the rocky coast of Maine to the sunny fairways of Florida, he built a life rich in experiences, relationships, and memories that will endure for generations.
A private funeral service was held in Fort Myers, Fla., surrounded by close family and friends.
He will be deeply missed and fondly remembered.

title: Filmmaker and music video director Ray Tintori dies at the age of 43
text:
Filmmaker and music video director Ray Tintori dies at the age of 43
Ray Tintori, filmmaker and boyfriend of "Saturday Night Live" alum Heidi Gardner, has died.
People Magazine and Variety said the New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner said Tintori died in New York. He was 43 years old.
Officials said his death remains under investigation. No further details have been released.
The filmmaker was one of the founders of Court 13, the filmmaking collective that made "Beasts of the Southern Wild." He served as special effects unit director on the film, which was nominated for four Oscars.
Tintori, who was the boyfriend of "SNL" alum Heidi Gardner, also directed music videos for Chairlift, Bonnie Prince Billy, The Cool Kids, The Killers and Solange.
Variety said he most recently co-directed a performance of Ethan Coen's play "Waiting" in New York with Jordan Fish, with whom he hosted the podcast "To the White Sea" about the unproduced Coen brothers screenplay.
The outlets said Tintori was the son of film editor and NYU Kanbar Institute chair John Tintori and the late script supervisor Mary Cybulski. He attended and later graduated from Wesleyan University.

title: The ‘green wave’ is Maine’s next economic opportunity
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Jeff Marks is executive director of ClimateWork Maine.
The midterm election was a “blue wave,” arming Democrats to capture the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives and catapulting them into governors’ offices across the country. They have an opportunity to turn that momentum into a green wave — a renewed national commitment to clean energy, sustainability initiatives and practical and affordable climate solutions.
The opportunities are immediate. The International Energy Agency forecasts that renewables and nuclear combined are projected to generate 50% of the world’s electricity by 2030. The primary driver is pure economic advantage — over 91% of newly commissioned utility-scale renewable capacity costs less than the cheapest new fossil fuel alternatives. The clean energy sector already employs roughly 35 million people worldwide, with projections showing another 10 million jobs globally by 2030.
Artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing and more efficient transportation and buildings are creating new demand. We must build enough power and grid capacity to serve that demand without sacrificing affordability or reliability. That means jobs across construction, engineering, manufacturing and operations, with benefits reaching local communities.
But opportunity is not guaranteed. An August 2026 analysis by Environmental Defense Fund and Atlas Public Policy found that companies announced nearly $8 billion in new clean-energy manufacturing investments in the second quarter, while nearly $40 billion in planned projects and more than 53,000 announced jobs had been canceled since the start of 2025. Whatever one’s view of tax incentives, rebates or regulations, the warning is clear: policy uncertainty can cost the country investment, jobs and competitive ground.
Maine has a special stake in what happens next. ISO New England’s 2026 forecast projects regional electricity use will rise 9% between 2026 and 2035. Electrification of heating and transportation is expected to turn the region’s historic summer-peaking grid into a winter-peaking system sometime in the 2030s.
We must add generation, expand transmission and plan for seasonal reliability. Those are significant challenges — but also an invitation to invest in offshore wind, solar, hydropower, storage, advanced nuclear, efficiency and other resources that can work together to deliver dependable, affordable power.
Our businesses, research institutions, ports, colleges, skilled workforce and innovative communities are assets. Maine and its neighbors can attract investment, grow homegrown companies and build supply chains if we provide a clear path from project proposal to construction.
Efficiency and smart building upgrades can lower operating costs now; cleaner fleets and better resource management can make companies more resilient over time. Sustainability is not a branding exercise. It is a competitiveness strategy.
Election results across the Northeast — from congressional contests to state and local races — will shape the policymakers and priorities guiding this work. The message should not be that one party has a mandate to impose its preferred energy mix. It should be that voters expect leaders to address affordability, reliability, jobs and the future. Those goals require cooperation across party lines, technologies and sectors.
Congress can help by moving forward with the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026. The Senate bill offers a bipartisan framework for permitting reform. It deserves serious consideration and constructive work so needed energy infrastructure projects can move forward predictably, with appropriate environmental safeguards.
According to analysis by the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions, connecting more clean energy could reduce Americans’ electricity bills by $19 billion by 2040. Modeling from the nonpartisan Resources for the Future shows that this legislation could save consumers up to 7% in electricity costs annually, saving more than $350 billion through 2050 and providing much-needed relief for working families struggling to pay for high energy costs.
Permitting reform alone will not solve every energy challenge. We also need long-term planning, investment in transmission and distribution, a diverse mix of reliable resources, less dependence on fossil fuels such as oil and gas and workforce training and policies that reward efficiency and innovation. But we cannot build the future if essential projects remain stuck for years.
The midterms are over. The work ahead belongs to all of us — businesses, workers, communities, and elected officials. A green wave is not a partisan slogan. It is a practical choice to build more, innovate faster, waste less and compete harder. Maine can help lead that effort, and America’s lasting prosperity depends on it.

title: Mother charged after newborn dies from blunt force injuries 2 days after birth
text:
SMITH COUNTY, Miss. (WLBT/Gray News) - Authorities in Mississippi say a 25-year-old woman has been charged with capital murder following the death of her newborn.
Jantelle Sharon Jordan, 25, was arrested Friday and charged with capital murder in connection with the death of her newborn, according to the Smith County Sheriff’s Office.
The case began Oct. 18 when Polkville first reponders and Smith County deputies were called to a home in Polkville for a woman who was giving birth. Investigators learned Jordan had given birth about an hour before contacting emergency services and requesting medical assistance for the newborn.
The baby was taken to a Jackson hospital for evaluation and began experiencing medical complications. Hospital staff determined the newborn had suffered injuries after birth.
Despite medical efforts, the baby died two days later.
An autopsy was conducted at the Mississippi Crime Laboratory. The pathologist determined the cause of death was blunt force trauma and ruled the manner of death a homicide, according to the sheriff’s office.
Sheriff Joel Houston described the case as horrific.
“This is a horrific case for everyone involved in working on this investigation. These are the types of cases that are difficult for anyone to comprehend, especially when they involve the loss of an innocent child,” Houston said.
The investigation remains active. Investigators are continuing to collect and examine evidence before forwarding the case to the district attorney’s office for prosecution.
The sheriff’s office urged the public to rely on verified information from official sources and avoid speculation while the investigation continues.

title: Crews battle fire at home in Unity
text:
UNITY, Maine (WABI) - Fire officials say there were no injuries after a chimney fire caused “substantial damage” inside a Unity home Tuesday morning.
Fire crews were called to a home on Main Street around 6:30 am for a reported fire.
Officials say they found heavy fire and smoke on the driveway side of the home.
Officials say that all occupants of the home got out safely.
Firefighters were able to knock the fire down within 45 minutes.
Officials say a chimney fire had extended into the roof area and into the garage.
Unity Fire Capt. Blaine Parsons says regular chimney inspection is imperative come the winter season.
“If anybody’s got a trap door for their chimneys, take a mirror and look up it at least once a month, make sure there’s no creosote buildup. This is our second structure fire in the last couple weeks for the same exact thing, chimney fire with extension into the roof,” said Parsons.
Parsons says a quick response from mutual aid partners helped them save a major part of the house.
