title: Volunteers work to preserve ruins of historic Windham gunpowder plant
text:
Volunteers and Lakes Region groups are working to preserve and protect a historic gunpowder mill in Windham that supplied a quarter of the Union’s gunpowder in the Civil War.
The powder mill was founded by businessmen from Massachusetts and began operations in 1824. The mill was powered by the Presumpscot River and straddled the Gorham and Windham border.
Don Wescott, a longtime volunteer with the Presumpscot Regional Land Trust, formerly served as steward of the Gambo Preserve, home of the ruined Gambo Powder Mill.
When he was first asked to give tours of the area, including the ruins of the gunpowder mill, Wescott consulted his neighbor, Dr. Maurice Whitten. A retired chemistry professor at the University of Southern Maine, Whitten wrote a book titled, “The Gunpowder Mills of Maine,” including an extensive section on the Windham-Gorham mill.
Presumpscot Regional Land Trust’s primary focus in regard to land stewardship at Gambo Preserve is cutting back overgrowth to ensure the area of the ruins is accessible to visitors, said Emily Southard, director of development and marketing for the land trust. In addition, Southard said the trust is working with local authorities to keep an eye on vandalism at its properties, which she said is a problem at highly visited sites such as Gambo Preserve.
The Gambo mill was one of several powder mills in Maine, with others located in North Buckfield, Camden and Warren. The powder was made with saltpeter imported from India.
The mill is most notable for producing a quarter of all gunpowder used by the Union Army during the Civil War.
Mill employees were considered as important as the soldiers on the front lines, Wescott said. Employees were exempted from the draft after the head of Oriental Powder Co., which operated the mill, sent a letter to Maine Gov. Israel Washburn Jr., which said that the mill’s productivity would be diminished if employees were drafted.
The mill’s contributions to the war effort were not without setbacks. According to a PBS documentary, Britain, which favored the Confederacy during the early years of the war, embargoed Indian saltpeter exports to the United States, critical in gunpowder manufacturing. It took the intervention of Lammot du Pont, of the DuPont chemical family, to convince Britain to lift its embargo. In addition, Westcott explained how, one month after the war broke out, the mill’s operations were crippled by a flood that emptied “virtually the entire contents of Little Sebago Lake” into the Presumpscot River.
In addition to its service to the Union war effort, the mill also provided powder to the Russian Empire during the Crimean War and the Russo-Turkish War of 1877.
The site also serves as a memorial for the 46 men who died in explosions during the mill’s 81 years of operation. One of the deadliest incidents occurred in 1855, when an explosion killed seven men, including the brother and grandson of mill owner Oliver Whipple.
Despite the risks of the job, Wescott said, whenever an employee died in an accident, there was always a lengthy line at the employment office of people looking to fill the vacancy, due to the high pay of such a dangerous job.

title: Who should consider a measles booster?
text:
With elimination status gone, who may need a measles booster?
The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, the Pan American Health Organization announced Tuesday.
Measles is once again considered endemic in the country, due to more than a year of continuous local transmission. Measles is also re-established in Bolivia and Mexico, Dr. Jarbas Barbosa da Silva Jr., director of PAHO, said Tuesday, adding that the current situation requires “urgent action.”
“Losing measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation. It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization, and death,” Barbosa said.
Dr. Peter Hotez, co-director of the Center for Vaccine Development at Texas Children’s Hospital in Houston, put it simply: “Basically, measles is back.”
Countries that lose elimination status are required to submit a corrective action plan to PAHO that outlines how they’ll regain elimination status. The U.S. is expected to submit its plan in the coming weeks, Barbosa said.
Dr. Erica Schwartz, director of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said Tuesday that the agency knows where transmission is occurring and that it has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” Schwartz said in a statement. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.”
The United States held its measles elimination status for 26 years, and the vast majority of people in the U.S. are protected from the highly contagious virus.
But doctors say that if you haven’t been vaccinated, now is the time.
Although measles boosters aren’t typically recommended, certain people could use another shot, especially with so many outbreaks ongoing in the U.S. The country has tallied more than 5,000 cases this year, and the chance of being exposed to the virus is much higher than it has been in decades.
What the numbers say
At least 5,412 confirmed measles cases have been reported in the United States this year, mostly among unvaccinated people, according to the CDC. Experts say that figure is most likely an undercount.
This is the highest number of infections in the U.S. in more than three decades, and unless many more people get vaccinated, it will probably continue to grow.
Compared with the millions of people who get the flu each year, 5,000-plus cases may not sound like a lot. But measles is one of the most contagious viruses in the world. If a person with measles walked into a room with 10 unvaccinated people, about nine would catch the virus, research suggests. By comparison, the flu would probably spread to only one person. And measles sticks around: Even after an infected person leaves the room, the virus can linger in the air for at least two hours.
A few years ago, when the U.S. had only a handful of cases, most of them happened when someone traveled to countries where the disease was endemic and returned with the virus. Now, most cases in the U.S. result from exposure to someone in the neighborhood, research shows, so it may be at your door sooner than you think.
Most people in the U.S. have been vaccinated against the measles, but cases are rising because the vaccination rate has fallen. Experts say that about 95% of a population must be vaccinated to reach what’s called herd or community immunity: when there are enough people vaccinated that the virus can’t get a foothold and will fade away.
Before the vaccine was introduced in the US. .in 1963, the country had 3 million to 4 million measles cases every year, and 400 to 500 people died from the disease annually. Once communities reached the 95% threshold, case numbers fell to almost nothing.
What to know about the vaccine
The measles vaccine was combined with mumps and rubella vaccines in 1971 to help streamline childhood immunization schedules, improve vaccination rates and reduce the number of shots children would need.
The vaccine can be given to older children and adults, as well. And if an unvaccinated person is exposed to the virus, getting a shot within 72 hours could offer some protection or at least result in less serious illness, the CDC says.
The MMR vaccine is considered extremely safe. There may be mild side effects, such as soreness, redness and a mild rash at the injection site. Some children may briefly develop a fever or joint pain.
Rare risks include febrile seizures, which happen in about 1 in 3,000 to 4,000 children, resolve on their own and cause no long-term harm. Serious allergic reactions are extremely rare.
Although a later-retracted study in the 1990s suggested a link between the MMR vaccine and autism, large-scale research involving millions of children has established that there is no link.
Who gets the MMR shot
Typically, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that children get the first dose of the combined MMR vaccine between 12 and 15 months old and a second dose between ages 4 and 6. But anyone older than that can also get vaccinated.
With a flu or Covid-19 vaccine, doses are recommended every year because those viruses mutate more quickly. But the measles virus stays pretty much the same from year to year, and two doses of the MMR vaccine should provide good protection for life.
For people who live in a region where there’s an outbreak, some doctors suggest giving a dose of the MMR vaccine between 6 and 11 months of age in what’s called a zero dose. It’s then recommended that the child receive the first and second doses on the usual schedule.
Immunologist Dr. Elisabeth Adkins Marnik says you can also ask your pediatrician to give your child the second dose of the vaccine before age 4.
“I personally made the decision to get my daughter a second dose early when measles started circulating so much in the community and I knew we were also going to be doing a lot of traveling,” said Marnik, a science communicator who works to translate evidence into clear and empathetic public communication. “I just didn’t want to take any risks, and getting it a little bit early is fine. It just gave us extra peace of mind.”
Who might need more protection
There are other groups whose protection might be lacking and who can be vulnerable to infection, or who might be uncertain about whether they’re protected. Here’s what you need to know:
If you were born before 1957
The CDC considers adults born before 1957 to be immune to measles, essentially because, before the vaccine, nearly every child caught the virus at some point.
If you’ve gotten one dose
A single dose of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine is considered 93% effective at preventing measles. In fact, only one dose was recommended until 1989, when the U.S. government changed the recommendation to two doses after a measles outbreak among vaccinated school-age children.
Two doses of MMR boost measles protection to 97%. If you were vaccinated before 1989 and did not receive a second shot, you may want to consider getting one now.
If you’ve gotten two doses
Doctors don’t typically suggest boosters for people who received two doses of MMR.
If you aren’t sure
If you don’t know whether you were vaccinated as a child or whether you have been fully vaccinated, talk to your healthcare provider, who may want to give you another shot.
Other people who might want an additional shot are those who received the first version of the measles vaccine between 1963 and 1968, which used a killed virus and may not offer as much protection.
Testing for measles immunity
You can get tested at a doctor’s office or pharmacy. When you have an infection or get vaccinated, your immune cells produce antibodies against the virus that can stay in your body for years and help you fight infection. A simple blood test looks for these antibodies to determine whether you have immunity. Doctors also sometimes order these tests for people with weakened immune systems to see how much immunity they have.
The CDC does not recommend this kind of testing, and doctors say it is not necessary if you have had two doses of the vaccine. But this titer test may give you some peace of mind.
“Titer tests are not perfect, but certainly if they’re positive, a person likely has a good bit of protection,” said Dr. Jesse Goodman, a professor of medicine and infectious disease at Georgetown University and director of its Center on Medical Product Access, Safety and Stewardship. “But if you’re pretty sure you didn’t get vaccinated or you didn’t get a second dose, you might as well just go ahead. There’s no harm in being vaccinated again.”
Measles can cause serious problems
The disease can cause serious symptoms. About 11% of Americans who have had measles this year were so sick that they had to go to the hospital, according to the CDC. There have also been at least 10 deaths in people who had measles, according to state data — the most the country has seen in decades.
Measles can cause a rash, fever, red eyes, sensitivity to light and cough. It may also lead to severe complications such as pneumonia or encephalitis, a swelling of the brain that can cause convulsions, deafness or brain damage. For pregnant people, measles may cause premature birth or miscarriage, and they can pass the virus to their baby.
Measles can also trigger immune amnesia, a condition in which the immune system forgets how to fight other diseases.
Some groups are more vulnerable to measles complications, including older adults, infants and young children, as well as people who have suppressed immune systems because they take certain medications or are undergoing cancer treatment. But anyone can develop severe complications.
“Most children who get measles as young children are fine and recover, but it can make them pretty sick. Anywhere from 1 in 5 to 1 in 10 even healthy children will end up in the hospital,” Goodman said.
Spreading the word
Even if you have been vaccinated — and chances are, you have — herd immunity grows as more people get the shot. Although trust in the vaccine has slipped recently, most people still say they believe in it.
Studies show that peers and trusted community members can be persuasive, particularly because it can take time to convince people who are reluctant to get the shot.
Marnik advises not to get discouraged if people you know don’t change their minds right away. Misinformation about vaccines is increasingly sophisticated, and it can be spread through close friends, anonymous voices online or even leaders. “So it’s no wonder parents are confused and have questions.”
Talk to people who are hesitant about vaccines with empathy, she says. Most people just want what is best for their children.
“Oftentimes, it takes time and multiple conversations with somebody who is hesitant for them to entertain potentially making the decision to get vaccinated,” Marnik said. “Losing elimination status is a sad thing, but it really makes it so much more urgent to get vaccinated, because now we know that the likelihood people are going to be exposed to measles is so much higher.
“I think we can course-correct. We can rebuild trust. It’s just going to take time,” she said. “This didn’t happen overnight, and we’re not going to be able to change it overnight.”

title: ScreenCrush’s 2026 Holiday Gift Guide
text:
ScreenCrush’s 2026 Holiday Gift Guide For Film and TV Lovers
Chestnuts roasting on an open fire, Jack Frost nipping at your nose. And yeah, everybody knows a turkey and some mistletoe help to make the season bright. But you know what makes it really bright? Presents. Lots and lots of presents.
Just in case you’re a little worried whether or not Santa is on his way (with lots and toys and goodies on his sleigh) the entire assembled staff of ScreenCrush got together to offer some ideas for great gifts for the film and/or TV nerd in your life this year. They were even nice enough to include prices, links, and even a few items available in ScreenCrush’s merch store, where there’s plenty more stuff you can check out if you need to do a little extra shopping this year.
And so I'm offering this simple phrase, to kids from one to ninety-two. Although it's been said many times, many ways please enjoy this ad-supported free content.
LEGO Ideas Godzilla
If you know someone who won’t shut up about Godzilla Minus Zero, they will let out a primal radioactive lizard scream over this LEGO set, which contains over over 5,000 pieces and stands 27 inches tall. (It even has a fire breath accessory.) The appropriately enormous brick-laden behemoth can be posed after it’s built, thanks to its adjustable tail, head, arms, wrists and fingers. (King Ghidorah not included.) ($449.99)
The Cosmic Kiss Caper and Other Stories By Various Artists
For decades, Marvel and DC have kept to their own turf. Finally, in just the last few years, they started publishing new crossovers where their respective characters can meet, team up, and inevitably fight. This recently released hardcover collects several recent crossovers including Grant Morrison and Dan Mora’s Batman/Deadpool and Mark Waid and Jorge Jiminez’s Superman/Spider-Man, plus a slew of short stories containing other quirky DC/Marvel pairings. (Power Girl and Punisher?!?) If your shopping list includes someone who loves Marvel or DC movies or TV shows but hasn’t really gotten into reading the actual comics yet, the gorgeous artwork and off-the-wall character combos in this book might just get them hooked. ($36.99)
Rated R shirt
For those whose lives contain adult content and themes, vulgar or harsher profanity, violence with injury details more evident or distinct, and possibly some very frequent depictions of smoking there is this shirt, which pretty much lays it all out there for the world in a single letter. ($34.98)
Stranded on Earth by Max Evry
Max Evry, author of the exhaustive A Masterpiece in Disarray: David Lynch’s Dune oral history, is back with another deep dive into ’80s science fiction, this one all about the early stages of Steven Spielberg’s E.T. The Extra-Terrestrial, and its origins in a very different and much darker concept called Night Skies. The book features new interviews with Spielberg collaborators and insiders, and contains plenty of juicy tidbits you can use to impress your friends (or just drive them crazy) the next time they ask what you thought of Disclosure Day. ($28.95)
Beavis and Butt-Head Do America 4K
The folks at Vinegar Syndrome are doing a heroic job of restoring and releasing genre films that rarely earn any attention from other boutique home-video labels. It’s a Criterion Collection for weirdos like me, basically, and one of their latest releases is a doozy: Mike Judge’s Beavis and Butt-Head Do America, newly restored in 4K, with a huge batch of extras. The set includes multiple commentary tracks, new and archival featurettes, and a booklet containing writing on the film by BenDavid Grabinski, Christina Newland, Roger Ebert, and yours truly. This is technically a pre-order but according to the VS website it will ship before the holidays. (Heh. Heh heh. I said ‘but.’) ($69.98)
Rocky: Ultimate Knockout Collection
With I Play Rocky racing through theaters, and with more and more people cutting the cord so they can’t watch any more basic cable Rocky marathons, it’s an ideal time to get a big 4K box set of the entire franchise. This version includes all six Rocky movies, plus the director’s cuts of Rocky IV and Rocky Balboa, and more extras. Admittedly, there will likely be an Even-More-Ultimate Knockout Collection in a year or two with I Play Rocky in it, but for a purist who only wants the main films, this will do the trick. ($132.96)
Pac-Man Arcade in a Tin
Retro gamers who already have their own arcade cabinets (or can’t afford one) can instead go for a much cheaper (and much smaller) route with this officially licensed Pac-Man game housed inside a six inch by six inch by one inch tin. Take Pac-Man with you wherever you go, so the next time you feel like doom scrolling you can instead scroll through an endless maze chomping dots and power pellets. ($30.00)
We Pitch You a Movie Christmas
From the makers of the Cinephile card game comes this new holiday variation that seems cunningly calculated for maximum movie lover stocking stuffer potential. Players take turns pitching holiday films based on different genres, actors, and clichés packed onto the 150 cards included with the set. Winner gets to pick the movie everyone watches after opening presents. ($24.98)
Echo Base Hat
There’s no shortage of Star Wars merchandise out there, and between the release of Star Wars: Starfighter and the 50th anniversary of the original Star Wars in 2027, we’re about to get a whole lot more. But I do like this line of Heroes & Villains corduroy hats that look like souvenirs from exotic tourist destinations. They’ve got one for Echo Base, another for Endor or, if you’re a different flavor of dork, they’ve also got hats inspired by Spider-Man and Magic: The Gathering. ($30)
The Complete Kubrick
The Criterion Collection’s big box set this holiday season is a doozy: Every movie ever made by director Stanley Kubrick from 1955’s Killer’s Kiss to 1999’s Eyes Wide Shot in one massive, gorgeously-designed package. Extras include new audio commentaries on The Shining and 2001: A Space Odyssey, new interviews, and a metric ton of archival material. If you can find this thing — it’s currently sold out on Criterion’s website — it’s gonna make a very merry Christmas for the cerebral, emotionally distant physical media lover in your life. ($299.98)
Making Disney Magic By Ron Clements
Disney fans curious about the inner-workings of the company’s vaunted animation studio might want to check out the new book from animation titan Ron Clements, one of the men behind movies like Moana, The Little Mermaid, and Aladdin. This coffee-table book features behind-the-scenes stories from Clements’ 45+ years at Disney, along with over 1,000 pieces of artwork. ($57.00)
Funny Business By Matt Singer
Last but certainly not least, if you’ve ever wondered “What happened to movie comedies?” then you have asked the same question that inspired my new book. It chronicles the rise and fall of the last great era of Hollywood movie comedies, including titles like Zoolander, Anchorman, Wedding Crashers, The 40-Year-Old Virgin, and many more. Not only is it objectively one of the greatest books ever written, guaranteed to satisfy anyone on your holiday shopping list, you can also feel good about supporting the guy who wrote this list and maintains this website and never asks you for a dime. You’re welcome! ($32)

title: Aging Untold: Prostate health and symptoms men should not ignore
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we examine prostate health, highlighting early warning signs like frequent nighttime bathroom trips and explaining when men should get screened.
Then, we explore the financial, legal and family considerations of tying the knot later in life.
Finally, we meet a Navy veteran and former first responder providing free mental health resources and lifelines of support to struggling heroes.
The prostate is a small gland that slowly enlarges with age, and it can have a big impact on a man’s health.
Dr. Rhea Rogers said an enlarged prostate can be a sign of prostate cancer, which often has no symptoms.
Trouble urinating, frequent nighttime bathroom trips, back pressure and frequent urinary tract infections should not be treated as normal.
Don’t ignore urinary changes, the Aging Untold experts said. Talk to a doctor.
Getting married as an older adult means making a legal and financial decision as much as an emotional one, Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said older couples who are thinking about marriage should start with practical questions, including about money, caregiving and children.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose also recommends working with an estate planning attorney.
High school football coach Shannon Jones was diagnosed with colon cancer that had spread to his liver. His chances for survival were low.
Then, he sought a second opinion at Mayo Clinic from Dr. Denise Harnois, a liver transplant specialist. After months of testing, Jones was approved for a liver transplant.
Advances in chemotherapy and other treatments now prevent colon cancer cells from migrating around the body. Mayo Clinic and a few other centers now perform liver transplants for highly selected colon cancer patients.
(Editor’s note: This story discusses suicide. If you or a loved one needs help, call or text the Suicide Prevention Hotline at 988.)
Navy veteran Billy Bowering was packing for a weekend camping trip with his wife in 2022 when he felt what he said was “this incredible sense of loss and worthlessness.” Then he called his wife to say goodbye.
The call she made changed Bowering’s life.
Within two minutes, Bowering’s friend from church, a Vietnam veteran, knocked at his door. It was in that moment that Bowering realized “that it was time to be one of those interrupters.”
He has created the Day One, Week One nonprofit, which provides mental health resources, financial services and couples counseling for veterans and first responders, all for free.

title: Musician’s tour bus involved in deadly collision in Florida
text:
OCALA, Fla. (WCJB/Gray News) — A 64-year-old man from Louisiana died after the car he was driving collided with a musician’s tour bus, according to Florida Highway Patrol troopers.
What troopers say happened
Troopers said the crash happened around 9 a.m. on Southwest Highway 484 at the intersection of 20th Avenue Road in the Marion Oaks area.
The tour bus was stopped on 20th Avenue Road at the intersection, troopers said. The car, which was heading east on Highway 484, traveled off the roadway and hit the front of the bus, according to troopers.
The man driving the car died in the crash. Approximately nine people on the bus were not seriously hurt.
Bus occupants not confirmed
Residents posting on social media said the bus was transporting production crew to Miami for DJ John Summit.
State troopers have not publicly confirmed the identity of the people on the bus or the act they were working for. There is no indication Summit was on the bus at the time of the crash.
Authorities are continuing to investigate the crash.

title: Maine state representative charged with domestic violence resigns
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - Maine State Rep. Lucas Lanigan (R-Sanford) has submitted his resignation to the clerk of the House, according to a statement from Maine House Speaker Ryan Fecteau. Lanigan is charged in an ongoing trial, accused of strangling his wife during a domestic dispute.
Lanigan turned himself in to authorities on Oct. 28, 2024, after a warrant was issued for his arrest on one count of domestic violence aggravated assault. He made his first court appearance two days later. In March 2025, he pleaded not guilty to domestic violence charges.
According to the initial police report, Lanigan’s wife claimed he strangled her during a domestic dispute. But during Lanigan’s court appearance, his wife claimed the incident was a misunderstanding.
“Representative Lucas Lanigan should have resigned more than two years ago — days after he allegedly attempted to strangle his wife. He was charged with felony aggravated domestic violence in October of 2024, one of Maine’s most serious domestic violence charges,” Maine House Speaker Ryan Fecteau said in a statement. ”His case continues to be litigated in court. His refusal to step down – despite the extremely serious charges against him – was a disservice to the legislature and a profound disservice to every person in House District 141. Maine people expect and deserve far better from their elected officials.”
Lanigan is a Republican representing portions of Newfield, Shapleigh and Sanford in the Maine House.

title: Z107.3 annual ‘Free the Z’ Turkey Drive now underway
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BREWER, Maine (WABI) - Z107.3 annual Free the Z Turkey Drive got underway Tuesday morning at the Hannaford parking lot in Brewer.
Last year they collected 3,200 turkeys before wrapping things up at the Brewer Hannaford.
This is the first leg of a joint effort with Penquis and WABI.
On Thursday, Nov. 19 from 4 p.m. to 6:30 p.m., during WABI newscasts, members of the WABI team, the Penquis team and other volunteers will be waiting by the phones to take donations. Every $15 donation provides one turkey.
Local partners
A network of more than 40 local food pantries and nonprofit organizations are partners in the effort, making it possible to distribute turkeys to so many families throughout Penquis’ service area.
“Thanksgiving is a time to come together with family and friends, share traditions, and create lasting memories,” said Renae Muscatell, Community Relations Manager at Penquis. “Every turkey and every financial contribution helps make it possible for families to enjoy a holiday meal together. Donating a turkey or its cash equivalent is an easy and manageable way to support those in our community. The generosity we see year after year is a powerful reminder of how neighbors continue to support one another.”
How to donate outside the events
Those wanting to help outside of these events can donate online at turkey.penquis.org or Text TURKEY to 44321 to make a donation.

title: A Somali American Uber driver was strangled and run over by a passenger, authorities say
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — A Somali American man who drives for Uber is in critical condition after an alleged attack by a passenger, but authorities said they could not prove the attack was motivated by bias.
Mohamed Yusuf has broken ribs, a broken leg, spinal injuries, collapsed lungs and significant internal bleeding after being strangled with a seatbelt and run over by his own car early Saturday, according to court documents.
Passenger Samit Apurva Patel, 25, has been charged with attempted second-degree murder and carjacking. But prosecutors said the evidence could not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Patel’s behavior was motivated by bias. Though that “does not diminish the pain that the family and the Somali community are feeling right now,” Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said Tuesday.
Online court records do not list an attorney for Patel, who is due to make his first court appearance Tuesday afternoon. A person who answered a phone number associated with Patel’s address said, “No comment,” before hanging up.
Yusuf was on the phone with his brother, who is also an Uber driver, when Yusuf picked up the passenger just before 1 a.m. Saturday. Yusuf’s brother says he heard the passenger tell Yusuf he didn’t like the name Mohamed, the court document says. He later heard Yusuf screaming in Somali that he was being choked with a belt and run over by the car, according to the filing.
Moriarty said the motive remains unknown but said, “There were some serious issues going on with this gentleman at the time he went home that so alarmed his parents that they called 911.”
Patel’s parents called for a wellness check after Patel arrived home appearing intoxicated and “exhibiting signs of emotional distress and belligerent behavior,” according to the court filing. When officers arrived, they found Yusuf’s car in the driveway with the exterior and driver’s seatbelt damaged. The phone call with Yusuf’s brother was still active through the car’s system, court records show.
Officers said Patel told them he had been drinking and “admitted he took an Uber home, but he claimed not to know where his Uber driver was,” the filing says.
Officers found Yusuf in a patch of burs in a ditch off the side of the road using location data from his smartwatch and a drone with thermal imaging.
Uber said in a statement that it was horrified by the attack, has been in touch with the driver’s family and has banned the rider from the platform.
The incident in a Minneapolis suburb has increased fear after years of targeted rhetoric against Somali Americans, including from President Donald Trump, said Jaylani Hussein, executive director of the Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations.
“We feel as a community we’re under threat, constantly,” Hussein said. “Our community has, unfortunately, been feeling the brunt end of a disinformation and demonization campaign that has been going on now, and it’s coming from every corner.”
Minnesota has the largest Somali population in the U.S., with a concentrated share in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area. The overwhelming majority are American citizens.
The Trump administration’s largest immigration enforcement operation, Operation Metro Surge, targeted the Twin Cities. Trump has said immigrants from the war-torn East African country have “caused a lot of trouble,” and he wants them to leave. He also referred to Somali immigrants in the U.S. as “garbage.”
Hussein said dozens of community members have been stopping by the hospital to show support for Yusuf. While there’s widespread fear, Hussein said, it’s been particularly acute among Uber drivers.
“I also think for a lot of Uber drivers are also feeling extremely vulnerable because of the fact of the way that the incident happened,” Hussein said.
—
Fingerhut reported from Des Moines, Iowa. Associated Press/Report for America reporter Laura Turbay contributed from Little Rock, Arkansas.

title: Director Ray Tintori, boyfriend of SNL alum Heidi Gardner, dies at 43, according to reports
text:
(Gray News) - Ray Tintori, filmmaker and former Saturday Night Live cast member Heidi Gardner’s boyfriend, has died at the age of 43.
The New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner confirmed his death to People. People reported that his cause of death remains under investigation.
According to Variety, Tintori was one of the founders of the filmmaking collective the Court of 13, which made the Oscar-nominated 2012 film “The Beasts of the Southern Wild.”
Along with directing several short films, including one for the NBA about the 2016 finals, Tintori directed music videos for musicians and bands such as MGMT, The Killers and Arcade Fire.
According to People, the last music video he directed was MGMT’s “Dancing in Babylon” in 2024.
In 2025, Tintori made a cameo in the film “Marty Supreme” as a cameraman in the Wembley finals. According to an Instagram post he shared, he also shot black-and-white 16 mm footage that was used during a newsreel sequence in the film.
Also in 2025, Tintori made his relationship with Gardner public on Instagram. He posted a carousel of photos on her birthday, including several of the two of them.
“I remember the first time we saw each other and how you laughed with your whole body the second our eyes met, and I immediately fell so fast,” Tintori said in the caption.
Gardner’s reps have not responded to a request from People for a comment on Tintori’s death.

title: David Beckham sues for $41 million after his fragrance is sold in gas stations and discount stores
text:
David Beckham sues for $41 million after his fragrance is sold in gas stations and discount stores
A dispute over the sale of David Beckham perfumes has struck a sour note with the soccer star turned style icon.
Beckham’s commercial company is suing a beauty firm after his “luxury” fragrances were allegedly found for sale in discount stores and a gas station bargain bin.
DB Ventures has filed a claim in the New York Supreme Court against German beauty group Coty, which makes and distributes a range of Beckham-branded fragrances and toiletries. They include the Classic and Instinct lines and the eaux de toilette Intimately and Exquisite Leather.
Related video: ‘ER’ and ‘The Pitt’ are similar enough for lawsuit to move forward, appeals court finds
The claim argues that Beckham’s “world-renowned global brand is synonymous with excellence and refinement,” and “David Beckham products are a symbol of everyday luxury.”
“Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station,” the legal document says. “How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”
Lawyers for DB Ventures allege that Beckham-branded products “ended up in the bargain bin inside a gas station” and at British budget retailer Poundland, “allowing the product to be sold for dollar store prices and associating the David Beckham brand with cheap, discount products.”
DB Ventures is seeking at least $41 million in damages for breach of its licensing agreement.
Coty has asked a judge to dismiss the lawsuit, which was filed in April. The company argues that New York courts have no jurisdiction in the case, and says DB Ventures is using the claim to “manufacture its early exit” from its licensing deal and hand over the Beckham contracts to another firm, Interparfums.
The company told The Associated Press on Tuesday that “Coty strongly disputes the claims and has asked the court to dismiss them. As this is an ongoing legal matter, we will not comment further.”
DB Ventures' parent company, U.S. entertainment and lifestyles firm Authentic Brands, declined to comment.
Beckham, who played for a number of clubs including Manchester United and Real Madrid and captained the England men’s national team, parlayed success on the pitch into a lucrative business career that includes co-ownership of soccer team Inter Miami. He was knighted last year by King Charles III, becoming Sir David.
He also has had a very public persona as a fashion model, “Bend It Like Beckham” movie muse and husband of Spice Girl-turned-fashion designer Victoria “Posh Spice” Beckham. The couple have four children.
The Sunday Times Rich List earlier this year estimated the Beckhams' wealth at almost 1.2 billion pounds ($1.58 billion).

title: As outages persist, Puerto Rico finds a way to help keep the lights on with 'virtual power plant'
text:
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico (AP) — On nearly 20 days in October, an electric utility took energy from a battery attached to Hector Ríos’ house in Cabo Rojo, on the southwest corner of Puerto Rico, and used it to support the power grid.
Ríos was happy to share.
With the U.S. territory’s frequent power outages that disrupt daily life and restrain its economy, he likes the idea of helping prevent blackouts for other people. He’s also compensated for the energy.
“It just seems like a good deal, to contribute to the community and make money at the same time,” Ríos said.
Ríos, 75, is part of what has become one of Puerto Rico’s most effective tools for energy resilience amid nearly a decade of electricity woes: a “virtual power plant,” or VPP, that harnesses batteries from nearly 115,000 households to bolster the grid when its aging and fickle power plants can’t meet demand.
Nine years after Puerto Rico’s public power utility filed for bankruptcy and Hurricane Maria ravaged its already dilapidated energy grid, residents still face unpredictable blackouts and electricity rates higher than in almost any state. Few new utility-scale power sources have been built since Maria, and most of the federal dollars promised for grid recovery have not yet reached the territory.
But the VPP — the first of its kind in Latin America and the Caribbean, and the U.S.’ second largest in terms of capacity — showed its potential this summer, preventing or mitigating outages more than 60 times since June 1, according to Luma Energy, its transmission and distribution utility.
“There’s nothing virtual about it,” said Javier Rúa Jovet, chief policy officer at the Solar and Energy Storage Association of Puerto Rico. “It’s real, and it’s better than a power plant.”
Dozens of states now operate similar networks of distributed energy sources like battery storage systems, electric vehicles and smart thermostats to help manage the grid. Experts expect their role to grow in the U.S. amid energy constraints, rising utility prices, and tech companies’ push to build power-hungry data centers.
As President Donald Trump’s administration promotes fossil fuel expansion and redirects dollars away from solar adoption in Puerto Rico, proponents of the territory’s system say it highlights the value of distributed solar and storage, and shows how these systems can bolster resilience for other energy-vulnerable communities.
“There’s a way for this technology to benefit not just the individual buildings that they’re on,” but instead be “in service to the community all the time,” said Nathalie Jordi, community solar lead at Together New Orleans, a nonprofit that championed an upcoming $23 million city program to provide and network over 1,000 batteries on homes and businesses across New Orleans.
A solar revolution after Hurricane Maria
The opportunity to harness a vast network of residential batteries arose after Hurricane Maria in 2017, which left some communities without electricity for nearly a year. Experts linked the infrastructure failure to thousands of post-hurricane deaths.
“We had to procure resiliency in some other way,” said Rúa Jovet, “not a centralized system that will completely fail for a whole year.”
There are now over 207,000 rooftop solar systems on an archipelago of fewer than 3.2 million people, a 20-fold increase from before Maria that was propelled by households who could afford installations, philanthropy, and some federal dollars. Because of the territory’s unique need for resiliency, nearly every installation includes at least one battery, a necessary add-on to keep the system running in a blackout.
“The mindset was, get yourself ready for everything,” recalled Ríos, who after Maria bought a diesel generator for his house, then installed panels and a Tesla Powerwall battery in 2023. The system also cut his utility bill in half, from about $400 to $200 in the summer.
Solar panels create an energy boon during the day, charging batteries and sending excess power to the grid. But when the sun sets and demand rises, Puerto Rico barely has enough power to meet the need. Any power plant malfunction can prompt an outage.
In late 2023, Luma launched a small pilot program that would leverage residential battery capacity to offset the shortages. Ríos was among the first to enroll; now over half of solar customers participate.
If Luma predicts an energy deficit, customers are digitally notified that a battery sharing event is coming. They can opt out via app, or adjust how much of their battery — enrollees typically offer 30% — they make available.
The experiment has faced challenges. In a 2026 survey of solar customers by the nonprofit Solar United Neighbors, some participants criticized the compensation structure, which varies by solar provider. Others expressed hesitation to enroll in the program because they did not understand it or feared losing backup power.
Ríos said he’s only had that problem once — when a storm knocked out power right after he shared his battery. He now skips battery sharing events if there’s bad weather forecast.
He acknowledged the payment system is “a little vague.” He and his wife received $162 last year, which they happily redeemed as a Marshalls gift card.
Luma told The Associated Press that relying so often on battery sharing has contributed in part to recent rate increases. The utility pays solar providers three times the residential electricity price for the battery energy it takes, recovering the costs through rates.
Rúa Jovet says that expense doesn’t compare to the societywide economic losses of frequent power outages that spoil food, endanger health and shutter schools and businesses. The territory is also set to spend more than $1.7 billion this year importing fuel for most of its power generation.
Creating a consistent energy source
Luma said each battery sharing event, typically about four hours, supports the equivalent of about 80,000 residential customers. Enrolling more households would enable supplemental power for more hours.
But experts believe Puerto Rico can think bigger.
“The VPP in Puerto Rico is like an emergency escape valve, but the batteries should be a grid asset,” said Jigar Shah, director of the Department of Energy’s Loan Programs Office under former President Joe Biden and comanaging director of the advisory firm Multiplier.
Instead of only being tapped in an emergency, Shah said, the batteries could dispatch power every day — offsetting the need to burn fossil fuels — and help absorb excess energy across the grid when solar panels are producing at their peak. Several states, including California and Texas, use solar and batteries this way.
VPPs “could potentially play a larger role in Puerto Rico’s energy future,” Alejandro Figueroa, Luma chief regulatory officer, told The Associated Press. But, he said, a program used daily would require a different design and compensation structure to be sustainable.
Providing daily power is a natural next step, Rúa Jovet said, and could help Puerto Rico meet its own legal mandate that the archipelago reach 100% renewable energy by 2050. But a virtual power plant alone cannot solve the territory’s energy crisis.
That will require deploying billions of unspent federal recovery dollars, continuing improvements to transmission and distribution infrastructure and building new large-scale generation and storage.
“You don’t want the situation to be a persistent emergency forever,” he said.

title: FAA says it has paused installation of routers linked to nationwide ground stop
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Federal Aviation Administration has paused installing routers linked to last week’s ground stop that caused chaos for travelers, the agency said Tuesday.
The move comes amid growing scrutiny over the nation’s air traffic control system and as the Trump administration is making a new request for $50 billion to improve air travel. Democrats in the Senate are demanding that the administration provide clear answers about what went wrong.
FAA spokesperson Ian Gregor said the agency paused new installations of Juniper routers and disabled the functionality of all existing ones on Friday after technicians linked the problems to a new router in El Dorado, Arkansas.
Maker of routers says devices were working properly
The system became overloaded when the federal contractor that maintains the FAA’s telecommunications network was replacing outdated copper wires with fiber optic lines across the nation.
The ground stop was needed, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said, after the installation of a new router by L3Harris in Arkansas resulted in a cascade of intermittent communications and radar signals at 17 of the 22 regional air traffic control centers. The centers direct planes cruising at high altitudes. A radar site in Amarillo, Texas, where a router had been installed three weeks earlier also contributed to the trouble.
The FAA said that “excessive data” was flooding the system “at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds.” That deluge created instability with “aircraft communications and radar feeds,” the agency said.
For now, the FAA is relying on older Cisco routers that have been in place for 25 years to continue operating the network while they investigate the cause of Friday’s trouble.
The routers at issue last week are being tested in a lab at the headquarters of L3Harris.
Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, said the company believes the routers were working properly when the ground stop occurred. “Based on what we know today, the device functioned as it was configured to by the installer,” the statement said.
Duffy said Tuesday that 68 previous installations involving the same routers worked well before this latest problem.
“We’ve been able to recreate what happened in El Dorado,” he said. “But the root cause of what happened, we don’t have clarity yet.”
Problems with FAA equipment are decades-old
Upgrading the nation’s air transportation system is an effort that Congress has dedicated significant sums to in recent years. Duffy has pushed Congress for billions more dollars, saying just this week much more is needed.
Democrats on the Senate Commerce Committee said that knowing which device was part of last week’s meltdown isn’t enough.
“FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues,” the Democrats said in a letter sent to Duffy.
Money would go to control towers, airport infrastructure
The Trump administration on Tuesday sent a letter to key lawmakers outlining its request for $50.1 billion to modernize the system and make other improvements at airports.
“Congressional approval of these funds will equip the FAA to deliver to the American people a brand-new air traffic control system that is safer, smarter, faster, and more efficient,” the letter said.
Several Republican senators voiced skepticism following a closed-door meeting Tuesday with the transportation secretary.
“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related,” said Sen. Ted Cruz, chair of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, & Transportation, which has jurisdiction over air safety issues.
Sen. Rick Scott of Florida said he believes the airline industry should pay for the upgrades.
Duffy, meanwhile, said he’s open to other options that could include Congress breaking up the request into pieces, with the initial focus on the most critical needs for air safety.
Congress approved $12.5 billion last year for replacing outdated technologies, but much of that money will also go toward runway upgrades and other construction.
Ground stop cost big airlines over $300 million
Equity research and brokerage firm Bernstein estimated the ground stop and the weekend work needed to recover from it cost the four biggest U.S. airlines $345 million combined.
The airlines had to offer cash refunds, credits or rebooking options to customers who decided to cancel their trips, Bernstein analysts said.
The lost revenue and additional costs from the ground stop still are enough to have a measurable effect on the quarterly earnings for American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Southwest Airlines, the analysts wrote in a Monday research note.
“A booking slowdown before Thanksgiving, or a second outage, would cost more than the weekend’s cancellations did,” the analysts said, adding they did not see any signs of waning ticket demand.
___
Associated Press writer John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed to this report.

title: Another busy Thanksgiving travel week expected despite high airfare, gas costs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FORT COLLINS, Colo. (AP) - Pricey plane tickets and expensive gasoline are expected to keep some Americans from traveling this Thanksgiving, but not enough to make much difference in airport security lines and highway traffic, AAA said Monday.
The auto club federation predicted that 81.5 million people would travel at least 50 miles (80 kilometers) from home between the Tuesday before Thanksgiving and the Monday after the holiday.
That’s about 121,000 fewer than traveled domestically over Thanksgiving last year, or a one-tenth of a percent decline, AAA said in its annual forecast. If proven accurate, the small drop would end three years of record-setting Thanksgiving travel that followed the COVID-19 pandemic, according to AAA’s calculations.
“After three years of record highs, the number of travelers is slightly lower partly because of higher travel costs this year. But travelers won’t notice much of a difference,” AAA Travel Vice President Stacey Barber said in a statement.
Officials: Normal air traffic expected after ground stop
AAA prepared its forecast weeks before problems with U.S. air traffic control communications and radar feeds on Friday prompted the Federal Aviation Administration to impose a nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours and disrupted weekend flights.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford said they expected air traffic to normalize well before the start of the Thanksgiving travel rush.
AAA doesn’t think Friday’s unusually long ground stop will have a major impact on Thanksgiving travel unless it happens again, spokesperson Aixa Diaz said.
“Travelers are resilient, and from what AAA has seen in the past, it takes a lot to keep holiday travelers home,” Diaz wrote in an email Sunday.
As in past years, AAA expects the vast majority of holiday travelers to opt for car trips over flights. Meanwhile, it expects buses, trains and cruise ships will serve 4% more passengers than last year combined.
Flights got more expensive as airlines’ jet fuel costs increased
Last November, a government shutdown that led the FAA to order flight cuts at 40 of the busiest U.S. airports created extra stress for airline passengers with Thanksgiving week tickets.
Air travelers who didn’t cancel their plans were rewarded; Congress ended the longest shutdown in history, and the FAA lifted its order 10 days before Thanksgiving.
This year, fuel prices that surged during the U.S. war with Iran are a concern. The overall inflation that influenced this month’s midterm elections may also have made some Americans more cautious about venturing far afield for their Thanksgiving meals.
With U.S. airlines spending more on jet fuel, airfares were more than 22% higher in September than the same month a year earlier, according to the most recent government data. Carriers also raised fees for checked bags.
Visa’s economic research group said an analysis of September credit card transactions revealed that spending on plane tickets and related travel for trips starting between Nov. 1 and Jan. 15 were down from a year earlier for households of every income level except those earning more than $200,000.
Aviation analytics firm Cirium said Thanksgiving flight bookings were running 1.6% behind last year as of late October.
Gasoline could set a Thanksgiving Day price record
Compared to last year, round-trip domestic flights booked through AAA for the Thanksgiving period were 17% more expensive, averaging $800 per ticket.
AAA expects nearly 6 million people to fly from Nov. 24 through Nov. 30, about 12,000 fewer than last year. Three Florida cities — Orlando, Fort Lauderdale and Miami — are the top three domestic destinations for Thanksgiving flights, the auto club said.
Other organizations have come up with different projections based on the data they reviewed. Trade organization Airlines for America said it expected U.S. carriers to serve more passengers during the same seven-day period, though it did not specify if that includes international flights.
The group said airfares have risen much more modestly than jet fuel prices this year.
Gasoline prices have fallen over the past week, but motorists can expect to pay more than last year heading to and from Thanksgiving destinations, AAA’s forecast said. Regular gas averaged $3.82 a gallon on Sunday compared to $3.08 a year earlier, AAA said.
If prices hold, gasoline would be more expensive this Thanksgiving Day than any previous. AAA’s previous Thanksgiving Day record was $3.58 in 2022.
___
AP writers Lisa Leff in London and Rebecca Boone in Boise, Idaho, contributed to this story.

title: Maine panel floats ‘Taylor Swift’ luxury home tax after being told it’s unconstitutional
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine — A property tax task force wrapped up more than a year of work Tuesday by asking lawmakers to consider a “Taylor Swift tax” on high-value second homes, an idea it was previously told violates the Maine Constitution.
The second-home tax was a late addition. It did not appear on the draft recommendations circulated before the meeting. Members took it up at 4:57 p.m., in the closing minutes of a meeting that began at 10 a.m.
Lawmakers are responding to a pandemic-era surge in home prices, fueled partly by out-of-state buyers, that has set off tax fights in towns across the state. Now the new Legislature and Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree, a Democrat who campaigned on making out-of-state owners pay more, will have to decide if they are going to try to rewrite the constitution to do it.
The task force stopped short of recommending details on Tuesday. The nickname comes from Rhode Island’s tax on high-value homes that sit empty most of the year, a reference to the pop star’s estate in Westerly’s Watch Hill neighborhood.
Analysis shared with the task force outlined a tax on residential property that is neither the owner’s primary home nor rented out, with an exemption for property worth less than $1 million. A 0.5% tax on those homes would affect about 12,000 Maine properties and raise roughly $50 million a year, according to the Progress and Poverty Institute.
The constitution says property taxes must be “assessed equally according to the just value” of property. Changing that takes a two-thirds vote in both chambers of the Legislature before the question goes to voters, which gives House Republicans a chance to veto the idea despite resounding Democratic margins in this month’s election.
In September, a Maine Revenue Services lawyer, told the panel that the Maine Constitution rules out almost any way of taxing second homes differently from other property, including Rhode Island’s approach. He said that was as close to an unconditional answer as a lawyer could give.
Pingree has said she is prepared to pursue an amendment. She also ran on doubling the homestead exemption, which the task force endorsed Tuesday. But the group could not agree on how to pay for that.
Much of the panel’s work over the past year went into that relief program and the Property Tax Fairness Credit. Its consultants modeled ways to expand both by reallocating existing relief money rather than adding new state spending, a constraint the Legislature will also face with a $1 billion budget gap.
Two proposals for paying to double the exemption and expand the credit both failed Tuesday, and the task force moved on without one.
“It appears the task force would like to remain agnostic as to how this shall be funded,” state Sen. Nicole Grohoski, D-Ellsworth, a co-chair of the task force, said.
An earlier draft of the recommendations would have paid for the relief by cutting the state’s revenue sharing payments to towns. Without a funding source, municipal officials warned that the cost could fall on residents who don’t qualify for the breaks.
That plan would “very severely hit a very small number of remaining taxpayers” in Bangor, City Manager Carollyn Lear, a task force member, said.
“So many of our taxpayers either enjoy the credit or don’t pay any property taxes at all, and what’s left are the folks who are going to bear the burden,” Lear said.
Rep. Bob Nutting, R-Oakland, made the same point.
“I think without new money from the Legislature, in some amount, we’re not talking about property tax relief,” Nutting said. “We’re talking about property tax shifting within your community.”
The group hedged elsewhere, too. Members split on a plan for the state to pay towns for the taxes they would collect if tax-exempt property, such as land owned by the state and nonprofits, were taxable.
They did recommend letting towns levy local sales taxes, lodging taxes and other optional revenue sources to ease their reliance on property taxes. On local service fees, uptake of relief programs, audit requirements and regionalization, the group asked only for further study.
The new Legislature will be sworn in Dec. 2, and Pingree takes office in January. Grohoski joked that Tuesday’s votes summed up the group’s message to them.
“We ran out of time, so please continue the work if you want to,” she said.
Daniel O’Connor is a Report for America corps member who covers rural government as part of the partnership between the Bangor Daily News and The Maine Monitor, with additional support from BDN and Monitor readers.

title: Who's meeting with President Trump for historic nuclear summit in Asia?
text:
Who's meeting with President Trump for this week's historic nuclear summit in Asia?
President Donald Trump is in Asia for a three-day trip, focusing on trade agreements, regional diplomacy, and discussions on nuclear stockpiles with world leaders.
Who's meeting with President Trump for this week's historic nuclear summit in Asia?
President Donald Trump is in Asia for a three-day trip, focusing on trade agreements, regional diplomacy, and discussions on nuclear stockpiles with world leaders.
The president is currently in the Philippines, where he is meeting with leaders who look to the United States for help in addressing Beijing's aggression in the region. According to the White House, Trump plans to sign a trade deal with Thailand during his visit.
Before that, Trump met with leaders from India, Japan, and Australia. This marks the first time the group, known as the Quad, has convened since Trump began his second term.
"Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable and prosperous Indo-Pacific. We have outstanding relationships and coordinate closely on matters of regional security, economic security and diplomacy, and we talk quite often," Trump said.
Trump will then travel to China to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit, also known as APEC.
For the final portion of his trip, Trump is scheduled to participate in the first-ever three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump has indicated that the meeting will primarily focus on nuclear stockpiles, though the leaders are also expected to discuss Iran.
A spokesperson for China's foreign ministry said China’s looking to have in-depth discussions about safeguarding world peace and promoting stability, adding the talks will be of "groundbreaking significance."
How could the Nvidia fallout impact Trump's China trip?
Trump administration officials have been trying to downplay the president's relationship with the former Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang, who resigned from the company after admitting he had an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent.
Despite the administration trying to show distance between Trump and Huang, the former CEO accompanied the president on Air Force One during Trump's last trip to China in May. Huang has also popped up at the White House a few times.
Last week, Trump was asked if he would bring up Huang with President Xi, and he said, "No, I don't think so. I mean, maybe. I'm sure President Xi will ask me about it."
There are a number of people accompanying the president on his trip to Asia this week, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Elon Musk.
Keep watching for the latest from the Washington News Bureau:

title: Man gets more than 27 years in US prison for assassination plot that he said was steered from Iran
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A man who admitted trying to get a U.S. politician killed — and said Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard drove him to it — was sentenced Tuesday to nearly three decades in prison.
Asif Merchant, a Pakistani businessman, had faced the possibility of life in prison for what the judge called an exceptionally serious crime. Possible targets of the thwarted plot included then-candidate and now-President Donald Trump, then-President Joe Biden or then-candidate and former U.N. Ambassador Nikki Haley, according to trial testimony.
“Not many charges … are more serious than the contemplated, targeted killing of a U.S. president or other senior government official,” said U.S. District Judge Eric Komitee, a Trump appointee.
Merchant, 48, shifted in his chair but otherwise showed no visible reaction when he was sentenced to a little more than 27 years. One of his lawyers, Avraham Moskowitz, said after court that Merchant plans to appeal but was grateful that the judge turned down prosecutors’ bid for a life term.
“I think what it shows is that our judiciary remains independent, thankfully,” Moskowitz said.
Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement that Merchant was “justly sentenced.”
The sentencing capped a remarkable trial about an alleged Iran-driven plan to kill a prominent U.S. political figure in the thick of the 2024 campaign season. The Iranian government has denied trying to kill U.S. officials.
Merchant, who was convicted earlier this year of murder for hire and attempted terrorism, declined to speak at his sentencing. But at his trial, he bluntly told jurors that he researched Trump rally locations and spoke of carrying out an assassination at a political rally, using objects on a hotel napkin to illustrate the scenario for an acquaintance. Merchant then lined up people he thought were hit men and paid them $5,000 in cash that he’d borrowed from a relative.
He testified that he was just playing along with instructions from a Revolutionary Guard intelligence operative in order to protect relatives in Iran. Merchant said he figured that U.S. authorities would foil the plan, that he would cooperate and that he might get immigration help as a reward.
U.S. law enforcement was, indeed, onto him: The supposed killers-for-hire actually were undercover FBI agents, tipped by the acquaintance who saw Merchant’s napkin demonstration. Merchant was arrested in Texas while packing for a flight back to Pakistan on July 12, 2024, a day before an unrelated attempt on Trump’s life in Butler, Pennsylvania.
“This plot was incompetent from the very beginning,” defense lawyer Christopher Neff said in court on Tuesday. “Mr. Merchant’s participation was half-hearted.”
Merchant worked for Pakistani banks for decades and then got into businesses ranging from car sales to banana exports, and he traveled periodically to the U.S. for work and to see relatives. He also traveled to Iran for Shiite Muslim religious pilgrimages and visits with kin.
After meeting a Revolutionary Guard operative several years ago, Merchant imagined intelligence work would be exciting and profitable, and he feared for his relatives’ safety if he defied the powerful paramilitary, according to his defense.
“My family was under threat, and I had to do this,” Merchant testified in March. He said his handler named Biden, Haley and Trump as potential targets.
Prosecutors challenged Merchant’s claim that he acted under duress. They noted that he had shared anti-American and anti-Trump social media posts after the U.S. killing of top Iranian military leader Qassem Soleimani in 2020, during Trump’s first administration.
Merchant’s defense portrayed the posts as venting, and Neff insisted that his client wasn’t an extremist or inclined to turn his beliefs into violence.
But Assistant U.S. Attorney Sarah Winik countered that Merchant did “the most extreme thing you can do: Plot the assassination of a government official.”
The judge said he believed Merchant had some concern for his family but also was “highly motivated to do harm to this country.”

title: US loses measles-free status as virus reaches highest rate in decades. What we know
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — With the U.S. experiencing its worst year for measles in decades, international health experts have decided that the U.S. has lost its status as a country that eliminated the continuous spread of the disease.
The U.S. has racked up more measles cases than in any year since 1991, with confirmed cases surpassing 5,000 in 2026, according to the latest data. Pennsylvania alone has seen more than 1,500 cases.
The Pan American Health Organization’s decision underscores a significant public health setback for the United States as the Trump administration reshapes federal vaccine policy.
Experts say that while the Trump administration did not create the underlying vaccination problem, which predates President Donald Trump’s return to office, many argue the Republican administration’s policies and public messaging may have exacerbated it.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an anti-vaccine activist before he entered politics who has worked to overhaul vaccine policy, promised in a social media post Tuesday that the Trump administration will stop measles outbreaks and work to regain the lost status. He said he recommended the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine and pointed to COVID-era disruptions as having led to a gap in protections, not only in the U.S.
“We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust,” he said.
Nationally, 92.4% of kindergartners received their required MMR shots in the 2025-26 school year, down from 92.5% the previous year and 95.2% in 2019-20, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That is below the approximately 95% coverage needed to prevent measles outbreaks, and some communities have substantially lower vaccination rates.
Here’s a look at how the Trump administration has handled the worst year for measles in more than three decades:
Mixed messages from the administration
Kennedy, who has a long record of questioning vaccine safety, has repeatedly promoted claims that vaccines are associated with autism, despite extensive scientific evidence finding no causal relationship.
And he has delivered mixed messaging on measles specifically. He has occasionally endorsed the MMR vaccine as “effective,” and again on Tuesday said he recommended the shot. But he also continues to raise unfounded safety concerns about the shots. In August, he told CNN: “I believe that the MMR vaccine prevents measles.” In that same interview he questioned the safety of the vaccine.
Trump reinforced those doubts at an event over the summer where he signed an executive order calling for splitting up the MMR vaccine. He said falsely that taken together the shot was “quite lethal.” Doctors say, and years of real-world evidence prove, that the combination MMR vaccine is both safe and effective at protecting children from illness.
Separate vaccines for measles, mumps and rubella are not available in the United States and producing them that way would be a logistical feat for drugmakers.
Josh Michaud, associate director of global and public health policy at healthcare research nonprofit KFF, said past administrations back to the 1990s, when confronted with measles outbreaks, were aggressive in telling the public how important vaccination is against the disease. That’s not happening now, he said.
“What we’re not seeing from the administration is strong communications about the need for vaccinations,” he said.
During the most recent measles outbreak, Kennedy promoted vitamin A as a possible treatment, which created concern among medical professionals that the administration was giving undue attention to alternatives rather than emphasizing vaccination.
Questioning measles deaths
Throughout the surge of measles cases, Kennedy has repeatedly challenged health officials’ accounts of deaths from the disease.
In August, Pennsylvania officials reported two measles-related deaths. The county coroner later said they involved infants too young to be vaccinated, with the virus itself causing one of the deaths.
After Gov. Josh Shapiro stressed that vaccinations could have averted the deaths, Kennedy said the deaths “may even have been altogether fabricated.” He later acknowledged that one of the deaths was due to measles.
The remark echoed similar statements he made after last year, when three measles-related deaths were recorded. Kennedy questioned whether one of the children who died was killed by measles.
Medical experts said the political quarreling over the deaths diverted focus from an exploding public health threat.
The overhaul of vaccine policy
As health secretary, Kennedy has spearheaded an overhaul of the nation’s vaccine policy. Last year, he fired all 17 members of a key vaccine advisory committee and hired vaccine critics among the replacements. In January, his department downsized the childhood immunization schedule. The moves were temporarily halted by a judge earlier this year.
Kennedy also acknowledged personally directing the CDC to update its website late last year to contradict its longtime guidance that vaccines don’t cause autism.
Critics say the overhaul and the administration’s overt questioning of immunization safety have fueled skepticism about vaccines.
Surveys indicate growing public wavering over support for the MMR vaccine. An August 2025 Annenberg survey found that 82% would be “very” or “somewhat” likely to recommend that an eligible child in their household get the MMR vaccine, compared to 90% in November 2024.
Kennedy has defended his upending of federal health policy by saying the changes will restore trust in America’s public health agencies. Doctors counter that the false and unverified information he promotes and the vaccine policy changes undermine confidence in vaccination and leave more people vulnerable to preventable disease.
In his statement Tuesday, Kennedy said the CDC has worked along multiple states to “help bring their outbreaks rapidly and successfully under control.”
Along with freezing and canceling billions in research under Kennedy’s leadership at the start of the Trump administration, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services laid off more than 10,000 workers and shut down entire offices and programs. Experts say those cuts may have impacted state and local health departments’ ability to adequately respond to outbreaks.
Measles designation won’t change federal response, CDC chief says
PAHO officials expect the U.S., along with Bolivia and Mexico, which also lost their elimination status, to each submit a plan “in the coming weeks” for how they will go about trying to stop transmission for at least a year and regain measles elimination status, said Dr. Daniel Salas, PAHO’s executive manager for immunizations.
A decision to strip the U.S. of its measles elimination status will not change how federal health officials are addressing outbreaks, CDC Director Erica Schwartz said.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans,” she said. “Vaccination does.”
She said federal officials have invested $100 million to help state and local health departments to reach communities with measles outbreaks. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.”
Michaud said the designation change is “a marker for how we backtracked on public health, particularly related to measles prevention, and particularly related to vaccines.”
“It encapsulates this idea that the United States is more vulnerable than ever to infectious diseases,” he said.

title: Facing outdoor adversity on a northern Maine lake
text:
Loons were calling when my son, Adam, and I awoke to a cold, partly cloudy morning at our campsite in Jackson Cove on remote Lobster Lake in a wilderness area northeast of Moosehead Lake. Our heavy-duty parkas and insulated pants coupled with a toasty campfire were invaluable in fending off the cold while cooking breakfast and breaking camp.
The second day of a two-day trip, we had kayaked to our campsite and climbed Lobster Mountain the previous day. Our plan for the day was to circumnavigate the lobster-shaped body of water and then paddle out on Lobster Stream. Two factors were a concern: the remnants of a tropical storm were expected to arrive later in the day and water levels on the lake, which are governed by releases from nearby Seboomook Dam on the West Branch of the Penobscot River, appeared to be low.
The southern sector of Lobster Lake consists of two long coves called Little Claw and Big Claw and they are separated by a substantial island in the middle named Big Island. We had observed a narrow channel on the southern end of Big Island from a mountain overlook the previous day that connects Little Claw with Big Claw on the eastern side of the lake. That attenuated corridor was our immediate goal.
We departed Jackson Cove, which is situated at the approximate midpoint on the western side of the lake, and began kayaking south on Little Claw beneath the slopes of Lobster Mountain assisted by a moderate tailwind. As we approached the southeastern sector, a search for the entrance to the tiny channel ensued.
After a determined investigation, we finally found the obscure entrance. When we paddled a short distance, it became apparent the depth was insufficient for our loaded kayaks. Since the underwater base was deep mud, our best option was to use kayak paddles to pole through what turned out to be two approximately 50-yard, shallow sections.
Our strenuous efforts concluded, we emerged into elongated Big Claw. Views of Spencer Mountain in the south were obscured by developing storm clouds. After paddling to the southern end of the claw where a campsite is situated on a sandy beach, we started north along the jagged eastern shore of Big Island.
Approaching an escarpment on the rugged northern tip of the island, we could hear northwest winds gusting and see large white caps in the expansive northern reaches of the lake. Anticipating turbulent conditions, I removed my cap and engaged my rudder before rounding the point.
A powerful headwind and large breaking waves greeted us as we struggled west across the northern end of Little Claw to temporary shelter from the gale on boulder-strewn Ogden Point. The entrance to Lobster Stream was about 2 miles northeast but an open water traverse was too dangerous. We decided to skirt along the shore until reaching the western terminus where protection from the wind and relatively calm waters seemed likely.
After turning the point in choppy waves and eddying behind a huge boulder for a respite, we labored mightily for about a mile to the western end. Once shielded from the wind and waves, we kayaked north along the shore in predominantly calm waters in search of the entrance to Lobster Stream.
When we found the apparent mouth of the stream, it lacked the depth we recalled from the previous day. More poling through deep mud was necessary. After a short distance, we realized the presumed stream was in fact a cul de sac and returned to the lake; again in search of our elusive goal.
Exploring first east and then backtracking west, we finally found the well-concealed entrance. Since the narrow outlet angles abruptly west when joining the stream, it wasn’t obvious when we first kayaked past.
This time, poling was unnecessary as we paddled easily as the stream flowed north through forested terrain providing partial protection from the wind. The approximate 2-mile trip to the landing just before Lobster Stream enters the West Branch of the Penobscot River was problem-free.
While we were loading our vehicle, it began to rain. Despite the many obstacles, we managed to avoid the worst of the storm.
Read about more exciting surf and turf trips on Moosehead Lake and Donnell Pond in my book “Maine Al Fresco: The Fifty Finest Outdoor Adventures in Maine.”
The author of “The Great Mars Hill Bank Robbery” and “Mountains for Mortals – New England,” Ron Chase resides in Topsham. His latest book, “Maine Al Fresco: The Fifty Finest Outdoor Adventures in Maine,” is available at North Country Press and through online retailers. Maine state representative charged with domestic violence resigns
