Maine State Rep. Lucas Lanigan (R-Sanford) has submitted his resignation to the clerk of the House, according to a statement from Maine House Speaker Ryan Fecteau. Lanigan is charged in an ongoing trial, accused of strangling his wife during a domestic dispute.
Lanigan turned himself in to authorities on Oct. 28, 2024, after a warrant was issued for his arrest on one count of domestic violence aggravated assault. He made his first court appearance two days later. In March 2025, he pleaded not guilty to domestic violence charges.
According to the initial police report, Lanigan's wife claimed he strangled her during a domestic dispute. But during Lanigan's court appearance, his wife claimed the incident was a misunderstanding.
“Representative Lucas Lanigan should have resigned more than two years ago — days after he allegedly attempted to strangle his wife. He was charged with felony aggravated domestic violence in October of 2024, one of Maine’s most serious domestic violence charges," Maine House Speaker Ryan Fecteau said in a statement. "His case continues to be litigated in court. His refusal to step down – despite the extremely serious charges against him – was a disservice to the legislature and a profound disservice to every person in House District 141. Maine people expect and deserve far better from their elected officials.”
Lanigan is a Republican representing portions of Newfield, Shapleigh and Sanford in the Maine House.

title: Maine’s Amy Allen could win third songwriter Grammy
text:
Maine’s Amy Allen has a chance to win the songwriter of the year Grammy for the third consecutive time.
Allen, who grew up in Windham and South Portland, was nominated for the award this week on the strength of songs she wrote or co-wrote for Noah Kahan, Olivia Rodrigo, Ed Sheeran, Megan Moroney and others. She won her second consecutive songwriter of the year Grammy in February.
Allen has been nominated for the award four of the five years it has been given out. She would become the first person to win it three consecutive times. Other nominees for the songwriter Grammy this year include Edgar Barrera, RAYE, Joybeth Taylor and Theron Thomas. The Grammys will be presented Feb. 7 in Los Angeles.
Allen could win a Grammy for her work as a songwriter in the album of the year category, for her work on Rodrigo’s “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So In Love.”
Also nominated for a Grammy this week was recording engineer Wellington Gordon, who graduated from Skowhegan Area High School in 1993. Gordon was nominated along with five others in the category of best engineer Classical Album, for their work on “Forward Into Light” by Sarah Kirkland Snider. Gordon now lives in Virginia.
Allen graduated from Waynflete School in Portland in 2010. She performed with her band, Amy and The Engine, before moving to Los Angeles around 2017 and beginning her career as a songwriter.
By 2019, she had co-written the Selena Gomez hit “Back to You” and the Halsey hit “Without Me.” The latter song reached No. 1 on Billboard’s Hot 100 pop chart. Allen has become one of pop music’s most in-demand songwriters in the past half-dozen years, working with Gomez, Sabrina Carpenter, Harry Styles and many others.
“This award belongs to every single songwriter out there,” Allen said, after accepting the songwriter Grammy in February. “To all the songwriters out there continuing to fight the good fight, thank you for teaching me and inspiring me.”

title: Even a Maine winter can yield a beautiful garden
text:
Flowers are a major attraction for many gardeners. We enjoy seeing them from inside the house and while outdoors. We cut them and bring them indoors. For some, gardens also provide food.
Much of that ends with the first frost, but not all of it. A garden contains many attractive features that last well after the flowers have faded, many of which are accentuated by a coating of snow.
One way to make a winter garden look better is to avoid cutting back all of the perennials as soon as they are hit by the first hard frost. The leaves and some of the blossoms might have been killed and the leaves fallen off, but the seed heads often are attractive, and some of the seeds will fall to the ground and sprout when temperatures warm in the spring.
My favorite winter blossoms are echinacea, with the common name coneflower. They stand up after the leaves have fallen and the seed heads, as the name implies, are cone-shaped and will last through a good part of the winter.
Rudbeckia, or Black-eyed Susan, is another plant where the blossoms will last well through the winter and drop seeds through the spring.
Autumn Joy Sedum is true to its name, but the joy continues throughout the winter with the flower heads showing above any snow that has fallen.
A garden with winter interest also includes evergreens. The first six plants we bought after we had our house built in 1975 included three evergreens that are still growing: two yews, one on each side of the steps to our front door, and a Rosebay rhododendron, which, in addition to a bounty of pink blossoms in spring, has a glossy foliage that lasts all year.
The yews have grown as tall as we want them, so we prune them once each summer. Rosebay, at 12 feet tall and wide, has required some pruning over the past half century, but it is gorgeous and has been well worth the effort.
At the far end of our property is technically an evergreen that is highly attractive. It is a Chamaecyparis ‘Filiocodes Gold,’ a Fernspray Gold False cypress with shades of yellow and green in fan-like foliage.
Even the shrubs that drop all of their foliage have a lot of winter interest. Three of them have a prime spot near a door to the house.
We first planted a hydrangea, Paniculata Grandiflora, which grows about 12 feet tall, and has white blossoms that change to pink as the year progresses. It has a nice structure and holds onto its blossoms well into the winter. The red blossoms look great when snow falls on them.
Another plant we bought shortly thereafter was a redtwig dogwood, which, in addition to thin red stems, has small white flowers in late spring that turn into berries, which birds might take before you see them. There is also a yellow twig dogwood but the yellow doesn’t show as well as the red does.
My absolute favorite plant grown for stems has the common name Harry Lauder’s Walking Stick, but it can also be called contorted hazelnut or contorted filbert. Its botanical name is Corylus. It has small catkins that are easy to overlook as its flowers. Some leaves have a reddish foliage in summer. When the plant really shows well is after the leaves have fallen and the twisted branches are on full display. A sticky snow will make it especially attractive.
We don’t have white birches – the trees most famous for their attractive foliage – on our property, but I like the look of bark on oaks and maples, especially on the north side when a bit of moss is growing in the cracks.
We built our house on what was once farmland, and there were stone walls when it was built. Any stones we have dug up while planting or doing other ground work were added to the existing walls. They look good all year long, especially in winter.
If you have a bird house in your garden you should also have a bird bath or two, and they always look terrific when it snows.
Things to do
Raking season has begun. We will rake leaves off the patio, the driveway and the places we mow, but will leave them until spring in the ornamental gardens. The leaves we rake will be ground up and saved in bins for use as compost and mulch in the vegetable garden next year.

title: James N. Stevens
text:
James Nathaniel Stevens, longtime resident and native of Boothbay region, died Nov/ 10, 2026 in Seattle, Washington.
Nathaniel, son of James P. and Evelyn (Thurston) Stevens, was born in Boothbay Harbor on Oct. 24, 1944. Home in those days was in East Boothbay, and baby "Natty" became the newest member of the lively and growing Stevens "tribe" on Barlow's Hill. Eventually, the number reached seven siblings.
During his early years, Nat attended the East Boothbay Grammar School, walking each morning down through the village with his brothers and sisters and the family dog "Butch."
In 1955 the family moved to a farm on the River Road in Boothbay. For the next several years, Nat and his brother Jake spent a good deal of their spare time in the barn feeding, watering and milking cows, raising pigs and often chasing sheep.
Nat finished his grade school years at the Boothbay Center School then entered Boothbay Region High School, graduating with the class of 1963.
After high school Nat attended New England College in Hennicker, New Hampshire, majoring in mathematics. He graduated in 1967. During semester breaks and summer vacations, Nat worked with his father, uncles and brothers at Goudy & Stevens Shipyard.
At the height of the Vietnam Conflict, Nat was drafted into the Army. He was fortunate to be assigned stateside for his tour of duty, having been selected to serve as a specialist in finance and accounting. He was posted in Kentucky, Michigan and finally Denver, Colorado.
After his military stint, Nat decided to go back to school and enrolled in a four-year program in engineering at University of Maine in Orono.
It was during these years that he met the love of his life, Barbara Speirs, of Bangor, Maine.
Barbara and Nat became a unique and devoted couple, sharing their love of studying, gardening, camping, traveling and even working together. Nat built houses on spec., while Barbara handled all the finances and book work for the projects.
Eventually, Nat and Barbara moved to Seattle, where they lived for several years. Sadly, on Thanksgiving morning 2008, Barbara died suddenly, leaving Nat bereaved and in his words "like a rudderless boat." It is safe to say that Nat's happiest and most productive years were those spent with his beloved Barbara.
During the years following Barbara's death, Nat traveled many times back and forth from Seattle to Maine, but never found a place to settle permanently. While in Maine, Nat enjoyed visiting with old friends and his sisters and never failed to make the trip to Bangor to call on Barbara's Mother and two brothers.
To his siblings and friends it seemed as though his final years were sad and very solitary, but as the saying goes: "He did it his way."
Our Nat will be remembered for his ready smile, his quick wit and his quirky habit of correcting our choice of words in conversation. The dictionary was his favorite book! He often showed up unannounced and was perfectly happy to just sit and observe whatever was going on. He had a very unassuming presence, preferring to remain in the background, usually disappearing when no one was paying attention.
In addition to wife Barbara, Nat was predeceased by his parents, his two older siblings, Joel Stevens and Elizabeth Smith. He is survived by three sisters, Edith Stevens, Ella lbarguen and Ellen Newton and brother Jacob Stevens. Uncle Nat is also fondly remembered by several nieces and nephews.
The family plans to have a celebration of life for Natty at a later date. We will endeavor to reach out to family and friends when we know the time and place of this gathering.

title: Standard-offer electricity supply prices to rise in Maine on Jan. 1
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) -Many Mainers will pay more for electricity supply starting Jan. 1 after the Maine Public Utilities Commission selected suppliers for next year.
What customers will pay
For the average standard-offer residential customer, the increase is about $4.99 more a month for CMP customers. For Versant customers in the Maine Public District, it is about $2.30 more a month.
Why prices are rising
“The biggest factor in Maine and all of New England is the price of natural gas,” said Patrick Scully, chair of the Maine Public Utilities Commission.
Scully said limited pipeline capacity and global factors, including the Iran war, push up gas prices.
National think tank Third Way projects a Maine household electricity bill could total about $951 from November through March.
How suppliers are chosen
The commission chooses standard-offer suppliers through competitive bids.
“Well, we’re satisfied that it was a competitive process and that these were the best prices that we can get,” Scully said. “Obviously, we’re never happy to see prices go up.”
About the standard offer
The standard offer is the default supply option for customers who don’t choose a supplier. Delivery is a separate charge.
CMP and Versant bill on behalf of suppliers. They don’t play a role in setting the supply price.
The commission will choose suppliers for Versant’s Bangor Hydro District standard offer Wednesday.

title: Family calls for kratom ban after 17-year-old’s overdose death: ‘This is a problem’
text:
EDMONDS, Wash. (KIRO) - A Washington state family is pushing to ban kratom sales after their 17-year-old son died from an overdose.
Aedan Morgan, 17, died Aug. 1 in what the medical examiner later reported was an overdose related to kratom. Now, his mother and stepfather have started a petition to ban the substance.
“It’s a big void in our home, and we are struggling with it every day,” said Aedan’s mother, Sorine Morgan. “Just keep waiting for him to come home.”
Kratom, at its most basic, is leaves from a tree in Southeast Asia used to make teas or chew on with effects similar to those of opioids. In gas stations and smoke shops across Washington state, it’s sold in highly concentrated, synthetic or partially synthetic versions that are potentially deadly.
“When we learned that Aedan had had an accidental overdose due to kratom-related products, then we kind of realized the connection with the signs we’ve seen in the stores, the gas stations,” said Cal McGrath, Aedan’s stepfather. “We realized how dangerous these substances are.”
When McGrath learned substances related to kratom were to blame for Aedan’s death, he tried to figure out how the teenager got hold of it. He found five stores advertising the substance around Edmonds and even more in neighboring communities.
Washington and 16 other states have no regulation on the sale of kratom, not even age restrictions.
Shannon Sessions is the executive director of Support 7, a non-profit that responds with first responders to unexpected death cases. She says Aedan Morgan’s death was the fifth from kratom she’s responded to this year.
“It’s not just a youth issue. It’s not just somebody who doesn’t have a home and lives on the streets and who’s drug addicted on the street. This is all of our problem, and it is seen at all ages,” Sessions said.
Aedan Morgan’s family now hopes people sign their petition to ban the substance in Edmonds and remains optimistic that may lead to more regulations at the state and county level.
“The main message is ‘do something.’ I mean, it’s pretty obvious this is a problem,” McGrath said.
“We hope that this can bring awareness and honor Aedan by hopefully saving other people,” Sorine Morgan said.

title: Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang signals interest in returning to the company following scandal
text:
Nvidia chairman says board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said Tuesday that the company's board of directors does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, a statement that came hours after Huang said he would come back to lead the chipmaker if the board invited him.
It was Huang's first public statement since he abruptly left the company last week following revelations of an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Huang said in a social media post that if the board decided that his return was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company and the country, he would be “honored to answer these calls.” He acknowledged making “serious mistakes” in his personal life.
Some tech industry figures, including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, have called for the reinstatement of Huang, a high-profile booster for the artificial intelligence industry who oversaw Nvidia's development as the key provider of chips driving advanced AI models. President Donald Trump, a Huang ally who has spoken with him frequently, has also endorsed the comeback bid.
Huang acknowledged making “serious mistakes” in his personal life but said that he’s received an “outpouring” of support from employees, investors, business partners and customers for his return.
Company's earnings report made no mention of Huang
In its third-quarter earnings statement released Tuesday, Nvidia did not mention Huang's ouster or his possible return.
The turmoil notwithstanding, Nvidia blew past Wall Street expectations for the quarter, pulling in more than $116 billion in revenue, double the level from a year ago. The company also posted net income of $2.70 per share, beating estimates of $2.48 per share.
Santa Clara, California-based Nvidia did not respond to an earlier AP request for comment on Huang’s statement.
Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was expected to speak with Wall Street analysts on the earnings call for the first time since being named interim CEO.
A “Stand with Jensen” petition set up last week has gathered momentum, gaining signatures from current and former Nvidia staff, investors and other Silicon Valley supporters. The petition calls on the board to bring back Huang while an independent investigation proceeds or until there’s “compelling evidence” that his departure is in the company’s best interests.
“We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process,” the organizers said in an open letter. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy.”
Trump suggested Monday that the ex-CEO could return, saying Huang “learned a big lesson” and that he “would certainly not mind” if he was reinstated.
Huang resigned last week from Nvidia, apparently ousted by the board after revelations that he had extramarital affairs, both with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of being an intelligence asset for Beijing and with a senior executive who reported to him.
The businesswoman Huang was seeing who reportedly had links to Chinese intelligence was an executive at Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed International, a company being investigated by the U.S. for allegedly violating U.S. export controls by illegally diverting advanced Nvidia AI chips to Chinese companies.
Huang faces questioning by Congress
Also Tuesday, key House lawmakers said that Huang has voluntarily agreed to appear for transcribed interviews as the company faces intensifying national scrutiny over sales of its advanced computer chips.
Huang will appear before congressional committees on Dec. 1, followed by the company’s general counsel, Tim Teter, on Dec. 2.
“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” said a statement from the chairmen of three House committees with oversight of China and intelligence issues.
“The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous PRC actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal,” the lawmakers said, referring to the People’s Republic of China.
Meanwhile, Nvidia said it’s creating a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance following the revelations about Huang.
In the statement detailing its August-to-October results, Nvidia said revenue in a key business segment — data centers — more than doubled to $107.6 billion. It also projected that revenue for the current quarter running through January would hit $130 billion, more than Wall Street had expected.
Nvidia’s advanced chips are in high demand because they’re essential for cloud computing and data centers that underpin the AI boom, but they face restrictions on their sale to China. Trump said it was “good” that Nvidia had created the new oversight committee.
“Yes, that’s a good idea. It’s a great company,” Trump said shortly after arriving Tuesday evening in the Philippine capital of Manila, where he participated in a photo opportunity with the leaders of Australia, India and Japan. “It’s a great idea.”

title: Here's Why Maine is The 3rd Best State to Raise a Family
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Here’s Why Maine is The 3rd Best State to Raise a Family
I am in the middle of my journey, raising a family in Maine and so far, it's been pretty great. And if you've ever raised a family here in Maine, you probably already know there's a whole lot to love about living here.
We have the most beautiful views, fresh clean air, forestry, tight communities, and plenty of Hallmark style small town charm.
But there's one little detail that can make family life a challenge.. the cost of living!
According to a new report from ConsumerAffairs, Maine ranks # 3 in the nation among the best states to raise a family.
Pretty impressive! But before we start celebrating, there's a catch..
Maine also ranks # 42 out of 50 states for affordability. Pretty cool, however as a Maine parent, I am stretched pretty thin. But this is compared to all of our states.
So, in other words, Maine is a great place to raise kids, but keeping a roof over everyone's heads can get expensive.
One example? Moving from a one bedroom to a two bedroom rental in Maine costs an about $420 MORE per month. That's a lot higher than the national average difference of $189.
And childcare isn't exactly cheap, either.
The report says that the average annual cost of full-time, care for an infant, toddler, and 4 year old in Maine is $15,290, compared with the national average of $13,184.
Read More: Maine Ranks Among America's Top 10 Potato-Producing States
Still, Maine has consistently ranked near the top, coming in at No. 2 in both 2024 and 2025.
So here's the question: Is Maine one of the best places to raise a family? Apparently, yes. Is it one of the easiest places to afford it? Not so much!
What do you think, Maine parents? Is raising a family here worth the extra expense?

title: Winslow singer-songwriter Bella Ann releases holiday record Nov. 27
text:
WINSLOW, Maine (WABI) - Isabella Loubier, known by her stage name, Bella Ann, would get in trouble for humming in class as a child in Winslow. Now, she is now signed with Slumbo Labs, an artist development company that is a partner of RCA Records.
Winslow High School student Isabella Loubier, who performs as Bella Ann, will release a Christmas EP titled “Hope for the Holidays” on Nov. 27. She recently spent five days in Los Angeles working with producers.
Loubier is a three-sport varsity athlete at Winslow High School and a songwriter. She said she is happy with the impact her music has made in her community.
“Little girls that come to my shows with, like, Bella Ann hoodies, and, like, and they’re singing along. It already matters to people,” Loubier said. “So, even if this is as far as it goes, what a beautiful thing that I have accomplished, you know?”
She cited artists from Olivia Rodrigo to Bob Dylan as inspirations.
Studio sessions in Los Angeles
In Los Angeles, Loubier worked with producers for five days. She said she has a catalog of original music.
“I have a lot of original music. The problem isn’t that I don’t have any music,” Loubier said. “It’s, like, here’s five songs. Which one do you want to produce today?”
Her mother, Meg, attended the studio sessions. Loubier said her mother has been her biggest influence.
“She really, I think, found her voice and her independence and her way to communicate,” Meg Loubier said.
Holiday EP recorded in Maine
Loubier also continues to make music in Maine. She worked with Hallowell producer Bob Colwell well on her Christmas EP, which features three covers and one original song.
“He really just has, like, brought what is in my head to life,” Loubier said.
“Hope for the Holidays” comes out Nov. 27. Bella Ann’s music is available on streaming platforms. More information is available at BellaAnnMusic.com.

title: 103-year-old Rosie the Riveter honored, shares favorite part of working at bomber plane manufacturer
text:
103-year-old Rosie the Riveter honored at event shares favorite part of working at bomber plane manufacturer
A new exhibit at the Wyandotte County Museum celebrates the Kansas City, Kansas, Fairfax plant’s production of B-25 bombers during World War II and honors the thousands of workers who contributed to the effort.
At 103 years old, Frieda Renick reflected on her time working at the B-25 manufacturing plant.
"I always look forward to that paycheck," Renick said.
Renick, one of the thousands of workers at the plant, was honored at the exhibit this weekend, where she signed her name on one of the wings she helped build.
"Fairfax plants made 6,680 B-25s," said Dan Desko, founder of the B-25 History Project.
The exhibit features hundreds of artifacts and tells the story of the Kansas City, Kansas, Fairfax plant’s role in building bombers during the war.
"There’s a total of 59,337 people working at that plant. If your family lived in the area about that time, you’ve got a relative that worked at the plant," Desko said.
Desko said that the Kansas City plant produced more medium bombers than any other plant in the world during World War II.
"There’s about 35 or 40 of them that are still flying today," Desko said.
The exhibit is free and open to the public, running through Memorial Day of next year.
Renick, who was a Rosie the Riveter during her time at the plant, said her favorite part of working there was the people.
"Everyone had respect for each other," Renick said.

title: Some of the world’s most-visited websites targeted by cyberattack
text:
Some of the world’s most-visited websites targeted by cyberattack
A massive cyberattack hit 178 major organizations, potentially exposing visitors to malicious code designed to target vulnerable phones and tablets.
The cyberattack took place Monday, sending malicious code to visitors of websites like BBC, CNN, Zoom and IKEA, according to numerous reports.
The code came through Optimizely, a service companies use to test and update their websites.
It was designed to steal payment card details and browser information, and to redirect cryptocurrency payments.
Related video above | How to keep identity thieves at bay with these tips
Researchers also found code that could target vulnerable iPhones and iPads.
The breach did not mean that the organizations’ internal computer systems were hacked. But people who visited affected pages could have been at risk, officials say, depending on what information they entered and what device they used.
Report URI said it confirmed that some cryptocurrency was stolen.
Optimizely said it fixed the flaw, removed the malicious code and secured affected accounts, Infosecurity Magazine reported.
Report URI said most of the infected code had been removed by late Monday.
The scope stretched across banking, technology, retail, news, travel and entertainment. Other affected names included Salesforce, GitLab, Equifax, Fox News, NPR, Bitly, ASOS, Mattel, Peacock, Alaska Airlines, Air France-KLM, Ledger, Change.org, UNICEF USA, Starbucks Canada and Stamps.com. Report URI published a full list of affected organizations and websites.

title: How do new House members pick their offices? An inside look at the bipartisan tradition
text:
How do new House members pick their offices? An inside look at the bipartisan tradition
Freshman lawmakers picked their offices through a lottery system on Tuesday, continuing a tradition dating back to 1908.
How do new House members pick their offices? An inside look at the bipartisan tradition
Freshman lawmakers picked their offices through a lottery system on Tuesday, continuing a tradition dating back to 1908.
Getting elected to Congress takes hard work, but for freshman lawmakers arriving on Capitol Hill, choosing an office comes down to luck.
New members from both parties gathered Tuesday for the House office lottery, continuing a tradition dating back to 1908.
Each lawmaker draws a number that determines their place in line to select an available office. Those who draw the lowest numbers get first pick, while lawmakers with higher numbers must wait their turn and often settle for less desirable spaces.
Congresswoman-elect Shannon Taylor of Virginia had an extra reason to celebrate Tuesday. She drew the first pick on her birthday, prompting the entire room to sing "Happy Birthday."
Even the last pick drew bipartisan cheers and a standing ovation. Congressman-elect Mark Teixeira of Texas shouted "105!" before high-fiving several of his new colleagues.
While scouting office buildings, Rep.-elect Dan Koh of Massachusetts said many members prioritize proximity to the House floor.
"I think it's good to get the steps in, so I don't really care about that," Koh said. "I think we’re optimizing for raw square footage."
Once lawmakers select their offices, they can make the spaces their own, choosing everything from paint colors to carpeting and drapes.
"I will defer to my wife on decor," Koh said.
And while the incoming lawmakers are eager to get to work, some are already planning ways to make their offices a little more fun.
"The one thing I learned when I came up here is you're actually allowed to enjoy a cigar in your office, and I'm going to do that," said Rep.-elect Chris Stigall of Missouri, who added that he'll prioritize an office with functioning windows.
"We're already talking about our snack selection. Of course, it's Iowa, so we're going to have to have a popcorn machine," said Rep.-elect Lindsay James of Iowa. "I'm also a redhead, so we're going to have ginger snaps and ginger ale."
For Rep.-elect Zach Dembo of Kentucky, the focus is on making constituents feel at home.
"It's their office. They are my boss. So I want them to feel welcome," Dembo said.
Rep.-elect Adrian Boafo of Maryland said the lottery marks a special milestone for incoming lawmakers hoping to leave their mark on Capitol Hill.
"You are reminded as you walk through this building that it is history all the time, history everywhere, and hopefully we do our jobs and make a small part of history," Boafo said.
New members of Congress are scheduled to be sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027.

title: Producers of Portland's Back Cove Music Festival are canceling the event
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Producers of Portland's Back Cove Music Festival are canceling the event, terminating agreement with city
The entertainment companies that produce the Back Cove Music and Arts Festival in Portland have informed city officials that they are canceling the event and will terminate their multiyear agreement with the city.
The inaugural Back Cove Music and Arts Festival was held at Payson Park in August 2025, but this year's event was canceled due to logistical reasons. When the 2026 festival cancellation was announced in January, organizers said they planned on bringing the event back in August 2027.
The city's director of communications, Jessica Grondin, shared an email with Maine's Total Coverage that was sent by Shore Sound Entertainment owner Jordan Wolowitz and GoodWorks Entertainment co-founder David Rosenfeld to Ethan Hipple, the director of the Portland Parks, Recreation and Facilities Department.
In their email to Hipple, Wolowitz and Rosenfeld said their companies must cancel the festival and terminate their agreement with the city of Portland.
"After careful consideration, we've determined that the current capacity limit does not support a financially sustainable long-term model for the festival that benefits all parties," Wolowitz and Rosenfeld said in their email. "We truly appreciate all the time, effort, and support you and the entire city dedicated to the festival. It has been a pleasure working with you, and we hope to have the opportunity to work together again in the future."
In October 2025, the Portland City Council unanimously approved an agreement with Portland Maine Festival, LLC to produce the Back Cove Festival annually for three years from 2026 through 2028 with an option to renew for an additional three years afterward. Portland Maine Festival, LLC is a joint venture formed by GoodWorks Entertainment and Shore Sound Entertainment.
Grondin shared another email with Maine's Total Coverage, in which city attorney Michael Goldman informed Mayor Mark Dion and the City Council that the organizers of the Back Cove Music and Arts Festival determined the event "is not financially viable and that they will not be moving forward with it."
Goldman said in his email that city officials were drafting a termination agreement that Wolowitz and Rosenfeld would need to sign in order to formally end the contract with the city.

title: Veteran turns depression struggle into free lifeline for first responders
text:
MYRTLE BEACH, S.C. (Aging Untold) — A Navy veteran and former first responder outside Myrtle Beach is sharing his struggle with depression to help break the stigma around mental health challenges that first responders, including firefighters, paramedics and police, face.
Billy Bowering started Day One, Week One in June 2023. The nonprofit provides mental health resources, financial services and couples counseling for first responders and veterans, all for free.
“I understand the traumas. I understand some of the dark days,” he said. “I wanted to do something different. I didn’t want to just talk about, ‘Hey, let’s have awareness.’”
Nonprofit and podcast aim to reach first responders and veterans
Day One, Week One also has a podcast where first responders and veterans can share what keeps them up at night.
“The concept behind it is we really want to be able to reach that person that may not look for counseling,” Bowering said.
Former paramedic shares her story
Parker McBryde, a former paramedic, listened to the podcast and decided to take part in an episode. She spoke about battling PTSD and depression.
McBryde also faced losing her eyesight after learning she could not afford cataract surgery.
A few days later, Bowering called back with the message, “I’ve secured it. We’re going to help you,” McBryde said.
“It was such a huge relief to know that my eyesight was finally going to at least be restored, or at least to a level where I’d have glasses or something that I could at least see,” McBryde said. “So I’m very thankful for Day One.”
The faith-based organization also helped seven others by paying off almost $4,000 in bills last year.
“You wonder sometimes if things are tangible, if you’re making a difference and there’s a tangible difference,” Bowering said.
Name comes from boot camp
Bowering said the name Day One, Week One came from his company commander in boot camp.
“He’s like, ‘All right, boys, today is Day One, Week One. This is the first day of the rest of your life, and it kind of stuck with me,’” Bowering said. “And he said, ‘My voice will stay in your head the rest of your life, and it did.’”
A day in 2022
The phrase is also a reminder of Bowering’s own Day One, Week One story.
In 2022, while packing for a weekend camping trip with his wife, Bowering said he felt “this incredible sense of loss and worthlessness” and had made a decision.
“I can’t do this anymore,” he said.
He called his wife to say goodbye. She then called his friend from church, a Vietnam veteran.
Bowering said that within about two minutes, there was a knock on the door. His friend was there.
“I realized in that moment that it was time to be one of those interrupters,” Bowering said.
Sharing stories to break the stigma
Bowering now shares stories and helps others pay it forward.
“I think the more that we share them, I think it does help to break that stigma,” McBryde said.
“Whenever someone is struggling, we’re going to try to be that source of strength and that hope for tomorrow,” Bowering said.

title: Director Ray Tintori, boyfriend of SNL alum Heidi Gardner, dies at 43, according to reports

The New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner confirmed his death to People. People reported that his cause of death remains under investigation.
According to Variety, Tintori was one of the founders of the filmmaking collective the Court of 13, which made the Oscar-nominated 2012 film “The Beasts of the Southern Wild.”
Along with directing several short films, including one for the NBA about the 2016 finals, Tintori directed music videos for musicians and bands such as MGMT, The Killers and Arcade Fire.
According to People, the last music video he directed was MGMT’s “Dancing in Babylon” in 2024.
In 2025, Tintori made a cameo in the film “Marty Supreme” as a cameraman in the Wembley finals. According to an Instagram post he shared, he also shot black-and-white 16 mm footage that was used during a newsreel sequence in the film.
Also in 2025, Tintori made his relationship with Gardner public on Instagram. He posted a carousel of photos on her birthday, including several of the two of them.
“I remember the first time we saw each other and how you laughed with your whole body the second our eyes met, and I immediately fell so fast,” Tintori said in the caption.
Gardner’s reps have not responded to a request from People for a comment on Tintori’s death.

Related video above: Remembering those we've lost in 2026
Carney was “an entrepreneur, philanthropist and proud Shocker whose impact on our university and community will be felt for generations,” WSU said on its social media.
Carney and his brother Frank, who died in 2020, opened the first Pizza Hut in Wichita, Kansas, in 1958.
Born in 1931, he was the second of seven children and grew up in the city, where he and his brother would build one of the best-known restaurant brands in the world, WSU said.
With a $600 loan from their mother, Carney and his brother opened their first restaurant after seeing a magazine article about pizza’s growing popularity, WSU’s Pizza Hut Museum said.
Prior to that, Carney had served two years in the Air Force in Georgia before returning to Wichita for a master’s degree in business, the school said.
The first Pizza Hut was opened on the same street corner where Carney’s father ran a grocery store. After his father's death in 1948, at 17 years old, Carney took on more of the work there, taking orders, running deliveries and managing customer pickups.
At 26 years old, Carney and his brother founded Pizza Hut, which saw huge success – with its first franchised location opening in Topeka, Kansas – and eventually expanded to 90 countries, according to the museum.
In 1977, the Carney brothers sold the chain to PepsiCo, which moved the headquarters to Texas and later spun off its restaurant division, including Pizza Hut, to a separate company.
The original Pizza Hut has since been moved to WSU’s campus, where it was preserved and transformed into a museum.
Carney also served as a chairman for the Board of the Cerebral Palsy Research Foundation of Kansas for decades, receiving honors for his work with the foundation, among other achievements.
The Cerebral Palsy Research Foundation hailed Carney as “a devoted champion of our mission,” whose “influence reaches far beyond his years of leadership, touching the lives of countless individuals and families who have benefited from the work he helped make possible.”
“We are proud that Wichita State was part of his journey and even prouder that his values of service, innovation and pride in the Wichita community will continue to inspire future generations of Shockers,” WSU said, praising his continued commitment to the community.
“Through his humility, wisdom and unwavering belief in the power of giving back, Dan shaped the lives of those who had the privilege to learn from him, work alongside him and benefit from his mentorship,” the university added.
He is survived by his wife, Gayla, and his children and grandchildren.

title: Congress agrees on civilian plane locator mandate after deadly American Airlines-Black Hawk crash
text:
Congress has agreed to require airliners and other civilian aircraft to carry systems that help pilots locate nearby aircraft. But lawmakers still have to resolve the provisions that apply to the military.
Senators Ted Cruz and Maria Cantwell announced the agreement Tuesday at a demonstration on the lawn outside the Capitol building. A group representing families of the 67 people killed when an American Airlines flight collided with an Army Black Hawk helicopter near Washington, D.C., on Jan. 29, 2025, organized the event.
“When military aircraft fly in the same airspace, they must meet the same standards as everyone else,” said Cantwell, a Democrat representing Washington state.
Cruz, a Texas Republican, said he believes Congress can pass the bill before the end of the year.
On the night of the collision, the Army helicopter flew without the key ADS-B Out system that broadcasts an aircraft’s location because of security concerns, even though it was only on a training flight.
Any aircraft flying in crowded airspace is already required to carry systems that broadcast its location but isn’t required to carry complementary ADS-B In systems that show pilots where nearby aircraft are flying.
“Pilots can’t avoid what we can’t see,” said Capt. Jason Ambrosi, who leads the Air Line Pilots Association union. He said Congress must require these systems on both military and civilian aircraft because the Federal Aviation Administration hasn’t. “Everyone in shared airspace must be seen. Period.”
The Senate and House each passed competing aviation safety reform bills, and lawmakers have been working since the spring to craft a compromise bill addressing 50 recommendations from the National Transportation Safety Board.
Everyone aboard the American Airlines jet, flying from Wichita, Kansas, and the helicopter died when the two aircraft collided. It was the deadliest plane crash on U.S. soil since 2001, and the victims included 28 members of the figure skating community.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford assured the victims’ families that safety remains the agency’s top priority. The FAA has been in the spotlight since grounding all flights nationwide on Friday because of a technical problem.
The FAA has already taken some steps to prevent helicopters and planes from sharing the same airspace around Reagan airport. Air traffic controllers are now prohibited from relying solely on pilots to see and avoid other aircraft. But the victims’ families and NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy have been pressing for the locator systems.

title: Presque Isle airport director says flight timing matters for holiday travel
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Travelers planning to fly home for the holidays should consider when they fly as well as where they are going.
Presque Isle International Airport Director Scott Wardwell said some of the busiest travel days fall right before the holidays. He recommends building extra time into travel plans.
“Don’t fly on Christmas Eve or the day before Thanksgiving,” Wardwell said. “Try to plan in a little extra time in case something happens. You still got time to recover and get there on Turkey Day or on Christmas.”
Wardwell also encourages travelers to factor in mileage, travel time, and parking when comparing flights. The airport has a travel cost calculator to help estimate those costs.

title: USPS proposes shipping rate increases. Here’s when they would start

text:
(CNN) - After the holidays, it could cost you more to ship packages with the U.S. Postal Service.
The Postal Service wants to raise the prices of shipping services starting Jan. 17.
The cost for domestic shipping would go up roughly 6%.
That includes Priority Mail, Priority Mail Express, Ground Advantage and Parcel Select.
International shipping rates would be raised roughly 8%.
There will also be a permanent 8% domestic fuel surcharge.
The USPS Board of Governors believes these new rates will keep the service competitive while providing the agency with much-needed revenue as it continues to struggle with financial issues.
The proposed increases still need to be reviewed by the Postal Regulatory Commission before they take effect.

title: Court blocks Pentagon from expelling several transgender troops from US military
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal appeals court on Tuesday blocked the Pentagon from forcing more than two dozen transgender troops out of the military, several months after it found that President Donald Trump’s administration unlawfully imposed the ban.
The decision — implementing an earlier ruling by the same appeals court panel — could set the stage for the issue to return to the Supreme Court, which previously allowed the ban to go forward for now in a different case.
Trump’s administration had asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit to delay the June 1 ruling’s implementation while it petitions the Supreme Court to take up the case. A three-judge panel voted 2-1 on Tuesday to reject the administration’s request for a stay of the circuit’s decision.
The Supreme Court had ruled in the administration’s favor last year, allowing the Pentagon to start enforcing the ban while the litigation proceeded.
Circuit Judge Robert Wilkins, partially joined by Judge Judith Rogers, ruled in June that the Pentagon’s policy was designed to exclude people from the military based on their gender identity. Their majority decision would bar the military from kicking out current service members named in the lawsuit, but it wouldn’t allow new transgender recruits to join.
Plaintiffs’ attorneys challenging the Pentagon ban say 27 service members are covered by Tuesday’s order. Shannon Minter, legal director of the National Center for LGBTQ Rights, said the plaintiffs are all “decorated troops who have met every standard the military sets.”
“The Trump administration asked the court to let it keep pushing these service members toward the door while it tries to get a different answer from the Supreme Court. Today, the D.C. Circuit said no,” Minter said in a statement.
On Tuesday, Wilkins said the administration hasn’t shown how retaining the plaintiffs currently serving in the military would cause any irreparable harm to the government or endanger national security. Wilkins also noted that the scope of the June 1 majority opinion was narrower than the injunction that the Supreme Court stayed last year.
“To the extent the government suggests that any injunction against the Executive Branch imposes irreparable harm, I am also unpersuaded,” Wilkins wrote.
The panel’s June 1 majority opinion partially upheld a March 2025 ruling by U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, who concluded that Trump’s executive order to exclude transgender troops from military service likely violates their constitutional rights.
A spokesperson for Hegseth’s office declined to comment on the court’s ruling.
In January 2025, Trump signed an executive order that claims the sexual identity of transgender service members “conflicts with a soldier’s commitment to an honorable, truthful, and disciplined lifestyle, even in one’s personal life” and is harmful to military readiness.
In response, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a policy that presumptively disqualifies people with gender dysphoria from military service. Gender dysphoria is the distress that a person feels because their assigned gender and gender identity don’t match. The medical condition has been linked to depression and suicidal thoughts.
Wilkins was nominated to the court by Democratic President Barack Obama. Rogers was nominated by President Bill Clinton, also a Democrat.
Circuit Judge Justin Walker, who was nominated by Trump, a Republican, wrote a dissenting opinion in June that said judges lack the power to second-guess the decision to exclude transgender troops. Walker also voted to grant the government’s request to suspend the decision.

title: Football coach receives Mayo Clinic’s first liver transplant for metastatic colon cancer
text:
(Aging Untold) — A high school football coach received the first liver transplant performed at Mayo Clinic for metastatic colon cancer, and he is back on the field and has been cancer-free for two years.
Shannon Jones was diagnosed with colon cancer that had spread to his liver. Treatments had damaged his liver when he sought a second opinion at Mayo Clinic.
Diagnosis and treatment
Several years ago, Jones could not keep up during football practices.
“I got to where I’d have to stop and sit down,” Jones said. “I just, I was out of energy.”
Jones was diagnosed with colon cancer. His doctor told him it had spread to his liver.
He began treatment immediately with surgery to remove part of his colon. He also received other treatments, including chemotherapy and radiation.
The disease had spread to both sides of his liver, and Jones’ chances for long-term survival were low.
Dr. Denise Harnois, a Mayo Clinic transplant hepatologist, said the five-year survival rate for those patients is 9%, even with systemic chemotherapy.
“It was difficult, it was hard to push through sometimes,” Jones said. “I always felt like there was something bigger in it and that it was leading to something and that I just couldn’t quit.”
His family and his love of coaching kept him going.
“What I always tell people is gotta keep on keeping on,” Jones said.
Seeking a transplant
Jones’ treatments were working to kill the cancer, but they were also damaging his liver and making him very sick.
Jones said he told his hometown doctor he wanted a liver transplant.
“He said, ‘You’ll never have a liver transplant.’ And I said, ‘I’m going to,’” Jones said. “And I remember him saying, ‘No, you’re not.’ I said, ‘Watch.’”
Jones traveled to Mayo Clinic for a second opinion from Dr. Harnois, a Mayo Clinic liver transplant specialist.
“One of the fields of transplantation that’s really been expanding is what we would call transplant oncology,” Harnois said.
Changes in transplant eligibility
Until recently, liver transplantation for colon cancer that had spread to the liver was not an option for several reasons, Harnois said.
One reason was the risk of cancer cells spreading throughout the body, making the likelihood of recurrence in a newly transplanted liver high.
People who have transplants take medication to suppress their immune systems so their bodies do not reject the new organ, and cancer cells can erupt in that environment.
“When transplants were done, they very frequently developed recurrence of disease and often very quickly after the transplant was done,” Harnois said.
Harnois described the patients as those who have disease in the liver and not outside of it. The disease is not in the lymph nodes, and it has not gone to the lungs or other organs. Their colon cancer itself has been treated.
“Now transplantation represents an option for those patients,” Harnois said.
Transplant at Mayo Clinic
Jones went through a month of testing at Mayo Clinic to find out if he was a transplant candidate. After he was approved, he waited for a donor liver to become available.
“It was just one miracle after another that worked,” Jones said. “You know, it worked out for me.”
Jones received the first liver transplant for metastatic colon cancer performed at Mayo Clinic.
He is back on the field and has been cancer-free for two years.
Jones and Harnois said their real heroes are the organ donors and their families.

title: Speeding crash involving 2 Waymo vehicles caught on camera
text:
PHOENIX (AZFamily/Gray News) - One person is in critical condition after a crash involving an SUV and two Waymo cars.
The crash happened at about 11 a.m. Monday at an intersection in central Phoenix.
Video from Sunland Auto Service shows two Waymo vehicles, a white sedan and a blue SUV, stopped at an intersection. A moment later, a speeding SUV comes barreling toward them through the intersection and crashes into them.
Skid marks found at the crash led to the discovery of a fourth vehicle, found upside down and severely damaged near a business.
Phoenix Police Sgt. John Buchanan said the driver of the SUV was taken to the hospital in extremely critical condition.
One person in the white Waymo sedan was taken to the hospital with injuries that aren’t considered life-threatening, while the two people in the blue Waymo did not require hospitalization.
Firefighters said a third person was taken to the hospital but their condition is unknown.
Buchanan said police do not have an estimate of how fast the SUV driver was going and police are still working to determine what led up to the crash.
Waymo employees are on the scene assisting investigators and providing them with the vehicle’s videos of the crash.
“The safety of our riders and other road users is our top priority. We are working with first responders to ensure the well-being of our riders,” a Waymo spokesperson said in a statement provided to Arizona’s Family.

title: US Catholic bishops meet after Democrats' big wins help reshape immigration and abortion debates
text:
U.S. Catholic bishops are holding their annual fall meeting in Baltimore this week. The gathering comes just after Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories reset the political dynamics around some of the bishops’ priorities, including immigration, abortion and artificial intelligence.
The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops is now facing a divided government as it seeks to influence both the faithful and public policy.
“Midterm elections are the opportunity for people to assess where we are as a country and where we hope to go,” said Bishop Michael Burbidge of Arlington, Virginia. “I think what the citizens are asking — and we’re certainly praying for — is that those who are elected will be devoted to doing all that is right and just and true and somehow find a way to begin working together and addressing the issues that impact individuals and families.”
Catholics overall are politically mixed. Catholic voters split roughly evenly between Republican and Democratic candidates for the U.S. House, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters.
There was a split between white Catholics and Latino Catholics: Just over half of white Catholics supported the Republican House candidate in their area, while about two-thirds of Latino Catholics supported the Democratic House candidate in their area.
Nationally, just over half of Catholics said the Trump administration’s actions on immigration enforcement had “gone too far,” according to The AP Voter Poll. A similar share disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement was doing its job.
During the first half of Republican President Donald Trump’s second term, Catholic leaders emerged as strong critics of the administration’s immigration crackdown. Last fall, U.S. bishops issued a rare “special message” on immigration, decrying “the vilification of immigrants” and “indiscriminate mass deportation.”
Bishops are expected to hear updates Wednesday from their committees that deal with migration and abortion. They will also hear from a new task force on “preserving human dignity in the age of artificial intelligence.”
Catholic theology does not fit neatly into American political categories. While Catholic leaders have criticized current Republican immigration policies, they have also taken Democratic leaders to task over support for abortion rights. Targets of criticism included former Democratic President Joe Biden, who is Catholic.
“I think we’re still trying to wrap our minds around what actually just happened,” said Bishop Robert Boxie III, an auxiliary bishop of the Archdiocese of Washington, while speaking about the midterms at a Georgetown University forum. He added the elections showed the power of “collective action” over money, including in “communities that had been sort of written off.”
Ahead of the midterms, U.S. bishops led a campaign urging Catholics to exercise their right to vote while putting faith before politics.
“The Church’s contribution to the public life of a nation is not a political or partisan program; rather, it reflects our commitment to the dignity of every person, who is created in the image and likeness of God,” Archbishop Paul Coakley, the conference’s president, said in a statement.
That message became muddled in late October, when the White House released images and a video of a group of Catholic bishops praying over Trump in the Oval Office. At least two bishops expressed regret during the ensuing backlash.
“I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purpose,” Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, Iowa, wrote in a statement. “I pray I am more prudent and wise going forward, even as I remain resolute in my openness to engaging and praying for political leaders at all levels.”

title: New Hampshire hospital server outage due to 'cyber incident'
text:
New Hampshire hospital server outage due to 'cyber incident,' officials say
New Hampshire's Monadnock Community Hospital said on Monday its week-long server outage is due to a "cyber incident."
The ongoing investigation now includes determining what data was affected. If any sensitive information was involved, patients will be directly notified, according to the hospital.
The phone network was restored as of Sunday, and the emergency department remains open. Clinical office, rehabilitation and physical therapy appointments will continue as scheduled. 
Other services are not functioning and some elective major surgeries have been cancelled through Nov. 23. All affected patients will be notified.
The hospital is diverting ambulance emergencies to other facilities.
Hospital officials said they are evaluating and will update security measures to protect sensitive information.

main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Mann Law, a female-led personal injury law firm, has added five team members as it strengthens its legal staff, operations and client support services.
“Each of our new team members brings valuable experience and a shared commitment to ensuring that every client feels heard, valued, informed and supported throughout the process,” said Chrissy Mann, founder and principal attorney at Mann Law. “As we grow, we’re building on what has always mattered most to us: personal attention, strong advocacy and helping our clients move forward.”
Before the new team members joined, the firm had just two employees.
New hires
Liam Morrissey has been hired for the role of associate attorney. A 2026 graduate of the University of Maine School of Law, Morrissey brings experience in private practice and public service. He clerked at a general practice law firm in Portland, externed with the Maine District Court in Augusta and interned with the Maine Department of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Standards.
Alexis Fowlie has been hired for the role of practice manager. Fowlie oversees Mann Law’s daily operations, human resources and staff development. She previously built a career in healthcare leadership, including serving as a director of human resources, gaining extensive experience in employee relations, operations and team management.
Cindy Rogers has been hired as a legal coordinator. Rogers brings a background in executive-level support, with experience coordinating day-to-day responsibilities in fast-paced professional environments. Her organizational and communication skills support the firm’s work on behalf of its clients.
Liv Neuhauser has been hired as a legal intern. A second-year student at the University of Maine School of Law, Neuhauser first joined Mann Law as an intern in 2023. Before attending law school, she studied history and secondary education.
Zaina Maist has been hired for the role of front office assistant. Maist is a recent graduate of Colby College, where she majored in government and minored in creative writing. She brings a strong interest in the law and plans to pursue a career in the legal field.
About the firm
Founded by Mann in 2018, the firm combines personal injury advocacy with an understanding of how insurance companies handle claims.

title: Forensics expert says Jeffrey Epstein’s injuries indicate he was likely killed while in custody
text:
(Gray News) - A forensics expert says new findings point to Jeffrey Epstein having been killed while in custody.
According to a report by CNN, Michael Freeman, a scholar and consultant in forensic medicine epidemiology, teamed up with Anders Eriksson, a forensic pathologist and professor of forensic medicine at Umea University in Sweden, and Itiel Dror, a cognitive neuroscientist and researcher, as part of an investigation into Epstein’s death.
Their research was presented Monday in London, which said there was no evidence a hanging took place, contradicting what officials have previously said they found.
The New York City medical examiner ruled Epstein’s death in August 2019 a suicide by hanging. Epstein was reportedly found unresponsive in his cell at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York.
However, the team of researchers and forensic experts said that after reviewing the entire autopsy file and completing a reconstruction using autopsy photos, they found Epstein’s injuries were more consistent with an assault and struggle, and that he was killed.
“The ligature marks are most consistent with homicidal strangulation from behind, most likely using a narrow knotted fabric ligature,” a portion of the presentation was quoted as sharing with the London legal society.
The New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner continues to stand by its determination that Epstein died by suicide and that the manner was hanging.
Epstein was said to have been on a brief suicide watch in the weeks before his death, but questions have remained. There were reportedly no photographs taken of his hanging in his cell or his body positioned at the scene.
The BBC reports that Freeman shared that he would have expected in an investigation of a death by hanging in custody for there to be a photograph before the body was taken down.
Freeman continued, saying that he didn’t know who may have killed Epstein.
“That is not something I have an opinion about. That isn’t any part of any investigation that I’ve done,” Freeman was quoted in the interview.
Freeman said he has based his conclusions on the files and photographs from the examiner’s report provided to him by Epstein’s brother, Mark Epstein, who has maintained that his brother was murdered.
Jeffrey Epstein pleaded guilty in a Florida state court in 2008 to one count of soliciting prostitution from a minor, and was required to be a registered sex offender.
He was said to have escaped a heavy jail sentence as a result of a plea deal.
In 2019, the billionaire financier was then charged with sexually abusing dozens of underage girls along with running a network of sex involving minors.
Jeffrey Epstein was awaiting trial when he was found dead.
Freeman said he has based his conclusions on the files and photographs from the examiner’s report provided to him by Epstein’s brother, Mark Epstein, who has maintained that his brother was murdered.

title: What is a dirty bomb and is the US a target?
text:
What is a dirty bomb and is the US a target?
What is a dirty bomb and is the US a target?
The White House has stated there is no credible dirty bomb threat to the United States.
Some reports have indicated that U.S. intelligence suggested Iran may be considering targeting Trump administration officials in Washington, D.C., with a dirty bomb.
A dirty bomb is not a nuclear weapon but uses a conventional explosion to spread radioactive material. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the biggest immediate danger from such a device would be the blast itself.
Iran has denied the report. U.S. officials have reiterated that there is no imminent threat but said they are monitoring all situations.

title: United Way to deliver books to Aroostook County maternity wards
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - United Way is delivering books for new babies to Aroostook County’s two maternity wards through a new program called First Pages.
Sarah Duncan, executive director of United Way of Aroostook, said the organization has books ready to give out.
“We have over 300 books that we’re giving out in anticipation that we’ll have over 300 births in Aroostook County,” Duncan said.
Four titles in each bag
The program includes 300 copies each of four titles: “Owl Babies,” “Llama Llama ABC,” “The Circus Ship” and “Two at the Zoo.”
The plan is for each new baby in the county to receive a bag with all four books.
How the books were obtained
Duncan said United Way worked with Neighborhood Books to purchase the books.
The program comes after the local Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library program lost state funding this year.
Distribution at hospitals
AR Gould and Cary Medical will give the bags out as new parents are discharged.
“The hospitals are going to each have so many bags to give out. And as soon as they are starting to run low, we’ll go and replenish them and make sure that this program keeps continuing,” Duncan said.
