title: Gloria Steinem’s famed talking circles are still going strong. This one had a twist: Men only
text:
Gloria Steinem’s famed talking circles are still going strong. This one had a twist: Men only
For more than half a century, Gloria Steinem welcomed guests into her inviting, art-filled Manhattan living room, gathering women from all walks of life to discuss issues of vital importance in health, education, business, politics and beyond.
It was her long-held dream that these “talking circles” continue after she was gone — and, two months after her death, they’re indeed going strong. Last week, though, marked a first that close associates say would have particularly delighted the feminist trailblazer: a men-only circle, focused on male well-being.
“I know Gloria would have loved this,” exclaimed Jill Heller of Gloria’s Foundation, which is working on preserving the home as a permanent center, as she welcomed the men. “Wherever she is, I hope she’s tap-dancing,” she added — a wry reference to one of Steinem’s lesser-known talents.
Then the circle's facilitator, Janna Meyrowitz Turner, explained the genesis of the idea to bring the guests — advocates, academics and others working with men and boys — into one room.
“If she were here, Gloria would tell you that men’s liberation and men’s well-being have always been a part of feminism,” said Meyrowitz Turner, CEO of Antenna Up, a media and events platform that aims to build trust between men and women. “She would say that healthier men mean healthier women.”
The circle, she noted, had been planned with Steinem's enthusiastic support before her death in September at age 92. Originally scheduled for the summer, the event had been postponed due to travel schedules.
“We’ll forgive her for not getting to this one,” Meyrowitz Turner said, to chuckles. “Gloria owes us nothing.”
One man was thanked for ‘bringing tears’ into the room
Hundreds of admirers will bid farewell to Steinem this week at a New York memorial service expected to feature luminaries from political figures to pop stars to poets, all there to remember, to laugh — and of course, to cry.
But there were tears, too, on a much smaller scale at the talking circle last Tuesday, with 12 men detailing the paths that had brought them to this moment in a feminist icon’s living room.
When Brendan Kwiatkowski-Hartman’s turn came to speak, he soon found he was overcome. The sociologist, who specializes in the emotional life of teen boys, was describing his journey away from a religious childhood in which he was taught to believe that feminism was “anti-Christianity.”
“I knew nothing about Gloria Steinem other than as a bogeyman,” he said.
In college, he met a professor who was a Christian feminist, and his views began to shift. Now, seated in the home of Steinem herself, he said: “Feminism has given me a mirror to see myself better.”
He began to choke up as he said it, drawing thanks from another circle member for “bringing tears into this space.”
“You've done one of the bravest things in this conversation,” said Johnny Cole, an advocate who also works with men and boys. One thing young men really need, he said, is “to see more men crying, and willing to do it in front of men.”
Like many in the room, Cole spoke of the need for self-esteem among men. “You can’t enact change … if you don’t have self-esteem,” he said.
Educator and author Jackson Katz, meanwhile, urged those assembled to remember that “We wouldn't be here without women's leadership.” Katz had written in Ms. Magazine, upon Steinem's death, about how she had changed men’s lives, too.
“This didn’t come out of nowhere,” he told the group about their conversation. “The driving energy is women’s leadership.”
Steinem first moved into her home in the late '60s, with a roommate
Steinem first made her home in the Upper East Side brownstone in 1967, Heller explained to the room. Then, it was a one-floor rental; she and her roommate fashioned a loft bed space in the living room, which remains.
“That’s the OG bed,” said Heller, pointing upward; whichever roommate came home first got the bed. Two decades later, Steinem bought the floor below, where the foundation now works. It also has space on the third floor, and the hope is that eventually the foundation can occupy the entire building.
Ms. Magazine, co-founded by Steinem in the early ’70s, had its early meetings in the living room, where many groups and initiatives were also born. The talking circles began almost from the start, and still usually take place a few times a week. Exactly one week after Steinem died, women gathered to discuss leadership and style in a circle hosted by the Argent fashion label.
Steinem explained the circles' meaning in an interview with this reporter earlier this year, six months before her death.
“There's a continuing series of meetings going on in my living room, sometimes initiated by me, sometimes initiated by other people,” she said, adding that she also usually had a guest or two staying in the spare bedroom.
“We are communal animals, you know,” Steinem said. “We don’t generate the famous oxytocin, the chemical that allows us to empathize with each other, unless we’re physically together. It’s why solitary confinement is the worst punishment everywhere in the world. We do need to be together.”
The home, including Steinem’s own bedroom down the hall from the living room and past a small kitchen, is filled with mementos from her constant travels. Every surface seems to contain an expression of her personality. Her fireplace bears a banner that says “Hope.” On the mantel above sits a colorful matchbox emblazoned with the words “Wonder Woman” — a character Steinem had a particular fondness for and even placed on Ms. Magazine's cover.
The men were urged to be a support system for each other
As the speakers took turns last Tuesday, each man recounted why he was there and what he hoped to accomplish.
Nate Glasser, an internist and pediatrician at the University of Chicago, told of how, during his residency, “the curriculum was telling us almost explicitly not to pay attention to the interior lives of men.”
His own colleagues, he said, “miss that boys have interior lives. That is what brings me here.”
CJ Goulding spoke about his work with a group called Boyz N The Wood, providing healing spaces in nature. “We are a part of something bigger when we're in nature,” he said.
Rawle Andrews Jr., executive director of the American Psychiatric Association Foundation, injected a note of humor when he quipped that some women on his team had asked him: “Why do YOU get to go to Gloria’s house? Take us!”
There were more laughs when two of the men, sitting on a small piece of furniture, thought they’d broken it. “The first time we get men in the room!!” joked Meyrowitz Turner, in mock horror. Heller assured everyone the damage had been there previously.
Meyrowitz Turner closed out the session by urging the men to serve as a support system for each other — as women more often do. “This work can be really lonely,” she said. The men, in turn, thanked her for “nudging” them to answer her emails.
Heller returned at the end with a tearful note of thanks.
“This is just what Gloria envisioned for this space,” she said, noting that Steinem had hoped she could “just go to sleep, and the work would go on.”
And she invited them all back.
“Consider it your living room, too,” she said.

title: Measles is no longer considered eliminated in the US and Mexico
text:
The U.S. has lost its measles-free status, international health officials said Tuesday, as the highly contagious virus once relegated to medical textbooks has spread — largely among the unvaccinated — at the highest rate in more than 30 years.
Mexico also lost its measles-elimination status, following a resurgence of the virus there that included a massive outbreak in Chihuahua state. Bolivia, too, lost its status.
The Pan American Health Organization declaration has few practical implications and is largely symbolic, but it marks a sharp turnabout in a disease largely controlled through decades of scientific advances. It also may be seen as the beginning of an era in which diseases of the past become deadly problems for the modern world.
Measles has been spreading throughout the Americas since 2024. The outbreaks in North America started in close-knit Mennonite communities and have since spread to areas with low vaccination rates. Last year, Canada lost its measles-free designation for the first time since 1998.
International health officials consider measles eliminated when the virus is not locally spreading among residents. The designation hinges on whether a single measles chain has spread uninterrupted for at least 12 months.
Tuesday’s announcement signals an erosion of public health preparedness.
Vaccination rates have been falling against a number of diseases, in the U.S. and globally. And as one of the most infectious diseases known to medicine, measles was seen as likely to be one of the first vaccine-preventable diseases to re-emerge when vaccinations falter.
That means others are likely to follow, some experts said.
“It can be the canary in the coal mine to other things,” said Dr. Susan Kansagra, chief medical officer of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials.
Vaccine rates fall and cases go up
Measles vaccines have safely stopped the virus’ spread in the U.S. for 30 years.
It takes a community vaccination rate of 95% to prevent outbreaks, experts say. But as fewer parents vaccinate their children and federal leaders sow doubt and confusion about the importance of getting vaccinated, the virus has found footholds in communities across the U.S. All but three states have reported a confirmed case of measles this year.
“This humiliating determination is the tragic yet predictable result of an ongoing campaign by grifters, quacks and charlatans to put their own greed and self-worth ahead of the health and safety of children,” said Sen. Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon.
The last two years have been the worst in a generation in the U.S., with more than 7,000 cases and 11 deaths. Nearly all of those people were either unvaccinated or didn’t report whether they were vaccinated. More than 10% of those infected had to be hospitalized.
The illness typically begins with a high fever followed by a telltale rash that starts on the face and neck. Most people recover, but it’s one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization. Serious complications, including blindness and swelling of the brain, are more common in young children and adults over age 30.
Ten measles-associated deaths have been reported in the U.S. this year. Health officials have not released detailed information on each death, but at least five of the dead were children.
This year’s measles death count is higher than what has been seen in any previous year in more than three decades.
And the U.S. is experiencing its worst year for measles illnesses since 1991.
The U.S. has seen major outbreaks in Texas, Utah, South Carolina and Pennsylvania
Since the U.S. eliminated measles in 2000, public health officials usually logged less than 200 cases a year, most of them tied to international travel.
But since 2025, measles has sickened thousands. It started with a major outbreak in the southwest.
In Texas, more than 760 people got sick and two children died. And in New Mexico, about 100 people got sick and one adult died.
In the summer of 2025, measles exploded in extremely rural border towns in Arizona and Utah. And a major outbreak in South Carolina in the winter and spring sickened nearly 1,000 people to become the fastest growing measles outbreak the nation has seen in decades.
Bad as 2025 was, this year has been much worse. The more than 5,400 confirmed cases so far this year are already double the 2025 tally, driven largely by an outbreak in Pennsylvania that has dwarfed the earlier ones.
And the outbreak tallies are almost certainly an undercount, public health experts say.
Critics say the US response is falling short
U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has no formal medical training, was a leading voice in the anti-vaccine movement before President Donald Trump appointed him to oversee federal health agencies.
Kennedy and other federal leaders have argued that vaccination rates were waning for years before Trump took office a second time, that measles is not an “American phenomenon,” and that the U.S. government is handling measles better than other countries. In January, a CDC leader told reporters that the loss of the nation’s elimination status would be the “cost of doing business” globally.
It’s true that other countries are struggling with measles, and some also have lost their measles-elimination status. But some experts say the outcome in the U.S. wasn’t inevitable.
The government has been taking some steps. In August and September, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention awarded $100 million — in two tranches — to support state and local measles-response work. And Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz have made statements that vaccination is the best way to prevent measles from spreading.
But state and local health officials say the cost is far higher than that.
“It wasn’t a lot of money, frankly,” said Chrissie Juliano, executive director of the Big Cities Health Coalition, which represents three dozen of the largest U.S. city health departments.
Experts also say the moment demands a louder federal voice — and a bigger push for vaccinations — than Kennedy and Schwartz are providing. Some noted that neither Kennedy nor the CDC has scheduled a news conference for this week to address how they plan to try to regain measles-elimination status.
“When the people at the front of the room are not speaking loudly and frequently in support of vaccination, the program starts to falter. And that’s what we’re seeing in the U.S.,” said Noel Brewer, a University of North Carolina public health professor who chairs a committee that presented an analysis of U.S. measles data to PAHO last week.
“The federal government has had such a ho-hum response,” he said. “How many kids have to die before they start getting concerned?
“At what point is this relic of the past, stealing children from us, going to create outrage and action from the federal government?”
What’s next?
After hugely successful vaccination campaigns, the Americas became the first region in the world to be free of measles in 2016. Health officials estimate the measles vaccine prevented 6.2 million deaths in the Americas between 2000 and 2023.
Now, the entirety of North America faces the task of earning back the designation.
Some individual countries have achieved, lost, and then regained measles-elimination status. Brazil is one example. Another is the United Kingdom, although it lost its status a second time — this year.
___

title: FAA says it has paused installation of routers linked to nationwide ground stop
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Federal Aviation Administration has paused installing routers linked to last week’s ground stop that caused chaos for travelers, the agency said Tuesday.
The move comes amid growing scrutiny over the nation’s air traffic control system and as the Trump administration is making a new request for $50 billion to improve air travel. Democrats in the Senate are demanding that the administration provide clear answers about what went wrong.
President Donald Trump has blamed old technology and Democrats for the nationwide grounding of all planes and upheaval at the nation’s airports. But the FAA has been struggling to modernize the air traffic control system for decades — going back well before the first Trump administration.
FAA spokesperson Ian Gregor said the agency paused new installations of Juniper routers and disabled the functionality of all existing ones on Friday after technicians linked the problems to a new router in El Dorado, Arkansas.
Maker of routers says devices were working properly
The system became overloaded when the federal contractor that maintains the FAA’s telecommunications network was replacing outdated copper wires with fiber optic lines across the nation.
The ground stop was needed, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said, after the installation of a new router by L3Harris in Arkansas resulted in a cascade of intermittent communications and radar signals at 17 of the 22 regional air traffic control centers. The centers direct planes cruising at high altitudes. A radar site in Amarillo, Texas, where a router had been installed three weeks earlier also contributed to the trouble.
The FAA said that “excessive data” was flooding the system “at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds.” That deluge created instability with “aircraft communications and radar feeds,” the agency said.
For now, the FAA is relying on older Cisco routers that have been in place for 25 years to continue operating the network while they investigate the cause of Friday’s trouble.
The routers at issue last week are being tested in a lab at the headquarters of L3Harris.
Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, said the company believes the routers were working properly when the ground stop occurred. “Based on what we know today, the device functioned as it was configured to by the installer,” the statement said.
Duffy said Tuesday that 68 previous installations involving the same routers worked well before this latest problem.
“We’ve been able to recreate what happened in El Dorado,” he said. “But the root cause of what happened, we don’t have clarity yet.”
Problems with FAA equipment are decades-old
Upgrading the nation’s air transportation system is an effort that Congress has dedicated significant sums to in recent years. Duffy has pushed Congress for billions more dollars, saying just this week much more is needed.
Democrats on the Senate Commerce Committee said that knowing which device was part of last week’s meltdown isn’t enough.
“FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues,” the Democrats said in a letter sent to Duffy.
Money would go to control towers, airport infrastructure
The Trump administration on Tuesday sent a letter to key lawmakers outlining its request for $50.1 billion to modernize the system and make other improvements at airports.
The request calls for $10.1 billion for updating the nation’s air traffic control system. Similar amounts would go toward boosting airport infrastructure, replacing or refurbishing terminals at high-impact hubs, constructing five new traffic control centers and improving or replacing up to 140 FAA-owned air traffic control towers.
“Congressional approval of these funds will equip the FAA to deliver to the American people a brand-new air traffic control system that is safer, smarter, faster, and more efficient,” the letter said.
Several Republican senators voiced skepticism following a closed-door meeting Tuesday with the transportation secretary.
“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related,” said Sen. Ted Cruz, chair of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, & Transportation, which has jurisdiction over air safety issues.
Sen. Rick Scott of Florida said he believes the airline industry should pay for the upgrades.
Duffy, meanwhile, said he’s open to other options that could include Congress breaking up the request into pieces, with the initial focus on the most critical needs for air safety.
Congress approved $12.5 billion last year for replacing outdated technologies, but much of that money will also go toward runway upgrades and other construction.
Ground stop cost big airlines over $300 million
Equity research and brokerage firm Bernstein estimated the ground stop and the weekend work needed to recover from it cost the four biggest U.S. airlines $345 million combined.
The airlines had to offer cash refunds, credits or rebooking options to customers who decided to cancel their trips, Bernstein analysts said.
The lost revenue and additional costs from the ground stop still are enough to have a measurable effect on the quarterly earnings for American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Southwest Airlines, the analysts wrote in a Monday research note.
“A booking slowdown before Thanksgiving, or a second outage, would cost more than the weekend’s cancellations did,” the analysts said, adding they did not see any signs of waning ticket demand.
___
Associated Press writer John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed to this report.

title: Hannah Pingree talks plans for first 100 days in governor's office
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree talks plans for first 100 days in office
In her first sit-down interview since being elected, Governor-elect Hannah Pingree talks about what she plans to accomplish in her first 100 days as Maine's governor.
Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree talks plans for first 100 days in office
In her first sit-down interview since being elected, Governor-elect Hannah Pingree talks about what she plans to accomplish in her first 100 days as Maine's governor.
It's been two weeks since Hannah Pingree was elected Maine's 76th governor. In the days following, she appointed a 22-person transition team tasked with finding the best people to be in her cabinet.
"I was campaigning for almost 18 months, and then you win. And you're deeply honored by the support that Maine people placed in you. But then you got to immediately get to work to ramp up a new administration," Pingree said.
She's wasting no time after her victory earlier this month. Some issues she said need to be tackled sooner than others.
"We are talking right now with leaders across the aisle about how we deliver on an urgent issue like heating oil relief," she said. "I've talked to Republican leaders and Democratic leaders on how on day one we are putting a bill before the legislature to ensure that Maine people can safely get through this winter."
The cost of heating oil got up to more than $6 a gallon earlier this year. According to the Maine Department of Energy Resources it is now $5.84.
Pingree is promising to provide heating oil relief while also passing tribal sovereignty in her first 100 days. In that time frame, she also needs to submit her first budget. That's due on February 5, just a month after her inauguration.
"The budget is what reflects your priorities," she said. "It's where you put things like, you know, the funding to build more housing, the funding to shore up our health care system, how we ensure that kids are getting a high-quality education."
The state budget currently has a $1.3 billion structural gap, or shortfall, in the general fund. In the highway fund, another $256.7 million gap.
"There is some talk in Washington about putting off some of the cuts to Medicaid. And I am hopeful that they will get that done either in the lame-duck session or early in January, because obviously that would make our work in Maine much easier," she said.
"There is nothing easy. I mean, most of the money in the state of Maine goes to health care and education. A lot of the other agencies, you know, honestly, the funding is very small. And I think both in health care and education, we're going to have to ensure that we are delivering the core services that people rely on, at the same time doing it in the most efficient way possible. And honestly, that's going to require hard conversations. There are no easy solutions to how we actually get it done," she said when asked what specifically could be removed from the budget.
Pingree will be sworn in as governor on January 6.

title: Standish, Maine, Man Was The Most Accomplished Jeopardy! Champion in State History
text:
Standish, Maine, Man Was The Most Accomplished Jeopardy! Champion in State History
For so many people across Maine, watching the game show Jeopardy! is an evening tradition.
First hosted by Alex Trebek and today's version hosted by former superchampion Ken Jennings, the modern-day evening edition of Jeopardy! was not the first iteration of the show.
Launched in 1964, there was a daytime version of Jeopardy!, hosted by Art Fleming. The original daytime Jeopardy! was filmed in New York City instead of Hollywood, which allowed for more contestants from the east coast to participate.
Including the greatest Jeopardy! champion in Maine history.
Burns Cameron of Standish, Maine, Remains Greatest Jeopardy! Champion in Maine History
First appearing on Jeopady! in December of 1965, Burns Cameron of Standish, Maine, still remains the greatest Jeopardy! champion in the history of the state.
Cameron dominated the Jeopardy! stage for five consecutive games, which was the maximum win-streak allowed for several decades.
Cameron amassed more than $7,000 in winnings which would be the modern-day equivalent of over $60,000. He accomplished that feat at just 27-years-old.
Burns Cameron went on to dominate the Tournament of Champions as well, becoming the first-ever male contestant to win the competition while adding another $4,000 to his total.
Cameron made one more Jeopardy! appearance, 25 years after his initial run, during a 1990 Super Jeopardy! tournament.
There Have Been Other Recent Jeopardy! Champions From Maine
Over the last decade, there have more Jeopardy! champions from Maine than any other stretch in the show's fabled history.
Jason Singer and Susan McMillan, a husband-and-wife from Portland, Maine, both became Jeopardy! champions in separate years. McMillan in 2021 and Singer in 2025.
In 2019, a librarian from Augusta, Maine, named Jessica Garsed won three consecutive games of Jeopardy!
In 2020, Dennis Coffey of Old Orchard Beach, Maine, won three games on Jeopardy! to match Jessica Garsed's streak.
The most recent Jeopardy! champion from Maine was Emily Burnham. who won a game in September of this year.

title: Air travel rebounds, but future disruptions are possible during modernization
text:
Air travel rebounds, but future disruptions are possible during modernization
A government watchdog report warns that the Trump administration's approach to modernization could be prioritizing speed at the cost of air traffic disruptions.
Air travel rebounds, but future disruptions are possible during modernization
A government watchdog report warns that the Trump administration's approach to modernization could be prioritizing speed at the cost of air traffic disruptions.
Air travel is recovering on Monday after a rare nationwide ground stop, but future disruptions are possible as the Trump administration continues to modernize the air traffic control system, according to federal officials and a government watchdog report published earlier this year.
With the busy Thanksgiving travel season just around the corner, officials have stressed that it's safe to fly and the system is stable. The tracking website FlightAware showed cancellations were in the hundreds on Monday, down from the thousands reported over the weekend.
As flight schedules rebounded, United Airlines separately confirmed a system outage that delayed departing flights on Monday but was later resolved.
Speaking publicly for the first time about Friday's hourslong ground stop, President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he doesn't "take any responsibility." He praised his administration's response and faulted the nation's outdated air traffic control infrastructure — a problem that stretches back decades — for the disruptions.
"Essentially, what you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack," Trump said.
Federal officials believe the disruptions were caused by a routine system upgrade when a router flooded the air traffic control network with data. The FAA and the contractor in charge of the maintenance are still looking into why that happened.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CNBC on Monday that future disruptions are possible if Congress doesn't approve a $50 billion funding request to modernize the system.
"If we don't make those investments, is there a guarantee that these things maybe, in varying forms, don't happen in the future? We can't make those guarantees. We’re going to make sure we keep people safe," Duffy said.
With an injection of cash, Duffy estimates that the system overhaul could be complete in roughly two years.
A nonpartisan Government Accountability Office report published in September agreed with the need to significantly accelerate the modernization process and applauded the FAA's initial progress, but it also raised questions about the Trump administration's timeline and the price tag.
"In the interest of expediency, FAA is introducing additional risk," the report concludes. "In essence, the FAA is buying delivery speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and potential disruptions. The net effect could be that air traffic controllers are forced to continue to rely on severely outdated systems that are prone to failure, leading to more system outages, ground stops, flight delays, or worse—safety incidents."
Kevin Walsh,  director of the information technology and cybersecurity team at the GAO, said it's a tricky balancing act because there are also risks associated with moving too slowly. 
"If we go very, very slowly, then systems continue to age and fray and may break in the meantime. So I don't know that there is a good option here, but I do think that there could be some more forethought and planning at the strategic level in terms of how we can schedule these things," Walsh said in an interview on Monday.
The report urges the administration to come up with a reliable cost estimate and an integrated master schedule. The Department of Transportation didn't directly respond to emailed questions about those recommendations.
However, the agency is currently reevaluating when upgrades are made in the wake of Friday's ground stop, according to Duffy. He explained that work at big facilities, like Chicago and Atlanta, is usually done at night, but the incident on Friday afternoon occurred at a remote location.
"This was a remote facility in Arkansas, and we didn't anticipate that this could take down the system, which is why it was done during the day, but we're going to review our whole procedures on when we do this work, how we do this work, so the system doesn't go down," Duffy told CNBC.

title: She married at 16. Now she’s fighting to end child marriage in Ohio
text:
CLEVELAND, Oh. (InvestigateTV) - Protecting children from forced marriages in recent years, several states have taken action to stop what some call abuse.
Before 2017, every state allowed marriage under 18, according to the nonprofit Unchained At Last. Since then, a growing number of states have outlawed child marriage with no exceptions, not even parental consent.
Ohio is the latest considering a change. In 2019, the state raised the minimum age to 17. But advocates and some lawmakers believe the age should be 18 with no exceptions.
Ohio’s current marriage law
Before 2019, Ohio had no minimum age to marry. The current minimum is 17. Ohio Senate Bill 341 would raise that age to 18 years old.
According to the nonprofit Unchained at Last, which advocates for banning child marriage, more than 5,000 children in Ohio have been married as minors since 2000.
Seventeen states have already banned child marriage, the organization reports. Nationwide, nearly 315,000 minors were legally married between 2000 and 2021.
Currently in Ohio, 17-year-olds cannot marry anyone older than 21.
Survivor speaks out
Stephanie Lowry survived child marriage and now advocates for others. She grew up in a religious family in Ohio. After her father died unexpectedly, her mother struggled, and her older sister married a man she had just met at age 19. Stephanie went to live with her sister and later became pregnant.
“I was 15 at the time I became pregnant. So, it would have been statutory rape for him,” Lowry said. “So one of the options is you need to marry her. And then that statutory rape goes away because you married her.”
A month after her 16th birthday, Lowry said her mother found a legal pathway that allowed the marriage.
“And at that time my mom looked up some laws around the marriage and back then you could be 16 with your parental signature and a psychologist letter,” Lowry said.
In 2001, four months pregnant, Lowry married the baby’s father at a courthouse. He was 19 years old.
“So, you’re going through having a baby, having a wedding with zero joy around it, just shame built up around you,” she said.
‘Your brain isn’t developed’
Once married, Lowry’s husband, not her mother, became her legal guardian.
“Basically, you’re just surviving in it. Because your brain isn’t developed to understand all the adults that were supposed to protect you can sometimes fail you,” Lowry said.
Lowry says the relationship turned abusive. At 17, with a 6-month-old baby, she called police after a fight became physical. She said they did not know what to do.
“He took me to the police station, and it was me and my son sitting there and he bought me a bag of Skittles. And just like a child, because I was a child,” she said.
Lowry could not return to her mother’s home or enter a battered women’s shelter because she was not 18. Foster care would have separated her from her baby. The shelter gave her and her baby a temporary placement, but their time there ran out. Because she was a minor, she could not independently file for divorce.
“Ultimately, I had to end up back with my abuser husband until I turned 18. A month after my 18th birthday, I was able to file another protection order on top of the other ones I already had on him. And I was able to leave the marriage,” Lowry said.
Life after child marriage
Lowry hid from her ex-husband for years after the divorce. She says he later died by suicide. She eventually rebuilt her life.
“I’ve been married for eight years, and we have a blended family,” she said.
Her son, born when she was 16, is now 24 years old.
“And all the healing I’ve done is where it’s brought me today, where I can be a voice and I can share my story with being vulnerable without any shame that I carried for so many years of being that young mom and a single mom,” Lowry said.
Lowry said Ohio’s current minimum age of 17 would not have protected her in 2001.
“So, the new law would have not protected me in 2001. They need to make it 18, no exceptions, because the new law still did not close the legal loopholes,” she said.
Advocates say child marriage can be a loophole for statutory rape, abuse and child trafficking.

title: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang signals interest in returning if company board chooses
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Nvidia on Tuesday rejected Jensen Huang’s offer to return as CEO, putting to rest for now any possible reinstatement of the celebrated artificial intelligence billionaire and industry evangelist, despite pressure from Silicon Valley and President Donald Trump’s support.
The embattled company’s board of directors “unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call before yielding to Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who is running the company as a permanent replacement is sought.
The rejection caps a whirlwind few days triggered by Huang’s admission to extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman and suspected spy for the country, his stunning ouster and a surprising split in the Trump administration over the fate of the disgraced business leader.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a wholesale cleaning at Nvidia on Sunday, only for Trump to come out in support of Huang’s return the next day despite investigations into whether Nvidia had allowed AI chips banned from China to slip through the cracks because of the alleged spy at the center of the controversy.
Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said in a social media post that if the board decided that his return was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company and the country, he would be “honored to answer these calls.” He acknowledged making “serious mistakes” in his personal life.
Company reports blowout financial results
The turmoil notwithstanding, Nvidia blew past Wall Street expectations for the third quarter, pulling in $116 billion in revenue, double the level from a year ago. The company also posted net income of $2.70 per share, beating estimates of $2.48 per share.
Nvidia stock shot up 5.2% in after-hours trading.
Referring to Huang’s replacement, Jones said, “We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.”
Some tech industry figures, including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, called for the reinstatement of Huang, a high-profile booster for the AI industry who oversaw Nvidia’s development as the key provider of chips driving advanced AI models.
Huang said he received an “outpouring” of support from employees, investors, business partners and customers for his return.
A “Stand with Jensen” petition set up last week gathered momentum, gaining signatures from current and former Nvidia staff, investors and other Silicon Valley supporters.
In comments Monday, Trump suggested that the ex-CEO could return, saying Huang “learned a big lesson” and that he “would certainly not mind” if he was reinstated.
The Chinese businesswoman whom Huang was seeing and who reportedly had links to Chinese intelligence was an executive at Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed International, a company being investigated by the U.S. for allegedly violating U.S. export controls by illegally diverting advanced Nvidia AI chips to Chinese companies.
Huang faces questioning by Congress
Also Tuesday, key House lawmakers said that Huang has voluntarily agreed to appear for transcribed interviews as the company faces intensifying national scrutiny over sales of its advanced computer chips.
Huang will appear before congressional committees on Dec. 1, followed by the company’s general counsel, Tim Teter, on Dec. 2.
“The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous PRC actors to access our most advanced chips,” said a statement from the chairmen of three House committees with oversight of China and intelligence issues, referring to the People’s Republic of China.
Huang also is expected to appear before the Senate Banking Committee, two people familiar with the matter said.
In the statement detailing its August-to-October results, Nvidia said revenue in a key business segment — data centers — more than doubled to $107.6 billion. It also projected that revenue for the current quarter running through January would hit $130 billion, more than Wall Street had expected.
Nvidia’s advanced chips are in high demand because they’re essential for cloud computing and data centers that underpin the AI boom, but they face restrictions on their sale to China.
Meanwhile, Nvidia said it’s creating a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance following the revelations about Huang. Trump said it was “good” that Nvidia had created the new committee.
“Yes, that’s a good idea. It’s a great company,” Trump said shortly after arriving Tuesday evening in the Philippine capital of Manila, where he participated in a photo opportunity with the leaders of Australia, India and Japan. “It’s a great idea.”
Nvidia later that day signaled it was already moving ahead without Huang.
“Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating,” interim CEO Kress said at the end of the quarterly conference call with investors. “We’ve got this.”
___
Chan reported from London. Associated Press writers Darlene Superville, Seung Min Kim and Kevin Freking in Washington, Alex Veiga in Los Angeles and Josh Boak in Shenzhen, China, contributed.

title: AARP scam alert: How an active pause can foil the perpetrator
text:
Most scams come at us with three elements – let’s call them together a trigger: a contact out of the blue, that yields a surge of emotion, and contains urgency. Criminals use this trigger to move our brains past logic and right into action through emotion. When this trigger comes at you, let that be your signal to Pause, Reflect, Protect – what AARP calls taking an “active pause.”
For example: Is your grandson calling you late at night (out of the blue), saying he’s in jail across the country (fear), and he needs you to send money right away (urgency)? The active pause means taking an intentional step back (pause) to think about what you might know of this scenario (reflect). This helps you engage with the logic center of your brain, allowing you to see the attempt and avoid having money stolen from you (protect).
The active pause gives you the opportunity, for example, to remember that you saw your grandson just the other day, so he’s not likely across the country, which prompts you to call him or his parents to confirm he’s okay, and so you hang up on the perpetrator, and avoid becoming a victim.
Know the trigger, know the safe response: Pause. Reflect. Protect.

title: Mother charged after newborn dies from blunt force injuries 2 days after birth
text:
SMITH COUNTY, Miss. (WLBT/Gray News) - Authorities in Mississippi say a 25-year-old woman has been charged with capital murder following the death of her newborn.
Jantelle Sharon Jordan, 25, was arrested Friday and charged with capital murder in connection with the death of her newborn, according to the Smith County Sheriff’s Office.
The case began Oct. 18 when Polkville first reponders and Smith County deputies were called to a home in Polkville for a woman who was giving birth. Investigators learned Jordan had given birth about an hour before contacting emergency services and requesting medical assistance for the newborn.
The baby was taken to a Jackson hospital for evaluation and began experiencing medical complications. Hospital staff determined the newborn had suffered injuries after birth.
Despite medical efforts, the baby died two days later.
An autopsy was conducted at the Mississippi Crime Laboratory. The pathologist determined the cause of death was blunt force trauma and ruled the manner of death a homicide, according to the sheriff’s office.
Sheriff Joel Houston described the case as horrific.
“This is a horrific case for everyone involved in working on this investigation. These are the types of cases that are difficult for anyone to comprehend, especially when they involve the loss of an innocent child,” Houston said.
The investigation remains active. Investigators are continuing to collect and examine evidence before forwarding the case to the district attorney’s office for prosecution.
The sheriff’s office urged the public to rely on verified information from official sources and avoid speculation while the investigation continues.

title: Widespread outage hits Apple services, including Apple Pay, iCloud, reports say
text:
(AP) - An update gone awry Tuesday at Apple followed a rash of major outages in recent days, including problems affecting the Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines and Microsoft.
Apple acknowledged on its system status page that its Apple Music, App Store and AppleCare services suffered full outages and that its iCloud sign-in interface was also having issues. The technology monitoring site Downdetector.com also showed a spike in user complaints about Apple Pay.
“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” the company said in an emailed statement. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”
EN ESPAÑOL | Reportan interrupciones en los servicios de Apple
Marriott International, the largest U.S. hotel operator, also had technology issues, according to users posting on Reddit. Downdetector.com also reported that Marriott was experiencing an outage.
In an emailed statement, Marriott said it has “resolved a technical issue” that affected sign-in capabilities on Marriott.com and the Marriott Bonvoy app. The company added that a company review found no sign the problem “was cybersecurity-related.”
The outages are the latest in a string of technology breakdowns.
On Monday, a system outage at United Airlines lasted more than 90 minutes, forcing the carrier to delay departing flights. The problem at United came just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop that delayed hundreds of flights and stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country.
Chicago-based United said there was no indication its outage was cybersecurity-related.
Also Monday, thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
Chase said Monday the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and on Tuesday confirmed the bank’s systems were operating normally.
Last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business chatter and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted.
The tech giant said there was “no indication” that malicious activity caused the disruptions, specifically noting on Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.

title: US loses its measles elimination status
text:
The U.S. has lost its measles-free status, international health officials said Tuesday, as the highly contagious virus once relegated to medical textbooks has spread — largely among the unvaccinated — at the highest rate in more than 30 years.
Mexico also lost its measles-elimination status, following a resurgence of the virus there that included a massive outbreak in Chihuahua state. Bolivia, too, lost its status.
The Pan American Health Organization declaration has few practical implications and is largely symbolic, but it marks a sharp turnabout in a disease largely controlled through decades of scientific advances. It also may be seen as the beginning of an era in which diseases of the past become deadly problems for the modern world.
“Measles elimination is not a trophy that is won once and placed on a shelf,” Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO’s director, said at a news conference. “It is an achievement that must be safeguarded every day by closing immunity gaps and ensuring we reach every community.”
PAHO expects the U.S., Bolivia and Mexico to submit plans “in the coming weeks” for how each country will go about trying to stop transmission for at least a year and regain measles elimination status, Dr. Daniel Salas, the organization’s executive manager for immunizations, told reporters.
Measles has been spreading throughout the Americas since 2024. The outbreaks in North America started in close-knit Mennonite communities and have since spread to areas with low vaccination rates. Last year, Canada lost its measles-free designation for the first time since 1998.
International health officials consider measles eliminated when the virus is not locally spreading among residents. The designation hinges on whether a single measles chain has spread uninterrupted for at least 12 months.
Tuesday’s announcement signals an erosion of public health preparedness.
Vaccination rates have been falling against a number of diseases, in the U.S. and globally. And as one of the most infectious diseases known to medicine, measles was seen as likely to be one of the first vaccine-preventable diseases to reemerge when vaccinations falter.
That means others are likely to follow, some experts said.
“It can be the canary in the coal mine to other things,” said Dr. Susan Kansagra, chief medical officer of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials.
Vaccine rates fall and cases rise
Measles vaccines have safely stopped the virus’ spread in the U.S. for 30 years.
It takes a community vaccination rate of 95% to prevent outbreaks, experts say. But as fewer parents vaccinate their children and federal leaders sow doubt and confusion about the importance of getting vaccinated, the virus has found footholds in communities across the U.S. All but three states have reported a confirmed case of measles this year.
The last two years have been the worst in a generation in the U.S., with more than 7,000 cases and 13 reported deaths. Nearly all of those people were either unvaccinated or didn’t report whether they were vaccinated. More than 10% of those infected had to be hospitalized.
The illness typically begins with a high fever followed by a telltale rash that starts on the face and neck. Most people recover, but it’s one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization. Serious complications, including blindness and swelling of the brain, are more common in young children and adults over age 30.
Ten measles-associated deaths have been reported in the U.S. this year, making it the deadliest in more than three decades. Health officials haven’t released detailed information on each death, but at least five of the dead were children.
Major outbreaks in four states
Since the U.S. eliminated measles in 2000, public health officials usually logged fewer than 200 cases a year, most of them tied to international travel.
But since 2025, measles has sickened thousands. It started with a major outbreak in the Southwest.
In Texas, more than 760 people got sick and two children died. In New Mexico, about 100 people got sick and one adult died. Then measles exploded in rural border towns in Arizona and Utah, followed by a major outbreak in South Carolina in the winter and spring that sickened nearly 1,000 people.
This year has been much worse — the worst for measles cases since 1991. The more than 5,400 confirmed cases so far this year are already double the 2025 tally, driven largely by an outbreak in Pennsylvania that dwarfed the earlier ones.
And the outbreak tallies are almost certainly an undercount, public health experts say.
Maine reported its first measles case since 2019 in February. There have been five more confirmed cases since then, according to the Maine CDC’s most recent update on Sept. 22. Five of the six cases were in Penobscot County.
Critics say the US response is falling short
U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was a leading voice in the anti-vaccine movement before President Donald Trump appointed him to oversee federal health agencies.
Kennedy and other federal leaders have argued that vaccination rates were waning for years before Trump took office a second time, that measles is not an “American phenomenon,” and that the U.S. government is handling measles better than other countries. In January, a U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention leader told reporters that the loss of the nation’s elimination status would be the “cost of doing business” globally.
It’s true that other countries are struggling with measles, and some also have lost their measles-elimination status. But public health experts and others say the outcome in the U.S. wasn’t inevitable.
“This humiliating determination is the tragic yet predictable result of an ongoing campaign by grifters, quacks and charlatans to put their own greed and self-worth ahead of the health and safety of children,” said Sen. Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon.
The government has been taking some steps. In August and September, the CDC awarded $100 million to support state and local measles-response work. And Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz have made statements that vaccination is the best way to prevent measles from spreading.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” Schwartz said in a statement Tuesday. “We know where transmission is occurring and we’ve invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities.”
But state and local health officials say the cost is far higher and that the moment demands a louder federal voice — and a bigger push for vaccinations — than Kennedy and Schwartz are providing.
“When the people at the front of the room are not speaking loudly and frequently in support of vaccination, the program starts to falter. And that’s what we’re seeing in the U.S.,” said Noel Brewer, a University of North Carolina public health professor who chairs a committee that presented an analysis of U.S. measles data to PAHO last week. “How many kids have to die before they start getting concerned?”
Some experts noted that neither Kennedy nor the CDC has scheduled a news conference to address their plans to fight measles. When the AP asked for Kennedy’s reaction to the U.S. losing its measles-free status, an HHS spokesperson pointed to Schwartz’s statement. During the PAHO news conference, the health department did issue a news release promoting the latest episode of Kennedy’s online cooking show.
What’s next?
After hugely successful vaccination campaigns, the Americas became the first region in the world to be free of measles in 2016. Health officials estimate the measles vaccine prevented 6.2 million deaths in the Americas between 2000 and 2023.
Now, the entirety of North America faces the task of earning back the designation.

Dan and Frank Carney opened the first Pizza Hut to cater to students. The business expanded to various Kansas locations and then became a national chain.

Wichita State University said Dan Carney’s legacy extended beyond his business success.

Dan Carney served as chair and a member of both the Wichita State University Foundation Board of Directors and the Wichita State University Board of Trustees.
Dan Carney is survived by his wife, Gayla, and numerous friends and family.

title: A low dose lung cancer screening can save your life
text:
As November marks Lung Cancer Awareness Month, Northern Light Health is highlighting the critical importance of early detection and encouraging eligible Mainers to consider a low-dose CT lung cancer screening because when things are caught sooner, there are usually more paths forward and that can change everything for the better.
Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death in Maine. According to the most recent data from the Maine CDC Cancer Registry (2023), there were 1,448 new cases of lung and bronchus cancer diagnosed in the state, a rate that is significantly higher than the national average.
In Maine, only about 32% of lung cancers are detected at an early (localized) stage, when the chance of surviving is substantially higher. But we know we can do better as a majority of cases are found at more advanced stages.
“Early detection is one of the most powerful tools we have against lung cancer,” John Klemperer, MD, cardiothoracic surgeon and lead physician for the Northern Light Lung Cancer Screening program, said. “When lung cancer is found early, patients often have more treatment options and better outcomes. Low-dose CT screening is a simple, quick exam that can detect cancer before symptoms appear.”
Low-dose CT lung cancer screening is covered by most insurances for individuals who meet established high-risk criteria (generally adults ages 50–80 with a significant smoking history). The scan uses lower radiation than a standard CT, requires no preparation or IV contrast, and typically takes only a few minutes.
Lung Cancer Screening is available at several Northern Light Health facilities across Maine, including: Northern Light A.R. Gould Hospital in Presque Isle, Northern Light Blue Hill Hospital, Northern Light C.A. Dean Hospital in Greenville, Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor, Northern Light Maine Coast Hospital in Ellsworth, Northern Light Mayo Hospital in Dover-Foxcroft, Northern Light Mercy Hospital in Portland and Northern Light Sebasticook Valley Hospital in Pittsfield.
Individuals at higher risk for lung cancer are encouraged to talk with their primary care provider today to see if a low-dose lung cancer screening is recommended.
Learn more about lung cancer screening and resources at northernlighthealth.org/lungcancer.

title: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ is almost here. What to know about the characters, music and billions at stake
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — “Grand Theft Auto” has never been much for following the rules.
Nearly three decades after a video game built around stealing cars, outrunning police and embracing criminal mayhem first arrived, the franchise has survived controversy, transformed open-world gaming and become one of the biggest sellers in entertainment.
Now, after a 13-year wait since its last main installment, “Grand Theft Auto VI” is preparing for another big score. The latest chapter arrives Thursday with a return to the neon-soaked streets of Vice City with two protagonists.
For longtime fans, “GTA VI” is a highly anticipated return. For everyone else, here’s what to know about the blockbuster video game, its characters and the enormous business riding on its release.
The game also picked up eight nominations Tuesday for the Game Awards, including game of the year, best game direction, narrative, art direction, score and music, audio design, action/adventure and performance. The awards will be presented Dec. 10.
Why is ‘Grand Theft Auto’ such a big deal?
The franchise began in 1997 as a relatively simple, top-down game that allowed players to roam fictional cities, steal vehicles, evade police and commit crimes.
The release of “Grand Theft Auto III” in 2001 helped redefine open-world gaming. It gave players greater freedom to explore a sprawling three-dimensional city, pursue missions and interact with their surroundings.
Later installments expanded that freedom with larger environments, cinematic storytelling, social satire and detailed worlds. The influence reached far beyond games about stealing cars.
Ubisoft’s Assassin’s Creed series brought open-world exploration to historical settings, while Bethesda’s The Elder Scrolls games expanded their own longstanding tradition of open-ended fantasy role-playing. Nintendo’s “The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild” later emphasized experimentation and discovery, allowing players to use the environment itself to solve problems.
For “Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas” and “Grand Theft Auto V,” Rockstar Games recruited real-life gang members to help bring authenticity to background characters and dialogue. Former writer and audio director Lazlow Jones has said some performers challenged scripted lines, prompting developers to let them use language drawn from their own experiences.
That attention to detail helped create the sense of a living world that became a hallmark of the franchise, even as the series drew criticism for its depictions of violence, crime and women.
But controversy did not stop the franchise’s commercial rise.
According to publisher Take-Two Interactive, the franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those units and reached $1 billion in retail sales in just three days.
Its online multiplayer component, “Grand Theft Auto Online,” has helped keep players engaged through years of updates, new activities and in-game purchases.
When can players start playing ‘GTA VI’?
“Grand Theft Auto VI” will become playable at midnight local time on Thursday on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X’S, according to Rockstar Games.
That means players can begin playing at 12 a.m. in their respective time zones. In the United States, the game unlocks at midnight Eastern, Central, Mountain and Pacific time as that day begins in each region.
Players who preordered the game digitally can already preload it, allowing the game files to be downloaded before launch. Preloading does not provide early access.
How closely is Vice City based on Miami?
“Grand Theft Auto VI” returns players to Vice City, Rockstar Games’ fictional version of Miami and South Florida. Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities, flying over the Everglades and researching the area’s history and architecture. Rockstar has promised its largest and most detailed open-world experience yet.
Miami is also leaning into its fictional alter ego ahead of the release. Miami-Dade County struck a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant “Welcome to Vice City” display atop the Miami Heat’s Kaseya Center, while Miami and Miami Beach have launched their own promotions tied to the game. The Heat will also wear black-and-pink “Vice City” jerseys on the eve of the release.
Not everyone has embraced the connection. Some South Florida officials have criticized using public resources to promote a franchise known for crime and violence, while supporters argue the campaign allows the region to capitalize on the enormous attention surrounding the game.
What’s the story behind ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’?
This time, the action returns to Vice City, Rockstar’s fictional version of Miami, and expands across the surrounding state of Leonida, a Florida-inspired setting filled with beaches, highways, nightlife and criminal enterprises.
At the center are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple trying to improve their circumstances through a life of crime. Lucia has recently been released from prison while Jason, a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys, is looking for a different path.
Their plans become more complicated when a seemingly straightforward criminal job goes wrong, drawing them into a conspiracy that stretches across Leonida.
The trailers suggest a story mixing romance, robberies, betrayals and the series’ familiar satirical take on American culture.
Rockstar has revealed several supporting characters, including bank robber Raul Bautista, aspiring music executive Dre’Quan Priest and nightclub owner Boobie Ike.
Who’s in the cast?
Rockstar has kept much of the voice cast under wraps, including the performers behind Lucia and Jason.
One familiar actor has confirmed his involvement: Stephen Root, known for his work in “Office Space,” “King of the Hill” and “Barry.” He told The Associated Press in September that he appears in the game, adding that fans had already recognized his distinctive voice in promotional footage.
Root has been identified in reports as the voice of Brian Heder, an aging drug runner operating out of the Leonida Keys. Rockstar has introduced the character but has not publicly confirmed Root’s casting in that specific role.
What makes this installment different?
Beyond the return to Vice City, one of the biggest changes is the focus on two protagonists whose relationship drives the story.
“Grand Theft Auto V” featured three playable main characters. The new installment centers on Lucia and Jason as partners navigating the criminal underworld together.
Rockstar has promoted a larger, more detailed setting that stretches beyond the city into the wider state of Leonida. The game also arrives in a vastly different technological landscape from its predecessor, with newer consoles capable of supporting more elaborate environments and character interactions.
But not every detail is known. Rockstar has offered trailers and promotional previews, while questions remain about the full range of activities, how the game’s systems will work and the future of its online multiplayer experience.
What about the music?
Music has long been part of Grand Theft Auto’s identity. It has included everything from fictional radio stations to the songs accompanying players as they cruise through the game’s cities.
“Grand Theft Auto VI” is expanding that tradition with an original score by Justice, the Grammy-winning French electronic duo of Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay.
Rockstar says the score adapts to players’ actions and experiences throughout the game, shifting with the environments and situations they encounter.
A 30-track score album is scheduled for Dec. 11, featuring collaborations with artists including Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.
The game also features in-game radio stations and a separate collection of original songs, continuing the franchise’s connection to popular music.

title: Congress agrees on civilian plane locator mandate after deadly American Airlines-Black Hawk crash
text:
Congress agrees on civilian plane locator mandate after deadly American Airlines-Black Hawk crash
Congress has agreed to require airliners and other civilian aircraft to carry systems that help pilots locate nearby aircraft. But lawmakers still have to resolve the provisions that apply to the military.
Video above: Family members who lost loved ones in D.C. plane crash hold press conference outside the Capitol
Senators Ted Cruz and Maria Cantwell announced the agreement Tuesday at a demonstration on the lawn outside the Capitol building. A group representing families of the 67 people killed when an American Airlines flight collided with an Army Black Hawk helicopter near Washington, D.C., on Jan. 29, 2025, organized the event.
“When military aircraft fly in the same airspace, they must meet the same standards as everyone else,” said Cantwell, a Democrat representing Washington state.
Cruz, a Texas Republican, said he believes Congress can pass the bill before the end of the year.
On the night of the collision, the Army helicopter flew without the key ADS-B Out system that broadcasts an aircraft’s location because of security concerns, even though it was only on a training flight.
Any aircraft flying in crowded airspace is already required to carry systems that broadcast its location but isn’t required to carry complementary ADS-B In systems that show pilots where nearby aircraft are flying.
“Pilots can't avoid what we can't see,” said Capt. Jason Ambrosi, who leads the Air Line Pilots Association union. He said Congress must require these systems on both military and civilian aircraft because the Federal Aviation Administration hasn't. “Everyone in shared airspace must be seen. Period.”
The Senate and House each passed competing aviation safety reform bills, and lawmakers have been working since the spring to craft a compromise bill addressing 50 recommendations from the National Transportation Safety Board.
Everyone aboard the American Airlines jet, flying from Wichita, Kansas, and the helicopter died when the two aircraft collided. It was the deadliest plane crash on U.S. soil since 2001, and the victims included 28 members of the figure skating community.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford assured the victims' families that safety remains the agency's top priority. The FAA has been in the spotlight since grounding all flights nationwide on Friday because of a technical problem.
The FAA has already taken some steps to prevent helicopters and planes from sharing the same airspace around Reagan airport. Air traffic controllers are now prohibited from relying solely on pilots to see and avoid other aircraft. But the victims' families and NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy have been pressing for the locator systems.

title: FAA ground stop forces organ donation team to race against the clock
text:
FAA ground stop forces organ donation team to race against the clock
A nationwide ground stop on Friday did more than leave travelers stranded. It also put the gift of life at risk.
The Federal Aviation Administration halted flights, disrupting the time-sensitive transportation of donated organs. When every second counts, hours without flights can make a big impact for patients waiting for an organ.
At LifeShare Oklahoma, staff members had to quickly change their plans, even delaying surgeries due to the nationwide flight grounding.
"At that point in time when we had the alert, we instantly started looking at the cases we had going," said Justin Johnson, chief operating officer of LifeShare Network.
That meant racing against the clock. Donated organs have a limited window to reach the patients waiting for them. With planes grounded, the team at LifeShare had to pivot.
"What we were able to do quickly was to switch and work with our families to change those OR times," Johnson said.
One Oklahoma donor was set to give two kidneys Friday, but LifeShare asked the family to delay the procedure. Both kidneys were then transported by ground instead of air.
One reached its originally intended recipient, but the other had to be diverted to a different transplant center and a different patient.
"If all flights were stopped and only ground can be done, then that changes the address of where that gift is going to be and the person it would go to," Johnson said.
LifeShare said despite the flight disruption, no donated organs from Oklahoma were lost, and two lives were saved that day.
Federal officials believe the disruptions were caused by a routine system upgrade when a router flooded the air traffic control network with data. The FAA and the contractor in charge of the maintenance are still looking into why that happened.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CNBC on Monday that future disruptions are possible if Congress doesn't approve a $50 billion funding request to modernize the system.
"If we don't make those investments, is there a guarantee that these things maybe, in varying forms, don't happen in the future? We can't make those guarantees. We’re going to make sure we keep people safe," Duffy said.

title: Speeding crash involving 2 Waymo vehicles caught on camera
text:

The crash happened at about 11 a.m. Monday at an intersection in central Phoenix.
Video from Sunland Auto Service shows two Waymo vehicles, a white sedan and a blue SUV, stopped at an intersection. A moment later, a speeding SUV comes barreling toward them through the intersection and crashes into them.
Skid marks found at the crash led to the discovery of a fourth vehicle, found upside down and severely damaged near a business.
Phoenix Police Sgt. John Buchanan said the driver of the SUV was taken to the hospital in extremely critical condition.
One person in the white Waymo sedan was taken to the hospital with injuries that aren’t considered life-threatening, while the two people in the blue Waymo did not require hospitalization.
Firefighters said a third person was taken to the hospital but their condition is unknown.
Buchanan said police do not have an estimate of how fast the SUV driver was going and police are still working to determine what led up to the crash.
Waymo employees are on the scene assisting investigators and providing them with the vehicle’s videos of the crash.
“The safety of our riders and other road users is our top priority. We are working with first responders to ensure the well-being of our riders,” a Waymo spokesperson said in a statement provided to Arizona’s Family.

title: Main Street in Unity reopens following structure fire

Chimney fire may have sparked Unity house fire, officials say
Firefighters say a quick response from crews helped save much of a home after a fire broke out Tuesday morning
A possible chimney fire may have sparked a fire that caused extensive damage to a home in Unity Tuesday morning, according to fire officials.
The Unity Fire Department and mutual aid crews responded to 245 Main Street around 6:33 a.m. for a reported structure fire.
Firefighters arriving on the scene found heavy fire and smoke in the kitchen area that had spread to the garage.
The department said crews were able to quickly knock down the fire with help from mutual aid departments, saving a large portion of the home.
Despite extensive damage to the home, all occupants escaped safely and no injuries were reported.
Fire officials believe the fire may have started in a chimney before spreading to other parts of the home.
The American Red Cross was contacted to provide resources for those affected by the fire.
Part of Main Street was closed between Depot Street and Thorndike Road (Route 220) for two hours while the crew responded. The road has since reopened.
Unity Fire Captain, Blaine Parsons reminded residents of the importance of regularly cleaning their chimneys.

title: AMHC Grants Support Recovery in Aroostook County
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) - AMHC has been awarded two federal grants to expand treatment, outreach, and recovery services across Aroostook, Hancock, and Washington counties. The awards represent a multi-year investment in addressing the opioid and substance use crisis in the state’s rural communities.
AMHC has been awarded $7.5 million in federal funding to expand substance use treatment and recovery services across rural Maine. AMHC officials say the funds will strengthen their ability to reach individuals who are often disconnected from traditional healthcare systems.
Kayla Moutinho, the Specialty Substance Use Initiatives Manager for A.M.H.C. said: “We’re gonna be able to meet more people where they’re at. So, in emergency rooms, in homeless situations, and provide them a service that they might not have been receiving before without the expectation for them to fully jump right in.”
AMHC’s CEO Christy Daggett says these grants won’t have anything to do with the state’s needle exchange programs. “This grant specifically funds nursing services to help people detect and treat conditions like HIV or hepatitis. This grant does not fund needle distribution of any kind but it does fund testing resources and treatment resources for people that might be affected by these conditions.”
Instead, the grants will focus on medication and substance use disorder treatment. “We’re going to make certain medications that treat or support substance use disorder treatment more available for people. There’s a lot of barriers that we discussed before like transportation, appointment times, housing. Teaching them what is substance use disorder treatment, what does that look like, what’s expected of me, what resources are available to them, and how can we support them getting there. Medication can be a great tool to get people where they need to or want to be in conjunction with the treatment,” added Moutinho.
Moutinho says it is sometimes difficult for those with substance use disorder to reach out for help and she has a message to give those struggling. “You matter, you’re worthy. I think a lot of people stay stuck in the mess for a really long time because they don’t think that they can change, or that they don’t matter, they don’t offer anything to this world, and that just simply isn’t true. Almost everybody I’ve worked with over the last 5 years has something great to offer the world. Whether that is in their family unit, their community, even in a rehab, or outpatient setting. What other addicts get from working with and collaborating with their fellows is beyond measure. Sometimes I believe that’s even beyond what I can offer them as a clinician. So, they do matter. They can change. I see it every day and it can be scary but there is people out there that want to help. You just have to pick up the phone or even message us and we can try our best to get them where they need to be.”
AMHC is working with other organizations to expand substance use treatment and recovery services including AR Gould and the Homeless Services of Aroostook. Anyone looking for help with substance use disorder or recovery can reach out through AMHC.org or call their referral center at 1-800-244-6431.

title: Fan ejected from Lambeau Field for spreading ashes on field after Packers game, police say
text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. (WBAY/Gray News) - Authorities in Wisconsin say a fan was removed from Lambeau Field after Sunday’s Green Bay Packers game for spreading ashes on the field.
According to the Green Bay Police Department, officers responded to a report of a person who was seen releasing what appeared to be ashes onto the field from the stands following the conclusion of Sunday’s game.
Officers confirmed the fan in question had dispersed the cremated remains of a loved one onto the field.
Police said this was a violation of Green Bay Municipal Code 24-117, Unlawful Conduct at a Public Event, and the person was ejected from the stadium.
The Green Bay Packers said that while they understand the desire of some fans to have their loved ones’ ashes spread at Lambeau Field, it is against the law and prohibited at the stadium.
“To honor a loved one’s legacy appropriately at Lambeau Field, we refer fans to the commemorative brick program. We also suggest they can coordinate tributes in other appropriate ways with their funeral home,” the team shared in a statement.
Police said Sunday’s violation could have resulted in an $890 citation, but it wasn’t immediately known if the person was officially cited.
The Packers dropped Sunday’s home game to the Minnesota Vikings 30-10.
