title: New restaurant in 18th century farmhouse is Buxton’s only sit-down dinner spot
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BUXTON — A landmark yellow farmhouse at the intersection of routes 22 and 202 has come alive again as a new restaurant.
Stephanie Keene and her husband, Ethan Owens, opened Mustard Public House in the 1790 building this fall. With no other sit-down dinner spots in the growing town of Buxton, they saw a hole to fill.
“We’ve always said there needs to be a good, family friendly, elevated comfort food, good price point restaurant in this area to serve the community,” Keene said.
The restaurant’s 145 seats have been full almost every night, all night, since it opened in late September, Keene said.
Previous owner and chef Max Brody added the kitchen and bar space to the original house in 2018 to run his restaurant, The Buxton Common, until the COVID-19 pandemic forced him to close, according to Keene. Shannon Keefe then headed farm-to-table restaurant Oak & Ember there from September 2023 to April 2025. Keene and Owens bought the building from the bank through an auction in July.
Owner of Hearts & Horses Riding Center in Buxton, Keene was a “more of a crockpot sally” before the opening. Now, she chops carrots and celery for soups and salads, boils apples for warm bourbon apple crisp, and bakes garlic bread, learning from the award-winning chefs she hired to launch the business. Nearly all of the food is homemade, and many ingredients are sourced from local farms.
The most popular menu items, Keene said, are the fried chicken sandwich with hand-cut fries ($18) and the house steak tips ($32), representing two ends of the main dishes’ price range. The restaurant has a meat smoker and a wood fire pizza oven, the latter of which the cooks have yet to start using.
Specials rotate daily, including for beverages. The most sought-after drink is the lumberjack old fashioned ($12), and head bartender Wendy Bunny makes new cocktail specials each night and signature flights on Mondays, most recently a candy flight with a Twix and Almond Joy candy bars on top.
The chefs are Matt Norton, formerly of now-shuttered Noble Barbecue in Portland; Josh Black, who Keene said won awards for his sauces, chili and baked beans in Wyoming before coming to Maine via the Appalachian Trail; and a third Keene said only goes by “Chef Chino,” who previously worked at MK Kitchen in Gorham.
On the walls of the cozy dining rooms are framed photographs Owens found at the Buxton-Hollis Historical Society that chronicle the town’s past, including a photo of Keene’s great great uncle bringing kids to Hollis High School in a horse-drawn sleigh.
Keene said Mustard Public House’s popularity was overwhelming in the first few weeks, but that the staff have entered a flow she hopes will keep them successful. The online show Chowdown Roadshow, which documents the stories of independent restaurants across the U.S., plans to feature the business in September 2027.
The restaurant is open Thursday through Monday from 4 p.m. to 10 p.m., but Keene said it may close earlier in the evening come winter.

Just one day after the Atlantic Asphalt tanker ship collided with an American Heritage cruise ship in New Orleans, four cruise ship crew members filed a lawsuit seeking compensation for physical injuries and emotional trauma.
According to the lawsuit, crew members went overboard after the collision on the Mississippi River, "not knowing if they were going to live or die."
The lawsuit names the vessel's management and operating companies, Thome Ship Management PTE LTD, operated out of Singapore, and Nave Shipping S.A., operated out of Liberia.

title: FAA halts installation of routers that led to nationwide ground stop
text:
FAA halts installation of routers that led to nationwide ground stop
The Federal Aviation Administration announced on Tuesday that it was pausing the installation of the routers that were linked to last week’s national ground stop, and turned off any Juniper routers that were already installed.
The decision was made after technicians linked Friday’s disruption of key air traffic control systems to one of these routers that had just been installed in El Dorado, Arkansas.
For now, the FAA is relying on older Cisco routers that have been in place for 25 years to continue operating the network while they investigate the cause of Friday’s problems at 17 of the nation’s 22 regional air traffic control centers.
The routers that malfunctioned last week are being tested in a lab at the headquarters of the company that installed them, named L3Harris.
The decision comes amid intense scrutiny of the causes of the malfunction. Democrats in the Senate on Tuesday called for pausing the replacement of thousands of routers across the nation’s air traffic control system. They also demanded that the Trump administration provide clear answers about what went wrong.
“Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed. FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues,” said the letter sent to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
President Donald Trump has blamed old technology and Democrats for the nationwide grounding of all planes and upheaval at the nation’s airports. But the FAA has been struggling to modernize the air traffic control system for decades — going back well before the first Trump administration.
The system became overloaded when a federal contractor that maintains the FAA’s telecommunications network was replacing outdated copper wires with fiber optic lines across the nation.
The closure of U.S. airspace was needed, Duffy said, after a new router that L3Harris installed in El Dorado, Arkansas, resulted in a cascade of intermittent communications and radar signals at 17 of the 22 regional air traffic control centers. The centers direct planes cruising at high altitudes.
The Federal Aviation Administration said that “excessive data” was flooding the system “at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds.” That deluge created instability with “aircraft communications and radar feeds” when those connection attempts overwhelmed the 25-year-old routers throughout the network, the agency said.
Democrats on the Senate Commerce Committee said they believe that only 400 out of more than 3,600 routers have been installed. Work on installing the new devices should be stopped until “the root cause of the failure has been identified,” the letter stated.
Upgrading the nation’s air transportation system is an effort that Congress has dedicated significant sums to in recent years. The problems with aging equipment at the FAA date back decades and past efforts to modernize the system have come up short.
Duffy has pushed Congress for billions more dollars to upgrade a system he said had been neglected for decades, saying on Friday that $50 billion is needed.
The Trump administration on Tuesday sent a letter to key lawmakers updating its request for $50.1 billion to modernize the system and make other improvements at airports.
The request calls for $10.1 billion for updating the nation’s air traffic control system. Similar amounts would go toward boosting airport infrastructure, replacing or refurbishing terminals at high-impact hubs, constructing five new traffic control centers and improving or replacing up to 140 FAA-owned air traffic control towers.
“Congressional approval of these funds will equip the FAA to deliver to the American people a brand-new air traffic control system that is safer, smarter, faster, and more efficient,” states the letter, which was obtained by The Associated Press.
Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to modernize much of the key infrastructure that more than 45,000 flights a day rely on to reach their destinations safely. The funds were earmarked for replacing outdated technologies such as copper wires, floppy discs and radars built in the 1980s, but much of that money will also go toward runway upgrades and other construction projects.

With the London-born actor officially named as the next James Bond, we wanted to revisit his connection to Maine.

Robert Pattinson starred alongside Willem Dafoe in the 2019 psychological horror film “The Lighthouse,” which takes place on a fictional island off the coast of Maine in the 1890s.
Directed by Robert Eggers, the black-and-white film follows Pattinson’s character, Ephraim Winslow, a young lighthouse keeper assigned to work alongside Dafoe’s character, Thomas Wake, for four weeks.
As the two men struggle with isolation, harsh weather and growing tensions, their mental states begin to deteriorate, leading to increasingly disturbing events.
Although the story is set in Maine and draws inspiration from our state’s maritime history, coastal scenery, and regional dialects, filming took place in Nova Scotia, Canada, where crews constructed a lighthouse specifically for the production.
Amazon MGM Studios announced Monday, Nov. 16, that Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond, succeeding Daniel Craig in the role.
Pattinson will star in the franchise’s next film, directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Steven Knight, with a release date yet to be officially announced.
And there you have it! Maine has an unexpected connection to the newly announced James Bond through one of Pattinson’s most distinctive film roles.

title: The Latest: Trump arrives in Philippines to kick off three-day Asia trip
text:
President Donald Trumparrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he was scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.
Manila, the Philippine capital, is Trump’s first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea’s leader Kim Jong Un.
Here’s the latest:
Classified network at NSA offline, defense official says
A network the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what one U.S. official described as “routine maintenance.”
A defense official said Tuesday that the problem affected NSANet, a classified internal network. A U.S. official said that the NSA “experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance” and that though “while some internal systems were affected, mission/critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues.” Another person familiar with the matter said the issue occurred during routine patching.
The three individuals spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss non-public information.
The NSA episode is the latest in a series of cyber-related disruptions to critical government and private sector functions, including one Friday that resulted in a ground stop of air traffic in the United States, and a technical issue that affected the banking industry on Monday.
FAA halts installation of routers that led to ground stop
The Federal Aviation Administration has paused the installation of the routers that were linked to last week’s national ground stop, and turned off any Juniper routers that were already installed.
The decision was made after technicians linked Friday’s disruption of key air traffic control systems to one of these routers that had just been installed in El Dorado, Arkansas.
For now, the FAA is relying on older Cisco routers that have been in place for 25 years to continue operating the network while they investigate the cause of Friday’s problems at 17 of the nation’s 22 regional air traffic control centers.
The routers that malfunctioned last week are being tested in a lab at the headquarters of the company that installed them named L3Harris.
Republican in Alaska’s governor’s race praises Democrat who withdrew to help his fellow Democrat
The top-finishing Republican in Alaska’s gubernatorial race praised as a statesman the Democrat who dropped out of the race to support a fellow Democrat.
Republican Bernadette Wilson, endorsed by President Donald Trump, had urged the other two Republicans in the race to withdraw after the open primary to create a clearer lane for her against Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins in the Nov. 3 ranked vote general election, which Kreiss-Tomkins won.
The two Republicans, a former mayor and a former state attorney general, stayed in the race, highlighting differences in experience and priorities with the business owner Wilson. They urged voters to rank the GOP candidates, calling that an important strategy.
After advancing from the August primary, Democrat Tom Begich withdrew and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins. His campaign said it was the best way to bring Democratic donors and voters together.
Wilson said Begich’s decision showed a willingness “to put pride and ego aside.”
Newsom visits Democratic leader Jeffries on Capitol Hill
Jeffries said they talked about disaster assistance and also priorities for health care and lowering the high costs of living.
“We’re committed to making sure that we deliver disaster relief to the people of Altadena and the Pacific Palisades,” he said, calling it unacceptable that those communities have gone without aid nearly two years after the devastating wildfires.
He said he also thanked Gov. Gavin Newsom for his leadership around the state’s response to nationwide Republican redistricting efforts.
Jeffries demands briefings for Congress about outages, ground stop
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said he spoke to Duffy on Sunday but there are still more questions and answers about the airline disruptions.
Taken together with other recent outages, he said it’s unclear if it’s infrastructure related or whether there’s “malignant activity.”
He mentioned the Microsoft email outage, the FAA ground stops and reports of problems at the NSA.
“I think it’s time for the administration to come up to the Hill and explain themselves,” he said, “so we can be informed about the steps that need to be taken.”
He panned the administration’s request for $50 billion to modernize the air traffic control system as Congress assesses the situation.
Duffy says no more ‘piecemeal’ on aviation investments
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is pitching to lawmakers the Trump administration’s request for $50 billion to fully modernize the nation’s air traffic control system.
Duffy said there has been a historic underinvestment in aviation. And now lawmakers have a choice.
“They have to make a decision. What do they want to do? Everything? Or do they want to give me some piecemeal?” Duffy said. “ I hope they don’t piecemeal it. There’s been too much piecemeal happening over the course over 20 or 30 years. I hope we get the full investment.”
Duffy’s comments came as he prepared to meet with GOP senators Tuesday on Capitol Hill. Earlier in the day, the administration made a formal request for the funding and detailed where it hopes to invest the money. The beefed-up request comes after the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years.
Cao’s nomination hearing for Navy secretary wraps up following clash over Navy suicide attempts
The Senate committee hearing to consider Acting Navy Sec. Hung Cao for the permanent job wrapped up after 2.5 hours that focused largely on the Iran war’s costs and conditions aboard Navy ships supporting the war.
The hearing ended with a clash between Cao and Democratic New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand over sailors’ suicide attempts aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, which supported the war during a record-breaking deployment.
Gillibrand targeted Cao’s assertions that reports of mental health concerns were dishonest. She also dismissed Cao’s use of the term “suicide mitigations” to describe suicide attempts.
Cao said a sailor who jumped off the Lincoln was not attempting suicide because he later admitted as much and was wearing a life preserver. Gillibrand pushed back: “What was he trying to do, swim to Guam?”
Trump administration nominates officer to top Army post
The Trump administration has nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to Chief of Staff of the Army — the top uniformed post in the service — after he stepped into the job for months following the unexplained firing of Gen. Randy George in April.
Adam Telle, the man currently serving as the acting Secretary of the Army following the departure of Dan Driscoll from the top civilian post in August, said that LaNeve “is the right leader at the right time to modernize the Army and ensure our Soldiers are prepared to dominate on any battlefield” in a post to social media.
LaNeve has seen a meteoric rise through the ranks since the start of the Trump administration. LaNeve was promoted to be Hegseth’s top military aide shortly after he arrived at the Pentagon and was suddenly nominated him to be the Army’s vice chief of staff last October even though there was an officer in the job at the time.
US House Oversight chairman James Comer to run for Kentucky governor
The Kentucky Republican congressman announced he’s running for Kentucky governor in 2027.
Comer said in an online town hall Monday night that serving Kentucky “is a calling for me.”
“With your support, we can restore hope and create growth all across Kentucky,” Comer said.
As head of the House Oversight Committee, he’s conducted extensive investigations of former President Joe Biden and his family as well as the Trump administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files.
Comer has served as Kentucky’s agriculture secretary and was also a state lawmaker.
Two Democrats have announced their campaigns for governor: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and Rocky Adkins, a former top adviser to Gov. Andy Beshear.
Beshear, who’s been mentioned as a potential presidential candidate, will leave office next year after serving two terms.
Mullin defends use of government plane to go to college football game after ground stop
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday defended his use of a government plane to fly to a college football game shortly after a nationwide ground stop which caused massive travel disruptions and left people stranded across the country.
Mullin, speaking on CNBC, acknowledged earlier reporting in the New York Post that he flew to the LSU-Texas college football game a day after all planes were grounded.
Mullin answered in the affirmative when asked whether he’s required to fly on government planes and that he paid for the trip personally.
“We would have never went if the airways weren’t completely open,” he said on CNBC. “They’d been completely open for 21 hours.”
He added: “We would have never taken airspace if airspace wasn’t open. And we still gotta live our lives at the same time.”
Hours before his flight, Mullin was at the White House alongside Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy giving updates on the ground stop.
The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from U.S. airports.
Cao confirms US Navy blockade of Iran costs about $32 million a day
Cao confirmed the figure during his Senate confirmation hearing Tuesday for the position of Navy secretary. He was being questioned by Democratic Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who cited reports on the blockade’s costs.
“That means the American taxpayers are spending about $1 billion a month just on this blockade,” Warren stated.
Navy secretary nominee dismisses lawmakers’ questions on food shortages on destroyers
Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly asked Cao about the current conditions on the various destroyers that are deployed around the world, including reports of diminishing rations that have caused some sailors to lose an alarming amount of weight.
Cao responded, “Well, senator, it’s just not what they want. It’s like my kids opening up the refrigerator door and saying there’s nothing to eat in here.”
“Mr. Secretary, somebody doesn’t lose 45 pounds just because they don’t like the options. I don’t think that’s a fair assessment,” Kelly said.
Cao says Navy still hasn’t assessed damage to US base in Bahrain hit by Iranian strikes
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao told Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren that he doesn’t know the cost of the damage to a U.S. Navy base in Bahrain that was struck by an Iranian attack. Cao previously told The Epoch Times that Iranian strikes “blew the hell out of” the installation.
Cao told Warren the Navy hasn’t been able to conduct a full damage assessment because it’s in a “nonpermissive area for us to go.” He did not confirm a Wall Street Journal report that estimated the cost to be $400 million. But Cao said he would find out the costs.
Warren noted that the base is home to U.S. Naval Forces Central Command and the 5th Fleet.
Republican senator rejects Trump’s plan to return to steam catapults on aircraft carriers
The Republican chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee has rejected President Trump’s plan to return to the use of steam-powered catapults to launch jets off aircraft carriers.
“Returning to steam is a nonstarter, and everybody needs to understand that,” said Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi. Wicker was speaking to Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao during his nomination hearing to become Navy secretary.
Democrats have also expressed an aversion to returning to steam.
In August, Trump ordered the U.S. Navy to remove the advanced electromagnetic system used to launch fighter jets from its newest type of aircraft carrier and return to older steam catapults he has long said he prefers.
Trump’s mandate would likely cost billions of dollars and revert the Navy’s most advanced ships to a system that takes more sailors to operate and is more difficult to maintain.
Navy secretary nominee says Iran war is ‘stressing’ naval resources but says it’s a worthy cause
After back-to-back questions about the impact of the ongoing war, Cao acknowledged the extent that Washington’s targeting of Tehran has had on naval resources.
“But again, I’ve grown up where I lost a country where I didn’t have a flag to stand under,” he responded to a question from Democratic Sen. Mazie Hirono. “And I’m telling you right now that I will fight every single day to keep that from happening to my children or my grandchildren.”
Cao notes boost in production of cruise missiles and use of expired munitions
He says there’s been a boost in production of Tomahawk cruise missiles and other weapons, addressing a concern that the Iran war has drawn down the nation’s stockpiles of key munitions.
“When I was in uniform, we only produced 125 tomahawks a year. Right now we’re well above 60 every month,” Cao said.
Cao said efforts are also underway to boost the production of interceptors that are used by Navy ships to shoot down incoming missiles.
Cao also said the Navy is using expired munitions, comparing the practice to adding water to expired bread and putting it in the microwave. He didn’t say what kind of munitions those were.
“For some of these munitions, we recoded them. And so we’re able to shoot off the expired munitions,” Cao said.
Democratic senator says Navy nominee is ‘failing these sailors’ over long deployments
Sen. Richard Blumenthal grilled Cao on the concerns that lawmakers have raised over sailors’ mental health, following reports of crew stress and supply shortages on the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier. The warship endured a record-breaking deployment supporting the Iran war before returning to its homeport of San Diego in October.
“Your solution seems to be to continue just asking these sailors and their families for more without giving them or us the truth about what the nature and length of their deployment is going to be,” the Connecticut lawmaker said.
“I don’t control the deployment lengths,” Cao said. “You see as eight suicide attempts, I see it, eight suicide mitigations.”
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to appear before Congress next month
Key House lawmakers say Huang and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter have voluntarily agreed to appear for transcribed interviews.
Huang will appear before the committees Dec. 1, and Teter will appear Dec. 2.
“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” said a statement from the chairmen of three House committees with oversight over China and intelligence issues.
“The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous PRC actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal,” the lawmakers said.
Cao says Navy didn’t tell Congress about sub mishap to protect sailors’ identities
As he vies to become Navy secretary, Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao faced pointed questions from a Democratic senator about why the Navy failed to inform Congress that it fired the entire leadership team of a submarine after an underwater collision.
Rhode Island Sen. Jack Reed, the ranking member on the Senate Armed Services Committee, noted that lawmakers received no notice of what happened despite a requirement for accountability from Congress.
“We need to have details, promptly,” Reed said. “And you have to do that. And you didn’t do it.”
Cao said there was a near mishap involving the USS South Dakota submarine and the Navy is still investigating what happened. He said the sub’s leadership did not live up to their ethos of honor, courage and commitment but declined to provide further information. However, Cao said the Navy didn’t release details to protect the sailors’ identities. He said he would provide more information to the senator.
Trump administration details its $50 billion request for aviation system improvements
The Trump administration has formally updated its request to lawmakers for $50.1 billion to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system and to make other improvements at airports.
A letter to key lawmakers dated Tuesday says that less than 24 hours after the administration’s request of $30.1 billion, “the urgent need for this investment became undeniable.” That’s when outdated equipment disrupted aircraft communications and radar feeds, forcing the Federal Aviation Administration to initiate a nationwide ground stop.
The request to lawmakers calls for $10.1 billion for updating the nation’s air traffic control system. Another $10 billion would go to boosting airport infrastructure.
Meanwhile, $10 billion would go to replace or refurbish terminals at high-impact hubs. Another $10 billion would go to construct five new traffic control centers and $10 billion would go to improving or replacing up to 140 FAA-owned air traffic control towers.
Trump’s pick to lead the Navy focuses on shipbuilding in his opening statements
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao told senators at his confirmation hearing Tuesday that he’ll focus on revitalizing shipbuilding in an effort to expand the nation’s fleet of warships.
But Cao avoided potentially thorny topics that are likely to come up before the Senate Armed Services Committee. Those include the Iran war, the recent firings of Navy admirals and the waiver Cao will need from Congress to become Navy secretary because he left active duty less than seven years ago.
Cao also spoke of his biography, which includes fleeing Vietnam with his family right before the fall of Saigon in the 1970s. He also focused on his 25 years of service in the Navy.
“I spent my entire adult life serving in the United States Navy special operations community with multiple combat deployments to Iraq, Afghanistan and Somalia,” Cao said.
Bipartisan concerns arise over forces being ‘stretched thin’ during Navy secretary hearing
Despite deep divisions over the Iran war, the Republican and Democratic leaders of the Senate Armed Services Committee voiced a unified concern over the impact the ongoing military operation and internal issues at the Department of Defense have had on the U.S. Navy.
“Our sailors and Marines are our greatest asset, but they cannot sustain an increasingly demanding operational tempo without adequate support,” GOP Sen. Roger Wicker, the committee chair, said during his opening statement.
His Democratic counterpart, Sen. Jack Reed, echoed his worry, saying that “disruption” from high-ranking officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, “sends the wrong signal to our sailors and Marines.”
Confirmation hearing for Trump’s nominee to lead the US Navy gets underway
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, a Trump loyalist and combat veteran, appeared Tuesday before the Senate Armed Services Committee as he seeks the permanent top civilian job during a particularly volatile time in Washington. It’s the first step in a nomination process that could turn into a fierce debate over the Iran war, military transparency and the well-being of American sailors.
Cao also faces the extra hurdle of needing a waiver from Congress, because he left active-duty service less than seven years ago.
ASEAN-US dinner menu features American surf and turf
The main course was a pairing of U.S. beef tenderloin and lobster tail, served with a truffle potato puree, glazed baby carrots, oyster mushrooms and a wine sauce, according to details shared by the White House.
Courses before the main included ratatouille, goose liver mousse and burrata cheese salad with heirloom tomatoes, walnuts, balsamic glaze and olive oil.
Chocolate-covered cake with roasted almonds and salted caramel ice cream was served for dessert.

title: How 911 dispatchers are using AI to assist callers
text:
O’FALLON, Mo. (InvestigateTV) — Artificial intelligence is on the frontlines of fighting crime and being used in many 911 dispatch centers around the country.
The police dispatch in O’Fallon is using artificial intelligence-based technology to assist dispatchers who answer 911 calls. Dispatchers there said a person will always answer the call.
Based on the call, the technology displays a specific list of questions for the dispatcher to ask. It also listens in, transcribes the call in real time and suggests information the dispatcher might have missed.
Paul Jokerst, emergency communications administrator for O’Fallon Police, said the technology is there to assist dispatchers.
“It is clearly here to assist. It’s just to assist them,” Jokerst said.
He said the technology is not intended to replace dispatchers.
“It’s not here to replace anybody. It’s not here to take a job away or hamper somebody’s job,” Jokerst said.
O’Fallon police dispatcher Mike Conte said he supports the use of AI.
Conte said the technology helps when dispatchers are trying to pick out information they cannot understand from a caller.
“It’s very helpful when we’re trying to pick out pieces of information that we can’t understand the caller,” Conte said.
He said he supports the technology as long as he is also on the line.
“You will always talk to a human. One of us is always here. And we’re always ready to answer your call,” Conte said.
The use of AI in 911 is expanding rapidly.
In Fairfax, Virginia, AI translates calls into more than 170 languages instantly.
In New Orleans, AI automatically answers calls about accidents officials already know about. The system will inform the caller about the incident and if they are involved in any way the person can stay on line to talk to a dispatcher.
Experts say AI would not replace dispatchers at the moment because humans are better at compassion, processing emotion and keeping people calm.
AI in law enforcement continues to evolve.

title: A painting was buried in a New York apartment closet. It could sell for up to $5 million
text:
A long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe painting was buried in a New York apartment closet. It just sold for $4.8 million
A long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe painting that had been buried in the closet of a Manhattan apartment for decades sold at auction Tuesday for $4.8 million.
The 1930 landscape painting “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” is likely the first in a series of three works depicting Lobo Peak in northern New Mexico, according to Christie’s auction house. Its existence was known from a 1931 photograph, but its whereabouts had been kept secret until recently.
A Manhattan woman in her 90s nonchalantly told her niece one day in 2022, “Oh, by the way, there’s a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet.” Her family believes she received the painting as a graduation gift from her mother, who had purchased it in 1963 from a New York gallery for $3,800.
The woman, who died recently, displayed it in her East Village apartment for many years until the mid-’80s when she noticed a guest looking at it a little too closely. From then on, she kept it in her closet, safely hidden behind coats and boxes.
When the family finally unboxed it this year, they discovered it has all the hallmarks of O’Keeffe’s work, including her signature marking on the back: a star with her initials scrawled in the middle.
The 10-x-24-inch (25.4-x-61-centimeter) oil painting is among O’Keeffe's early love letters to New Mexico, where she settled and lived for decades. The identity of the winning bidder was not disclosed; it sold for $4,878,000.
Known as the “mother of American modernism,” O’Keeffe maintained a home and studio in Abiquiu and a nearby summer residence tucked between the red-rock cliffs of Ghost Ranch. She died in 1986 at age 98 and is best known for her paintings of flowers and American Southwest landscapes.
The second piece in the “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico” collection is at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, and the other, for many years, was in the collection of the Rockefeller family.

title: Highly classified US national security communications network goes down, reports say
text:
Highly classified US national security communications network goes down, reports say
At this point, there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources say
Highly classified US national security communications network goes down, reports say
At this point, there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources say
The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter.
The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said.
Related video above — JUST A TEST: FEMA conducting nationwide Emergency Alert System test on Tuesday
As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said.
CNN has asked the National Security Agency for comment.
"We see no evidence that this was a cyberattack," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said Tuesday on Newsmax. "There is no crisis, or anything like that, for Americans to be worried about."
A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One.
Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president, who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country.
All flights nationwide were grounded for hours on Friday after a massive systems failure, leading to thousands of flights being delayed or canceled. The Federal Aviation Administration traced the problem to a single router in Arkansas.
Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Teams meetings.
And in recent weeks, banks and other services have experienced outages; on Monday, thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts.
There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security.
The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence-sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official.
Tuesday’s outage was not the first time the NSA’s internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson said at the time.
This story has been updated with additional information.

title: Kennebunk animal shelter seeks homes for chinchillas rescued from Ohio breeder
text:
Michael, Dwight and a few other characters from “The Office” were among hundreds of chinchillas rescued from a large-scale breeding facility in Ohio. Now, they’re in Kennebunk — and could go home with you.
The Animal Welfare Society announced Tuesday that it had taken in 10 of the 951 chinchillas, which are now up for adoption. Four have already found their forever homes, but Michael, Dwight, Meredith, Jim, Holly and Erin are still searching.
According to a news release from the society, the hundreds of chinchillas were rescued over the past few weeks by the Humane World for Animals. The organization carried out the operation at the request of the Department of Justice after years of documented violations of the Animal Welfare Act by R & R Chinchilla in Jenera, Ohio.
Veterinary staff found chinchillas with matted fur, missing limbs and an assortment of other injuries, according to the Humane World for Animals. The breeding facility has been shut down.
According to Bernadette Juarez, a deputy administrator from the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, inspectors documented animals with untreated medical conditions, “excessive fecal accumulation” and more.
“USDA has a responsibility to ensure that licensed facilities meet the standards required under the Animal Welfare Act, and the conditions identified at this facility reflected a prolonged failure to provide basic animal care,” said Juarez.
Humane World for Animals worked with shelters across the country to coordinate finding homes for the nearly 1,000 chinchillas.
AWS Executive Director Heidi Marston said the organization was grateful to be able to send a small team to Ohio on Nov. 2 to assist with initial care after the rescue before welcoming some of the animals to the shelter when the team came back on Nov. 3.
“When nearly a thousand animals need help, it takes organizations and communities working
together to give them a fresh start,” Marston said. “Every adoption opens the door for another animal in need, and with the support of our community, we hope to continue being part of this incredible rescue effort.”
Assisting with animal care after rescue operations like this is something the society tries its best to do whenever it’s able, said Marston. She said she believes the work AWS has been doing has helped to build relationships with other animal welfare groups, leading to more opportunities for the organization to help in similar situations.
Marston also said that many of the chinchillas were frightened when they arrived, but have warmed to the shelter with time.
“Since they’ve been with us, we’ve definitely seen them come out of their shell more,” said Marston. “It’s been super cute to see them enjoying their little dust baths and see their personalities come out.”
The chinchillas were named after characters from “The Office” due to their tendency to jump, Marston said. Staff at AWS made jokes about their “parkour” skills, referencing a famous scene in the show.
Chinchillas require specialized care, including spacious habitats and regular dust baths, the AWS noted, and they can live 15 years or more. The shelter encouraged prospective new owners to learn about chinchillas’ unique needs before considering adoption.
The society said it hopes to welcome additional chinchillas as needed, depending on community interest and support.

title: Standish, Maine, Man Was The Most Accomplished Jeopardy! Champion in State History
text:
Standish, Maine, Man Was The Most Accomplished Jeopardy! Champion in State History
For so many people across Maine, watching the game show Jeopardy! is an evening tradition.
First hosted by Alex Trebek and today's version hosted by former superchampion Ken Jennings, the modern-day evening edition of Jeopardy! was not the first iteration of the show.
Launched in 1964, there was a daytime version of Jeopardy!, hosted by Art Fleming. The original daytime Jeopardy! was filmed in New York City instead of Hollywood, which allowed for more contestants from the east coast to participate.
Including the greatest Jeopardy! champion in Maine history.
Burns Cameron of Standish, Maine, Remains Greatest Jeopardy! Champion in Maine History
First appearing on Jeopady! in December of 1965, Burns Cameron of Standish, Maine, still remains the greatest Jeopardy! champion in the history of the state.
Cameron dominated the Jeopardy! stage for five consecutive games, which was the maximum win-streak allowed for several decades.
Cameron amassed more than $7,000 in winnings which would be the modern-day equivalent of over $60,000. He accomplished that feat at just 27-years-old.
Burns Cameron went on to dominate the Tournament of Champions as well, becoming the first-ever male contestant to win the competition while adding another $4,000 to his total.
Cameron made one more Jeopardy! appearance, 25 years after his initial run, during a 1990 Super Jeopardy! tournament.
There Have Been Other Recent Jeopardy! Champions From Maine
Over the last decade, there have more Jeopardy! champions from Maine than any other stretch in the show's fabled history.
Jason Singer and Susan McMillan, a husband-and-wife from Portland, Maine, both became Jeopardy! champions in separate years. McMillan in 2021 and Singer in 2025.
In 2019, a librarian from Augusta, Maine, named Jessica Garsed won three consecutive games of Jeopardy!
In 2020, Dennis Coffey of Old Orchard Beach, Maine, won three games on Jeopardy! to match Jessica Garsed's streak.
The most recent Jeopardy! champion from Maine was Emily Burnham. who won a game in September of this year.

title: Trump arrives in Philippines to kick off Asia trip with economic deals and talks with allies
text:
Trump arrives in Philippines to kick off Asia trip with economic deals and talks with allies
President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he met with regional partners, sought to formalize a trade deal and get a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.
Manila, the Philippine capital, is Trump's first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un.
The visit marks Trump's first travel abroad since his party suffered deep losses in midterm elections. The White House and stock market alike have been rattled by the departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved.
But Trump could not escape all the controversies still swirling in the U.S. Reporters asked him about the recent service outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration and online banking with JPMorgan Chase. The president played down the problems that caused mass flight cancellations and disrupted workdays.
“It’s life,” Trump said. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”
The president was also asked about a CNN report that Iran was putting together plans to attack Washington with a dirty bomb or chemical weapons.
“Well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before,” Trump said, adding, “I hope it’s not. But we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy.”
Trump to be feted at the annual ASEAN summit
Trump's first hours in the Philippines included all the reassuring optics from Washington’s oldest treaty ally in Asia, such as a cocktail reception and dinner with other world leaders, an intermission from some of the thorniest issues at home. He's being feted Tuesday night at a gala as the “guest of honor” at the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
The ASEAN leaders have been working on a non-aggression pact with China in the contested waters of the South China Sea, a key global trade route. Confrontations have escalated in recent years, particularly between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals.
After landing in Manila, Trump met with the leaders of the Quad nations, comprising the U.S., Australia, India, and Japan, that have aimed to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific, for the first time since he returned to the White House last year.
“We’re all friends," Trump said. "It’s a lot easier that way.”
The president announced that the Quad would conduct an exercise featuring maritime patrol aircraft and launch an accelerator to speed the development of artificial intelligence.
Trump signed a trade statement with Thailand, the type of agreement he has relished striking since launching a trade war last year buttressed by steep tariff threats. The president said that he was looking forward “to finalizing the details of our formal agreement in the coming weeks.”
The joint statement included details that were posted more than a year ago by the U.S. government. Thailand would remove tariffs on most American goods, as well as barriers for importing American autos, food products and pharmaceutical drugs. Trump said Tuesday that Thailand would buy $2.6 billion in U.S. agricultural products.
Before the gala dinner Tuesday night, Trump will participate in what's billed as a “special summit” with the ASEAN leaders, where they are expected to discuss efforts to deepen trade and security ties as well as the region’s longstanding conflicts, including yearslong violence in Myanmar and escalating disputes in the South China Sea, which Beijing claims virtually in its entirety.
Washington rejects China’s expansive claim in the waterway, and has repeatedly stated that it’s obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces come under an armed attack.
Anti-Trump protesters are gathered in Manila
About 1,500 left-wing protesters held a noisy rally in a downtown Manila square ahead of Trump’s arrival, calling on Philippine leaders not to take their foreign policy cues from the U.S.
They waved red flags and held up a large streamer that read, “Resist U.S. war and plunder!” They planned to burn an effigy of Trump. Riot police with shields and wooden truncheons stood nearby.
“The Philippine government should not deal with such a loser so our call to the Marcos administration is to stop being a puppet of Donald Trump and to uphold an independent foreign policy for the Philippines,” protest leader Teddy Casiño told The Associated Press at the Liwasang Bonifacio square, referring to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Nearly 23,000 police personnel and other law enforcers, including SWAT teams, were deployed to secure the ASEAN summit.
Planned meetings with the Philippine president — and possibly an old friend
On Wednesday, Trump is set to receive a red-carpet welcome and full military honors from Marcos Jr., followed by a state banquet as part of his visit to the Malacanang presidential palace. Trump and Marcos are expected to affirm their commitment to their countries' longstanding treaty alliance.
Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion in Malacanang with an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she’s well enough and gets her doctors’ nod.
Now 97 and using a wheelchair, the former jet set Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a strongman leader, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 “People Power” public uprising.
But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: “How’s Imelda?” Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press.
“Personal connections are very important to him,” Romualdez said.
When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. “President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, ‘please say hello to your mother,’” according to Romualdez.
Trump is also expected to announce a series of commercial deals and investments in the aviation, defense, energy, and technology sectors, before heading to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
___
Boak reported from Shenzhen, China.

title: AIO to distribute Thanksgiving meals to 600 households in Knox County
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine (WABI) - With Thanksgiving on the horizon, AIO Food & Energy Assistance in Rockland will be a recipient of roughly 200 turkeys from Penquis’s yearly turkey drive.
“This is an amazing time of year where so many different partners, so many different community members come together, and they help us prepare for a massive Thanksgiving distribution on Sunday,” said Alan Kearl with AIO Food & Energy Assistance.
AIO says it has seen an uptick in the number of people relying on pantries. The food drive will help to get local organizations and community members involved in helping families put Thanksgiving meals on the table
“We’ve seen an increase of members coming to the food pantry, we’ve seen a pretty significant increase. Over the past two weeks, we know that this is even more needed than in years past,” said AIO’s new executive director Nicole Chaplin.
With the help of local donations, AIO will help pack Thanksgiving meal packages this weekend for about 600 households. Meal packages include essentials such as dressing and gravy, and a choice of either turkey, turkey pot pie or a vegetarian offering.
A distribution event will be taking place this Sunday at AIO’s new location on 5 Payne Ave in Rockland, bringing in a new era of growth for the pantry
“People will actually be able to drive through the building in one way, out the other, pick up their box, and then we’ll be able to go on their way,” said Chaplin.
For AIO, the distribution is about more than a holiday meal.
“Being able to reach 600 families at this time of the year, or really any point in the year, but this time of year in particular, is part of why we’re here,” said Chaplin.
“For events like this, we have even more volunteers throughout the community that come and support us. This wouldn’t be possible without them either.”
The distribution event will be taking place this Sunday, Nov. 22, from 1:30 to 5:30 p.m. at 5 Payne Avenue off of Route 1.
You can donate to Penquis’s yearly turkey drive during our Turkey Telethon this Thursday, Nov. 19, from 4 to 6:30 p.m.

title: James N. Stevens
text:
James Nathaniel Stevens, longtime resident and native of Boothbay region, died Nov/ 10, 2026 in Seattle, Washington.
Nathaniel, son of James P. and Evelyn (Thurston) Stevens, was born in Boothbay Harbor on Oct. 24, 1944. Home in those days was in East Boothbay, and baby "Natty" became the newest member of the lively and growing Stevens "tribe" on Barlow's Hill. Eventually, the number reached seven siblings.
During his early years, Nat attended the East Boothbay Grammar School, walking each morning down through the village with his brothers and sisters and the family dog "Butch."
In 1955 the family moved to a farm on the River Road in Boothbay. For the next several years, Nat and his brother Jake spent a good deal of their spare time in the barn feeding, watering and milking cows, raising pigs and often chasing sheep.
Nat finished his grade school years at the Boothbay Center School then entered Boothbay Region High School, graduating with the class of 1963.
After high school Nat attended New England College in Hennicker, New Hampshire, majoring in mathematics. He graduated in 1967. During semester breaks and summer vacations, Nat worked with his father, uncles and brothers at Goudy & Stevens Shipyard.
At the height of the Vietnam Conflict, Nat was drafted into the Army. He was fortunate to be assigned stateside for his tour of duty, having been selected to serve as a specialist in finance and accounting. He was posted in Kentucky, Michigan and finally Denver, Colorado.
After his military stint, Nat decided to go back to school and enrolled in a four-year program in engineering at University of Maine in Orono.
It was during these years that he met the love of his life, Barbara Speirs, of Bangor, Maine.
Barbara and Nat became a unique and devoted couple, sharing their love of studying, gardening, camping, traveling and even working together. Nat built houses on spec., while Barbara handled all the finances and book work for the projects.
Eventually, Nat and Barbara moved to Seattle, where they lived for several years. Sadly, on Thanksgiving morning 2008, Barbara died suddenly, leaving Nat bereaved and in his words "like a rudderless boat." It is safe to say that Nat's happiest and most productive years were those spent with his beloved Barbara.
During the years following Barbara's death, Nat traveled many times back and forth from Seattle to Maine, but never found a place to settle permanently. While in Maine, Nat enjoyed visiting with old friends and his sisters and never failed to make the trip to Bangor to call on Barbara's Mother and two brothers.
To his siblings and friends it seemed as though his final years were sad and very solitary, but as the saying goes: "He did it his way."
Our Nat will be remembered for his ready smile, his quick wit and his quirky habit of correcting our choice of words in conversation. The dictionary was his favorite book! He often showed up unannounced and was perfectly happy to just sit and observe whatever was going on. He had a very unassuming presence, preferring to remain in the background, usually disappearing when no one was paying attention.
In addition to wife Barbara, Nat was predeceased by his parents, his two older siblings, Joel Stevens and Elizabeth Smith. He is survived by three sisters, Edith Stevens, Ella lbarguen and Ellen Newton and brother Jacob Stevens. Uncle Nat is also fondly remembered by several nieces and nephews.
The family plans to have a celebration of life for Natty at a later date. We will endeavor to reach out to family and friends when we know the time and place of this gathering.

title: How to make a Thanksgiving dinner on a budget
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
How to make a Thanksgiving dinner on a budget
Delish trims the holiday bill by making smart swaps and leaning on pantry staples.
How to make a Thanksgiving dinner on a budget
Delish trims the holiday bill by making smart swaps and leaning on pantry staples.
Does a classic homemade Thanksgiving feast have to come with a big bill?
The National Consumer Unit put our Hearst partners at Delish to the test: make a Thanksgiving dinner for four in New York for as little as possible.
Delish food editor Taylor Ann Spencer breaks down her strategy and what swaps she had to make.
Turkey
The biggest expense was the turkey, Spencer said. She chose turkey breast tenderloin instead of a full bird or drumsticks.
"You're paying for the bone. With the tenderloin, you're eating all of the ounce-age that you bought," she said.
Spencer recommends searing the tenderloin on a pan, baste with herbs and butter and finish the cooking off in the oven.
She says the cooking technique is similar to searing a steak, which you can find the Delish recipe here.
Gravy
For the gravy, Spencer saved the pan used to sear the turkey to preserve the browned bits at the bottom.
She then added butter, flour and chicken stock to the drippings to make gravy.
Check out Delish's recipe on their "perfect" gravy here.
Stuffing
Spencer chose boxed stuffing as the budget-friendly base.
She upgraded it with fresh onion and celery that had been sweated down, some chicken stock that would also be used for the gravy, and an egg.
For a great boxed stuffing, check out Delish's rankings here.
Mashed potatoes
For the mashed potatoes, Spencer swapped regular milk for evaporated milk.
"This can was $1.25, and I had trouble finding regular milk that I could get that for that amount," Spencer said.
For perfectly creamy mashed potatoes, check out Delish's recipe here.
Steamed green beans and crispy onions
Instead of green bean casserole, Spencer kept it simple by steaming fresh green beans and using the remaining onions from the stuffing to make a crispy onion topping.
She found that premade crispy fried onion toppings were expensive and only used occasionally.
She also chose fresh green beans that were not pre-bagged, which saved money.
Cranberry sauce
For the cranberry sauce, Spencer chose the canned version because it was slightly cheaper than buying fresh cranberries.
Mini apple crisp pies
For dessert, Spencer opted for mini apple crisp pies instead of pumpkin pie, since the premix for the latter was more expensive.
"When we were looking at pricing, pumpkin pie mix was $5.99," Spencer said. "It blew the budget right out of the water."
For the mini apple crisp pies, Spencer only needed one apple per recipe.
She used pantry staples like flour, butter, sugar, salt and oats for the crust and the crispy topping.
To make a pie dough, see Delish's recipe here.
For a great apple crisp filling and topping, see Delish's recipe here.
Cost breakdown
In the end, the full meal for four people came to $36.11, around $9 per person.
Spencer says planning ahead and relying on pantry staples can help save you money and stress.
"Decide what matters to you and then be okay with going to multiple stores to shop," she said.

title: A man destroyed a $60 million US military plane at an Irish airport, prosecutors say
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — An ax-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked overnight at an Irish airport, cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks, U.S. prosecutors said. The man’s supporters attributed the attack to his anger at the United States’ involvement in Middle East conflicts.
An indictment unsealed Tuesday in Manhattan charges Daithi O’Corrain, 48, with destruction of U.S. government property in connection with the April incident at Shannon Airport, an international gateway in the west of Ireland that serves as a hub for American troops and military equipment.
O’Corrain isn’t in U.S. custody and his arraignment on the new charge hasn’t been scheduled. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison. Online court records do not list an attorney who might speak on his behalf.
The plane, a $60 million U.S. Air National Guard C-130 Hercules that had been en route to a military assignment in another country, was rendered inoperable and won’t fly again, U.S. prosecutors said. The attack jeopardized critical military operations, the FBI said.
O’Corrain, described by supporters as an independent peace activist, was arrested immediately after the attack by Ireland’s police force, An Garda Síochána. He was charged there with causing criminal damage and trespassing. The Limerick Post reported he is from Cork, about 60 miles (97 kilometers) southeast of Shannon.
Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said the indictment sends “a clear and powerful message that attacks on U.S. military assets — and thus our national security — will not be tolerated.”
An online fundraiser organized by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends and comrades said he disarmed the C-130 in protest of the U.S.’s war with Iran and support for Israel’s war in Gaza — a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians.
“An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide,” organizer Tracey Ryan wrote.
O’Corrain plotted the attack for months, U.S. prosecutors said. He searched online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel, and looked up coordinates for sneaking onto the airport’s grounds, prosecutors said.
He subscribed to a cellphone app that provided live flight tracking, including for military aircraft, and ordered capsules of gallium, a chemical that can corrode steel and break down aluminum, the primary material used to build the C-130, prosecutors said.
He even tried to get in touch with someone who had been involved in a prior breach at Shannon Airport, prosecutors said.
“This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism,” James Barnacle, the head of the FBI’s New York office, said in a statement.
O’Corrain attacked on April 11, breaching the airport’s perimeter at around 4:40 a.m. and breaking into the C-130 as it was parked on a taxiway by destroying a locking mechanism on the rear crew door, his indictment said.
He used the crew’s hammocks to cover the plane’s windows but left the cockpit windshield exposed, the indictment said. He then barricaded himself inside the aircraft, securing the doors with straps, brackets and screws, and putting ball bearings mixed with epoxy in door tracks to prevent doors from being opened or closed, the indictment said.
O’Corrain laid waste to the plane over the next few hours, pulling, snipping and otherwise disabling its key components, the indictment said. He sliced wire bundles, crimped a liquid oxygen line, punctured air ducts and shattered every gauge in the cockpit, the indictment said.
Had O’Corrain cut the oxygen line instead, he would’ve risked blowing up the plane, prosecutors said.
Returning to the airport after resting elsewhere, the C-130 crew spotted O’Corrain through the uncovered cockpit at around 9:40 a.m. and alerted security, the indictment said.
Crew members then saw him emerging through a roof hatch and swinging an ax at the plane’s exterior, according to the indictment, which included images taken from a video recording that show a man standing on the roof of the plane. O’Corrain then poured substances and objects into the fuel tanks, including ball bearings, before being arrested.
Shannon Airport, which was used by President Donald Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September, has had several security breaches in the last 18 months, including three people who were accused of spray-painting a U.S. military plane and three others who drove to a restricted area where a U.S. military jet was parked.

title: Recount confirms Clement winner of Lewiston House District 96 seat
text:
The Maine Secretary of State’s Office confirmed Tuesday that a recount shows Republican Kerryl Lee Clement won the race for Maine’s House District 96 seat in Lewiston.
District 96 includes parts of Wards 4, 6 and 7.
In the original tally following the Nov. 3 election, Clement defeated his Democratic rival Luke Jensen by 40 votes, 2,226 to 2,186.
After the recount, Clement’s win stood, though by a narrower margin of 24 votes, 2,232 to 2,208.
Clement succeeds outgoing Rep. Michael Lajoie, a Democrat, who did not seek reelection.

title: Hathaway Holiday Lights Returns Bigger, With Donations Going To Northern Light EMMC NICU
text:
Hathaway Holiday Lights Celebrate 15 Years Of Lighting Up Eastern Maine For A Special Cause
What started as a way for Rick and Deanna Hathaway to honor their twin sons who were born prematurely, and spent time in the NICU, has turned into a much anticipated and loved Holiday Lights Event in the Eastern Maine.
The Hathaway Holiday Lights Display was first set up 15 years ago, on Hillside Drive in Bangor.
Read More: Show Us Bangor + Eastern Maine Holiday Light Displays
This interactive display boasting tens of thousands of lights grew so big, so quickly, that around 2020, they Hathaways moved the entire operation to the lawn of the Veazie School, where there was a parking lot across and the street and less disruption to their neighbors.
Each year, it has grown and expanded, with extra elements and lights added season after season. But the heart of what the display represents has not changed.
The display is free to explore, but visitors are encouraged, if they see fit, to leave a donation. All donations go straight to the Northern Light EMMC NICU, in honor of the couple's boys, Alex, who passed away just four days after he was born, and Warren, who spend over 50 days in the NICU, but is thriving today.
Those who visit the display are thrilled with thousands of lights, expertly programmed to a number of holiday songs. There are paths to walk, buttons to push, and plenty of opportunities to take photos along the way.
Read More: Stillwater River Trail Of Lights Returns To Orono This December
A team of hard-working volunteers have finished setting up this year's display, which they say is bigger and better than the one next year.
Rick Hathaway says the display will officially open on December 1st and run through the 25th. He thanks the community and volunteers for helping in such a special way each year.
"Hathaway Holiday Lights may have started as a family project, but it truly takes a community to bring this display to life. Without all of you, we wouldn’t be nearly as far along as we are today!"
He says this year folks can expect over 15,000 more lights, a talking grinch face and some more fun surprises.

title: Maine Marathon participant raises more than $9K for Alzheimer's Association
text:
Maine Marathon participant raises more than $9,000 for Alzheimer's Association
A woman raised more than $9,000 for the Maine Chapter of the Alzheimer's Association by taking part in the 2026 Maine Marathon.
Maine Marathon race director Bob Dunfey visited the Alzheimer's Association's local office in Scarborough on Monday to present a check for $9,405.12 on behalf of Meghan Cushing.
Cushing raises money for the Alzheimer's Association in memory of her grandmother, Eve, who lived with Alzheimer's disease for 10 years.
In addition, Cushing and her mother, Michele, serve as committee co-chairs for the Greater Portland Walk to End Alzheimer's.
Meghan and Michele reached out to Dunfey earlier this year to see if the Alzheimer's Association could be a beneficiary of the race, and he said yes.
"With no expectation, you're kind of like, 'Yeah, maybe a couple hundred dollars would be great.' Then for us to kind of blow it out of the water and get nearly $9,500 is super exciting for us and it's a great stepping point for us to raise awareness about the foundation," Meghan Cushing said.
Dunfey said he has seen first-hand how donations can help advance Alzheimer's research as his best friend is living well with the disease after taking an FDA-approved medication to reduce cognitive decline.
WMTW is a proud sponsor of the Maine Marathon, Half Marathon, and Relay, which is a volunteer-run nonprofit event. The race is held annually in Portland and directs net proceeds to Maine-based charitable organizations.

title: Obituary: Alden N. Perry
text:
BRUNSWICK – Alden N. Perry, 83, died Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, at his home. He was born April 11, 1943 in Bath, Maine, a son of Herbert and Jeanne Bellanger Perry.
He was a graduate of Brunswick High School, class of 1961, and Southern Maine Vocational Institute. Mr. Perry served in the Airforce National Guard from 1965-71.
He met the love of his life Pamela Buell while camping on Sebego Lake. The couple was married on Sept. 20, 1969, in Portland and together built a life of adventure, traveling through Europe, Central America, Alaska and Hawaii. The couple enjoyed cruises, which they shared with their parents and close friends.
The couples love of camping brought them from Sebago to Cathedral Pines, Eustis Maine, where they returned annually for over 50 years.
Mr. Perry was a surveyor for the Maine DOT for over 40 years, retiring as supervisor, and having been instrumental in the construction of the Casco Bay Bridge and the State’s railway system.
He loved all sports and followed the Celtic and New England Patriots. He was especially passionate about the Boston Red Sox, having made several trips for Spring training in Fort Meyers, Fla. and regular games at Fenway.
Friends and family are invited to visit 3 – 6 p.m. Wednesday. Nov. 18, 2026, at the Brackett Funeral Home, 29 Federal Street, Brunswick. A funeral service will be held 10 a.m. Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, at the funeral home. A committal with military honors will follow in Riverview Cemetery, Topsham.

title: Watch: Deering girls, Westbrook boys basketball gearing up for season
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Editor’s note: Maine high school basketball practices began Monday for most of the state. To tip off the hoops season, we’re sending reporter Gideon Aigner on a tour of southern, western and central Maine. First up were stops at the Deering girls and Westbrook boys practices.
On the first day of winter sports practices, excitement was in the air for the Deering girls basketball team and smiles were all around the gym.
“I’m ready to start fresh,” Rams forward Blake Gayle said Monday. “Last season, we didn’t get as far as we wanted to, and we wanted to prove ourselves more.”
Third-year coach Michael Atkins has nine seniors on the roster, and the hope is experience will benefit the Rams late in close games. Last season, the Rams went 3-14, with half of those losses coming by 10 points or fewer.
“We were one or two (wins) away from getting into playoffs,” Atkins said. “It’s just a matter of finishing those last-minute possessions and getting over the hump with this group. That’ll put us exactly where we want to be.”
Senior guard Angie Keo said another point of emphasis is cohesion on defense.
“Our key is communication,” Keo said. “On the court, we’re just really quiet. We just need to work on talking to each other.”
About 3 miles east, the Westbrook boys basketball team is going to be vastly different than in previous seasons. The Blue Blazes graduated nine seniors after last season, leaving plenty of opportunities for new talent.
“I’ve been pushing kids to get in the gym more,” said Westbrook guard Faiz Omar. “Since it was mostly seniors, and I was the only sophomore starting, I’ve just been pushing (the younger players) to get on the same level (the seniors) were last year.”
Senior power forward Jelson Binda says the Blue Blazes are trying to build the fortitude that came with experience last year.
“The team has really changed in maturity,” Binda said. “It’s going to be real different having younger guys.”
Coach Jim Seavey’s points of emphasis are improving 3-point shooting and using other teams’ low expectations of Westbrook against them.
“A lot of people are gonna write us off because we graduated nine seniors,” Seavey said. “I hope they do that, because I think they’re going to be in for a surprise. … I don’t think (the players are) going to accept people writing us off.”

title: Letter: Chris Van Hollen should be Senate majority leader
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
“Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” What a relatable soundbite for Sen. Angus King to express his support for Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader.
Except I believe that King knows what blue voters in this election likely know. Schumer does not deserve credit for this blue wave. In fact, if he had been willing to support popular progressive candidates, we may have seen an even bigger wave. Florida likely would be blue right now, too.
Voters handed the World Series to Democrats in a historic repudiation of Donald Trump and MAGA — and in spite of their frustration with donor-purchased establishment Democrats like Schumer. Voters’ top concerns include: corruption, war/genocide, ICE, AI/data centers/crypto, affordability, and Medicare for All. One of Schumer’s top priorities is providing weapons to Israel. He said so himself, right out in public.
Handing Senate leadership to Schumer will completely alienate voters who came out for change. I think it’s like winning the World Series and then using the win to sell the team to your rich out-of-town venture capitalist buddy.
Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen has announced a run for majority leader. This is a public servant who flew to El Salvador to fight for the civil rights of his constituent — and won! I don’t think this would be a hard choice if donor dollars didn’t factor into the decision.
I believe Van Hollen is the right choice for what voters have demanded — real change, a government for the people, not the donors.
Sydney Michalski
Columbia

title: This Maine-Made Eggnog Tastes Like Christmas in a Glass
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This Maine-Made Eggnog Tastes Like Christmas in a Glass
If there's one thing that tastes like the holidays in a glass, it's eggnog. And if there's one sip that instantly gets me in the Christmas spirit, it's that first taste of the creamy holiday classic! But what happens when you combine traditional eggnog with the buttery sweetness of a freshly baked sugar cookie? You get Oakhurst Dairy's newest seasonal treat (and my newest obsession!).
Oakhurst Sugar Cookie Eggnog is bringing a little extra holiday magic to the dairy aisle. The festive flavor "combines rich, creamy eggnog with the sweet taste of freshly baked sugar cookies". It's available for a limited time in 16-ounce pints and quart-sized containers, making it perfect for sharing (or drinking it all yourself... like me LOL).
Every time the holidays roll around, I'm always looking for a new holiday flavor or treat to try.
One local wrote on Oakhurst social media announcement, "Super sweet but it made *the best* pancakes!"
So, OBVIOUSLY I had to give this one an immediate shot! And let me tell you, this was one of my favorites thus far.
