title: Another wipeout hits Wall Street as Nvidia, other jittery AI stocks swing lower
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The U.S. stock market shook again Tuesday as Nvidia and other jittery stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry led widespread losses on Wall Street.
The S&P 500 sank 1% and at one point was on track for its first back-to-back losses of at least 1.5% since March. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 848 points, or 1.6%, and the Nasdaq composite fell 0.7%.
The center of the action was again Nvidia, which resumed its whipsaw moves. After flipping between modest gains and losses in the morning, it veered lower and dropped as much as 3.7% before trimming the loss down to 0.4%.
The swings came ahead of the chip company’s latest earnings report, which arrived after trading ended for the day and once again came in above analysts’ expectations. It was Nvidia’s first earnings report since interim CEO Colette Kress took over for Jensen Huang, the leather-jacketed star who became one of the most famous faces of the AI boom.
The pressure is on Kress and Nvidia to show whether the company’s tremendous growth can continue following the stunning resignation of one of AI’s strongest influencers. Nvidia is creating a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance following revelations that Huang had a relationship with an alleged spy for China.
Huang said on the X social-media network Tuesday that he would come back as CEO if “the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America.”
Other AI stocks also swung sharply. Advanced Micro Devices went from an early gain of 1.6% to a drop of 4.7% before trimming its fall to 0.2%. CoreWeave initially climbed 1.8%, flipped to a loss of 6.1% and then finished nearly unchanged.
AI-related stocks have been shaky for months because of a rolling chain of worries. At first, it was concerns that AI stock prices had broadly shot too high in their frenzy. Then it was worries that high interest rates would mean less borrowed money to fund further growth. More recently, it was concerns that Democratic victories in this month’s U.S. midterm elections could mean tougher regulations and restrictions on AI data centers.
Such stocks can almost single-handedly set the U.S. market’s course because they’ve grown into some of Wall Street’s most valuable and most influential.
Most of Wall Street was weak Tuesday, as 17 out of every 20 stocks within the index fell,
Home Depot sank 2.4% even though it reported profit for the latest quarter that edged past analysts’ expectations.
The retailer has been hampered by a housing market chilled by expensive mortgage rates, which have climbed with Treasury yields because of high oil prices, high inflation and other factors.
The 10-year Treasury yield climbed toward 5.15% Tuesday morning from 5.12% late Monday before later pulling back to 5.10%. It erased its gain after the sharp drops for AI stocks pushed investors to herd into investments seen as safer bets.
In the morning, yields got support from a report showing better growth in an underlying measure of spending at U.S. retailers than economists expected. Such spending, along with big investments in AI, has helped the U.S. economy continue to grow despite frustration with high inflation.
Elsewhere on Wall Street, stocks of banks fell amid concerns about how much pain the broad U.S. economy will feel from any pullback in AI-related spending.
JPMorgan Chase fell 2.4%. A day before, a technical issue at the bank had slowed transactions for customers trying to use the Zelle payment system.
Apple and Marriott had only modest moves following outages in their systems. Apple slipped 0.2%, and Marriott International fell 0.7%.
United Airlines had its own operational struggles, as a system outage forced the carrier to delay departing flights Monday. That came just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop.
United’s stock lost 4%, but it was also hurt by a rise in oil prices.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 0.8% to $93.14. It’s been yo-yoing amid uncertainty about what will happen in the war with Iran.
The downward momentum on Wall Street was strong enough to erase early gains for The Walt Disney Co. and pull it down 1.5%, even though it reported stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 76.06 points to 7,340.53. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 848.75 to 50,759.42, and the Nasdaq composite sank 181.37 to 24,328.38.
Stock prices generally tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term, depending on how interest rates behave. The big businesses across the S&P 500 index are on track to deliver earnings per share for the summer that are nearly 32% higher than a year earlier, according to FactSet.
In stock markets abroad, indexes sank across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi fell 2.6% and dropped to its lowest closing level since February.
___
AP Writers Elaine Lai and Matt Ott contributed to this report.

title: Outage math at the airport: When a four-hour Uber beats waiting out a ground stop
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — New airline tickets: $300. Hours waiting for luggage: four. And the topper: a four-hour Uber ride from Detroit to Chicago that cost $400.
Call it outage math, a hellish calculation spawned by ever-more-common flight delays. This one was part of Angelina and Kyle Phoenix’s anniversary trip to Chicago.
On Friday, they flew from Jacksonville, Florida, into the maw of the Great Ground Stoppage of 2026 with as many as a million other travelers. Instantly, the financial and emotional toll of the four-hour flight outage radiated outward from the airports as everyone involved scrambled for costly workarounds to a crisis no one expected, can fully explain or wants to pay for.
Emergency child care. Outrageous taxi ride fees. Rebooked tickets, lost vacation rentals and little idea what expenses might be reimbursed.
But beyond finances, travelers told The Associated Press on Monday, perhaps the most consequential cost is also the most intimate: Stress and grief over time lost — a cumulative toll that is generally not, as customer service might say, eligible for reimbursement.
It’s not your imagination: Outages are getting worse
Kyle Phoenix got a whiff of it more than 12 hours and hundreds of dollars of unexpected expenses into the couple’s journey, as he watched chaos unfold in the baggage claim area of Detroit airport. Officials, he noticed, had stopped announcing which canceled flights would disgorge checked baggage onto which turnstiles.
Answers were hard to come by. That made decisions about what to do next increasingly difficult.
“A lot of confusion, a lot of scrambling from a lot of people,” Kyle recalls of the scene. “I think that was probably the roughest part, not knowing anything.”
When the couple finally retrieved their luggage at midnight, the $400 Uber ride began to look like the best option. They forfeited their rebooked flight — as well as a hotel room they would have stayed in for a few hours — and embarked on the four-hour ride to Chicago.
“We just took the loss,” Angelina Phoenix said.
Dread lingers around such events because they’re getting more commonplace, with no end in sight.
Even as travelers spoke to the AP about Friday’s ground stop, United Airlines suffered a malfunction and halted its flights for 90 minutes. Several top U.S. banks reported significant slowdowns. And that was after AI chaos and Microsoft’s global meltdown just a few days earlier. Ahead loomed the busy Thanksgiving travel week, when TSA agents typically screen more than 2 million passengers nationwide.
It was enough to make any thinking person ask: Could everything be broken? And it forced humanity to reckon once again with the fragility of the systems that anchor modern life.
The government agrees that lost passenger time is worth money
Delays are accelerating faster than the increase of scheduled passenger flights since the COVID-19 pandemic, the International Air Transport Association reported in July. Between 2015 and 2025, delays affecting scheduled passenger flights generated about $10.9 billion in costs for airlines and travelers, with sharp increases in holdups starting in 2021.
The issues are costing travelers time, which even the Federal Aviation Administration agrees is worth money.
Federal guidance issued a decade ago valued airline passengers’ time at $47.10 an hour, expressed in 2015 dollars. That’s about $66 an hour today. The figure accounted for travel time that would otherwise be available for work or leisure.
More recently, an economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond estimated that last year’s 43-day federal government shutdown caused roughly 1 million additional hours of passenger delays at six airports. Economist Russell Wong calculated the lost time’s value at $66 million, based on metro area wage data and the higher-than-average incomes of people who take flights. Wong excluded canceled flights.
Harder to measure is the loss absorbed by the population downstream from the airports, including hourly workers, freelancers and caregivers — in short, everyone affected by the ripples.
On trust: ‘I’m super-skeptical about what we’re being told’
Another cost: Trust in government, which has been low for years.
The nationwide shutdown, the nation’s longest in 25 years, could cost billions of dollars, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said over the weekend. He blamed a contractor and aging infrastructure. President Donald Trump testily pointed to Democrats, who in turn demanded answers about how the administration has spent billions it’s already been given and why its funding request has soared to $50 billion.
Downplaying the event as a glitch with a faulty router raised questions, if not suspicions, one communications expert says.
“It wasn’t simply a crisis, it was an actual emergency of impending disaster-level scale,” Shannon A. Bowen, a journalism and mass communications professor at the University of South Carolina told “The Conversation.”
Inside airports, travelers weren’t easily accepting the official explanation.
“I’m super skeptical about what we’re being told as to why this event happened at all,” said Sonia Saini Simpson, 56, whose flight from Orlando, Florida, landed in Philadelphia after hours of uncertainty, during which she said she considered renting a car to drive the nearly 1,000 miles (1,587 kilometers). “I look forward to getting some answers that are believable.”
Days after the stoppage, questions arose among some travelers about delays that sound like routine maintenance issues.
Glenn Anthony Cooper, a disc jockey, said he was told his flight from Philadelphia to Toronto on Monday had been delayed nine hours for “a hole in the tire.”
“It’s like, what’s really going on, you know? Is there something behind it, or what are they doing?” he said in an interview at the Philadelphia airport. “It’s just a bummer to just have these types of situations happen and you can’t really control it.”
The most cursory scroll through social media reveals the nightmare of Friday’s historic stoppage in all its dramatic detail, much of it posted live: The 10-hour drives, the epic Uber rides, the lost wages, the stunned faces.
There’s advice, too: Buy travel insurance, advised some. Don’t check luggage if it’s avoidable. Be nice to airline and security workers. And skip, if you can, to the acceptance phase of grief — because there’s a limit to what you can control.
For young father William Ware, 24, the peak of stress may have been the moment he realized the shutdown created overwhelming traffic outside LAX that was keeping his Uber from dropping him off in time to make his flight home to Chicago to care for his child.
Ware was rebooked for the next day and could only find a hotel in Long Beach more than 20 miles away — “scary, but that was the only hotel that was available.” That meant another two Uber rides round trip back to the airport.
Maybe, Ware thinks, he’ll get a refund for the ticket. But there was another cost: his time.
“I actually had to get home to my kid and I couldn’t, so it was horrible for me,” he told the AP Monday, back in Chicago at last. “I got a great support system, so my family was able to watch my child.”
___
Kellman reported from London. AP writers Lisa Leff in London and Mingson Lau in Philadelphia contributed to this report.

title: Dessert auction for Rape Response Services
text:
BANGOR — Rape Response Services, a Penquis subsidiary, will be hosting a dessert auction on Friday, Nov. 20. The fun-filled event, featuring a live auction, will include over 60 delicious desserts made by local Maine bakers, ready for winning bidders to take home and enjoy. This event is sponsored by Versant Power and Bangor Savings Bank.
The dessert auction will take place at the Hilton Garden Inn, 250 Haskell Road in Bangor. Doors open at 6 p.m. and the auction starts at 6:30 p.m. There is no entry fee, and a selection of appetizers and desserts will be served. Cash, checks and online payments will all be accepted during the event.
The funds raised by the dessert auction will support advocacy and prevention services throughout Penobscot and Piscataquis counties.
“The dessert auction is more than just a fun evening,” Tamar Mathieu, executive director of Rape Response Services, said. “It is a way for our community to show support for survivors and speak out against sexual violence.”
“This dessert auction has a tremendous impact supporting survivors in our community when they need it most,” Marissa McKay, supervisor of communications & brand for Versant, said. “Versant Power is happy to sponsor this event and help support Rape Response Services’ important work.”
According to Maine Coalition Against Sexual Assault, one in five Mainers will experience sexual assault at some point in their lifetime. Rape Response Services provides advocacy (one-to-one support) to survivors via their 24/7 helpline, accompaniment to hospital, law enforcement, medical and court appointments and referrals to other supportive services, such as legal assistance, medical follow-up and counseling services. Outreach, education and prevention efforts are designed to provide children, adults and communities in Penobscot and Piscataquis counties with the tools needed to address and prevent sexual violence.
For more information, contact Amanda Chambers at 207-947-2436 or Mathieu at 207-973-3595.
Rape Response Services, a member center of the Maine Coalition Against Sexual Assault, has served as the sexual assault support services center for Penobscot and Piscataquis counties since 1988. It became a subsidiary of Penquis, the community action agency for Penobscot, Piscataquis and Knox counties, in 2008. The mission of RRS is to offer hope, support and advocacy to survivors and people affected by sexual assault and stalking and to provide education about sexual violence and promote prevention. Services include a 24-hour crisis and support line; information and support for survivors and their family and friends; advocacy; accompaniment to the hospital, including forensic exams and medical or legal appointments; support through the court process; and information and referral to other resources and alternative paths to healing. Rape Response Services also facilitates multidisciplinary teams, provides community education and school-based primary prevention programming and engages in social change through community engagement.

Recently unsealed court documents are shedding new light on alleged MaineCare fraud.
In October, federal officials arrested six people connected to Community Home Health Care LLC in South Portland.
A grand jury indicted the agency’s owner and operator, Noora Abd, and five other people who worked at the agency.
8 Investigates had visited the office last summer after the company was suspended from the MaineCare program.
Court documents offer new insight into how officials try to prevent fraud and how Community Home Care allegedly got around those safeguards.
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services requires home health care providers to use an Electronic Visit Verification tool to log visits. The system verifies when and where services are provided while workers are on-site.
A MaineCare member handbook says health aides may ask patients to sign a digital form or speak into a phone to verify a visit.
MaineCare claims must correspond with the Electronic Visit Verification logs, but care agencies can also add or update the logs manually through an online portal.
According to the indictment, one employee, Adel al Rashid, used his own and other workers’ usernames and passwords to enter false visits into the verification system.

title: Senate Democrats demand clear-cut answers on what caused grounding of planes
text:
Democrats in the Senate on Tuesday called for pausing the replacement of thousands of routers across the nation’s air traffic control system after the work was blamed for setting off last week’s air traffic snarls.
They also demanded that the Trump administration provide clear answers about what went wrong.
“Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed. FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues,” said the letter sent to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
President Donald Trump has blamed old technology and Democrats for the nationwide grounding of all planes and upheaval at the nation’s airports. But the FAA has been struggling to modernize the air traffic control system for decades — going back well before the first Trump administration.
The system became overloaded when a federal contractor that maintains the FAA’s telecommunications network was replacing outdated copper wires with fiber optic lines across the nation.
The closure of U.S. airspace was needed, Duffy said, after a new router that L3Harris installed in El Dorado, Arkansas, resulted in a cascade of intermittent communications and radar signals at 17 of the 22 regional air traffic control centers. The centers direct planes cruising at high altitudes.
The Federal Aviation Administration said that “excessive data” was flooding the system “at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds.” That deluge created instability with “aircraft communications and radar feeds” when those connection attempts overwhelmed the 25-year-old routers throughout the network, the agency said.
Democrats on the Senate Commerce Committee said they believe that only 400 out of more than 3,600 routers have been installed. Work on installing the new devices should be stopped until “the root cause of the failure has been identified,” the letter stated.
Upgrading the nation’s air transportation system is an effort that Congress has dedicated significant sums to in recent years. The problems with aging equipment at the FAA date back decades and past efforts to modernize the system have come up short.
Duffy has pushed Congress for billions more dollars to upgrade a system he said had been neglected for decades, saying on Friday that $50 billion is needed.
The Trump administration on Tuesday sent a letter to key lawmakers updating its request for $50.1 billion to modernize the system and make other improvements at airports.
The request calls for $10.1 billion for updating the nation’s air traffic control system. Similar amounts would go toward boosting airport infrastructure, replacing or refurbishing terminals at high-impact hubs, constructing five new traffic control centers and improving or replacing up to 140 FAA-owned air traffic control towers.
“Congressional approval of these funds will equip the FAA to deliver to the American people a brand-new air traffic control system that is safer, smarter, faster, and more efficient,” states the letter, which was obtained by The Associated Press.
Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to modernize much of the key infrastructure that more than 45,000 flights a day rely on to reach their destinations safely. The funds were earmarked for replacing outdated technologies such as copper wires, floppy discs and radars built in the 1980s, but much of that money will also go toward runway upgrades and other construction projects.

Robert Pattinson starred alongside Willem Dafoe in the 2019 psychological horror film “The Lighthouse,” which takes place on a fictional island off the coast of Maine in the 1890s.
Directed by Robert Eggers, the black-and-white film follows Pattinson’s character, Ephraim Winslow, a young lighthouse keeper assigned to work alongside Dafoe’s character, Thomas Wake, for four weeks.
As the two men struggle with isolation, harsh weather and growing tensions, their mental states begin to deteriorate, leading to increasingly disturbing events.
Although the story is set in Maine and draws inspiration from our state’s maritime history, coastal scenery, and regional dialects, filming took place in Nova Scotia, Canada, where crews constructed a lighthouse specifically for the production.
Amazon MGM Studios announced Monday, Nov. 16, that Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond, succeeding Daniel Craig in the role.
Pattinson will star in the franchise’s next film, directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Steven Knight, with a release date yet to be officially announced.

title: Measles officially no longer considered eliminated in the US and Mexico
text:
Measles officially no longer considered eliminated in the US and Mexico
The U.S. has lost its measles-free status, international health officials said Tuesday, as the highly contagious virus once relegated to medical textbooks has spread — largely among the unvaccinated — at the highest rate in more than 30 years.
Mexico also lost its measles-elimination status, following a resurgence of the virus there that included a massive outbreak in Chihuahua state. Bolivia, too, lost its status.
The Pan American Health Organization declaration has few practical implications and is largely symbolic, but it marks a sharp turnabout in a disease largely controlled through decades of scientific advances. It also may be seen as the beginning of an era in which diseases of the past become deadly problems for the modern world.
Measles has been spreading throughout the Americas since 2024. The outbreaks in North America started in close-knit Mennonite communities and have since spread to areas with low vaccination rates. Last year, Canada lost its measles-free designation for the first time since 1998.
International health officials consider measles eliminated when the virus is not locally spreading among residents. The designation hinges on whether a single measles chain has spread uninterrupted for at least 12 months.
Tuesday's announcement signals an erosion of public health preparedness.
Vaccination rates have been falling against a number of diseases, in the U.S. and globally. And as one of the most infectious diseases known to medicine, measles was seen as likely to be one of the first vaccine-preventable diseases to re-emerge when vaccinations falter.
That means others are likely to follow, some experts said.
“It can be the canary in the coal mine to other things,” said Dr. Susan Kansagra, chief medical officer of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials.
Vaccine rates fall and cases go up
Measles vaccines have safely stopped the virus’ spread in the U.S. for 30 years.
It takes a community vaccination rate of 95% to prevent outbreaks, experts say. But as fewer parents vaccinate their children and federal leaders sow doubt and confusion about the importance of getting vaccinated, the virus has found footholds in communities across the U.S. All but three states have reported a confirmed case of measles this year.
“This humiliating determination is the tragic yet predictable result of an ongoing campaign by grifters, quacks and charlatans to put their own greed and self-worth ahead of the health and safety of children,” said Sen. Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon.
The last two years have been the worst in a generation in the U.S., with more than 7,000 cases and 11 deaths. Nearly all of those people were either unvaccinated or didn’t report whether they were vaccinated. More than 10% of those infected had to be hospitalized.
The illness typically begins with a high fever followed by a telltale rash that starts on the face and neck. Most people recover, but it’s one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization. Serious complications, including blindness and swelling of the brain, are more common in young children and adults over age 30.
Ten measles-associated deaths have been reported in the U.S. this year. Health officials have not released detailed information on each death, but at least five of the dead were children.
This year’s measles death count is higher than what has been seen in any previous year in more than three decades.
And the U.S. is experiencing its worst year for measles illnesses since 1991.
The US has seen major outbreaks in Texas, Utah, South Carolina and Pennsylvania
Since the U.S. eliminated measles in 2000, public health officials usually logged less than 200 cases a year, most of them tied to international travel.
But since 2025, measles has sickened thousands. It started with a major outbreak in the southwest.
In Texas, more than 760 people got sick and two children died. And in New Mexico, about 100 people got sick and one adult died.
In the summer of 2025, measles exploded in extremely rural border towns in Arizona and Utah. And a major outbreak in South Carolina in the winter and spring sickened nearly 1,000 people to become the fastest growing measles outbreak the nation has seen in decades.
Bad as 2025 was, this year has been much worse. The more than 5,400 confirmed cases so far this year are already double the 2025 tally, driven largely by an outbreak in Pennsylvania that has dwarfed the earlier ones.
And the outbreak tallies are almost certainly an undercount, public health experts say.
Critics say the US response is falling short
U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was a leading voice in the anti-vaccine movement before President Donald Trump appointed him to oversee federal health agencies.
Kennedy and other federal leaders have argued that vaccination rates were waning for years before Trump took office a second time, that measles is not an “American phenomenon," and that the U.S. government is handling measles better than other countries. In January, a CDC leader told reporters that the loss of the nation's elimination status would be the “cost of doing business” globally.
It's true that other countries are struggling with measles, and some also have lost their measles-elimination status. But some experts say the outcome in the U.S. wasn't inevitable.
The government has been taking some steps. In August and September, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention awarded $100 million — in two tranches — to support state and local measles-response work. And Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz have made statements that vaccination is the best way to prevent measles from spreading.
But state and local health officials say the cost is far higher than that.
“It wasn't a lot of money, frankly,” said Chrissie Juliano, executive director of the Big Cities Health Coalition, which represents three dozen of the largest U.S. city health departments.
Experts also say the moment demands a louder federal voice — and a bigger push for vaccinations — than Kennedy and Schwartz are providing. Some noted that neither Kennedy nor the CDC has scheduled a news conference for this week to address how they plan to try to regain measles-elimination status.
“When the people at the front of the room are not speaking loudly and frequently in support of vaccination, the program starts to falter. And that's what we're seeing in the U.S.," said Noel Brewer, a University of North Carolina public health professor who chairs a committee that presented an analysis of U.S. measles data to PAHO last week.
“The federal government has had such a ho-hum response," he said. "How many kids have to die before they start getting concerned?
"At what point is this relic of the past, stealing children from us, going to create outrage and action from the federal government?”
What's next?
After hugely successful vaccination campaigns, the Americas became the first region in the world to be free of measles in 2016. Health officials estimate the measles vaccine prevented 6.2 million deaths in the Americas between 2000 and 2023.
Now, the entirety of North America faces the task of earning back the designation.
Some individual countries have achieved, lost, and then regained measles-elimination status. Brazil is one example. Another is the United Kingdom, although it lost its status a second time — this year.

title: Maine’s transportation is inadequate, expensive and harming our environment
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Matt Cannon has been a staffer with Sierra Club Maine since 2019, coordinating the chapter’s conservation and energy work. He is also on the steering committee of Transportation for Maine (T4ME) and the board of the Moving Maine Network.
All Mainers are impacted by our state’s inadequate, expensive, and climate-damaging transportation system.
The average Mainer spends more than $1,000 a month on transportation needs. For some, this can exceed the cost of food and housing, forcing many to make difficult choices about where to go and what they can afford. Additionally, our state’s over-reliance on highways drives sprawling development, destroys natural spaces, and exacerbates air and water pollution. These choices have increased social isolation, driven the decline of downtown areas, and reduced spaces for walking, cycling, and recreation.
I have been watching these impacts become more and more significant, and this is a critical moment to act before our landscape is irreparably harmed.
Even with all these highways, getting from one place to another is far more difficult than it should be. Whether it’s going to work, a doctor’s appointment, or school, too many people lack affordable, reliable transportation options. These challenges disproportionately affect rural communities, where tens of thousands of households lack access to a personal vehicle or public transit that meets their needs.
Beyond the necessary travel we all take, inaccessible transit leaves Mainers disconnected from community life as well, harming the mental and physical well-being of residents of our state. That’s especially true for older adults, young people, low-income families, and anyone who doesn’t or can’t drive.
Even short trips can become major undertakings for those without a car. Taking public transit from Portland to Scarborough can take almost an hour, compared with about 12 minutes by car. And these barriers extend beyond everyday commutes to the places that make Maine special. On a recent Sierra Club Maine trip to the Katahdin Woods National Monument, my colleague traveling from the Sebago Lake area faced a journey of more than 13 hours using public transit. Others drove electric vehicles, only to find no charging stations in the park. Even the roads in the park are most suited for trucks or SUVs, limiting access for folks who arrived in other types of vehicles.
These are more than inconvenient trips. They are examples of how a transportation system shapes who can access jobs and essential services, participate in community, and experience the beauty of our state.
Other states and countries have demonstrated it’s possible to expand transit in rural areas. Maine can do the same. For too long, our leaders have prioritized building infrastructure for cars and trucks while neglecting our public transportation and other alternatives. Although some progress has been made in recent years, much more remains to ensure Mainers have affordable, reliable transit.
That’s why, earlier this year, organizations across the state formed a coalition called Transportation for Maine. We are working to address these issues and fight for more investment in transportation systems that support walking, cycling, rolling, shared rides, public transportation, and downtown revitalization. More than a dozen organizations working on issues as diverse as economic development, social services, land use, climate, conservation, and fiscal responsibility have come together to push for more resilient, connected, and thriving communities across Maine. Just to name a few: The Katahdin Collaborative is working to foster community, build economic growth and increase outdoor recreation and access; the Aroostook Regional Transportation system is doing amazing mobility management work in the County; and the Moving Maine Network is expanding transportation access for all Mainers.
Today, Transportation for Maine is hosting a summit to bring people together who believe Maine can do more to address the issues we face and get started shaping an agenda that demands government action that prioritizes people, lowers costs, and creates healthier, more resilient, and more connected communities. But that is just the start. We hope this moment inspires even more people to join our cause and create a power shift toward justice.
To find out more about Transportation for Maine and join us at the upcoming summit, visit our website, t4me.org.

title: 'All hands on deck': South Portland says network outage may involve cybercriminal activity
text:
'All hands on deck': South Portland says network outage may involve cybercriminal activity
City Hall, Assessor's Office and public library will remain closed through Thursday
'All hands on deck': South Portland says network outage may involve cybercriminal activity
City Hall, Assessor's Office and public library will remain closed through Thursday
South Portland officials announced Tuesday evening that City Hall, the Assessor's Office and the public library will remain closed through Thursday, Nov. 19, due to a continuing network outage and related operational issues.
City Hall and the Assessor's Office will also be closed on Friday per the regular city schedule.
South Portland officials said the network outage that is disrupting some municipal services may involve cybercriminal activity. The city's IT team shut down the network Saturday night after discovering a cybersecurity issue.
South Portland is now working with state and federal agencies to investigate what they believe was a cyberattack. The city has hired an independent forensic investigator to assess the incident.
"Our IT team, staff leaders, and external partners are working tirelessly to conduct an exhaustive examination and resume all City services as soon as it is possible to safely do so," said City of South Portland IT Director Mike Dery. "It's all hands on deck."
Officials said their preliminary assessment indicates most city data is unaffected, but they have not determined the full extent of the incident. 
The city said residents should expect continued disruptions to its phone system, in-person credit card payments, some online administrative portals and mapping services, printed receipts and materials, and online streaming of city meetings.
Some South Portland residents told Maine's Total Coverage that they are losing faith in these systems that are supposed to be "secure."
The city postponed the property tax payment deadline to Monday, Nov. 23. Residents can still leave payments in secure drop boxes outside City Hall. The city is working on a solution for new vehicle registrations; renewals are available through the state's Rapid Renewal website.
Police, fire and EMS services are not affected.

title: Fan ejected from Lambeau Field for spreading ashes on field after Packers game, police say
text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. (WBAY/Gray News) - Authorities in Wisconsin say a fan was removed from Lambeau Field after Sunday’s Green Bay Packers game for spreading ashes on the field.
According to the Green Bay Police Department, officers responded to a report of a person who was seen releasing what appeared to be ashes onto the field from the stands following the conclusion of Sunday’s game.
Officers confirmed the fan in question had dispersed the cremated remains of a loved one onto the field.
Police said this was a violation of Green Bay Municipal Code 24-117, Unlawful Conduct at a Public Event, and the person was ejected from the stadium.
The Green Bay Packers said that while they understand the desire of some fans to have their loved ones’ ashes spread at Lambeau Field, it is against the law and prohibited at the stadium.
“To honor a loved one’s legacy appropriately at Lambeau Field, we refer fans to the commemorative brick program. We also suggest they can coordinate tributes in other appropriate ways with their funeral home,” the team shared in a statement.
Police said Sunday’s violation could have resulted in an $890 citation, but it wasn’t immediately known if the person was officially cited.
The Packers dropped Sunday’s home game to the Minnesota Vikings 30-10.

title: Trump blasts judge’s 2-week halt to his Washington golf project and says administration will appeal
text:
Trump blasts judge’s 2-week halt to his Washington golf project and says administration will appeal
President Donald Trump on Sunday decried a “highly destructive and political decision” from a federal judge who ordered a two-week delay on renovations at a historic Washington public golf course that he has been trying to redevelop into a championship-level venue.
Video above: Post-midterms, President Trump focuses on DC beautification projects
In a social media post, Trump said his administration will “immediately appeal, on an expedited basis,” the temporary restraining order from U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, which she issued just before East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months.
“It is in a terrible state of disrepair, as anybody can see by just looking at the pictures that are now circulating all over the Country, and in the Court,” said Trump, who spent much of the weekend posting photos on his social media site of the golf course. “They don’t call it Trash Island for no reason!”
Trump had announced work on the site along the Potomac River would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.
The plaintiffs argue that the president's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something Trump has denied. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would “irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest.”
The president’s public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the judge's decision.
Reyes, in her ruling Saturday, noted that those posts presented a problem for the government, indicating that Trump's redevelopment plan was final and that the National Park Service "will close the Park to implement it.”
Both points, she wrote, "favor granting Plaintiffs’ motion for another temporary restraining order.”
The order is in effect through Nov. 28. The park’s redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation’s capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.
Reyes’ order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump’s projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project.

title: Bangor Savings Bank helps Veggies to Table grow and share more with $5,500 grant
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new produce wash & pack station at Veggies to Table is one step closer to reality, thanks to a generous $5,500 grant from Bangor Savings Bank alongside $22,000 raised at the farm’s recent Harvest Dinner at The Contented Sole. The covered workspace will give staff and volunteers a sheltered place to wash, dry, and pack freshly harvested crops for donation.
The farm’s current setup is exposed to the weather and lacks proper drainage, making it more difficult to keep harvested produce fresh and beautiful through cold, damp days and summer heat. With shelter, electricity, better drainage, and more room to work, the team will be able to prepare donations more efficiently, freeing up time and hands to grow and share more nourishing produce and joyful flowers.
Bangor Savings Bank’s grant supports the project’s first phase: preparing the gravel pad and bringing electricity to the site. Growing community support from the bank and Harvest Dinner guests and supporters provides a strong foundation as fundraising continues for constructing and outfitting the station.
Veggies to Table is still raising funds to complete the project, and every gift helps. To be part of bringing more nutritious food, flowers, connection, and hope to the community, visit www.veggiestotable.org/donate or reach out to info@veggiestotable.org.
Everything Veggies to Table grows, they donate in collaboration with 35+ local partners, including food pantries, schools, summer lunch programs and hospitals—filling hungry stomachs and lifting spirits along the way. Since 2019, the organization has grown and donated more than 100,000 pounds of organic produce to communities throughout Midcoast Maine.

title: Police say pilot killed in Monday crash in Sweden was Lovell man
text:
SWEDEN — The pilot whose Cessna crashed near Smarts Hill Road on Monday afternoon has been identified as 65-year-old William Connelly of Lovell.
Investigators said Connelly had flown out of the Fryeburg airport Monday afternoon before he crashed about 3:45 p.m. in the area of 201 Smarts Hill Road.
His plane went down less than 12 miles from his home in Lovell.
Emergency crews who first responded to the crash site reported that the pilot was dead when they arrived.
The cause of the wreck remained unknown Tuesday. The Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation and Safety Board are investigating.
Connelly was alone in the Cessna 182 four-seat, single-engine plane when it crashed. The plane was registered in 2023, according to online aviation sources.
The crash site was closed overnight as federal investigators arrived at the scene and began probing for the cause.
On social media on Tuesday, friends and family of Connelly reacted to the news about the crash. In various conversations, he was described as “fun loving” and “talented.”
“He was an incredible human being,” one woman wrote.
“A great man in so many ways,” offered another.
Federal officials did not provide an estimate of how long their investigation will last or when their findings will be released.

title: Parts of Androscoggin County Courthouse closed due to elevated mold levels
text:
Parts of Androscoggin County Courthouse closed due to elevated levels of mold
The Maine Judicial Branch is no longer using parts of the Androscoggin County Courthouse after environmental testing revealed elevated levels of mold in some areas of the Auburn building.
Officials said the testing was conducted after concerns were raised about the courthouse's condition.
The Judicial Branch said it is working with Androscoggin County, which owns the building, to remove the mold and make needed repairs.
The parts of the courthouse with elevated mold levels will be retested to ensure that the problems have been eradicated before any of the affected areas of the building are reopened.

title: Norway Savings Bank donates $15,000 to United Way in Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — In recognition of their shared mission of improving lives and channeling the caring power of communities, Norway Savings Bank was pleased to recently donate $15,000 to three local United Way organizations: United Way of Southern Maine, United Way of Mid Coast Maine and United Way of Western Maine.
Though the programming is varied, all three organizations bring people, ideas, and resources together to tackle issues like food insecurity, housing challenges, literacy gaps and access to healthcare through initiatives that:
- move individuals and families from homelessness to safe housing
- increase access for those in need to high quality, nutritious foods and offer nutrition programs
- connect people with heating assistance
- mitigate the dangers of substance use
- coordinate essential medical and dental care
- provide referrals to mental health or addiction resources
- educate on violence prevention
- invest in community schools that offer before and after school programming
- host volunteer readers in classrooms and provide mentors
“Because of NSB’s generosity, many of our friends and neighbors will have a brighter future. Critical life-changing programs will be available, as well as programs that prevent serious problems from occurring in the first place,” Joleen Bedard, president and CEO of United Way of Western Maine, said.
“Norway Savings Bank’s investment makes it possible for United Way to bring people together to solve community challenges that a single organization wouldn’t be able to do on its own. Together, we’re building a connected community where everyone belongs, has the resources they need and can fulfill their potential,” Nicole Evans, executive director of United Way of Mid Coast Maine, said.

title: York County Food Hub distributes over 30K pounds of food in first month
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Just over a month in operation, a new resource to fight growing food insecurity in York County is already making a significant impact on anti-hunger organizations, local leaders say.
The York County Food Hub opened in Biddeford in early October and has already taken in close to 30,000 pounds of food and distributed it to 17 community resources.
Soon, schools will be picking up and using produce from the hub, board President Alex Gramling said.
“We’re just getting started,” he said Tuesday. “We’ve made significant progress in a short period of time.”
COST OF FOOD AN ISSUE
What makes the program possible is the sheer size of the hub, Gramling said. With 7,500 square feet of dry and cold storage, the hub can store and distribute far more food than the average pantry.
Because of its ability to store such large quantities of food, the hub is able to donate to pantries and anti-hunger resources throughout the county, filling a gap that they can’t always meet.
And with the cost of food on the rise, pantries are seeing more and more customers each month, increasing the amount of food pantries need to keep people fed.
“I had a leader at one pantry tell me that their food cost has quadrupled in the last five years,” Gramling said. “That’s not sustainable. We can help them stretch their budget.”
WORKING TOGETHER TO FIGHT HUNGER
The hub isn’t working alone. It’s partnered with Good Shepherd Food Bank — a nonprofit that’s the largest hunger-relief organization in Maine — and Farms for Food Equity, a network of farms that have agreed to sell their produce to anti-hunger and charitable food organizations at a significant discount.
Currently, Farms for Food Equity only distributes food to organizations in Cumberland County and other counties farther north. By working with the food hub, that distribution will also stretch to York County.
“That will give us access to hundreds of thousands of pounds of Maine-grown produce,” Gramling said.
On Tuesday, Hannaford Supermarkets also announced a partnership with the food hub, investing $40,000 to help expand access to nutritious food in southern Maine. The majority of that funding will be utilized for transportation and cold storage needs, while the remainder will be used to purchase fresh food to help stock the hub.
Hannaford President Mike Vail said in a news release that caring for the community means helping neighbors access the healthy food they need to survive.
“We’re proud to support York County Food Hub and the local partnerships that are bringing this important resource to life,” Vail said. “We’re helping strengthen the foundation for food access in York County in our continued commitment to communities across Maine.”
THE GIVERS AND RECEIVERS
The hub’s food supply comes from multiple different sources, Gramling said. The Maine Food Bank, operated by Good Shepherd, is a significant provider. Other resources include local farms and organizations like Farms for Food Equity, supermarkets and donations.
Last week, the hub received a donation of 2,500 pounds of apples from a local farmer. It was the end of his growing season, and he didn’t want to see the fruit go to waste.
Most food pantries wouldn’t be able to take that donation, Gramling said — they simply don’t have the space to store that much food.
“We’re able to,” he said. “We can store it and distribute it.”
The pantries and anti-hunger organizations receiving those donations are from all across York County. Gramling estimates there are about 50 such programs in the county, and all of them are welcome to use the hub.
So far, about 17 pantries and organizations have used the hub. Gramling expects that to grow as the resource gains traction.
“We’re very excited about the progress and feedback from other pantries and other small meal programs,” he said. “This is truly a countywide solution.”

title: Jackson Lab working with Maine oncologists on cancer biomarker testing
text:
BAR HARBOR, Maine (WABI) - Scientists at The Jackson Lab are working with oncologists around Maine on biomarker testing used to diagnose and treat cancer.
Lindsey Kelley, a board-certified genetic counselor for Jackson Lab, said biomarker testing can be a key component of diagnosing and treating cancer.
What biomarkers are
“Biomarkers in general are a test result that gives us an idea about someone’s health or a disease they might have. Biomarkers that people might be familiar with are things like blood pressure monitoring or cholesterol testing,” Kelley said.
Cancer is caused when the DNA in cells changes. Biomarkers can focus on a particular part of the body. HER2 is a biomarker for breast cancer, and EGFR is a biomarker for lung cancer.
Biomarkers can be tested through bloodwork or tissue samples.
Biomarker testing differs from genetic testing because it focuses solely on tumor cells, as opposed to inherited cells that could increase the risk for cancer.
How testing is used
“We actually do a testing of the tumor itself, or the tumor DNA in the bloodstream, and we use that information to give us a better idea about what might have caused that cancer, how it’s growing, how we expect it to progress and then how we might be able to treat it best,” Kelley said.
Kelley said biomarkers also can be used to monitor patients.
“We could monitor biomarkers to see if any of them are starting to look like there might be a presence of cancer. We can use biomarkers as another way to monitor response to treatment. In addition to that, patients who have finished their treatment, are being monitored to just ensure there’s no recurrence of that cancer,” she said.
Availability in Maine
Cancer biomarker testing is available in Maine. How readily a patient can get it depends on the cancer, the provider and insurance coverage.
Jackson Lab developed the Maine Cancer Genomics Initiative, which offers free support to oncologists throughout the state.
“Some oncologists will reach out to us when they have a result that they’re really struggling to understand. We have other oncologists that do send almost every test report to us, just for a second opinion. So that any cancer patient in Maine is really receiving the same type of cutting edge care no matter where they live,” Kelley said.
Legislation on insurance coverage
Last year, a bill to require health insurance coverage for biomarker testing was introduced in the Maine Legislature. It passed in the House but did not pass the Senate before lawmakers adjourned for the session.

title: Analysis: Team defense and goaltending put UMaine men’s hockey on positive path
text:
The University of Maine’s hockey team picked up a valuable four points in its two-game series against Vermont over the weekend.
Saturday’s 3-1 victory followed a scoreless tie Friday night, when Vermont won the shootout to earn the extra point in the standings.
In Hockey East, teams receive three points for a regulation win; two for a victory in overtime or the shootout; and one for an overtime or shootout loss. The NCAA doesn’t acknowledge shootouts.
But in the NCAA Power Index, which has replaced the Pairwise Rankings as the NCAA Tournament selection ratings process, an overtime victor receives credit for 60% of a win and the loser picks up 40% of a win.
If the game goes to a shootout, each team is credited with 50% of a win.
UMaine is currently 18th in the NCAA Power Index as the result of its 6-5-1 start.
UMaine will enter this weekend’s home series against Boston College as the country’s sixth stingiest team among 62 Division I programs, allowing only 1.83 goals per game.
That’s largely thanks to senior goaltender Albin Boija, who was named the Hockey East Goaltender of the Week after stopping 44 of 45 shots in the two games at Vermont.
Boija has now allowed only one goal over his last 208 minutes and 13 seconds.
He produced back-to-back shutouts against UMass and Vermont. The senior now has 13 career shutouts and is just two away from tying longtime Detroit Red Wings goaltender Jimmy Howard’s school career record.
Boija has been looking like the second-team All-American that he was two years ago, bouncing back well from last season’s forgettable campaign. He’s been tracking the puck more effectively, squaring himself to the shooters and hanging onto pucks rather than spilling rebounds. Boija has also done a better job against initial shots, which gave him issues a year ago.
His 1.51 goals-against average is seventh best in the country, and his .932 save percentage is 19th. His GAA was 2.59 a year ago with a save percentage of .899.
It should also be pointed out that the team’s overall defensive play has been much better this season. The defensive corps, according to sixth-year head coach Ben Barr, is the most mobile group he’s had at UMaine.
That’s helping the Black Bears spend less time in their own zone, because the defensemen can skate the puck out of the zone on their own if they don’t have someone available to receive a breakout pass.
The forwards have also been doing a much better job handling their defensive responsibilities.
UMaine is allowing almost a goal per game less than a year ago. Last year’s team surrendered 2.7 goals per game. The Black Bears are 19th in the country in blocked shots with 150.
Goal scoring is still an issue, as the team’s 2.33 goals per game is tied for 45th in the country.
The power play will come into the Boston College series without a goal in its last five games and 13 opportunities.
Goal scoring was always going to be an issue for this team due to the loss of last year’s top four point-getters. Still, as long as the Black Bears maintain their defensive prowess and continue to outwork teams, and if Boija continues to give them elite-level goaltending, they won’t need many goals to win games.
UMaine may not have any 20-goal scorers, but the Black Bears have enough players capable of producing 8 to 14 goals to carve out close, low-scoring victories.

title: Bruins shut out by Kings
text:
BOSTON — Darcy Kuemper stopped 29 shots for his 40th career shutout, including Morgan Geekie’s third-period penalty shot, and Mats Zuccarello scored an early goal as the Los Angeles Kings beat the Boston Bruins 3-0 on Tuesday night to snap a four-game skid.
Andre Lee and Erik Gustafsson also scored for the Kings, who picked up just their sixth win.
Michael DiPietro made 19 saves for the Bruins, who lost their third straight for the first time this season.
Kuemper made a left-pad stop on Geekie’s penalty shot wrister en route to his first shutout this season.
The previous eight games in Boston between the teams were decided in overtime or a shootout, with the Kings winning five.
DiPietro made a splendid glove stop on Quinton Byfield’s second-period penalty shot. Byfield went wide left and cut in before firing a backhand shot.
Boston lost its last two games against two of the league’s better teams — Minnesota and Montreal — by a combined score of 11-4.
Coming into the game a point ahead of the West’s basement, the Kings went ahead 1-0 when Zuccarello’s wrister from the left circle slipped inside the near post 15:46 into the game.
Cutting in front, Lee had Scott Laughton’s pass carom in off his left knee for a goal that made it 2-0 in the second.
Los Angeles defenseman Drew Doughty played his 1,297th game with the club, moving past Dustin Brown for second on the team’s all-time list behind Anze Kopitar’s 1,521.
Boston won 4-1 in Los Angeles on Oct. 17 in the teams’ other meeting this season.
The Kings came in with the NHL’s worst penalty kill percentage, allowing 11 goals in 22 chances, but kept Boston scoreless in two opportunities.
Artemi Panarin, who leads the Kings with 19 points in 17 games, missed his second straight game because of a family matter.
Up next
Kings: At Toronto on Thursday
Bruins: At Detroit on Wednesday

title: Experts say to ‘stop and verify’ before you click pay this holiday season
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Bank of America says phony shipping notices, “too good to be true” deals and fake donation QR codes are popping up as scammers gear up for the holiday rush.
Jen Ehresman, head of consumer client protection at Bank of America, said the bank’s top advice is to stop and verify.
“Our best piece of advice is stop and verify. And price is always a red flag. If it’s too good to be true, it’s too good to be true. But we also suggest beware of unexpected links. Unexpected messages asking you to click on a link or fix an issue or you have a problem with your account,” Ehresman said.
Ehresman said the best thing shoppers can do while hunting for deals and getting gifts shipped is slow down. That means stopping to verify before clicking a link or paying.
Ehresman also warned that artificial intelligence is making scams look more real.
“AI creates a lot of convenience for our clients. And there are definitely opportunities on that front. But obviously, AI has also made things look more authentic. It makes it difficult to spot suspicious emails, calls, texts,” she said.
Ehresman said shoppers should not click through from a text or a social media ad. Instead, they should leave the app, go straight to the retailer’s real website and do a quick search for complaints, such as “never got my merchandise.”
Anyone who falls for a scam should not wait. They should contact their bank right away, lock their cards and save any emails and texts. They should also tell friends and family so they do not fall for the same trick.

title: Owls Head official says neighboring fire department discharged toxic foam in town
text:
Officials in the Knox County town of Owls Head are weighing how to address a neighboring fire department’s discharge of what they believe is toxic firefighting foam in their town.
Owls Head Town Administrator Rodney Mason took to the podium to address the Select Board at Monday’s meeting, noting he is not only the town administrator but also a property owner.
He said, on the night of Nov. 2, he was near the intersection of Ash Point Drive and North Shore Road in Owls Head when he saw a fire truck spraying water.
Mason said he contacted the Owls Head fire chief, who said it wasn’t the local department. It was later confirmed to be a South Thomaston truck, Mason said, and “they accidentally released some firefighting foam” into their apparatus and were “flushing it out.”
That left Mason with several questions, he said, including, “What are they doing here at 8 o’clock at night cleaning out an engine or tanker?”
In the process of “flushing out” the foam, Mason said, water spread through the area and passing cars drove through it, and it washed away gravel and soil in the area.
The town administrator said he took photos the morning after the incident. A photo obtained by the Midcoast Villager, which was first to report the incident, shows foam in a culvert.
Mason said that samples have been taken and the matter has been referred to the Department of Environmental Protection’s PFAS unit, and that they plan to “expedite” the testing of the samples.
A spokesperson for the Maine DEP could not be reached Tuesday night.
Long-term exposure to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS, is linked to high cholesterol, liver damage, developmental delays and cancer. They are known as forever chemicals because they don’t break down in nature and build up in the body.
Firefighters use firefighting foam, which contains PFAS, to knock down fires through oxygen depletion. It is mainly used in instances when water can potentially make matters worse, such as chemical fires.
Mason explained that while “all these chemicals are really good at what they do” for firefighting, they are not safe for humans or the environment.
As awareness of the forever chemicals’ repercussions has spread, some fire departments have switched to PFAS-free firefighting foam. However, it is estimated that over 9,000 gallons of PFAS-laden chemicals are stored at local fire stations in Maine, and the state is trying to secure funds for cleanup.
Owls Head select board members are weighing how to address the issue with their neighboring town. Some at Monday’s meeting noted the potential availability of state funding for cleanup efforts, referencing the August 2024 spill at Brunswick landing in which 1,450 gallons of aqueous film-forming foam concentrate mixed with 50,000 gallons of water to create the biggest accidental discharge in Maine since it began keeping records in the 1990s.
Over the last decade, Maine has spent more than $100 million as it became a national leader in the fight against PFAS, but dwindling funds have complicated matters.
South Thomaston officials could not be reached for comment Tuesday night.

title: Maine House Republican accused of domestic violence resigns
text:
If you or someone you know is experiencing domestic violence and would like to talk with an advocate, call 866-834-4357, TTY 1-800-437-1220. This free, confidential service is available 24/7 and is accessible from anywhere in Maine.
A Maine House Republican facing domestic violence accusations has resigned.
Rep. Lucas Lanigan, R-Sanford, submitted his resignation Monday, according to the office of House Speaker Ryan Fecteau, D-Biddeford.
A profile for Lanigan on the Legislature’s website says he has resigned the seat for District 141, which includes part of Springvale, part of Sanford, Newfield and Shapleigh.
In October 2024, Lanigan’s romantic partner confronted him and another woman at Springvale Safe Storage on River Street about an affair, according to a police affidavit.
An argument ensued, during which Lanigan allegedly put his hands around his partner’s throat and “choked her for approximately 20 seconds,” Sanford police Sgt. Jeremy Riddle wrote.
She freed herself and returned home, where she called friends, who then reported the alleged assault to police that afternoon, according to the affidavit. The Bangor Daily News does not name victims of alleged violent crimes without their consent.
She was then taken to Maine Medical Center in Portland, where an examination found bruising around her neck, as well as small marks on her face and nose and in her mouth consistent with bleeding under the skin, according to the affidavit.
Lanigan turned himself in at the York County Jail in Alfred three days later. He made his first appearance in court on the domestic violence charge just before Halloween 2024. During that hearing, his partner denied the assault happened, saying the case should be dropped.
That case continues to wind through the court system.
Fecteau on Monday evening chastised Lanigan for not resigning sooner, calling the charges against him “most serious.”
“His refusal to step down – despite the extremely serious charges against him – was a disservice to the legislature and a profound disservice to every person in House District 141. Maine people expect and deserve far better from their elected officials,” Fecteau said in a statement.
The domestic violence aggravated assault charge made Lanigan’s political fate precarious heading into the 2024 election. Just two years earlier, he held onto the District 141 seat by 12 points. He ultimately prevailed over Democrat Patricia Kidder by a single vote. He did not run for reelection this year.
House District 141 will be represented in Augusta for the next two years by Republican Marc A. Boisse.
Before joining the Legislature, Lanigan served on the Sanford City Council from 2016 to 2021, and had a stint as the city’s deputy mayor.

title: Ground stop sparks Thanksgiving travel concerns
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Aging systems are being blamed for last week’s nationwide ground stop that disrupted an estimated 46,000 flights, as Americans prepare for the busiest travel week of the year.
Trump comments on the ground stop
President Trump blamed old infrastructure, broken equipment and Biden for the ground stop.
“I don’t take any responsibility,” Trump said.
Flight cancellations and delays
The Federal Aviation Administration estimates 18,000 flights were canceled and 28,000 were delayed as a result of the incident.
Thanksgiving travel outlook
AAA predicts 81 million Americans will travel for Thanksgiving. Nearly 6 million of them are expected to travel by plane.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said he expects air travel operations to be restored before the holiday.
“I think we’re going to be back up and operational as we head into the heat of the Thanksgiving travel operation,” Duffy said.
Questions about new AI system
The FAA maintains the ground stop was unrelated to the rollout of its new AI smart system overhaul.
Earlier this month, House Democrats sent a letter to the Government Accountability Office requesting a closer look at the new software, citing possible safety concerns.
Duffy said he will hold a news conference Tuesday to provide important updates.

title: Nationwide emergency alert test set for 2:20 p.m. today
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - A nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System will briefly interrupt television and radio programming at 2:20 p.m. today, Tuesday, Nov. 17.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency and the Federal Communications Commission will conduct the test. No action is required by the public.
The interruption is expected to last about one minute. Viewers and listeners will hear a message identifying the alert as a nationwide test. Cellphone alerts will not be part of today’s test.
If an actual emergency or significant weather event requires officials to postpone the test, the backup date is Dec. 3.
FEMA conducts nationwide tests to identify technical or operational problems before the system is needed during an emergency. Federal law requires testing at least once every three years.

title: Ogunquit family files federal lawsuit against town over rooster sculptures
text:
An Ogunquit family has filed a federal lawsuit against the town after being fined thousands for displaying tin rooster sculptures.
David and Sara LeBlanc announced the suit Tuesday morning amid months of debate over whether the 6-foot tin roosters are illegal advertising for The Omelette Factory — a restaurant owned by the family, which is also attached to their home.
The sculptures have nothing to do with the restaurant, the LeBlancs say, and are instead a source of comfort for their 6-year-old daughter, Pyper, who has autism. Town officials have held that the roosters are a violation of the sign ordinance and repeatedly ordered the family to remove them.
“Roosters are (Pyper’s) favorite animal,” reads the complaint, filed Monday in U.S. District Court in Portland. “She chose roosters as her own symbol. … The six-foot tin rooster became a landmark, a ritual, and a source of safety for her.”
Since June, the code enforcement office has fined the family more than $2,000. In October, the family warned town officials of potential litigation if the fines continued.
“The LeBlancs are asking the court to declare the town’s enforcement unconstitutional and to bar Ogunquit from fining, citing, or prosecuting them for displaying the roosters,” reads a news release from the Institute for Justice, the libertarian nonprofit law firm that’s representing the family.
The family is asking for a permanent injunction against the town that would exclude the roosters from sign code enforcement. The LeBlancs are also requesting the town pay for damages, including a reimbursement of the fines, as well as a symbolic $1 payment for violating their First Amendment rights.
The suit argues that the town’s sign code gives no guidance on how to distinguish decorations from signage, “so officials decide based on what they think a display means and who is displaying it.”
Daniel Woislaw, the LeBlancs’ attorney, said in October that town officials are misinterpreting what the sculptures represent by associating roosters with the egg-based restaurant — “notwithstanding that roosters don’t lay eggs.”
The issue has gained national attention, with 18,000 supporters following the “Roosters of Ogunquit” Facebook page. Hundreds of supporters have displayed their own sculptures in solidarity, and many now say they view roosters as a symbol for autism.
“According to the Town’s own records, no other person or business in Ogunquit has been fined, cited, or noticed for a violation of the sign code for displaying a rooster decoration on their property,” the suit reads.
Code enforcement officer Tyler McOsker has not responded to several requests for comment on the dispute since June; neither he nor Town Manager Matthew Buttrick immediately responded to renewed requests Tuesday. In a June statement, Assistant Town Manager Mandy Cummings defended McOsker’s actions as fulfilling the responsibilities of his office and said the town would not be commenting further on the dispute with the LeBlancs.
The town has roughly three weeks to file a response in court, according to a summons.

title: Widespread outage hits Apple services, including Apple Pay, iCloud, reports say
text:
(AP) - An update gone awry Tuesday at Apple followed a rash of major outages in recent days, including problems affecting the Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines and Microsoft.
Apple acknowledged on its system status page that its Apple Music, App Store and AppleCare services suffered full outages and that its iCloud sign-in interface was also having issues. The technology monitoring site Downdetector.com also showed a spike in user complaints about Apple Pay.
“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” the company said in an emailed statement. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”
EN ESPAÑOL | Reportan interrupciones en los servicios de Apple
Marriott International, the largest U.S. hotel operator, also had technology issues, according to users posting on Reddit. Downdetector.com also reported that Marriott was experiencing an outage.
In an emailed statement, Marriott said it has “resolved a technical issue” that affected sign-in capabilities on Marriott.com and the Marriott Bonvoy app. The company added that a company review found no sign the problem “was cybersecurity-related.”
The outages are the latest in a string of technology breakdowns.
On Monday, a system outage at United Airlines lasted more than 90 minutes, forcing the carrier to delay departing flights. The problem at United came just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop that delayed hundreds of flights and stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country.
Chicago-based United said there was no indication its outage was cybersecurity-related.
Also Monday, thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
Chase said Monday the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and on Tuesday confirmed the bank’s systems were operating normally.
Last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business chatter and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted.
The tech giant said there was “no indication” that malicious activity caused the disruptions, specifically noting on Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.

title: Pres. Trump travels for Asia summits
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President DonaldTrump is off to Asia for two high stakes summits.
Just weeks after Republicans were handed big losses during the Midterms, President Trump turns his attention to foreign affairs with two consequential summits in Asia.
The President’s first stop is Manila in the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit. There he will meet with the leaders of Japan, Australia and India. He will also sign a trade agreement with Thailand.
Then it’s off to Shenzen, China for the APEC Summit. The President said he does not plan to raise spying allegations regarding Nvidia with President Xi. Monday morning, President Trump told reporters upon departure from the White House, “You know, we’re heading to China, and I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get on your meeting.”
Also on the President’s agenda- an historic trilateral meeting with President Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin - where the three leaders are expected to discuss nuclear disarmament, and a possible meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. President Trump confirmed to reporters that the meeting is on the table, “Yes, we might have Kim Jong un. He may come, I don’t know. That’s up to President Xi.”
Three separate summits between Kim and President Trump have failed to lead to any curb in North Korea’s nuclear program.
This will be President Trump’s second trip to China this year. The U.S. and China just last week extended a trade truce that is due to expire in early January.

title: Trump nominates Army Chief of Staff after previous chief was asked to step down in April
text:
Trump nominates Army Chief of Staff after previous chief was asked to step down in April
The Trump administration has nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to be Chief of Staff of the Army — the top uniformed post in the service — after he stepped into the job as interim chief for months following the unexplained firing of Gen. Randy George in April.
Video above: President Trump names Stephen Miller chief of staff amid debate over immigration enforcement
Adam Telle, the man currently serving as the acting Secretary of the Army following the departure of Dan Driscoll from the top civilian post in August, said that LaNeve “is the right leader at the right time to modernize the Army and ensure our Soldiers are prepared to dominate on any battlefield” in a post to social media.
“For 36 years, I’ve served in the U.S. Army currently as the Vice Chief of Staff,” LaNeve said in a statement. “I’m deeply honored by the President’s trust and confidence for the nomination to serve as the Chief of Staff of the Army and if confirmed, I look forward to continuing to serve our Soldiers, their families and our nation.”
LaNeve has seen a meteoric rise through the ranks since the start of the Trump administration. LaNeve was promoted to be Hegseth’s top military aide shortly after he arrived at the Pentagon and was suddenly nominated to be the Army’s vice chief of staff last October even though there was an officer in the job at the time.

title: Janet Mills' transportation commissioner is resigning
text:
Maine’s transportation commissioner is resigning.
Dale Doughty plans to retire effective Nov. 28, according to the office of Gov. Janet Mills.
“Dale’s focus has always been creating safer, more reliable infrastructure for the next generation through his effective, pragmatic leadership. I’m grateful for Dale’s decades of service to Maine’s communities and for his leadership in my Administration. I wish him the best in retirement,” Mills said in a Monday statement.
That caps 30 years of public service for Doughty. He joined the Maine Department of Transportation in 1996, holding various roles during his career.
In 2018, he left the Department of Transportation for a stint as Lewiston’s public works director.
Doughty returned to the Department of Transportation in 2024, when he was appointed deputy commissioner. He then succeeded Bruce Van Note as transportation commissioner earlier this year.
“Serving the people of Maine alongside the dedicated employees of MaineDOT has been an honor,” Doughty said in a statement. “I’m grateful to Governor Mills for her trust and support, and to the colleagues and partners who work every day to keep our communities connected and our transportation system reliable. As I prepare to retire, I take the greatest pride in the people of this department and their commitment to Maine.”
Doughty earned bachelor’s degrees in geology and chemistry from the University of Maine at Farmington and graduate degrees from the University of West Virginia.
Before entering public service, he worked for geotechnical and geological engineering firms.

title: US monitoring reported Iran dirty bomb plans; White House says ‘no credible threats’
text:
WASHINGTON D.C. (CNN) - New U.S. intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans to detonate a so-called “dirty bomb” in Washington, D.C., according to a report.
Sources familiar with the information reportedly characterized the planning as an effort by Iran to give itself options, rather than an indication of an imminent attack.
But sources say the potential plot targeting senior Trump administration officials has prompted U.S. contingency planning.
In a statement, White House officials said the U.S. is “monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland.”
