title: Medication used to treat blood pressure recalled over possible metal contamination
text:
Medication used to treat blood pressure recalled over possible metal contamination, company says
A pharmaceutical company has issued a voluntary nationwide recall after it said a lot of medication used to typically treat blood pressure may be contaminated with metal.
Breckenridge Pharmaceutical Inc. issued a voluntary recall for one lot of 60 mg propranolol hydrochloride extended-release capsules. The effected lot, PK25110035, has an expiration date labeled as May 2029.
The company said the medication was distributed nationwide to wholesalers and pharmacies between Oct. 26, 2026, and Nov. 4, 2026.
Related video: How to stay ahead of recalls
"Use of product from the affected lot could potentially cause lacerations of soft tissues in the oral cavity, esophagus, stomach, or intestine," the company said on its website. "The affected lot shared intermediate material suspected to be the source of metal contamination identified in a separate lot that was not released to market."
Breckenridge Pharmaceutical said it is not aware of any adverse events assessed to be related to the recall.
Consumers are asked to stop use of the product from the recalled lot and contact their doctor or healthcare provider for medical advice and replacement instructions. The company also advised consumers to return any unused portion of the affected product to the pharmacy where it was picked up.
The company also urged wholesalers, pharmacies, and other retailers to check their inventories.
According to the Cleveland Clinic, propranolol hydrochloride extended-release capsules help to treat many conditions, including high blood pressure and heart disease. The clinic says the medication works by lowering blood pressure and heart rate, making it easier to pump blood through the rest of the body.

title: What to discuss before marrying later in life: Money, caregiving, kids
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — Falling in love later in life can be exciting and can feel like a fresh start. But when it comes to saying “I do,” there are some unique considerations for older couples.
Treat marriage as a legal and financial decision
“This is a legal and a financial decision,” Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “If you’re going to go into business with somebody, you better know who you’re going into business with, because business partners can absolutely take your feet out from underneath of you.”
Talk about money and caregiving
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said couples should start with the practical questions.
“Talk about money. How are you going to pay the bills? How are you going to mesh money? Are you going to mesh your money?” O’Rourke said.
She said caregiving should be part of the conversation, too.
Couples should ask: “If I need care, are you going to provide for it? Are you going to arrange it?” O’Rourke said.
Think about how the kids will get along
O’Rourke said couples should also talk about how their children will get along.
She described a couple whose children worked together for them.
“They were doing it beautifully,” O’Rourke said.
O’Rourke said she took one of the daughters aside and asked what the secret was.
“She said, ‘My parents didn’t give us an option,’” O’Rourke said.
The daughter told her the parents sat down with the children and said their expectation was that when they needed help, the children would work together, O’Rourke said.
“Not everybody can do that, but I think involving the children to some level, not to get permission, but involving them, is a really healthy thing to do,” O’Rourke said.
You’re marrying the whole family
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said marriage is a family affair.
“You’re not just marrying the person. You’re marrying the family. You’re marrying your history,” Rogers said.
“You’re marrying everything that came along with them. Everything that they are didn’t just happen at 40, 50 and 60. They’re bringing some stuff with them and you need to investigate that,” she said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said it’s “very complex.”
“Love is emotional, but this business arrangement, asset protection, is very practical, and it’s a matter of doing both,” Ambrose said.
Why adult children may want a say
Ambrose said adult children can feel they are in a position to give permission or weigh in, adding that it can become touchy and manipulative.
Loyalty can also play a role in a second marriage, Cradduck added.
“If it’s your mom getting married again, you could be loyal to your dad, and you’re concerned that he’s alone, or however the marriage ended, or if it was in death,” Cradduck said.
Inheritance can be another concern.
“What’s that mean to all the things that you and my parent, the other parent, developed and earned? And so what’s that going to mean to me in the future? And so a lot of times the kids weigh in,” Cradduck said.
Plan with an estate planning attorney
Even when children do not weigh in, they may need to be involved, Ambrose said.
“Death order has a big impact,” Ambrose said. “Which one dies first, and say, there’s legal implications here, so be sure to work with an estate planning attorney.”

title: Court blocks Pentagon from expelling several transgender troops from US military
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal appeals court on Tuesday blocked the Pentagon from forcing more than two dozen transgender troops out of the military, several months after it found that President Donald Trump’s administration unlawfully imposed the ban.
The decision — implementing an earlier ruling by the same appeals court panel — could set the stage for the issue to return to the Supreme Court, which previously allowed the ban to go forward for now in a different case.
Trump’s administration had asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit to delay the June 1 ruling’s implementation while it petitions the Supreme Court to take up the case. A three-judge panel voted 2-1 on Tuesday to reject the administration’s request for a stay of the circuit’s decision.
The Supreme Court had ruled in the administration’s favor last year, allowing the Pentagon to start enforcing the ban while the litigation proceeded.
Circuit Judge Robert Wilkins, partially joined by Judge Judith Rogers, ruled in June that the Pentagon’s policy was designed to exclude people from the military based on their gender identity. Their majority decision would bar the military from kicking out current service members named in the lawsuit, but it wouldn’t allow new transgender recruits to join.
Plaintiffs’ attorneys challenging the Pentagon ban say 27 service members are covered by Tuesday’s order. Shannon Minter, legal director of the National Center for LGBTQ Rights, said the plaintiffs are all “decorated troops who have met every standard the military sets.”
“The Trump administration asked the court to let it keep pushing these service members toward the door while it tries to get a different answer from the Supreme Court. Today, the D.C. Circuit said no,” Minter said in a statement.
On Tuesday, Wilkins said the administration hasn’t shown how retaining the plaintiffs currently serving in the military would cause any irreparable harm to the government or endanger national security. Wilkins also noted that the scope of the June 1 majority opinion was narrower than the injunction that the Supreme Court stayed last year.
“To the extent the government suggests that any injunction against the Executive Branch imposes irreparable harm, I am also unpersuaded,” Wilkins wrote.
The panel’s June 1 majority opinion partially upheld a March 2025 ruling by U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, who concluded that Trump’s executive order to exclude transgender troops from military service likely violates their constitutional rights.
A spokesperson for Hegseth’s office declined to comment on the court’s ruling.
In January 2025, Trump signed an executive order that claims the sexual identity of transgender service members “conflicts with a soldier’s commitment to an honorable, truthful, and disciplined lifestyle, even in one’s personal life” and is harmful to military readiness.
In response, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a policy that presumptively disqualifies people with gender dysphoria from military service. Gender dysphoria is the distress that a person feels because their assigned gender and gender identity don’t match. The medical condition has been linked to depression and suicidal thoughts.
Wilkins was nominated to the court by Democratic President Barack Obama. Rogers was nominated by President Bill Clinton, also a Democrat.
Circuit Judge Justin Walker, who was nominated by Trump, a Republican, wrote a dissenting opinion in June that said judges lack the power to second-guess the decision to exclude transgender troops. Walker also voted to grant the government’s request to suspend the decision.

title: Cruise ships bring $22M spending boost to Portland area: study
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
“When a passenger has lunch in the Old Port or picks out a gift at a local shop, that purchase matters,” said Lynn Tillotson, president and CEO of Visit Portland. “At an average of $76 per visitor, those purchases add up over a cruise season.”
Cruise ship passengers and cruise lines generated $22 million in total spending in the Portland area during the 2025 season and supported the equivalent of 300 full-time local jobs, according to a study released Monday.
The figure includes $14.3 million in passenger and crew spending on food, beverages and retail shopping and $7.8 million spent by cruise lines, including $4.3 million in port fees and $2.3 million in marine services. The study shows that the economic impact extends well beyond the areas where passengers disembark, with visits to other communities including South Portland, Kennebunk and Freeport.
Cruise ship passenger and crew spending boosted Maine’s GDP by $17.5 million, supported more than 300 jobs and provided nearly $2 million in state tax revenue in 2025, the study shows.
The study, prepared by Digital Research Inc. for Visit Portland, is based on surveys conducted at Portland’s cruise ship piers between April 17 and Nov. 5, 2025. Researchers collected responses from 1,565 passengers and crew members arriving on 42 cruise ships during the season.
Researchers also found that the 2025 cruise ship season generated $1.8 million in state tax receipts.
“When a passenger has lunch in the Old Port or picks out a gift at a local shop, that purchase matters,” said Lynn Tillotson, president and CEO of Visit Portland. “At an average of $76 per visitor, those purchases add up over a cruise season.”
For many passengers, it’s their first visit to Portland, Tillotson noted.
“As they head back to the ship, our staff and volunteers often hear them say they’ll be back,” she said. “That’s a credit to our community and the people who make them feel welcome here.”

title: Maine Farmland Trust sells Portland office, lists Belfast building for sale in wake of layoffs
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Farmland Trust is selling its Belfast office and moving into a smaller building.
The asking price is $760,000 — down from the original ask of $836,000. The value of the property was assessed at $445,500, according to city property tax records.
The three-story downtown building on Main Street sits on 0.03 acres. It was built in 1860 and renovated in 2012, and offers a mix of retail and office space.
Maine Farmland Trust is a not-for-profit organization that protects farmland from development, supports farmers to keep farmland in production, and advocates for conditions that keeps farms and farmers productive, the trust says on its website.
The organization doesn’t need as much office space because the majority of employees choose to spend most or all of their workdays working remotely, MFT Communications Director Emily Lad said. That’s especially true of those who live outside of Belfast.
Maine Farmland Trust eliminated 10 jobs in July, citing rising costs and a “significantly different funding environment.” Downsizing office spaces will help reduce operating costs, the organization said.
In August, MFT sold its Portland office for $915,550.00. Employees moved into a smaller space on Union Wharf at the city’s waterfront in October, Lad said. An open house for the new office took place Tuesday.

title: Melbourne Cup horse So You Are found dead in a waste facility, sparking an inquiry
text:
SYDNEY (AP) — The body of Melbourne Cup horse So You Are was found in a waste facility in Sydney less than two weeks after competing in the most prestigious event in Australian horse racing.
The Sydney Morning Herald newspaper reported Tuesday that racing stewards were investigating after a construction worker saw a dead horse in a dumpster at a licensed waste center and posted a video on Facebook.
Trainer Bjorn Baker had released a statement Monday saying So You Are died following a severe bout of colic. The 5-year-old gelding was rushed to a specialist equine hospital for emergency veterinary treatment but couldn’t be saved.
Baker posted an update Tuesday after discovering So You Are hadn’t been properly buried.
“Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are’s remains,” Baker said in a statement. “He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death.”
So You Are placed eighth in the Melbourne Cup on Nov. 3, with Point of Law winning the 166th running of the 2-mile classic.
REC Equine Specialists managing partner Dr. Jonathan Lumsden issued a statement saying So You Are had been “humanely euthanized under anesthesia” after receiving emergency treatment.
“After his death, So You Are was collected by our contracted service provider and taken to a licensed landfill. He should have been promptly and respectfully buried,” Lumsden said. “What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone who cared for him. We are deeply sorry.”
Lumsden said he was working with the service provider and the state’s horse racing authority, Racing NSW, to establish what went wrong and to put in processes to ensure it never happens again.
“So You Are was in our care. We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that,” he said. “We should have known exactly how horses were handled after leaving our hospital, and we did not. That process is not good enough, and it must change.
“No owner should have to go through what So You Are’s connections have experienced this week.”
Racing NSW said So You Are was being held temporarily, awaiting burial, when the video was recorded.
“These images are distressing for all involved and for all of us who care deeply about our horses,” Racing NSW said in a statement. “The way in which So You Are’s body was left is distressing and completely unacceptable. So You Are deserved to be treated with dignity and respect.”
The state’s racing regulator said under industry guidelines — now under review — a licensed landfill was the preferred option for animals which have been euthanized because of the chemicals involved in the process.
“That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner,” the statement continued. “If through the course of our ongoing investigation any wrongdoing is found, Racing NSW will not hesitate to take appropriate action.”

title: Crews battle fire at home in Unity
text:
UNITY, Maine (WABI) - Fire officials say there were no injuries after a chimney fire caused “substantial damage” inside a Unity home Tuesday morning.
Fire crews were called to a home on Main Street around 6:30 am for a reported fire.
Officials say they found heavy fire and smoke on the driveway side of the home.
Officials say that all occupants of the home got out safely.
Firefighters were able to knock the fire down within 45 minutes.
Officials say a chimney fire had extended into the roof area and into the garage.
Unity Fire Capt. Blaine Parsons says regular chimney inspection is imperative come the winter season.
“If anybody’s got a trap door for their chimneys, take a mirror and look up it at least once a month, make sure there’s no creosote buildup. This is our second structure fire in the last couple weeks for the same exact thing, chimney fire with extension into the roof,” said Parsons.
Parsons says a quick response from mutual aid partners helped them save a major part of the house.

title: How to cook Thanksgiving dinner on a budget
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
With the cost of food on the rise, many Mainers might be feeling the pressure to put a delicious Thanksgiving dinner on the table – without breaking the bank.
The average cost of a Thanksgiving dinner for eight people in New England ranges from just over $60 to around $120, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation, which reported an average price for dinner of $60.82 in 2025.
As more and more Mainers struggle to afford the essentials, many might be looking for ways to trim the costs, but still have all the trimmings.
To find the least expensive way to cook a Thanksgiving dinner for eight, we visited several grocery stores in southern Maine and compared the prices of popular holiday meal items to find some places where you might find the best deals for dinner.
What you’re getting: A 12-pound turkey (enough to feed eight), gravy, stuffing mix, cranberry sauce, carrots, celery, dinner rolls, sweet potatoes and ingredients for mashed potatoes, green bean casserole and pumpkin pie.
Price comparisons were conducted the weeks of Nov. 2-6 and Nov. 9-13.
MARKET BASKET: $52.37, or $6.54 per person
The grocery store with the lowest prices for ingredients for Thanksgiving dinner was Market Basket. For some, this will come as no surprise — the New England chain is well-known for its low prices and great savings.
The chain has locations in Biddeford and Westbrook, as well as a brand-new store in Scarborough.
This time of year, there are sales on almost every aisle. There’s the $2.99 pie crust, the two-for-$4 cans of pumpkin pie filling and the 99-cent cans of gravy (although gravy is easy to make yourself with the leftover turkey drippings).
But possibly the best deal — and the main reason Market Basket comes in at the top of this list — was the turkey. At 49 cents per pound, a 12-pound turkey big enough to feed eight people came in at just under $6. That’s less than a cup of coffee in some places.
WALMART: $52.48 or $6.56 per person
With locations across the state, including Biddeford, Sanford, Scarborough and Falmouth, Walmart is convenient and inexpensive for most Maine shoppers.
The most expensive component of a meal from Walmart wasn’t actually the turkey — it was the produce. Between sweet potatoes (a group of eight would need about four pounds), yellow potatoes, carrots and celery, the total came to about $15.
A 12-pound turkey, on the other hand, would cost just under $12 — not bad for the table’s centerpiece.
HANNAFORD: $53.98 or $6.74 per person
Maine’s largest supermarket chain is not its least expensive, but at just under $54 for a Thanksgiving dinner for eight, it’s still well below the New England average.
Hannaford is known for its fresh produce from local farms, and with 68 locations across the state, it’s widely accessible.
The supermarket is also running a host of Thanksgiving deals: 99-cent cans of cranberry sauce, $1.87 stuffing mix, or 99-cent cream of mushroom soup for that all-important green bean casserole.
And at only 69 cents per pound, the turkey isn’t a bad deal, either. A 12-pounder would cost under $9.

title: Pope Leo XIV hit in face with rosary during popemobile ride in South America
text:
LIMA, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV bid farewell to his beloved second homeland of Peru on Monday with an “hasta luego,” after a marathon 12-day South American tour that tested his stamina after lung cancer surgery.
During the traditional popemobile ride before Leo’s final Mass, someone threw an apparent rosary toward the pope that seemed to hit him in the face. The pope winced and touched his temple, but he proceeded on and the Mass began as planned. The Vatican said some 1.5 million people attended.
The faithful often toss rosaries, stuffed animals, sports jerseys and other items towards the popemobile and Leo has often wowed the crowd with his quick reflexes in catching them. His bodyguards, though, have lamented that such tossed objects are among their chief concerns in protecting the pope when he is out in public.
A trip and pontificate modeled on a missionary saint
For the Chicago-born Leo, who spent two decades in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop, the trip was an emotional homecoming to a place that he has credited with teaching him how to be a shepherd. Upon arrival, he declared that Peru was his “patria” or homeland, and he sang the national anthem alongside President Keiko Fujimori. Leo has American and Peruvian citizenship.
“It was here that you taught me how to be a bishop, and this time I learned a little more about serving as the Successor of Peter,” Leo said at the end of Mass as many in the crowd knelt on the dirt ground to receive his final blessing.
“I have felt at home, and you have reminded me that the Church truly is a family,” he said.
Over the course of the trip, it became clear that Leo modeled his ministry in Peru and now for the universal Catholic Church on the figure of the first archbishop of Lima, St. Turibius of Mogrovejo.
Mogrovejo, who lived from 1538-1606, is revered for having denounced abuses against Indigenous and enslaved people by Spanish colonizers. He is also remembered for having crisscrossed his vast diocese on foot and horseback to minister to his flock, learning Quechua and Aymara to better preach to its Indigenous members and overseeing the translation of church teachings so they could understand.
Following his example, Leo traveled across Peru to where the Catholic hierarchy rarely goes to minister to his flock, going high up in the Andes mountains and deep into the Amazon rainforest and points in between. On his final full day in Peru on Sunday, Leo went from his former diocese of Chiclayo on the north Pacific coast to the southeastern Andean city of Cusco, to the northeastern Amazonian city of Pucallpa and back to Lima on the coast.
The climatic and altitude changes alone were exhausting — from hot, humid Chiclayo to chilly and rainy Cusco (at an oxygen-challenging altitude of 3,400 meters or about 11,150 feet) to the steaming heat of the Pucallpa rainforest and back to the gray humidity of Lima.
It was a daylong lesson in what it means to be a shepherd. But it also served to say “So there!” to the nay-sayers, including some in the Vatican who had questioned whether Leo would have to change the course of his pontificate given his lung cancer diagnosis.
On Monday, Leo proceeded with his program as planned and made clear he wasn’t saying “adiós” or goodbye forever to Peru.
Speaking to the crowd outside the Vatican residence, Leo thanked Peruvians for having accompanied him on his trip. “Have a good day, thank you very much, and until later!” he said.
At the home for the elderly in Callao, where Leo visited with residents, Leo bid farewell again saying “hasta pronto, hasta luego,” another way of saying “see you soon.”
Callao Mayor César Pérez told The Associated Press that Father Roberto, as he is known to the Peruvian people, would drive approximately 12 hours from Chiclayo in northern Peru to Callao during the pandemic because he wanted to ensure the well-being of older residents.
Leo delivered food and other supplies to the home but didn’t enter the facility in order to protect the residents from the virus, Pérez said.
A visit that was questioned but went ahead
The Peru stop capped a visit that began on Nov. 6 in Uruguay and proceeded on to Argentina, the homeland of Leo’s predecessor Pope Francis, who never returned during his pontificate.
The trip itself was in doubt after Leo underwent lung cancer surgery Oct. 13 in Rome. But Leo said as the visit began that he had “no doubt” that he would make it.
Rosa María Flores, who was attending Leo’s final Mass, was glad he did. She said the most important thing about the pope’s visit was that he brought faith to the people of his homeland of Peru.
“We have so much crime, so many deaths; we’re in great need of peace, reconciliation and faith,” she said. “I know that he’s pouring blessings on Peru and that things will get better for all of us.”
Some people at the Mass complained they couldn’t hear the pope because the giant TV screens didn’t work. Others begged firefighters to spray them with water to cool off, and the firefighters obliged.
Paying homage to his inspiration
One of the most meaningful visits for Leo was to the sanctuary of Mogrovejo in the city of Zaña in the diocese of Chiclayo. Leo revealed that he had come there the night before he was ordained a bishop to pray, so important to him was the saint who died there after falling ill during one of his own missionary visits.
“This is a kneeling place for Robert Prevost,” the Rev. David Farfan, the parish pastor, told AP. Many of the pope’s actions, he said, “helping people in the world, as a peacemaker, he did them while also kneeling in this sacred place because a saint passed away here.”

title: Family calls for kratom ban after 17-year-old’s overdose death: ‘This is a problem’
text:
EDMONDS, Wash. (KIRO) - A Washington state family is pushing to ban kratom sales after their 17-year-old son died from an overdose.
Aedan Morgan, 17, died Aug. 1 in what the medical examiner later reported was an overdose related to kratom. Now, his mother and stepfather have started a petition to ban the substance.
“It’s a big void in our home, and we are struggling with it every day,” said Aedan’s mother, Sorine Morgan. “Just keep waiting for him to come home.”
Kratom, at its most basic, is leaves from a tree in Southeast Asia used to make teas or chew on with effects similar to those of opioids. In gas stations and smoke shops across Washington state, it’s sold in highly concentrated, synthetic or partially synthetic versions that are potentially deadly.
“When we learned that Aedan had had an accidental overdose due to kratom-related products, then we kind of realized the connection with the signs we’ve seen in the stores, the gas stations,” said Cal McGrath, Aedan’s stepfather. “We realized how dangerous these substances are.”
When McGrath learned substances related to kratom were to blame for Aedan’s death, he tried to figure out how the teenager got hold of it. He found five stores advertising the substance around Edmonds and even more in neighboring communities.
Washington and 16 other states have no regulation on the sale of kratom, not even age restrictions.
Shannon Sessions is the executive director of Support 7, a non-profit that responds with first responders to unexpected death cases. She says Aedan Morgan’s death was the fifth from kratom she’s responded to this year.
“It’s not just a youth issue. It’s not just somebody who doesn’t have a home and lives on the streets and who’s drug addicted on the street. This is all of our problem, and it is seen at all ages,” Sessions said.
Aedan Morgan’s family now hopes people sign their petition to ban the substance in Edmonds and remains optimistic that may lead to more regulations at the state and county level.
“The main message is ‘do something.’ I mean, it’s pretty obvious this is a problem,” McGrath said.
“We hope that this can bring awareness and honor Aedan by hopefully saving other people,” Sorine Morgan said.

title: John T. Gorman Foundation awards $525,000 to support students’ mental health
text:
MAINE (WABI) - More than half a million dollars is going toward supporting students’ mental well-being in Maine.
Grants from the John T. Gorman Foundation will go to five organizations.
The money will support programs focused on mentoring, building friendships, and keeping students engaged socially and academically.
A list of grant recipients can be found below.
Girl Scouts of Maine, Statewide – $125,000 to expand access to school-based, afterschool Girl Scouts programming for approximately 200 girls in grades 4-8 across 16 schools statewide. Programming is focused on helping students form lasting friendships, build resilience, and stay more engaged both socially and academically.
- Hearty Roots, Lincoln County – $100,000 to expand year-round programming in partnership with three middle schools in Lincoln County. Through this grant, approximately 220 middle school students will have regular access to outdoor experiences, small-group mentoring, behavioral-support programming, and interpersonal skill-building.
- Maine Seacoast Mission, Washington County – $100,000 to strengthen the Journey program, which provides about 90 Washington County students from grades 7 to 12 with mentoring, social connection, and experiences to build aspirations, supportive relationships, and academic and career pathways after high school.
- NorthStar 4-H, Oxford, Waldo Counties – $100,000 to bring the NorthStar program to middle school students in three school districts (two in Oxford County and one in Waldo). NorthStar combines in-school support, afterschool programming, multi-day expeditions, community engagement, and individualized mentoring.
- Tree Street Youth Center, Lewiston – $100,000 to support out-of-school-time programming for youth in Lewiston. Tree Street delivers a continuum of programming designed to strengthen social-emotional wellness, resilient relationships, future readiness, and access to meaningful recreation.

title: New American Lung Association report details lung cancer in Maine
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Nearly a third of lung cancer cases in Maine are diagnosed early, according to the American Lung Association’s ninth annual “State of Lung Cancer” report.
The report shows early detection works. Survival has improved 34% in five years.
Maine rankings
The report examines key lung cancer indicators and ranks Maine 44th out of 51 in the nation for rate of new lung cancer cases, at 65.1 per 100,000. The national rate is 52.1 per 100,000. The report says this represents a 13% improvement for Maine over the past five years.
Maine ranks 19th out of 43 in the nation for survival, at 31.8%. According to the report, most lung cancer cases are diagnosed at later stages when the cancer has spread, and treatment options are less likely to be curative.
Association response
Lance Boucher, assistant vice president of state public policy for the American Lung Association, said the report contains positive news.
“Overall, our report reveals positive news—more people in the U.S. are living longer after a lung cancer diagnosis than ever before, and more people are getting screened for the disease. While these findings give us hope, more must be done to end the burden of this devastating disease on families throughout Maine,” Boucher said.
“We need to increase screening rates among those at high risk to catch the disease early when it’s more likely to be curable, expand comprehensive biomarker testing to help identify targeted treatments, and improve access to clinical trials and the best lung cancer care,” he said.
Screening recommendation
Boucher urges anyone with a history of tobacco use to get screened.
“If you are in that risk group of tobacco use history, visit Saved by the Scan and look at being screened for lung cancer because early detection really is one of the most important ways to increase five-year survival and open access to many different courses of treatment,” Boucher said.
Biomarker testing and clinical trials
Boucher wants Maine to expand biomarker testing. It helps doctors find targeted treatments.
The American Lung Association urges lawmakers to pass the Clinical Trial Modernization Act to make trials easier to join.

title: Ground stop sparks Thanksgiving travel concerns
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Aging systems are being blamed for last week’s nationwide ground stop that disrupted an estimated 46,000 flights, as Americans prepare for the busiest travel week of the year.
Trump comments on the ground stop
President Trump blamed old infrastructure, broken equipment and Biden for the ground stop.
“I don’t take any responsibility,” Trump said.
Flight cancellations and delays
The Federal Aviation Administration estimates 18,000 flights were canceled and 28,000 were delayed as a result of the incident.
Thanksgiving travel outlook
AAA predicts 81 million Americans will travel for Thanksgiving. Nearly 6 million of them are expected to travel by plane.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said he expects air travel operations to be restored before the holiday.
“I think we’re going to be back up and operational as we head into the heat of the Thanksgiving travel operation,” Duffy said.
Questions about new AI system
The FAA maintains the ground stop was unrelated to the rollout of its new AI smart system overhaul.
Earlier this month, House Democrats sent a letter to the Government Accountability Office requesting a closer look at the new software, citing possible safety concerns.
Duffy said he will hold a news conference Tuesday to provide important updates.

title: What to discuss before marrying later in life: Money, caregiving, kids
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — Falling in love later in life can be exciting and can feel like a fresh start. But when it comes to saying “I do,” there are some unique considerations for older couples.
Treat marriage as a legal and financial decision
“This is a legal and a financial decision,” Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “If you’re going to go into business with somebody, you better know who you’re going into business with, because business partners can absolutely take your feet out from underneath of you.”
Talk about money and caregiving
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said couples should start with the practical questions.
“Talk about money. How are you going to pay the bills? How are you going to mesh money? Are you going to mesh your money?” O’Rourke said.
She said caregiving should be part of the conversation, too.
Couples should ask: “If I need care, are you going to provide for it? Are you going to arrange it?” O’Rourke said.
Think about how the kids will get along
O’Rourke said couples should also talk about how their children will get along.
She described a couple whose children worked together for them.
“They were doing it beautifully,” O’Rourke said.
O’Rourke said she took one of the daughters aside and asked what the secret was.
“She said, ‘My parents didn’t give us an option,’” O’Rourke said.
The daughter told her the parents sat down with the children and said their expectation was that when they needed help, the children would work together, O’Rourke said.
“Not everybody can do that, but I think involving the children to some level, not to get permission, but involving them, is a really healthy thing to do,” O’Rourke said.
You’re marrying the whole family
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said marriage is a family affair.
“You’re not just marrying the person. You’re marrying the family. You’re marrying your history,” Rogers said.
“You’re marrying everything that came along with them. Everything that they are didn’t just happen at 40, 50 and 60. They’re bringing some stuff with them and you need to investigate that,” she said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said it’s “very complex.”
“Love is emotional, but this business arrangement, asset protection, is very practical, and it’s a matter of doing both,” Ambrose said.
Why adult children may want a say
Ambrose said adult children can feel they are in a position to give permission or weigh in, adding that it can become touchy and manipulative.
Loyalty can also play a role in a second marriage, Cradduck added.
“If it’s your mom getting married again, you could be loyal to your dad, and you’re concerned that he’s alone, or however the marriage ended, or if it was in death,” Cradduck said.
Inheritance can be another concern.
“What’s that mean to all the things that you and my parent, the other parent, developed and earned? And so what’s that going to mean to me in the future? And so a lot of times the kids weigh in,” Cradduck said.
Plan with an estate planning attorney
Even when children do not weigh in, they may need to be involved, Ambrose said.
“Death order has a big impact,” Ambrose said. “Which one dies first, and say, there’s legal implications here, so be sure to work with an estate planning attorney.”

title: Fire in White Mountain National Forest remains about 60% contained for nearly a week
text:
Wild River Fire in White Mountain National Forest remains about 60% contained for nearly a week
A wildfire that has been burning in the White Mountain National Forest for more than two weeks has remained at the same level of containment for six days.
The U.S. Forest Service said that the Wild River Fire was 59% contained as of Tuesday and was burning 817 acres, figures that have not changed since last Wednesday, Nov. 11.
Officials said Tuesday that firefighters remain focused on suppressing hot spots, as well as monitoring, patrol and mop-up operations. There were 22 total personnel involved in the firefighting operations as of Tuesday, including a helicopter, an unmanned aerial system and a suppression module.
According to the Forest Service, fire behavior is minimal and infrared flights conducted by unmanned aircraft systems remain ongoing in an effort to identify and assess potential hot spots.
Officials said natural barriers such as brooks and conifer stands, in combination with strengthened fire lines, have helped contain the Wild River Fire to its existing footprint.
The Forest Service said full containment of the fire is expected with significant precipitation or a season-ending event. Officials added that safety remains the top priority in rugged and challenging terrain.
The Wild River Fire was first reported the afternoon of Nov. 1, just southeast of Gorham, New Hampshire, and just south of Gilead, Maine, near Evans Notch.
On Nov. 4, the Forest Service issued a closure order that remains in effect. Click here to see a map of the closure.
On Nov. 5, officials revealed that they believed the fire was caused by humans. Two community meetings have been held since then in order to share information with people who live in the area and to answer questions from residents.
The Forest Service announced on Nov. 10 that the Wild River Fire was more than half contained.

title: No evidence that a US blackout is expected Nov. 17
text:
There is no evidence a nationwide blackout is expected Nov. 17. Online claims are unfounded
A 90-day nationwide blackout is not looming for the U.S., despite social media call outs to prepare for such a doomsday scenario.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
Multiple TikTok posts say the blackout will start Nov. 17 and warn people to stock up with food and other supplies.
A Nov. 14 TikTok post went even farther, showing President Donald Trump purportedly saying the blackout is coming.
“A 90-day blackout is going to happen before the end of the year,” Trump appears to say from the White House press briefing room.
That video was manipulated. PolitiFact found the original video of Trump talking Nov. 9 in the press briefing room; he didn’t announce a 90-day blackout. Among many things, he talked about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and the Iran war. The TikTok account that posted the video uses the purported clip to promote buying cryptocurrency before the supposed blackout and has posted other manipulated videos of Trump.
Fact-checkers at Snopes also found similar manipulated videos of Trump shared on Facebook and Instagram promoting cryptocurrency and claiming that it would make people money during the “upcoming” blackout.
A Spanish-language TikTok post said the blackout already started, pointing to the Nov. 12 to 14 Microsoft outage and the Federal Aviation Administration’s Nov. 13 order to ground all flights because of faulty old equipment. Microsoft said in a Nov. 13 X post the outage was a technical issue, not a cyber attack, and the FAA allowed flights to resume Nov. 13.
What’s happening Nov. 17?
The Federal Emergency Management Agency announced Sept. 17 that on Nov. 17 around 2:20 p.m. ET, it and the Federal Communications Commission will conduct a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System.
The test will air only on radio and TV; the alert will not be sent to mobile phones. There is nothing the public has to do in response. This is a standard test that happens at least once every three years per federal law to ensure the alert system is ready in case of an emergency.
That test is not expected to announce a real emergency or a blackout.
The message will last one minute, have an alert sound and will say, “This is a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System, issued by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. This is only a test. No action is required by the public.”
FEMA also says on its website that if an actual emergency happens Nov. 17, the test will be postponed to Dec. 3.
Homeland Security secretary said no need to stockpile supplies
Fox News Senior White House Correspondent Peter Doocy asked Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Nov. 15 if Americans should start stockpiling food and supplies after the FAA ground stop. Mullin said Americans don’t need to stockpile supplies for potential disruptions to power, water and food supplies, although other countries such as the United Kingdom advised their residents to do so in late October.
The U.K. government released this guidance to ensure that households can survive weather, cyber or other serious emergencies with supplies to last 72 hours. The notice came before the winter storm season and amid concerns that the global phenomenon “super El-Niño” could affect global food supplies and energy systems.
Mullin said the U.K. doesn’t have the same safeguards and emergency preparedness the U.S has.
“That’s kind of running over the internet right now too, especially throughout social media. ‘Should I be worried? The 90 days?' Absolutely not,” Mullin said. “I’m not stockpiling, and I tell my kids all the time, don’t worry unless you see me worry. We’re in good shape here; the panic that people want to draw from is unfounded.”
Some social media users also said the blackout is related to the FORTRESS America project, which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Sept. 30. FORTRESS, which stands for Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply and Survivability, seeks to ensure that every major U.S. military installation generates its own independent power so that bases remain operational even if civilian electric grids are taken down by a cyberattack or sabotage.
Fox News reported Oct. 25 that according to documents it reviewed, the project is preparing the U.S. military bases to keep operating without outside power for at least 90 days. The network didn’t report that a 90-day blackout is coming.
This isn’t the first time these emergency tests triggered misinformation. We have fact-checked bogus claims saying the electric signals of these tests could turn people into zombies and activate COVID-19 vaccine ingredients in people’s bodies.
Our ruling
TikTok posts say a nationwide 90-day blackout will happen Nov. 17, 2026.
There is no evidence that is going to happen.
One video shows Trump purportedly saying a blackout is coming, but that clip is manipulated. The video is of a Nov. 9 news conference and Trump didn’t mention a nationwide power outage.
FEMA will do a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System on Nov. 17, which happens at least once every three years.
The Defense Department in late September announced a project to prepare military bases to operate for 90-days in case of a blackout of the civilian electric grid, that doesn’t mean a blackout is expected Nov. 17.
During the recent nationwide flights ground stop, the Homeland Security secretary said Americans don’t need to stockpile for widespread disruptions to power, water and food supplies and that related online claims are unfounded.
We rate this claim False.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: Federal review faults leadership failures in Grand Canyon fire that destroyed historic lodge
text:
Federal review blames leadership failures in Grand Canyon fire that destroyed historic lodge
Leadership failures, along with a lack of preparedness and poor communication, were the driving factors of a wildfire that destroyed a historic lodge and dozens of structures along the North Rim of Grand Canyon National Park.
Previous coverage from 2025 in the player above: Wildfire along Grand Canyon's North Rim destroys historic lodge in 2025
A federal review of the Dragon Bravo Fire, recently made public, noted that while drought conditions and extreme fire behavior contributed, systemic weaknesses in the National Park Service related to authority and qualifications hindered decision-making at critical moments.
The 2025 fire should be considered a warning, according to the multiagency team of experts that reviewed the handling of the fire.
“The findings indicated many of the challenges observed during the fire were foreseeable, preventable, and reflective of broader institutional issues that extend beyond a single park, region, or agency,” the report stated.
The Dragon Bravo Fire was sparked by lightning in July 2025. The park service allowed it to burn for days before it exploded into a fast-moving conflagration that forced evacuations and consumed the Grand Canyon Lodge, historic cabins, employee housing and other critical infrastructure. Suppression costs topped $141 million over three months.
The park service initially defended its handling of the fire, saying a sudden and extreme shift in the wind far exceeded forecasts.
Grand Canyon officials referred questions about the findings to the U.S. Interior Department, which oversees the park service. The Interior Department did not immediately answer emails sent by The Associated Press.
The review, ordered by the Interior Department's deputy secretary, provides a timeline that starts with the day the fire ignited. It details weather conditions and includes photos of the towering plume that could be seen from the South Rim, the lodge awash in flames and the charred remains of the historic building.
The review noted that it was known by park officials that the region was experiencing persistent drought and had dense fuels in close proximity to nationally significant historic structures. Fire planning and policy documents existed, but the review stated those plans “were not fully translated into effective preseason preparedness actions or operational readiness.”
The recommendations include requiring agency administrators to undergo the needed training to handle complex incidents and ensuring that communication flows through proper channels so that decision-makers get firsthand, accurate and timely information.
The review highlighted a breakdown in communication that resulted in a multiday delay in fire retardant being used as the flames intensified. The decision to use retardant came only after several structures, including the lodge, already had been lost, according to the findings.
The review also stated that the park service's continued authorization of the confine and contain strategy did not reflect awareness of changing conditions or escalating risk. The recommendations also call for fire leadership to reevaluate their strategies regularly and to reconsider weather conditions, fire behavior and the availability of resources.
The review team described the Dragon Bravo Fire as a defining event for Grand Canyon National Park and a consequential case study for the Interior Department and the U.S. Wildland Fire Service.
The experts stated in the review that the resulting loss of historic structures, the displacement of employees, the risks to firefighters and the significant suppression costs underscore the stakes associated with managing wildfires in complex landscapes.
“What began as a small, naturally ignited fire rapidly evolved into a high-consequence, cross-boundary incident that tested leadership, governance, preparedness, decision quality, and execution across multiple programs and agencies,” the team stated.
___
Montoya Bryan reported from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

title: Presque Isle airport director says nationwide ground stop highlights need for answers
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - The Federal Aviation Administration halted departures nationwide Friday after technical problems disrupted air traffic control communications and radar feeds, disrupting air travel across the country.
What the FAA said
Air traffic resumed at 8:15 p.m. Friday. The agency said all aircraft landed safely and the cause remains under investigation.
Airport director responds
Presque Isle International Airport Director Scott Wardwell said the disruption highlights a need for answers.
“In the history of aviation in the United States, there’s only been three ground stops nationwide. September 11th, 2001 was first one. Second one was in 2023, and then last Friday. Certainly the trend is not good. We’re starting to have them more frequently,” Wardwell said.
“I think the federal government, the FAA, the airlines, the entire industry have to really work together to identify what the issue was and to try to fix the issue. And because as you can see, it’s very disruptive to the traveling public,” he said.
Advice for travelers
Wardwell said affected passengers should check with their airlines about rebooking options and possible refunds.
With holiday travel approaching, he also recommended building extra time into travel plans so a delay or cancellation does not mean missing the holiday.

title: St. Francis home a total loss after fire
text:
ST. FRANCIS, Maine (WAGM) - A home at 691 Main Street in St. Francis is a total loss following a fire Monday afternoon. No injuries were reported.
According to St. Francis Fire Chief Voisine, the call came in around 2 p.m., and crews had the fire under control by 7 p.m.
Fort Kent, Allagash, Frenchville, Eagle Lake and North Lakes provided mutual aid. Fort Kent Public Works provided a tanker, and Ambulance Service Inc. provided support.
The Red Cross was notified, and the occupant is staying with family.
The fire remains under investigation by the Maine State Fire Marshal’s Office.

title: Annual dessert auction raises funds for survivors across Penobscot and Piscataquis Counties
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - An evening of irresistible desserts, community spirit, and meaningful giving returns to Bangor this November as Rape Response Services hosts its Annual Dessert Auction on Friday, November 20, at the Hilton Garden Inn, 250 Haskell Road. The event raises funds to support advocacy services for survivors of all ages throughout Penobscot and Piscataquis counties.
Guests will have the opportunity to bid on more than 60 delicious desserts while helping provide critical resources for survivors of sexual violence. Sponsored by Versant Power and Bangor Savings Bank, the event combines a fun annual tradition with a powerful mission: ensuring survivors have access to the services they need and working together as a community to prevent sexual violence.
Doors open at 6 p.m., with an array of appetizers available before the live auction begins at approximately 6:30 p.m. Attendees can expect to bid upon a tempting assortment of cakes, pies, cookies, cupcakes, cheesecakes, and other specialty treats. Gluten-free options will also be available. Returning this year, desserts will be displayed under a camera system, giving everyone a clear, up-close view of each item as bidding takes place.
In addition to the dessert auction, guests and others will have the opportunity to participate in our end-of year fundraising campaign and contribute their piece of the pie. Campaign contributions can be designated to support services for survivors or to provide practical immediate support when it is needed most such as special paddle raise dedicated to helping survivors access immediate support and emergency assistance. Every contribution helps provide practical resources that promote safety, stability, and healing.
All proceeds benefit Rape Response Services, a subsidiary of Penquis. The organization provides free, confidential support and advocacy for individuals affected by sexual violence in Penobscot and Piscataquis counties while also delivering prevention education and community awareness programs.
“This event is a wonderful reminder of what can happen when a community comes together for a shared purpose,” said Amanda Chambers, Division Manager for Rape Response Services. “Every bid, donation, and show of support helps us respond to real needs in real time. The generosity we see each year at the Dessert Auction allows survivors to access resources, regain stability, and know that their community stands beside them.”
Past auction favorites have included Whoopie pies, macarons, assorted pies, chocolate peanut butter cake, carrot cake, pumpkin rolls, assorted cheesecakes and cookies, brownies and more
Admission is free. Guests will enjoy appetizers and grazing selections prepared by the Hilton Garden Inn, along with coffee, dessert samples, and other refreshments throughout the evening. Auction purchases may be paid by cash, check, or mobile credit card.
Community members are encouraged to attend, enjoy an evening of sweet treats, and help support the life-changing work Rape Response Services provides to survivors throughout the region.

title: Rattle Shake Grill closes Cumberland location
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After six months of serving burgers and shakes, Rattle Shake Grill has closed its Cumberland location, citing unsustainable costs.
The retro-inspired diner opened in May inside the former location of Rise Pizza and Pub, which closed in July 2025. Business partners Michael Gatlin and Matt Moran, who also co-own Rattle Shake Grill’s first location in South Portland, said they wanted the Cumberland restaurant to be a “family spot” where the community could gather.
The restaurant hosted trivia, viewings of professional sports games and a chance for Greely High School sports spectators and athletes to grab a bite during or after a game.
A post on Rattle Shake Grill’s Instagram page Friday said the business would close after the weekend.
“We have loved meeting new friends and watching the kids come through for a shake but sadly we just can’t sustain the current costs,” the post said.
Gatlin and Moran could not be immediately reached for details about the decision.
The post also shared that if anyone is interested in hosting a holiday party or sports banquet at the Cumberland location, the owners would be happy to accommodate the event.
“Hopefully this isn’t a goodbye but a see you later,” the social media post said.

title: VIDEO: Cincinnati Zoo welcomes baby giraffe in first live-streamed birth
text:
VIDEO: Cincinnati Zoo welcomes baby giraffe in first live-streamed birth
There’s a new baby giraffe at the Cincinnati Zoo, and almost 8,000 people were able to watch the birth live.
See video of the baby giraffe in the player above.
Tessa the giraffe gave birth to her baby calf around 11:45 p.m. Monday.
The zoo livestreamed her labor and the moments after as her calf wiggled its way to stand.
It’s the 18th calf born at the zoo and the fifth calf for 19-year-old Tessa.
Zookeepers and volunteers were staking out shifts to keep watch of Tessa for a 24-hour period.
“People were definitely worried at times when the calf took a while to move and stand, but that is part of the process,” said Cincinnati Zoo veterinarian Dr. Jessica Heinz. “The baby is wobbly and still finding her footing, but we’ve been pleased to see nursing and good interactions with Tessa.”
The zoo said vets are planning to conduct a health check on the baby as soon as Wednesday and will be able to determine the sex at that time. After that, they will start the process of naming the calf. 
Zoo officials are giving one lucky member of the community a chance to name the calf. For $20, participants can enter for the chance to win the rights to the calf's name. Naming rules will be announced at a later date.
The baby is currently bonding with mom, so the pair will not be visible beyond the livestreams for now.
The calf will later join the rest of the group, including 5-year-old father Zeke, Zoey and half-brother Fennessy.
The zoo said the pairing was recommended by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) Giraffe Species Survival Plan (SSP), so the introduction of this genetic combination to the AZA population is important.
“We were blown away by the interest in the giraffe birth livestream,” Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said. “We launched the live cams on YouTube last month, toward the end of the birth window, and 4 million people have watched since then.”
The zoo said the addition is encouraging news as it looks to double the size of its herd over the next couple of years, compared with what the herd was when Giraffe Tower first opened.
The new habitat aims to expand space for the giraffe herd and provide more feeding and behind-the-scenes opportunities.

title: Trump arrives in Philippines to kick off Asia trip with economic deals and talks with allies
text:
MANILA, Philippines (AP) — President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he met with regional partners, sought to formalize a trade deal and get a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.
Manila, the Philippine capital, is Trump’s first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea’s leader Kim Jong Un.
The visit marks Trump’s first travel abroad since his party suffered deep losses in midterm elections. The White House and stock market alike have been rattled by the departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved.
But Trump could not escape all the controversies still swirling in the U.S. Reporters asked him about the recent service outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration and online banking with JPMorgan Chase. The president played down the problems that caused mass flight cancellations and disrupted workdays.
“It’s life,” Trump said. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”
The president was also asked about a CNN report that Iran was putting together plans to attack Washington with a dirty bomb or chemical weapons.
“Well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before,” Trump said, adding, “I hope it’s not. But we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy.”
Trump to be feted at the annual ASEAN summit
Trump’s first hours in the Philippines included all the reassuring optics from Washington’s oldest treaty ally in Asia, such as a cocktail reception and dinner with other world leaders, an intermission from some of the thorniest issues at home. He’s being feted Tuesday night at a gala as the “guest of honor” at the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
The ASEAN leaders have been working on a non-aggression pact with China in the contested waters of the South China Sea, a key global trade route. Confrontations have escalated in recent years, particularly between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals.
After landing in Manila, Trump met with the leaders of the Quad nations, comprising the U.S., Australia, India, and Japan, that have aimed to counter China’s influence in the Asia Pacific, for the first time since he returned to the White House last year.
“We’re all friends,” Trump said. ”It’s a lot easier that way.”
The president announced that the Quad would conduct an exercise featuring maritime patrol aircraft and launch an accelerator to speed the development of artificial intelligence.
Trump signed a trade statement with Thailand, the type of agreement he has relished striking since launching a trade war last year buttressed by steep tariff threats. The president said that he was looking forward “to finalizing the details of our formal agreement in the coming weeks.”
The joint statement included details that were posted more than a year ago by the U.S. government. Thailand would remove tariffs on most American goods, as well as barriers for importing American autos, food products and pharmaceutical drugs. Trump said Tuesday that Thailand would buy $2.6 billion in U.S. agricultural products.
As part of the gala dinner Tuesday night, Trump participated in what was billed as a “special summit” with the ASEAN leaders. They finalized a set of principles to tackle online scams, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said.
Leaders at the dinner were also expected to discuss efforts to deepen trade and security ties as well as the region’s longstanding conflicts, including yearslong violence in Myanmar and escalating disputes in the South China Sea, which Beijing claims virtually in its entirety.
Washington has rejected China’s expansive claim to the waterway, and has repeatedly stated that it’s obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces come under an armed attack.
Anti-Trump protesters are gathered in Manila
About 1,500 left-wing protesters held a noisy rally in a downtown Manila square ahead of Trump’s arrival, calling on Philippine leaders not to take their foreign policy cues from the U.S.
They waved red flags and held up a large streamer that read, “Resist U.S. war and plunder!” They planned to burn an effigy of Trump. Riot police with shields and wooden truncheons stood nearby.
“The Philippine government should not deal with such a loser so our call to the Marcos administration is to stop being a puppet of Donald Trump and to uphold an independent foreign policy for the Philippines,” protest leader Teddy Casiño told The Associated Press.
Nearly 23,000 police personnel and other law enforcers, including SWAT teams, were deployed to secure the ASEAN summit.
Planned meetings with the Philippine president — and possibly an old friend
On Wednesday, Trump is set to receive a red-carpet welcome and full military honors from Marcos Jr., followed by a state banquet as part of his visit to the Malacanang presidential palace. Trump and Marcos are expected to affirm their commitment to their countries’ longstanding treaty alliance.
Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion in Malacanang with an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she’s well enough and gets her doctors’ nod.
Now 97 and using a wheelchair, the former jet set Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a strongman leader, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 “People Power” public uprising.
But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: “How’s Imelda?” Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press.
“Personal connections are very important to him,” Romualdez said.
When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. “President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, ‘please say hello to your mother,’” according to Romualdez.
Trump is also expected to announce a series of commercial deals and investments in the aviation, defense, energy, and technology sectors, before heading to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
___
Boak reported from Shenzhen, China.

title: More bright days ahead with well above average temperatures
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The strong pressure over the Ohio Valley will remain in control over the pattern here for the rest of the week or so and bring with it unseasonably warm temperatures and sun filled skies. We do however remain in a fairly severe drought here and unfortunately for that there will not be a hint of precip the rest of the week while temperatures may reach as much as 15-20 degrees above normal by Friday with highs near or above 60. Lows will remain more seasonable with the clear skies but the days will be very warm for November.
Tuesday night: Seasonable lows and clear skies.
Lows will drop to right around 30 or so for most with the usual cold spots in the 20s. Light winds.
Wednesday: Warming up a few more degrees
Clear skies will continue for most with a few clouds possible up north and temps will continue to climb to the upper 50s for most with a light breeze from the W at 5-10 mph with gusts to 20 mph.
Wednesday night: Similar to previous nights
Lows will drop to near 30 for most with light winds.
Thursday: Near or above 60 for some
The warming trend will reach its peak Thursday into Friday with highs getting to near 60 on Thursday. Light winds.
Thursday night and beyond: Typical lows, not so typical highs
While lows will be quite typical, right around freezing or a bit below, the highs will most certainly be not. Friday highs will peak again near 60 which will be downright balmy for most across Maine this time of year. The warmth will continue likely into the weekend as well before the next chance for rain which may show up in the early portion of next week. That’s a long way away so lots of time to sort all of that out.
Tuesday night: Clear with lows in the 20s and 30s. Winds light.
Wednesday: The warmup continues with highs in the middle to upper 50s. Winds NW at 5-10 mph gusts to 20 mph.
Thursday: Very warm with highs near 60. Winds light.
Thursday night: Clear skies with lows near 30. Winds light.
Friday: Warm and clear with highs near 60 once again. Winds NW at 5-10 mph with gusts to 20 mph.

title: Experts say to ‘stop and verify’ before you click pay this holiday season
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Bank of America says phony shipping notices, “too good to be true” deals and fake donation QR codes are popping up as scammers gear up for the holiday rush.
Jen Ehresman, head of consumer client protection at Bank of America, said the bank’s top advice is to stop and verify.
“Our best piece of advice is stop and verify. And price is always a red flag. If it’s too good to be true, it’s too good to be true. But we also suggest beware of unexpected links. Unexpected messages asking you to click on a link or fix an issue or you have a problem with your account,” Ehresman said.
Ehresman said the best thing shoppers can do while hunting for deals and getting gifts shipped is slow down. That means stopping to verify before clicking a link or paying.
Ehresman also warned that artificial intelligence is making scams look more real.
“AI creates a lot of convenience for our clients. And there are definitely opportunities on that front. But obviously, AI has also made things look more authentic. It makes it difficult to spot suspicious emails, calls, texts,” she said.
Ehresman said shoppers should not click through from a text or a social media ad. Instead, they should leave the app, go straight to the retailer’s real website and do a quick search for complaints, such as “never got my merchandise.”
Anyone who falls for a scam should not wait. They should contact their bank right away, lock their cards and save any emails and texts. They should also tell friends and family so they do not fall for the same trick.

title: Cat rescued from abandoned drain pipe in midcoast Maine
text:
Neighbors came together last week to save a cat trapped in an abandoned drain pipe in Harpswell.
A woman heard a cat meowing in an abandoned drain pipe, and soon three of her neighbors came together to rescue the distressed feline, according to the town of Harpswell.
The cat needed all the help he could get, because he was stuck seven feet down the pipe.
Aside from being cold, this cat was not injured after getting trapped seven feet down an abandoned drain pipe in Harpswell. Credit: Courtesy of the town of Harpswell
The team dug, cut, coaxed and pulled the little cat to safety. One of the neighbors was a vet tech by training, and she gave the cat a thorough look over. Aside from being cold, the cat appeared uninjured, the town of Harpswell said Friday.
“This little kitty has no idea how lucky he is! Harpswell is so amazing to have people pull together to help others, people and animals, alike!” the town said in a social media post.
The search was on over the weekend for the cat’s owners. If he is a stray, he’ll be put up for adoption.

title: Here's Why Maine is The 3rd Best State to Raise a Family
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Here’s Why Maine is The 3rd Best State to Raise a Family
I am in the middle of my journey, raising a family in Maine and so far, it's been pretty great. And if you've ever raised a family here in Maine, you probably already know there's a whole lot to love about living here.
We have the most beautiful views, fresh clean air, forestry, tight communities, and plenty of Hallmark style small town charm.
But there's one little detail that can make family life a challenge.. the cost of living!
According to a new report from ConsumerAffairs, Maine ranks # 3 in the nation among the best states to raise a family.
Pretty impressive! But before we start celebrating, there's a catch..
Maine also ranks # 42 out of 50 states for affordability. Pretty cool, however as a Maine parent, I am stretched pretty thin. But this is compared to all of our states.
So, in other words, Maine is a great place to raise kids, but keeping a roof over everyone's heads can get expensive.
One example? Moving from a one bedroom to a two bedroom rental in Maine costs an about $420 MORE per month. That's a lot higher than the national average difference of $189.
And childcare isn't exactly cheap, either.
The report says that the average annual cost of full-time, care for an infant, toddler, and 4 year old in Maine is $15,290, compared with the national average of $13,184.
Read More: Maine Ranks Among America's Top 10 Potato-Producing States
Still, Maine has consistently ranked near the top, coming in at No. 2 in both 2024 and 2025.
So here's the question: Is Maine one of the best places to raise a family? Apparently, yes. Is it one of the easiest places to afford it? Not so much!
What do you think, Maine parents? Is raising a family here worth the extra expense?

title: President Trump appeals to state and federal courts to erase hush money conviction
text:
President Trump appeals to state and federal courts to erase hush money conviction
A federal appeals court is weighing whether it can — or should — intervene in President Donald Trump’s hush money case now that a New York State appellate court has heard arguments in his quest to erase the historic conviction.
Previous coverage in the video player above: "Blatant criminality:" White House warns Democrats on proposed investigations in letter
A three-judge panel of the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Monday spent more than an hour questioning Trump’s lawyer and a state prosecutor about the president's latest bid to shift the case from state court to federal court, where he could seek to have it dismissed on immunity grounds. There was no immediate decision.
The sides were in court for the second time in 11 days as Trump pursues a two-pronged legal strategy in an attempt to get the May 2024 verdict thrown out. Trump was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to obscure a $130,000 payment to adult film performer Stormy Daniels.
Along with his federal court fight, the Republican president is also waging a traditional appeal through New York’s state court system, which included arguments before the mid-level Appellate Division on Nov. 5. That court has yet to rule.
Regardless of the outcome, Trump will forever be associated with the case, which went to trial as he was campaigning for his return to the White House. Trump denies wrongdoing and was given no punishment. Now, with little over two years left in his presidency, he is steadfast in trying to rid himself of the dubious distinction of being the first U.S. president convicted of a crime.
Trump's lawyer says case could go to the Supreme Court
Trump’s lawyer, Robert Giuffra Jr., urged the 2nd Circuit judges on Monday to issue an order as soon as possible — even before writing their full decision — to take control of the case and stop the Appellate Division’s deliberations.
Without federal court intervention, Trump “will likely have to wait years” for state appellate courts to rule before he can take the matter to the U.S. Supreme Court, Giuffra said in a letter previewing his argument.
But Judge John M. Walker Jr., who was appointed to the appeals court by his cousin, President George H.W. Bush, and Chief Judge Raymond J. Lohier Jr., who was appointed by President Barack Obama, weren't so sure.
“How does that work?” Walker asked. “I mean, assuming we were to agree with you, there’s been an argument in the Appellate Division. Briefs have been filed in the Appellate Division. Will those briefs be refiled by everybody here?”
Federal law doesn't spell out precisely how such a move would play out.
Giuffra suggested the case would first go to a federal district court judge, who would adopt the state court verdict, before going to the 2nd Circuit for arguments and a decision on dismissal on presidential immunity grounds. The briefs, he said, would remain the same — albeit with different covers.
“You’re asking us to embrace an entire procedural mechanism that I don’t see anywhere authorized by Congress,” Lohier said.
“We think it is authorized,” Giuffra said, calling a provision of the law that allows such post-verdict transfer petitions “a safety valve that’s intended to protect against exactly the gamesmanship that’s gone on here.”
A federal judge declined Trump’s transfer bid 3 times
Trump asked the 2nd Circuit to step in after a federal judge in August ruled against the president for a third time. Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein, who died last month at 92, wrote in his decision that “paying hush money to an adult film star or engaging in a cover-up of an embarrassment are not subsumed in presidential immunity.”
Trump first sought to move the case to federal court weeks after he was indicted in March 2023. He tried again after his conviction and the Supreme Court’s July 2024 ruling that presidents and ex-presidents can’t be prosecuted for official acts and prosecutors can’t use official acts as evidence that unofficial actions were illegal.
Giuffra argued to both the state and federal appellate panels that prosecutors used the type of official acts evidence that was later barred by the Supreme Court's immunity ruling, including testimony about his Oval Office conversations, workflow and social media posts.
Giuffra also took issue with the prosecution’s description of the hush money payment as an illegal campaign contribution under the Federal Election Campaign Act, arguing that such allegations belong in federal court, not state court.
After Trump appealed Hellerstein’s second denial, the 2nd Circuit ordered the judge to reconsider, finding that he had failed to weigh “important issues relevant” to the president’s request to move the case.
That panel, which also included Lohier, said it expressed no view on how he should rule but instructed Hellerstein to closely review evidence that Trump claimed was related to official acts and whether Trump could argue those actions were taken as part of his White House duties.
Steven Wu, chief of the appeals division at the Manhattan District Attorney's Office, urged the 2nd Circuit panel to uphold Hellerstein’s ruling and leave the case in state court. Even if Trump were to prevail, he argued, the state appeals court would still be free to rule.

title: Former teacher pleads guilty in sexual abuse case involving 16-year-old student
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (WDRB/WAVE/Gray News) — A former teacher pleaded guilty Friday in Kentucky to charges stemming from a sexual relationship with a student.
Mary “Hanna” Mattingly, 32, broke down in tears as she pleaded guilty to first-degree sexual abuse and possession of matter portraying a sexual performance of a minor.
Arrest and investigation
Mattingly was arrested in March.
According to the Bardstown Police Department, she had sexual contact and exchanged nude photos with a 16-year-old student.
In a written statement at the time, Bardstown City Schools said the district received an anonymous letter outlining “alleged inappropriate conduct between a female substitute teacher and a student.”
Mattingly was initially placed on administrative leave, and district officials contacted police.
Police said the letter, received by the district on March 26, led to the investigation into Mattingly.
Court proceedings
During Friday’s hearing, a judge said the sexual contact happened between March 1 and July 31, 2025.
Under the plea agreement, Mattingly would serve five years in prison.
Final sentencing is set for Jan. 21, 2027.
