title: Seasons change, politics should too
text:
It’s time for Republicans and Democrats to think about what happened in the recent election.
Democrats should plan to reverse the bad things the previous administration did, such as pulling funding from necessary initiatives like USAID and Medicare. They should also work for the good of the people by reducing inflation, come to a conclusion of the war in Iran and reduce the deficit.
Republicans should see that the voters rejected the plans of President Trump and not blindly follow his lead. If Trump did something that was good for the country, enlarge upon it. But change those which are too expensive and unnecessary — such as the proposed arch. Following Trump now will prove disastrous in the future.
How about getting big money out of elections? Making a decision regarding the changing of the clocks?
If the two parties don’t change their goals and do things which are good for the country — and not for the pockets of their representatives and senators — there will be be another major change at the next election.
Robert Goldberg
Portland

title: Teen who was shot in head while friends showed off gun on FaceTime taken off life support
text:
Teen who was shot in head while friends showed off gun on FaceTime taken off life support
Family of Ja'Vohn Pitts said his brain wasn't showing any activity.
Teen who was shot in head while friends showed off gun on FaceTime taken off life support
Family of Ja'Vohn Pitts said his brain wasn't showing any activity.
A high school student has died after being shot in the head earlier this month in Kentucky.
Seventeen-year-old Ja'Vohn Pitts was shot in Kenton County, Kentucky, on Nov. 7. Elsmere, Kentucky, police believe one of his friends pulled the trigger. A week later, Pitts' family said his brain wasn't getting any oxygen.
Family confirmed on Monday that Pitts had died.
Reggie Pitts said his son planned to enlist in the Marines after graduating.
Last Saturday, Ja'Vohn was with friends in Elsmere. Police say the teenagers were showing off the gun during a FaceTime call when one of those friends shot him in the head.
Investigators say the person who shot Ja'Vohn was a juvenile and a friend of his. Police say the shooter cooperated with investigators and was charged with second-degree assault with a deadly weapon. Police did not release the juvenile's name, citing Kentucky law.
But there's a new question of whether the juvenile's assault charges could be upgraded since Ja'Vohn has died.
"It was senseless and careless," Pitts said. "I just lost a son for some mistake. I think justice needs to be served for that."
To support Ja'Vohn's burial costs, his family set up a fundraiser, which can be accessed here.

title: Apple reporting outages affecting some services
text:
Apple reporting outages affecting some services
Apple reporting outages affecting some services
An update gone awry Tuesday at Apple followed a rash of major outages in recent days, including problems affecting the Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines and Microsoft.
Video above: What caused the nationwide ground stop and where does the investigation stand?
Apple acknowledged on its system status page that its Apple Music, App Store and AppleCare services suffered full outages and that its iCloud sign-in interface was also having issues. The technology monitoring site Downdetector.com also showed a spike in user complaints about Apple Pay.
“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” the company said in an emailed statement. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”
Marriott International, the largest U.S. hotel operator, also had technology issues affecting reservations and check-ins, among other problems, according to users posting on Reddit. Downdetector.com also reported that Marriott was experiencing an outage.
Marriott, which has 10,200 properties and more than 1.8 million rooms under its corporate umbrella, did not immediately respond to an email inquiry from The Associated Press.
The outages are the latest in a string of technology breakdowns.
On Monday, a system outage at United Airlines lasted more than 90 minutes, forcing the carrier to delay departing flights. The problem at United came just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop that delayed hundreds of flights and stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country.
Chicago-based United said there was no indication its outage was cybersecurity-related.
Also Monday, thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
Chase said Monday the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and on Tuesday confirmed the bank's systems were operating normally.
Last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business chatter and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted.
The tech giant said there was “no indication” that malicious activity caused the disruptions, specifically noting on Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.

title: Maine runners sweep NCAA Division III East regionals, lead their teams to nationals
text:
Stephen White has enjoyed a strong season for the Colby College men’s cross country team, but was still seeking a breakout performance.
He found it Saturday at the NCAA Division III East Region championships and will get the opportunity to ride that momentum to nationals.
With a strong finishing kick, White passed Dylan Fiegener of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology to win the men’s 8,000-meter race with a time of 24 minutes, 00.20 seconds at the Wainwright Recreation Complex in South Portland.
“It’s just a huge confidence booster and I’m really excited,” said White, a junior from Southborough, Massachusetts. “I always thought that I had it in me, I just didn’t really have that breakthrough race this season, and I finally got it on Saturday.”
Charlotte Crum, a Bates College freshman, won the women’s 6,000-meter race in 21:08.19, beating runner-up Liv Girand of MIT by more than seven seconds.
“I was feeling confident in my body and preparation going into it,” Crum said. “We’ve been putting in a lot of work. I knew I’d be up near the front of the pack, but I really didn’t think about taking the win (at first) … I was trying to talk to myself and stay positive, even though I was in a lot of pain during the race.”
Both Bates teams, the Colby men and the Bowdoin women received at-large berths for the national championships Saturday in Northfield, Minnesota.
White was one of four Colby runners to finish in the top 10, joining Curtis Leachman (seventh), Eli Ziegler (ninth) and Henry Reichle (10th). The Mules finished second in the team competition.
“Going in, I had to visualize myself as being the best,” White said. “I just kind of thought that the people that race the best don’t really go into races thinking they’re going to lose. I really had to muster up all my confidence going in. I knew the field was going to be super strong. I just knew I had to (stay) with the top guys.”
The top five runners in the men’s race were separated by a mere eight seconds.
“It was a top-tier moment in the program for me as a coach, one of the most electric moments,” said Colby coach Jared Beers, who is in his 22nd season leading the program. “When he took over to lead the pack, it was electric. … Stephen is the one who got the W, but it’s really been about them working together, at least six months of them talking about building to this moment together.”
Crum’s peformance is the continuation of a strong first season in college. A highly recruited runner from Hinesburg, Vermont — Crum was the Vermont Gatorade Runner of the Year last season — she’s finished 12th or better in every race since mid-September. That includes a fourth-place finish at the Maine State Championship on Sept. 19 at Bowdoin College.
“When she made the final turn (of the race), I knew (Girand) wasn’t going to cover her move,” said Bates coach Danny Feldman, who is in his fifth year. “It was everything we wanted and then some, and was executed fantastically. … I saw her competing at this high of a level (this early). She had some national level experience (in high school). She made it very clear (Saturday) that she’s a force to be reckoned with.”
Two of Crum’s teammates, Leah White (sixth) and Zoe McCullough (10th), also finished in the top 10. Max Hoffman led the Bates men with an eighth-place finish (24:13.99). The Bates women placed third and the men took fourth. This is the sixth time that both teams have reached nationals in the same year.
“I’m so excited, and I know my team is as well going to nationals,” Crum said. “It’s so much better when you get to go with the team. It’s so much more fulfilling and exciting to go as a team.”
The Bowdoin women, led by Laura White’s ninth-place showing (21:36.33), finished fourth.

title: Fiona the hippo under close watch at Cincinnati Zoo after swallowing knit hat
text:
Cincinnati Zoo's Fiona the hippo under close watch after swallowing knit hat
Fiona the hippo is being monitored after swallowing a knit cap that a visitor accidentally tossed into her habitat, the zoo says.
"We probably couldn't make it happen again if we tried," Cincinnati Zoo's spokesperson said of the circumstance that led to Fiona ingesting the inedible object.
The knit cap was tossed into the air in front of the habitat and caught by a ceiling fan that catapulted it through a 1-foot opening above the 12-foot-tall viewing windows, Communications Director Michelle Curley said.
"Our veterinary team and hippo care staff are monitoring her around the clock and doing everything they can to help her pass the object safely," the zoo shared. "Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self."
Her caregivers are likely concerned the knit cap could cause an obstruction, according to Ron Magill, goodwill ambassador and conservation liaison for the Zoo Miami Foundation.
"The major concerns regarding Fiona ingesting a cap are primarily that it doesn’t cause an obstruction in her digestive tract, which could lead to impaction and damage leading to serious infection and sepsis," Magill told CNN.
As she's being monitored, she will be off habitat until it's resolved, the zoo said.
The zoo said it will share more information when possible and reminded visitors to be careful and secure their belongings when near habitats.
"If something falls into a habitat, please notify a Zoo staff member immediately," the zoo said.
Born six weeks premature at the Cincinnati Zoo on Jan. 24, 2017, Fiona weighed only 29 pounds at birth — 25 pounds less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species. She survived because of her animal care team's tireless efforts to save her and has inspired many to care about her species and wildlife. Her story captured the attention of many, making her known across the world.
CNN contributed to this report.

title: Portland City Council approves Franklin Street redesign plan
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Portland City Council approves Franklin Street redesign plan
The Portland City Council unanimously approved a plan Monday night to redesign Franklin Street, advancing the project to preliminary design with the Maine Department of Transportation.
Franklin Street is about 200 feet wide in some places. The plan would narrow the roadway and add raised crossings and separated bike lanes. It would reconnect streets and add sidewalks, traffic-calming features and on-street parking. The plan also keeps two through lanes in each direction on the northern stretch, from Marginal Way to Congress Street, and one lane each way on the southern stretch, from Congress to Commercial Street.
The conceptual plan aims to create more than 3.5 acres of land for housing and other development, expand Lincoln Park and make room to enlarge Boyd Street Park and Garden. The plan estimates that newly created parcels, combined with some adjacent city-owned land, could accommodate 530 to 720 homes.
The project grew from a 2024 city agreement with MaineDOT to update an earlier Franklin Street study. The Sustainability and Transportation Committee voted 3-0 in October to send the plan to the council.
Written comments submitted before the vote included support and objections. The Portland Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Committee supported the plan, citing safety and connectivity improvements, but urged further review of turn lanes and medians. The Urbanist Coalition of Portland also backed moving ahead while arguing some parking, medians and traffic lanes could be reduced to create more room for housing.
Other commenters raised concerns about tree loss, commuter traffic shifting to Pearl Street, parking for future residents and project costs.
The preliminary construction estimate is about $44.4 million, including $12.5 million for stormwater, sewer separation and green stormwater infrastructure. The estimate will be refined during design. The plan anticipates construction from 2031 to 2033.
The preliminary design phase is already funded at $2.5 million. After that, the project would need final design and construction funding.

title: Republican accused of attempting to strangle wife resigns from Maine House seat
text:
A Republican state representative from Sanford accused of attempting to strangle his wife has resigned from the House of Representatives.
House Speaker Ryan Fecteau, D-Biddeford, announced Monday night that Rep. Lucas Lanigan was stepping down. The House clerk confirmed that Lanigan submitted his resignation Monday via email.
In a written statement, Fecteau criticized Lanigan for not immediately stepping down after he was charged with felony aggravated assault more than two years ago.
Lanigan pleaded not guilty to the felony charges of domestic violence assault and domestic violence aggravated assault. His case is still pending in the courts.
“His refusal to step down — despite the extremely serious charges against him — was a disservice to the legislature and a profound disservice to every person in House District 141,” Fecteau said. “Maine people expect and deserve far better from their elected officials.”
Lanigan won reelection by a single vote in the November 2024 election, less than two weeks after he was charged with aggravated domestic violence. An affidavit says Lanigan grabbed his wife by the throat after she confronted him about an affair.
Democrats called for his resignation, but he remained in the House, with Republicans defending his right to due process.
His wife asked a judge and prosecutors to drop the charges, but Assistant District Attorney Linda Holdsworth-Donovan said victims regularly recant, sometimes because of pressure from the alleged perpetrators, and that the state was still pursuing charges against Lanigan.
Lanigan did not seek reelection for a third term this year, and his term expires next month. Republicans held the Sanford-area seat earlier this month; Marc Boisse will be sworn in to the District 141 seat on Dec. 2.
House Democrats voted in January 2025 to launch an ethics probe of Lanigan. But that effort never got off the ground because Lanigan’s case was tied up in the courts.
Lanigan is scheduled to appear next week in York County Superior Court for a status conference, according to court documents. His attorney, Chris Nielsen, did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
Staff Writer Morgan Womack contributed to this report.

title: FAA, NTSB investigating deadly plane crash in the Town of Sweden
text:
SWEDEN, Maine (WABI) - The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) are investigating a plane crash that happened in Sweden Monday afternoon.
An FAA spokesperson tells WABI that the crash happened around 3:45 p.m.
According to the FAA, the pilot was the only person on board the small aircraft.
Portland media partners WMTW report a male pilot was killed in the crash.
The model of the plane, which the FAA says is a Cessna 182, is a four-seat, single-engine light utility airplane.
The NTSB says two investigators are expected to arrive at the accident site on Tuesday. After the wreckage is documented, it will be recovered and moved to a secure facility for further examination.
The FAA is expected to release a preliminary incident report Tuesday. You can find the latest accident reports here.
This year has seen several high-profile plane crashes in Maine, including the private jet crash in Bangor that killed 6 people, the crash involving a Maine Warden Service plane in Avon that killed pilot Joshua Tibbetts, and the crash in Bristol that killed a New Hampshire man in August.

title: White House pulls FDA nominee Heidi Overton after wavering support from Senate Republicans
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House said Tuesday it has pulled the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration amid growing indications she didn’t have the votes needed to win Senate confirmation.
Overton, a physician and White House domestic policy adviser, has spent most of her professional career working directly for Trump or conservative groups aligned with his agenda. Her nomination in August was seen as a move to bring a stabilizing Trump loyalist to the FDA after a tumultuous year under Trump’s first FDA commissioner, Dr. Marty Makary.
But Overton faced bipartisan questions in the Senate about her willingness to break from Trump, particularly on his unsupported claims about the dangers of childhood vaccines.
Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana doctor who chairs the Senate health committee, said earlier in the day he remained undecided about Overton ahead of a critical vote on her nomination scheduled for Wednesday.
Cassidy had previously called Overton’s support for Trump’s plan to break up combination vaccines — including the measles, mumps and rubella shot— “almost disqualifying.” And he pressed her during a September hearing about her scientific independence and willingness to push back against Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine critic.
A spokesperson for Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, said Tuesday that she had not yet made a decision on Overton.
To win confirmation, Overton would have needed the votes of all 12 Republicans on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. Democrats hold 11 seats. Without support of the committee, Overton faced little chance of winning a full Senate vote on the chamber floor.
Republicans are racing to try to confirm all of Trump’s current nominees before they hand over power to Senate Democrats in January.

title: Pope forgives person who nailed him in the eye with a rosary in Peru
text:
Pope forgives person who nailed him in the eye with a rosary in Peru
Pope Leo XIV has forgiven the person who threw a rosary at him before his final Mass in Peru and nailed him in the eye, saying it was merely a sign of the person’s profound faith.
Leo got hit during a popemobile ride Monday through the estimated 1.5 million people who had flooded a Lima air base for the service. Leo grimaced and touched his eye but proceeded as if nothing had happened.
During an in-flight press conference en route home, a Peruvian reporter apologized for the incident. Leo, who lived in Peru for two decades and has Peruvian citizenship, brushed it off as merely someone trying to get close to the pope.
Related video: Pope Leo XIV rides in helicopter during Latin America trip
And he also joked about it.
“The nice thing about Peruvians, including the person who with a lot of faith simply wanted to offer me a rosary, are things you carry in your heart – or maybe in your eye – but that mark the life of someone,” he said.
“It tells you that here truly there is enthusiasm. Here there is profound faith. Here there is a desire to receive the blessing of the Lord,” he said.
People often toss rosaries, stuffed animals, sports jerseys and other items toward the pope when he is in the popemobile and he has often wowed crowds with his quick reflexes and ability to catch them. His bodyguards, however, say these tossed items are some of their biggest security concerns when he’s out in public.

title: Woman accused of posing as registered nurse earned two promotions before she was caught, authorities say
text:
MANITOWOC, Wis. (WBAY/Gray News) - A woman posed as a registered nurse and was even promoted twice before she was caught, according to authorities.
Angel Jacobson, 36, is accused of stealing the identity of another person to work as a registered nurse in Wisconsin. She is charged with theft of over $100,000 by false representation, identity theft for financial gain and practicing as a registered nurse without a license.
Jacobson started working in December 2025 as a floor nurse. She was promoted to unit coordinator in April and then director of nursing in September. The facility she worked at has not been named.
According to the criminal complaint, a credential screening vendor flagged Jacobson’s RN license number as inactive because the license holder became a registered nurse in Texas.
Several other discrepancies were discovered, including different birth dates on Jacobson’s resume and driver’s license. The name of the person she claimed to be was similar but not the same. The original RN license holder passed the RN licensing exam in 2007, but Jacobson’s resume said she passed in 2022.
When confronted, Jacobson blamed the mix-up on the Wisconsin Department of Safety and Professional Services.
Jacobson later admitted that she was looking for jobs that offered a lot of money and found someone with a similar name on Wisconsin’s license database, according to the complaint.
“Even though I don’t have formal schooling, I’m well knowledgeable in the field,” Jacobson said, according to the complaint.
Jacobson said she had EMT training and learned a lot from registered nurses over the years. She said she believes she would be able to pass an RN licensing exam.
“I could probably pass it with flying colors. I know a lot of stuff, and what I didn’t know, I just didn’t do,” she said.

title: THAW Radiothon Thursday to help local families stay warm this winter
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ELLSWORTH – As winter approaches, many families across Hancock and Washington counties are facing unprecedented financial pressures. Record high heating costs, combined with rising prices for groceries, housing, healthcare, transportation and other necessities, are leaving more households vulnerable to a heating emergency than ever before.
To help meet this growing need, Avec Community Action, Heart of Maine United Way and Star 97.7 Radio are partnering for the 2027 THAW Fund Radiothon, airing live on Thursday, Nov. 19, from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. The event will raise critical funds to support the THAW Fund, which provides emergency heating assistance to residents of Hancock and Washington counties.
For more than 30 years, the THAW Fund has helped local families, seniors and individuals facing a winter crisis keep the heat on when they have nowhere else to turn. This year, community support is more important than ever.
“Many of the people reaching out for help today are hard-working individuals and families who are employed and doing everything they can to make ends meet,” Matt Donahue, chief executive officer of Heart of Maine United Way, said. “The rising cost of living, especially home heating costs, is creating real challenges for households across our region. Many of these families earn too much to qualify for traditional assistance programs yet still cannot absorb the cost of a heating emergency. Funds raised through the THAW Radiothon may be the only source of help available to them, making community support absolutely critical.”
The emergency heating assistance provided by the THAW Fund does more than address the immediate need for heat, helping to prevent larger crises that can threaten a family’s health, safety and overall stability.
“The need we are seeing in our communities is greater than ever before, which inspires us to leverage our partnerships to help as many of our neighbors in Hancock and Washington counties as we possibly can,” Jason Parent, chief executive officer of Avec Community Action, said. “The THAW Radiothon is a powerful example of what can happen when organizations, businesses and community members come together to support their neighbors. Every donation helps ensure local families have somewhere to turn when a heating emergency threatens their well-being.”
Community members can support the THAW Fund by making a secure online donation at https://homeunitedway.org/thaw/, mailing a gift to THAW Fund c/o Heart of Maine United Way, 700 Mount Hope Ave., Suite 101, Bangor, ME 04401 or by donating during the live Radiothon broadcast on Star 97.7 Radio on Nov. 19.

title: This sculptor uses art to rise from grief
text:
RANDOLPH, Vt. (InvestigateTV) - In the hills of central Vermont, where the ocean is nowhere in sight, two massive mammals rise from the earth. Visitors who stumble upon them are often stopped in their tracks.
Whale Dance is the creation of local artist Jim Sardonis. “I mainly love nature in all its forms.”
The Randolph sculpture, installed in 2019, has an older sibling, Reverence, which migrated from Randolph to South Burlington in 1999, and is seen by thousands each day as they head up Interstate 89.
“Surprising how many people know about them when I go to Boston, or some place, people mentioned them,” Sardonis said.
People like the Perkins family from Connecticut, who every summer take selfies with friends and family at the whales, and who on this day got a special treat, meeting the sculptor himself.
“We always wondered who designed them and why,” Perkins said.
In Brookfield, Sardonis’ first piece is set in stone. It’s near the historic floating bridge in the village — two hippos called Father and Son.
“I did it shortly after my father died and my son was born,” Sardonis said. At the time, he was teaching and thought it would be a good summer project. “It’s given a lot of fun to kids over the years.”
The whales came later, in a dream. “I had been standing on a beach looking at the water, and these two tails came up at the same time.”
But Sardonis’ most poignant work wasn’t born from a dream. It was born of a broken heart. He and his wife, Dianne, lost an unborn daughter to anencephaly.
“The brain doesn’t develop for some unknown reason,” Sardonis said. “So, they knew she wouldn’t live when she was born. So, we had a tough weekend, knowing on Monday we would deliver her and spent an hour with her.”
Her name was Leah. Through the grief, Sardonis decided to make a sculpture to honor her and the care workers at nearby Gifford Hospital. It’s called Vermont Family.
“Spending the year working on the sculpture was, yeah, just what I needed,” he said. “We didn’t realize until the sculpture was done that we would have a baby girl.”
“Well, you seem very honest about what you’ve gone through and what this means to you,” reporter Joe Carroll said.
“We certainly have had a lot more joy in our lives than sorrow,” Sardonis responded.
Proof that even in the deepest valley of grief, art prevails.

title: Pro-choice Mainers pressure Susan Collins ahead of FDA confirmation vote
text:
Hours after reproductive and abortion-rights advocates called on Republican Sen. Susan Collins to oppose President Donald Trump’s choice to lead the Food and Drug Administration the White House withdrew the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton.
The administration took the move Tuesday night after it became clear that Overton didn’t have the votes needed for Senate confirmation.
The Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pension Committee, on which Collins serves, was scheduled to take up Overton’s confirmation on Wednesday. She would have needed the votes of all 12 Republicans on the committee. Democrats hold 11 seats. Without support of the committee, Overton faced little chance of winning a full Senate vote.
The prospect of Overton taking the top post at the FDA had alarmed abortion-rights supporters because she has celebrated abortion bans and refused to say whether she believes birth control is a form of abortion.
Standing in front of Americans for Contraception’s “FREEDA Womb,” a 20-foot-tall inflatable IUD, at Portland City Hall on Tuesday, Mark Gallagher, a 54-year-old Kennebunk resident, said the government has no right to restrict access to contraception for his two teenage daughters.
“I want them to make a decision about their own bodies,” said Gallagher, who identified himself as a Catholic. “I want them to be assisted and guided by doctors and scientists, and not Republicans in Congress, and certainly not the Trump administration.”
Collins’ office did not immediately respond to a request for comment late Tuesday night about Overton’s withdrawal. Last week, she told NBC News she had not yet taken a position.
Overton has been a vocal opponent of medication abortion and celebrated the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision that overturned Roe v. Wade. She serves as a White House policy adviser at a time when the administration is questioning the safety of certain drugs and vaccines.
Maine Rep. Anne Graham, D-North Yarmouth, a retired pediatric nurse practitioner, had called on Collins to oppose the nomination.
“Sen. Collins needs to stand up for the women of Maine, particularly rural women, who would not be able to access birth control under Overton’s oversight,” Graham said at the news conference Tuesday.
In addition to news the conference Tuesday, “say no to Heidi Vaperton for FDA commissioner” signs had sprouted up in Portland’s West End — a reference to the agency’s decision to authorized flavored vapes. Politico reported the signs are the work of Health in Office, a nonpartisan activist group targeting Collins and Sens. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and Bill Cassidy, R-La.
During a confirmation hearing in September, Collins questioned Overton about vapes and drugs for rare diseases. Democrats and Murkowski pressed the nominee on vaccines, contraception and abortion services, including her muddled stance on the abortion medication mifepristone.
Overton had previously called mifepristone “dangerous to women.” But she told senators that the drug is “safe and effective as labeled today” and noted that the FDA was currently reviewing its safety.
The head of the FDA oversees the evaluation and regulation of prescription drugs, vaccines and food safety. Whoever takes the post will oversee the FDA’s current safety study of mifepristone.
Overton was also pressed at her confirmation hearing about whether she would resist political pressure and make decisions based only on scientific evidence. She did not directly answer questions about whether Trump could be wrong, and stated that she’s had “robust” conversations with the president, saying he wants the best for people.
Several senators noted that she was in the Oval Office when Trump falsely claimed acetaminophen, commonly known as Tylenol, causes autism, and when he said a combined vaccination for the measles, mumps and rubella could be fatal to children.
Nicole Clegg, president and CEO of Planned Parenthood of Northern New England, said in a written statement that Overton’s “inflammatory briefs” about abortion and LGBTQ+ care, and her support of the “politically motivated” mifepristone review, are disqualifying.
“The truth is, a vote for Overton is a vote to install an FDA commissioner whose public statements and agenda are dangerous to women,” Clegg said.
Collins was seeking a sixth term when the confirmation hearing was held. Reproductive rights, including Collins’ 2018 vote to support Brett Kavanaugh’s nomination to the Supreme Court, were major issues during the campaign.
Collins continues to describe herself as pro-choice while also defending her vote for Kavanaugh, which reproductive rights advocates blame in part for the fall of national abortion protections. She lost her reelection race earlier this month.
Staff Writer Drew Johnson contributed to this story.
This story contains reporting by The Associated Press.

title: I followed a big buck into a Maine bog. Getting out was another story.
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
If you are a young, energetic deer hunter who likes to get deep into the woods and snoop about, Maine’s bogs hold an allure and fascination. Big bucks like bogs. Cedar trees cast long shadows and the green carpet of sphagnum moss underfoot makes for silent running. On a misty morning, a buck in one of these bogs is almost an apparition, a gauzy ghost.
But be careful, young fella. One of these seductive bogs can swallow you up in two ways.
The first happens when you step in the wrong place and, without warning, your boots sink beneath the moss. You can get stuck, really stuck, in the muck beneath that inviting green carpet. The harder you try to free yourself, the deeper you sink. It’s not the infamous quicksand, but it’s a near cousin.
Consider what happened last month at Sebasticook Lake. A duck hunter trying to retrieve a dead duck became stuck chest-deep in mud, roughly 300 feet from shore. His waders filled with muck, leaving him immobile and in need of rescue by the Newport Fire Department. Firefighters laid ladders across the mud and used a rope and sled to free him. Chief Jeff Chretien said he bet the hunter’s waders weighed 400 pounds by the time firefighters got him out.
The second way a bog can swallow you up happens when you get deep into one while tracking that monster buck on new snow. Bogs are uneven, with inlets, outlets and little cul-de-sacs that make them resemble a maze. Once inside, your exit plan can take an unexpected turn. The way out may be due north, but straight-line compass bearings are useless in these natural traps. The more you veer left or right to avoid blowdowns and standing water, the less reliable your compass heading becomes.
Orson Bog, north of Brownville and east of Route 11, is one of those classic, expansive Maine bogs that lies in wait for the supercharged but naive deer hunter. Years ago, I got my education there.
The place had always intrigued me. One November morning, a dusting of snow and a big deer track sucked me deeper and deeper into the cedar shadows and silent moss. I never saw the buck and abandoned the hunt in the late afternoon, figuring I had plenty of time to get out before dark. Or so I thought.
You guessed it. I had a hell of a time finding my way out. A light drizzle had erased my tracks, leaving me unable to backtrack. My compass bearing took me straight into standing water and blowdown tangles, just as I had described. I eventually found my way out as darkness was closing in, but not without some anxiety and sweaty palms.
My experience is hardly unique. Several documented incidents show just how easily people can become trapped or lost in Maine’s bogs.
Three hunters found themselves in that predicament in New Gloucester in November 2018. They became stuck hip-deep in a bog off Route 231 and needed help from the New Gloucester Fire and Rescue Department and Maine game wardens. Their call for help was sent through an Apple Watch, and cellphone coordinates helped rescuers pinpoint their location. Twenty fire and rescue responders went to the scene along with members of the Maine Warden Service.
A similar ordeal unfolded at Mount Blue State Park in July 2024. Michael Altmaier, a 75-year-old New Sharon man, was reported missing after failing to show up for a scheduled meeting in Weld. His car was found at the park’s overlook, and a search led game warden Kyle Hamilton and his K9 to Altmaier near a bog less than a mile away. He likely fell down an embankment and became disoriented. Unable to get up, he remained stuck there for four days before rescuers found him. He was flown out by helicopter and taken to a hospital.
In another incident, an 85-year-old Parkman man named Gene Wilbur was found at the edge of a bog in Piscataquis County in August 2023 after being reported missing from his home. Game Warden Chad Robertson and K9 Storm located him about a quarter-mile from his residence. His legs and feet were wet from wading into the bog, and he was suffering from hypothermia. He was helped out and taken to a hospital.
Maine bogs are peatlands. In some bogs, raised areas are ombrotrophic, meaning they receive most of their water and nutrients from precipitation rather than groundwater. Whatever their precise classification, these wet, tangled places deserve a hunter’s respect. Call them what you will, hunters need to approach them with caution and common sense.

Three Maine colleges — Bowdoin, Colby and Maine Maritime Academy — are heading to the 64-team NCAA Division III volleyball tournament that starts Thursday.
Colby (22-3), which won the NESCAC championship, is in the event for the first time in 21 years and will host the first two rounds, including an opening-round match Thursday against Baruch (16-13). The other two teams heading to Waterville are Emerson and Sarah Lawrence.

title: Hearts of Pine begin overhauling roster after disappointing season
text:
Hearts of Pine and Maine Wildness coverage is supported by Thomas College
Thomas College does college differently. Home to Maine's first and only athletic coaching degree and the first NCAA DIII NIL education and support program, Thomas College is empowering the next generation of leaders. thomas.edu
The major overhaul of the Portland Hearts of Pine roster has begun — with a lofty long-term goal guiding the decisions.
“My goal in coming here is to turn this club into a perennial top-four team, with a goal of being the first club to be promoted in American soccer history,” said Ray Saari, the Hearts of Pine’s sporting director, who was hired in late August.
United Soccer League plans to start a first-tier league, called Premier, in 2028 and introduce the promotion-relegation system common to European leagues. The Hearts of Pine play in USL League One, a third-tier league. USL Championship is a second-tier league.
After struggling to an 8-14-10 record in USL1 in 2026, the Hearts of Pine have determined that only six of its 28 players will definitely return for the franchise’s third season. Five other players are still in contract discussions with Portland and could return. That means 17 players, including retired team captain Mikey Lopez, will not be back on the pitch at Fitzpatrick Stadium for the home team.
The sweeping changes were expected after the Hearts finished 14th in the 17-team league and 12 points out of the playoffs. Portland never won more than two consecutive games and conceded winning or tying goals after the 80th minute in 10 matches, coughing up 21 potential points.
“We struggled in different parts of the game, improvement needed to be made,” Saari said.
Midfielders Ollie Wright and Masashi Wada and forward Titus Washington will return for a third season. All three players finished the 2026 campaign on the injured list. Wada (first team) and Wright (second team) were both all-USL1 players in 2025.
Wada suffered a lower-leg fracture on April 11 in the home opener. The club struggled to fill that void at the top of the midfield. Saari said the club has actively been in contact with Wada, his doctor in Japan, and the Hearts of Pine’s team doctor.
“We felt confident Sashi will be able to make a strong comeback,” Saari said.
Wright (six goals, team-high seven assists) had surgery in late September to repair the torn ACL in his right knee. Wright is expected to be out until at least late June or early July. Washington played in only seven USL1 games in 2026.
Also returning are outside backs Josh Drack and Eji Hata and midfielder Diego Letayf Escutia. All three were in-season additions in 2026.
Goalkeeper and 2026 team MVP Hunter Morse, midfielders Diego Gonzalez, Matteo Kidd and Tyler Huck and forward Aboubacar Camara are the other players who could be re-signed. Camara scored a team-high 10 goals in his first professional season.
Saari said there are “intricacies” to the negotiations for each of those players.
Morse has been a club mainstay.
“There’s free agency in pro sports. Some players, like Hunter, who have done very, very well, may have interest from other teams,” Saari said. “Hunter is a guy we’re very hopeful of bringing back.”
Gonzalez and Kidd were arguably the Hearts’ top performers in the center of the field. Gonzalez scored nine goals and had two assists in 21 games after joining the team on loan from the Houston Dynamo.
“Diego still has an option with Houston, so I can’t sign him until they make a decision,” Saari said.
Among those leaving Hearts are eight players who were in Portland for two seasons: dynamic dribbler Jay Tee Kamara, who led the 2026 squad in chances created; promising outside back Mo Mohamed; backup goalie Kash Oladapo; outside back Jaden Jones-Riley; center midfielder Michel Poon-Angeron; midfielder Khalid Hersi of Lewiston; center back Kemali Green; and forward Walter Varela.
Poon-Angeron was the first player signed to a Hearts of Pine contract and often wore the captain’s armband when Lopez was hurt or not playing. Varela scored the first goal in team history.
Green started 49 of the 53 USL1 games he played. The Hearts of Pine jettisoned their entire center-back rotation of Green, Brecc Evans, Serigne Mbacke Faye and seldom-used Esteban Espinosa.
“We conceded quite a bit of goals, and center back is very important to get right (to) build a successful team,” Saari said.
The other 2026 players not returning are outside back Zion Scarlett, forward Lagos Kunga, and midfielders Diogo Barbosa, Konstantinos Georgallides and Felipe Rodriguez Gentile.
Saari said announcements of player acquisitions could come within the next two weeks.

title: Fundraiser for 90-year-old veteran creates friendships across generations, state lines
text:
Fundraiser for 90-year-old veteran creates friendships across generations, state lines
The connections of three lives across generations and state lines started in 2024 with a fundraiser for a New Hampshire veteran.
Jenelle, a manager at U.S. Gold and Pawn in Manchester, noticed Donald, a 90-year-old veteran, regularly pawning his wife's jewelry to pay for her medical care.
Jenelle and her husband Jay started a fundraiser that raised $460,000 for Donald and his wife.
"She got to live out the rest of her life without any financial struggles and with the best care he could have given her. So that was the goal, and that was accomplished. So we're very happy about that," Jenelle said.
The story went viral on social media, catching the attention of Kathy Bull, who lived thousands of miles away.
"She was taking care of him out of the goodness of her heart. And the only little thing I can do is maybe help [her] plan an event," Bull said.
Bull said a stranger had helped her own family in their time of need, and felt a calling for her to pay it forward. She reached out to Jenelle with an offer to plan her wedding for free.
"We started with monthly planning calls and, I don't know, I fell in love with her in a way that I can't even explain," Bull said.
They finally met last month at the wedding after spending nearly two years planning through video calls and texts.
"We flew to Cape Cod and had a beautiful wedding with her and her family," Bull said.
Jenelle said she couldn't have asked for a better day.
She said Donald still comes to visit the store, but no longer out of necessity.
"I love seeing him come in now and not having to pawn his jewelry for money. Now it's just to say hi," Jenelle said. "He calls me his adopted granddaughter."
Janelle and Kathy are hoping that their story now inspires others to pay it forward.

title: Murder case in death of Tasia Fortune, found hanging from tree, sent back to police
text:
JACKSON, Miss. (WLBT/Gray News) - The case against a man charged with murder in the death of Tasia Fortune is being sent back to police for further investigation.
During a preliminary hearing Tuesday for 25-year-old Earnest Lloyd, the judge agreed there was not enough evidence against him.
The case was sent back to the Jackson Police Department.
Fortune’s mother questions investigation
Fortune’s mother, Christy Spivey, attended the hearing. She said she does not think Fortune will ever get justice.
“No, no. I think it was handled sloppily, and I’ve also come to realize that they’re so thin,” Spivey said.
Spivey said she spoke with Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney about the case. She said she had a “meeting with the chief” and does not think the department has the necessary resources.
“I just think they’re so thin that how do you even have time to investigate a case? There are only eight detectives, is what the chief told me, and 93 murders. Who does what?” Spivey said.
Spivey said she does not know how her daughter died.
“It’s hard. I don’t even know how she died. Her death certificate says homicide by unspecified means, and I can’t even see the autopsy. I don’t know. I don’t even know how she died,” Spivey said.
Spivey said she is working on a petition to sue the Jackson Police Department over how the case was handled.
Case background
Lloyd was arrested Sept. 22 and charged with murder for his alleged role in Fortune’s death. He was denied bond shortly after.
Three suspects have been arrested in connection with the investigation.
Fortune, 29, was found hanging from a tree behind a vacant house in the 500 block of Road of Remembrance in Jackson on Aug. 3.
Investigators have not publicly disclosed her exact cause of death.
The case has drawn national and local attention. Community leaders and activists have called for answers about the circumstances of Fortune’s death.

title: How 911 dispatchers are using AI to assist callers
text:
O’FALLON, Mo. (InvestigateTV) — Artificial intelligence is on the frontlines of fighting crime and being used in many 911 dispatch centers around the country.
The police dispatch in O’Fallon is using artificial intelligence-based technology to assist dispatchers who answer 911 calls. Dispatchers there said a person will always answer the call.
Based on the call, the technology displays a specific list of questions for the dispatcher to ask. It also listens in, transcribes the call in real time and suggests information the dispatcher might have missed.
Paul Jokerst, emergency communications administrator for O’Fallon Police, said the technology is there to assist dispatchers.
“It is clearly here to assist. It’s just to assist them,” Jokerst said.
He said the technology is not intended to replace dispatchers.
“It’s not here to replace anybody. It’s not here to take a job away or hamper somebody’s job,” Jokerst said.
O’Fallon police dispatcher Mike Conte said he supports the use of AI.
Conte said the technology helps when dispatchers are trying to pick out information they cannot understand from a caller.
“It’s very helpful when we’re trying to pick out pieces of information that we can’t understand the caller,” Conte said.
He said he supports the technology as long as he is also on the line.
“You will always talk to a human. One of us is always here. And we’re always ready to answer your call,” Conte said.
The use of AI in 911 is expanding rapidly.
In Fairfax, Virginia, AI translates calls into more than 170 languages instantly.
In New Orleans, AI automatically answers calls about accidents officials already know about. The system will inform the caller about the incident and if they are involved in any way the person can stay on line to talk to a dispatcher.
Experts say AI would not replace dispatchers at the moment because humans are better at compassion, processing emotion and keeping people calm.
AI in law enforcement continues to evolve.

title: 'Just a test:' FEMA to conduct nationwide Emergency Alert System test Tuesday
text:
'Just our legally mandated test:' FEMA conducting nationwide Emergency Alert System test Tuesday
The government is conducting a test of the nationwide Emergency Alert System (EAS) at approximately 2:20 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday.
If you are watching TV or listening to the radio, programming will be interrupted, and you will hear a test message. No action is required, and normal programming will resume once the test is complete.
The EAS is a national public warning system designed to quickly reach Americans in case of a major emergency. The government is required by law to conduct these tests once every three years to identify any issues.
Despite online rumors, the test has been scheduled for months. FEMA acknowledged those rumors in a post on X Monday, saying in part, "No blackouts, no secret emergencies. Just our legally mandated, routine test on TV and radio."
The test was first announced by the FCC in September.

title: Sources: US intel indicates Iran developing plans to potentially use 'dirty bomb' in Washington
text:
Sources: US intel indicates Iran developing plans to potentially use 'dirty bomb' in Washington
New U.S. intelligence indicates that Iran is developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in Washington, D.C., even as officials continue to debate whether Iran can or will attempt to execute such a plot, according to seven U.S. officials.
Sources familiar with the information characterized the Iranian planning as an effort to give itself options, rather than an indicator of an imminent attack.
Dirty bombs package radioactive materials into a conventional bomb. A dirty bomb is much different from a nuclear bomb, which relies on a nuclear-fission reaction and would be exponentially more destructive.
Dirty bombs can still disperse dangerous airborne radiation for blocks or even miles, but experts say that any casualties are likely to be caused by the bomb explosion, not radiation. While they are no harder to assemble than any conventional bomb, the hard part is acquiring the radioactive material.
According to CNN, sources said the potential plot targeting senior Trump administration officials has sparked a flurry of U.S. contingency planning.
In a statement, White House officials said the U.S. is "monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time, there is no credible threats to the homeland."
The news comes as President Trump arrived in the Philippines Tuesday, where he is scheduled to meet with regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, according to the Associated Press.

title: US loses measles-free status as virus reaches highest rate in decades. What we know
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — With the U.S. experiencing its worst year for measles in decades, international health experts have decided that the U.S. has lost its status as a country that eliminated the continuous spread of the disease.
The U.S. has racked up more measles cases than in any year since 1991, with confirmed cases surpassing 5,000 in 2026, according to the latest data. Pennsylvania alone has seen more than 1,500 cases.
The Pan American Health Organization’s decision underscores a significant public health setback for the United States as the Trump administration reshapes federal vaccine policy.
Experts say that while the Trump administration did not create the underlying vaccination problem, which predates President Donald Trump’s return to office, many argue the Republican administration’s policies and public messaging may have exacerbated it.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an anti-vaccine activist before he entered politics who has worked to overhaul vaccine policy, promised in a social media post Tuesday that the Trump administration will stop measles outbreaks and work to regain the lost status. He said he recommended the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine and pointed to COVID-era disruptions as having led to a gap in protections, not only in the U.S.
“We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust,” he said.
Nationally, 92.4% of kindergartners received their required MMR shots in the 2025-26 school year, down from 92.5% the previous year and 95.2% in 2019-20, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That is below the approximately 95% coverage needed to prevent measles outbreaks, and some communities have substantially lower vaccination rates.
Here’s a look at how the Trump administration has handled the worst year for measles in more than three decades:
Mixed messages from the administration
Kennedy, who has a long record of questioning vaccine safety, has repeatedly promoted claims that vaccines are associated with autism, despite extensive scientific evidence finding no causal relationship.
And he has delivered mixed messaging on measles specifically. He has occasionally endorsed the MMR vaccine as “effective,” and again on Tuesday said he recommended the shot. But he also continues to raise unfounded safety concerns about the shots. In August, he told CNN: “I believe that the MMR vaccine prevents measles.” In that same interview he questioned the safety of the vaccine.
Trump reinforced those doubts at an event over the summer where he signed an executive order calling for splitting up the MMR vaccine. He said falsely that taken together the shot was “quite lethal.” Doctors say, and years of real-world evidence prove, that the combination MMR vaccine is both safe and effective at protecting children from illness.
Separate vaccines for measles, mumps and rubella are not available in the United States and producing them that way would be a logistical feat for drugmakers.
Josh Michaud, associate director of global and public health policy at healthcare research nonprofit KFF, said past administrations back to the 1990s, when confronted with measles outbreaks, were aggressive in telling the public how important vaccination is against the disease. That’s not happening now, he said.
“What we’re not seeing from the administration is strong communications about the need for vaccinations,” he said.
During the most recent measles outbreak, Kennedy promoted vitamin A as a possible treatment, which created concern among medical professionals that the administration was giving undue attention to alternatives rather than emphasizing vaccination.
Questioning measles deaths
Throughout the surge of measles cases, Kennedy has repeatedly challenged health officials’ accounts of deaths from the disease.
In August, Pennsylvania officials reported two measles-related deaths. The county coroner later said they involved infants too young to be vaccinated, with the virus itself causing one of the deaths.
After Gov. Josh Shapiro stressed that vaccinations could have averted the deaths, Kennedy said the deaths “may even have been altogether fabricated.” He later acknowledged that one of the deaths was due to measles.
The remark echoed similar statements he made after last year, when three measles-related deaths were recorded. Kennedy questioned whether one of the children who died was killed by measles.
Medical experts said the political quarreling over the deaths diverted focus from an exploding public health threat.
The overhaul of vaccine policy
As health secretary, Kennedy has spearheaded an overhaul of the nation’s vaccine policy. Last year, he fired all 17 members of a key vaccine advisory committee and hired vaccine critics among the replacements. In January, his department downsized the childhood immunization schedule. The moves were temporarily halted by a judge earlier this year.
Kennedy also acknowledged personally directing the CDC to update its website late last year to contradict its longtime guidance that vaccines don’t cause autism.
Critics say the overhaul and the administration’s overt questioning of immunization safety have fueled skepticism about vaccines.
Surveys indicate growing public wavering over support for the MMR vaccine. An August 2025 Annenberg survey found that 82% would be “very” or “somewhat” likely to recommend that an eligible child in their household get the MMR vaccine, compared to 90% in November 2024.
Kennedy has defended his upending of federal health policy by saying the changes will restore trust in America’s public health agencies. Doctors counter that the false and unverified information he promotes and the vaccine policy changes undermine confidence in vaccination and leave more people vulnerable to preventable disease.
In his statement Tuesday, Kennedy said the CDC has worked along multiple states to “help bring their outbreaks rapidly and successfully under control.”
Along with freezing and canceling billions in research under Kennedy’s leadership at the start of the Trump administration, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services laid off more than 10,000 workers and shut down entire offices and programs. Experts say those cuts may have impacted state and local health departments’ ability to adequately respond to outbreaks.
Measles designation won’t change federal response, CDC chief says
PAHO officials expect the U.S., along with Bolivia and Mexico, which also lost their elimination status, to each submit a plan “in the coming weeks” for how they will go about trying to stop transmission for at least a year and regain measles elimination status, said Dr. Daniel Salas, PAHO’s executive manager for immunizations.
A decision to strip the U.S. of its measles elimination status will not change how federal health officials are addressing outbreaks, CDC Director Erica Schwartz said.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans,” she said. “Vaccination does.”
She said federal officials have invested $100 million to help state and local health departments to reach communities with measles outbreaks. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.”
Michaud said the designation change is “a marker for how we backtracked on public health, particularly related to measles prevention, and particularly related to vaccines.”
“It encapsulates this idea that the United States is more vulnerable than ever to infectious diseases,” he said.

title: Pres. Trump travels for Asia summits
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President DonaldTrump is off to Asia for two high stakes summits.
Just weeks after Republicans were handed big losses during the Midterms, President Trump turns his attention to foreign affairs with two consequential summits in Asia.
The President’s first stop is Manila in the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit. There he will meet with the leaders of Japan, Australia and India. He will also sign a trade agreement with Thailand.
Then it’s off to Shenzen, China for the APEC Summit. The President said he does not plan to raise spying allegations regarding Nvidia with President Xi. Monday morning, President Trump told reporters upon departure from the White House, “You know, we’re heading to China, and I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get on your meeting.”
Also on the President’s agenda- an historic trilateral meeting with President Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin - where the three leaders are expected to discuss nuclear disarmament, and a possible meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. President Trump confirmed to reporters that the meeting is on the table, “Yes, we might have Kim Jong un. He may come, I don’t know. That’s up to President Xi.”
Three separate summits between Kim and President Trump have failed to lead to any curb in North Korea’s nuclear program.
This will be President Trump’s second trip to China this year. The U.S. and China just last week extended a trade truce that is due to expire in early January.

title: LSU guard MiLaysia Fulwiley accused of hitting officer with vehicle, denies police account
text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB/Gray News) — Louisiana State Police said it is compiling all available dashcam, bodycam and video footage connected to the arrest of Louisiana State University women’s basketball guard MiLaysia Fulwiley for review by prosecutors.
Video footage and public release
In a statement Monday, the Louisiana Department of Public Safety said investigators are gathering evidence following Fulwiley’s arrest on Saturday. The incident involved a Department of Public Safety police officer.
“DPS personnel are compiling all available dash-camera, body-worn camera, and surrounding video footage, along with a comprehensive, documented report, for submission to the 19th Judicial District Attorney’s Office for review,” the department said.
The statement did not specify whether dashcam or bodycam recordings of the incident exist.
State police also addressed whether footage would be released publicly.
“In accordance with established procedures, camera footage related to ongoing investigations is not routinely released to the media,” the statement said.
Officials said requests for footage are handled through the public records request process.
Arrest details

title: Puppy wanders into car dealership after being abandoned and finds her forever home
text:
WICHITA FALLS, Texas (KAUZ/Gray News) - For an abandoned 6-month-old puppy, wandering into a Texas car dealership turned out to be the beginning of a second chance.
Nova, a 6-month-old Great Pyrenees, wandered into the Always Auto showroom in Wichita Falls after being abandoned. Instead of turning her away, the employees welcomed her with food, water and plenty of love.
“She ran right into the dealership, ran right up to me, and I just kind of knew it was meant to be,” Roman Letsis said. “I can’t believe somebody dumped her, too. It’s pretty sad. So, we took her under our care and just fell in love with her.”
However, just as Nova was settling in, her health took a frightening turn. She stopped eating and moving, showing signs of parvovirus, a potentially deadly disease in puppies.
Her new family knew they had to act fast. After struggling to find an available veterinarian nearby, they decided to make the drive more than 100 miles to Denton to get her the care she needed.
Josh Letsis, the dealership’s owner, said there was never any question about getting Nova help.
“There wasn’t even a thought. It was like, ‘Let’s just find somebody that can get her in tonight. It doesn’t matter if we have to go to Fort Worth or Dallas or whatever...’ So, it just wasn’t even a question. My son jumped in the truck with me, and we took her right in,” Josh Letsis said.
Roman Letsis said the trip was worth it, knowing Nova might not have survived without treatment.
“It was worth it taking her in, and we’re glad we did because she might have not made it another day,” he said.
Nova spent the next week in the hospital fighting for her life. Her family initially expected her treatment to last only a couple of days, but her condition remained uncertain.
Josh Letsis said there were two days when the family wasn’t sure whether Nova would pull through. She eventually began receiving food through a feeding tube and slowly started showing signs of improvement.
After a difficult week, Nova finally made it through. Roman Letsis said seeing her recover after everything she had been through was an incredible feeling.
“Seeing her pull through after that full week was amazing,” he said.
Now, Nova is continuing her recovery and has found a forever home with the Always Auto family. Roman Letsis said he plans to make Nova his own dog, and she will become a permanent fixture at the dealership.
“Yeah, I’m gonna make her my dog,” he said. “So, I’m glad she found me, and she found us. She’s gonna be a little dealership dog.”
After everything Nova has experienced, her family hopes her story encourages others to help animals in need. They recommend fostering puppies or donating to local animal shelters to give more animals a chance at finding their forever homes.

title: Football coach receives Mayo Clinic’s first liver transplant for metastatic colon cancer
text:
(Aging Untold) — A high school football coach received the first liver transplant performed at Mayo Clinic for metastatic colon cancer, and he is back on the field and has been cancer-free for two years.
Shannon Jones was diagnosed with colon cancer that had spread to his liver. Treatments had damaged his liver when he sought a second opinion at Mayo Clinic.
Diagnosis and treatment
Several years ago, Jones could not keep up during football practices.
“I got to where I’d have to stop and sit down,” Jones said. “I just, I was out of energy.”
Jones was diagnosed with colon cancer. His doctor told him it had spread to his liver.
He began treatment immediately with surgery to remove part of his colon. He also received other treatments, including chemotherapy and radiation.
The disease had spread to both sides of his liver, and Jones’ chances for long-term survival were low.
Dr. Denise Harnois, a Mayo Clinic transplant hepatologist, said the five-year survival rate for those patients is 9%, even with systemic chemotherapy.
“It was difficult, it was hard to push through sometimes,” Jones said. “I always felt like there was something bigger in it and that it was leading to something and that I just couldn’t quit.”
His family and his love of coaching kept him going.
“What I always tell people is gotta keep on keeping on,” Jones said.
Seeking a transplant
Jones’ treatments were working to kill the cancer, but they were also damaging his liver and making him very sick.
Jones said he told his hometown doctor he wanted a liver transplant.
“He said, ‘You’ll never have a liver transplant.’ And I said, ‘I’m going to,’” Jones said. “And I remember him saying, ‘No, you’re not.’ I said, ‘Watch.’”
Jones traveled to Mayo Clinic for a second opinion from Dr. Harnois, a Mayo Clinic liver transplant specialist.
“One of the fields of transplantation that’s really been expanding is what we would call transplant oncology,” Harnois said.
Changes in transplant eligibility
Until recently, liver transplantation for colon cancer that had spread to the liver was not an option for several reasons, Harnois said.
One reason was the risk of cancer cells spreading throughout the body, making the likelihood of recurrence in a newly transplanted liver high.
People who have transplants take medication to suppress their immune systems so their bodies do not reject the new organ, and cancer cells can erupt in that environment.
“When transplants were done, they very frequently developed recurrence of disease and often very quickly after the transplant was done,” Harnois said.
Advances in chemotherapy and other treatments now prevent colon cancer cells from migrating around the body. Mayo Clinic and a few other centers now perform liver transplants for highly selected colon cancer patients.
Harnois described the patients as those who have disease in the liver and not outside of it. The disease is not in the lymph nodes, and it has not gone to the lungs or other organs. Their colon cancer itself has been treated.
“Now transplantation represents an option for those patients,” Harnois said.
Transplant at Mayo Clinic
Jones went through a month of testing at Mayo Clinic to find out if he was a transplant candidate. After he was approved, he waited for a donor liver to become available.
“It was just one miracle after another that worked,” Jones said. “You know, it worked out for me.”
Jones received the first liver transplant for metastatic colon cancer performed at Mayo Clinic.
He is back on the field and has been cancer-free for two years.
Jones and Harnois said their real heroes are the organ donors and their families.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Sunshine and Warmer Temperatures Return to Northern Maine, But Dry Conditions Remain a Concern
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Monday! We’re starting off the new work week on a fairly quiet note across Northern Maine and Western New Brunswick, and it looks like that trend will continue for much of the upcoming week. High pressure will remain in control of our weather, bringing plenty of opportunities for sunshine and a gradual warming trend. By the middle of the week, we could see temperatures climbing into the lower 50s for many locations, which is well above average for the middle of November. Unfortunately, the extended stretch of dry weather isn’t necessarily good news for our ongoing drought conditions, which continue to impact much of the region.
Heading into the overnight hours tonight, we’re looking at mostly clear skies across the region as high pressure continues to dominate our weather pattern. With the lack of cloud coverage, temperatures will have a good opportunity to cool off throughout the overnight hours. Most locations will see temperatures falling back into the mid 20s, with a few upper 20 degree readings possible across western and northern portions of The County. I’m forecasting an overnight low of 26 degrees in Presque Isle, 24 in Caribou, and 24 degrees in Houlton. Winds will remain fairly light out of the west at around 5 mph. All in all, a quiet but seasonably chilly November night across the region.
As we head into the day tomorrow, we’re looking at another fairly nice day across the region, with plenty of sunshine expected during the morning hours. We’ll likely see a few more clouds beginning to work their way into the region as we head through the afternoon, but I still anticipate a good amount of sunshine throughout the day. Temperatures will begin to moderate as warmer air works its way into the region, with highs climbing into the mid to upper 40s for most locations. I’m forecasting a high of 48 degrees in Presque Isle, 46 in Caribou, and 48 degrees in Houlton. Some of our southern communities, including Millinocket, could even make a run at 50 degrees. Winds will pick up a little during the afternoon, with westerly winds around 5 to 10 mph and occasional gusts around 20 mph.
Looking ahead to Wednesday, we’ll continue to see temperatures warming across the region, although we may have to trade in some of that sunshine for additional cloud coverage. An increase in westerly flow across Northern Maine will help usher in some warmer air, bringing afternoon temperatures into the upper 40s and lower 50s. I’m forecasting a high of 53 degrees in Presque Isle, 50 degrees in Caribou, and 53 degrees in Houlton. For reference, the average high temperature in Caribou for this time of year is only around 39 degrees, meaning we’re looking at temperatures running more than 10 degrees above average! One thing you’ll notice Wednesday is a bit more of a breeze, with west winds around 10 to 15 mph and occasional gusts up to 25 mph. Despite the increase in cloud coverage, we’re still expecting dry conditions throughout the day.
Taking a look at our cloud cover forecast for the next several days, you’ll notice that Wednesday looks to feature the greatest amount of cloud coverage across the region. The good news is that we should begin to see more breaks in those clouds as we head into Thursday, with additional opportunities for sunshine expected Friday and Saturday. High pressure centered over the Ohio Valley will gradually shift eastward throughout the week, helping to keep any significant weather systems away from our region. This means we’re looking at an extended stretch of relatively quiet weather, with temperatures remaining above average for the middle of November.
For now, enjoy the sunshine and warmer temperatures while they’re here! I’ll continue to keep an eye on our next opportunity for precipitation as we get closer to the weekend. For more details on what to expect over the coming days, make sure to check out my First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening everyone!

title: Organizers cancel Portland’s Back Cove Music Festival — this time for good
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A two-day music festival that brought artists like Jack White and The Roots to Portland in 2025 will be remembered as just that — a one-off weekend that never became an annual tradition.
Organizers of the Back Cove Music & Arts Festival notified city staff earlier this month that the event planned for 2027 has been canceled, and a three-year contract would be terminated, citing financial viability.
“After careful consideration, we’ve determined that the current capacity limit does not support a financially sustainable long-term model for the festival that benefits all parties,” organizers Jordan Wolowitz of Shore Sound and David Rosenfeld of GoodWorks Entertainment wrote.
While the pair did not cite a specific barrier, the three-year agreement stipulated that no more than 12,500 people would be allowed entry to the festival per day.
City spokesperson Jessica Grondin said the promoters asked the city to increase the attendance cap to 15,000, but were told staff and officials were not likely to support the increase since the inaugural event didn’t reach the 12,500 limit.
According to previous statements from organizers, the 2025 festival drew about 12,000 people each day. However, records show the city was paid $14,122 in ticket fees, which were $1 per ticket for 2025.
“We truly appreciate all the time, effort, and support you and the entire city dedicated to the festival,” the organizers wrote. “It has been a pleasure working with you, and we hope to have the opportunity to work together again in the future.”
Wolowitz and Rosenfeld did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
Councilors were notified of the decision last week as city administration prepared to execute a termination agreement.
Early this year, the city and festival organizers signed an amended three-year contract after extended negotiations the previous fall led organizers to cancel a 2026 edition.
At the time, organizers said the delay — which was caused by councilor debate over the impact to the Back Cove neighborhood and financial compensation to the city — affected their ability to book talent, but that they were “dedicated to producing the Back Cove Festival in 2027.”
When the three-year contract was approved, a statement on the festival’s social media accounts said, “We have big things in store for the future of Back Cove, and we look forward to seeing you again in Payson Park in August 2027 and in the years that follow.”
Councilor Anna Bullett, who represents the Back Cove neighborhood, said Tuesday that she became worried about lost momentum when the council was “unable to follow the timeline necessary to ensure a 2026 festival could occur.”
“Today’s economic reality is very challenging for mid-size independent concert producers, so I understand (the organizers’) decision to terminate their contract,” she said, adding that she’s encouraged them to consider returning to Portland should the opportunity arise.
The inaugural, and only, iteration of the festival was largely seen as a success in Portland in August of 2025 due to a family-friendly atmosphere and low impact to Payson Park. Festival organizers had paid $100,000 to the Portland Parks Conservancy, which this past year was used for several pedestrian-friendly upgrades in the park.
Under the agreement, the promoters would’ve also paid the city $1.50 per ticket sold in 2027, increasing to $2 in 2028 and 2029.

title: InvestigateTV+: Firing college coaches can cost millions
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Firing college football coaches can cost millions of dollars, and InvestigateTV+ has uncovered how, in some cases, students are helping to foot the bill.
Then, one woman shares how she was forced to marry as a teenager and is now using her past to help protect young lives.
Plus, a grandfather says he’s counting his blessings after surviving a rattlesnake bite, and we talk to wildlife experts about where to tread carefully.
Billion Dollar Blitz
Across America, big-time college athletics is a $12 billion industry, in most cases, living beyond its means.
Ticket sales, TV deals, sponsorships and other revenue sources don’t bring in enough money to cover the bills.
So, universities are filling sometimes massive gaps from their general funds and charging students millions of dollars in mandatory fees to support athletics.
Ending children marriages
Protecting children from forced marriages in recent years, several states have taken action to stop what some call abuse.
Before 2017, every state allowed marriage under 18, according to the nonprofit Unchained At Last. Since then, a growing number of states have outlawed child marriage with no exceptions, not even parental consent.
Ohio is the latest considering a change. In 2019, the state raised the minimum age to 17. But advocates and some lawmakers believe the age should be 18 with no exceptions.
How to watch out for snakes
Wildlife experts say when the weather heats up, rattlesnakes can pop up anywhere — not just on hiking trails.
“Yesterday I removed a snake from a neighborhood garage, so it is possible for them to enter your home, backyard, all different kinds of areas. It’s really anywhere,” Clark said.
Using art to rise from grief
In the hills of central Vermont, where the ocean is nowhere in sight, two massive mammals rise from the earth. Visitors who stumble upon them are often stopped in their tracks.
“You come up here and you think you’re up in the mountains, you’re out in the wilderness, and all of a sudden you see two whale tails,” said Court Perkins, a visitor from Connecticut.
Whale Dance is the creation of local artist Jim Sardonis. “I mainly love nature in all its forms.”
