title: Doctors sound the alarm about US babies born with measles for the first time in decades
text:
(AP) - For the first time in decades, U.S. doctors are sounding the alarm about babies coming into the world with measles.
Congenital measles happens when a pregnant woman passes the virus to her fetus in the womb. It can lead to serious complications or even be deadly for newborns.
From the start of 2025 through the end of this September, 13 congenital measles cases were reported to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention during large measles outbreaks, according to preliminary figures published in a medical journal on Monday.
“This is a brand new phenomenon,” said Michael Osterholm, who directs the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy.
The condition’s emergence is driven by declining vaccination rates, which have fueled the virus’s spread so much that the Pan American Health Organization is expected to officially announce Tuesday that the U.S. has lost the measles-free status it’s had since 2000. In the past two years, according to the CDC, there have been more than 7,500 measles cases.
“We’re now seeing levels of measles that we haven’t seen in 30 years,” said Dr. Adam Ratner, a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics’ infectious diseases committee. “When you have measles under control,” congenital measles doesn’t happen.
The preliminary case figures were released in a public health alert published by NEJM Evidence in partnership with the center Osterholm directs. The alert also said there were 112 cases of confirmed measles during pregnancy — almost all among women who didn’t get vaccinated against measles beforehand or whose vaccination status was unknown. The alert said getting vaccinated before pregnancy and having high vaccination rates in the community “are important to prevent measles and related complications.” CDC scientists authored the alert.
Guidance on congenital measles from the pediatrics academy is already reaching doctors. And Pennsylvania’s health department published an advisory last month for healthcare providers, schools, childcare centers and others in the state, which currently has the largest measles outbreak in the nation.
A new reality allows congenital measles to emerge
People gain immunity to measles by getting the disease or the vaccine. Before the shots existed, lots of people were infected by the extremely contagious virus in childhood. Later, high vaccination rates protected everyone. But a new and historic reality — shaped both by the success of the vaccine and recent skepticism about it — has triggered congenital measles.
“What’s happening is we have so many women of childbearing age who were not vaccinated in the last 25 years, nor have they ever had exposure to measles because for the last 25 years we have beaten it back,” Osterholm said. “Now, this group is highly susceptible to measles.”
Doctors say the best way to prevent the disease is for women to get the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, before pregnancy. This protects the fetus too because antibodies pass from mother to baby through the placenta. Protection can last a few months after birth.
MMR can’t be given during pregnancy. Unvaccinated women who have never had measles and are exposed while pregnant can get a solution containing antibodies within six days to reduce the risk of infection and complications.
Congenital measles can seriously harm babies
If a woman gets measles toward the end of pregnancy, there’s a good chance she will pass it along. An estimated 25% to 30% of babies born to someone who gets measles shortly before delivery may become infected, the pediatrics group says.
Babies are considered to have congenital measles if they were exposed in the uterus and doctors find evidence of measles very soon after birth. Common symptoms include fever, jaundice and a measles rash. Severe complications include pneumonia, encephalitis and a rare condition known as SSPE, a brain disorder that generally develops many years after a measles infection and is almost always fatal.
Ratner, who wrote a book about measles, said there are indications that kids with congenital measles are at higher risk for SSPE and may develop it sooner after having measles than other children. “That’s something that sadly we’re learning more about,” he said.
Doctors worry things may get worse if vaccination rates keep dropping. Outbreaks are considered unlikely if a community has a 95% MMR rate, but rates in many communities have dipped below that threshold. Nationally, the CDC said, 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners in 2025-26 received required MMR shots.
This puts many vulnerable people at risk, including infants too young to be vaccinated. The first MMR dose is routinely given at 12 to 15 months old, and the earliest babies can get the shots is 6 months in outbreak areas.
“We need to get back to the point where everybody who can get vaccinated is getting vaccinated, and that’s gonna take some doing,” Ratner said. “It’s going to be a lot of work on the part of pediatricians and public health institutions and lots of others. But it’s an important thing for us to do.”

AP Medical Writer Mike Stobbe contributed from New York.

title: Beautiful Fall Weather Continues Across The State... Warmer Days Ahead
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Strong high pressure centered to our southwest will continue to bring us some beautiful fall weather for the next several days.
We’ll see mostly sunny skies today with a few clouds moving through the state later this morning through the afternoon as an upper-level disturbance crosses the state. Temperatures will be a bit above average with highs topping off in the mid-40s to low 50s from north to south across the state this afternoon. Skies will average clear to partly cloudy tonight with lows in the 30s.
We’ll see a few more clouds on Wednesday especially across the north as moisture slides along a stalled out front well to our north. Expect partly to mostly cloudy skies Wednesday with the bulk of the clouds across Aroostook County. Temperatures will be warmer with highs mainly in the 50s. Thursday and Friday look fantastic with sunshine and highs in the 50s to low 60s.
Of course it’s always great to get a beautiful stretch of weather like we have in store for the week ahead but it certainly doesn’t help us any with regard to the ongoing drought. With much of the state under moderate to severe drought conditions... we need rain badly. That being said... the next best chance of precipitation looks to be the potential for some showers later Sunday night into Monday as a cold front moves through. There is a storm system forecast to pass out to sea well south of the area Sunday night into Monday however we’ll still keep a close eye on it. If it were to move a bit quicker ahead of the approaching cold front... it may be able to make its way farther north and bring some steadier rain to the state Monday. At this point... it looks like it’s going to get swept out to sea but stayed tuned for updates.
Rest of Today: Mostly sunny. Highs between 43°-53°. West/northwest wind 5-10 MPH.
Tonight: Clear to partly cloudy. Lows in the 30s. Light and variable wind.
Wednesday: Partly to mostly cloudy... most clouds north. Highs mainly in the 50s. West wind 5-10 MPH with gusts to 15-20 MPH possible.
Thursday: Mostly sunny. Highs in the 50s to low 60s.
Friday: Mostly sunny. Highs in the 50s to low 60s.
Saturday: Partly to mostly sunny. Highs in the upper 40s to mid-50s.

CARIBOU, Maine (WABI) - A bridge replacement project in Caribou is delayed, meaning drivers will face a longer traffic disruption.
Crews are replacing the Prestile Brook Bridge on Route 164 with a large culvert. The culvert will improve fish and wildlife habitats while reducing crashes involving animals, according to MaineDOT.
Officials say delays in getting construction supplies have slowed the project.

title: Jared Golden’s lobster bill in doubt after state shift catches Washington off guard
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Bangor Daily News was the first to report this story. What you’re reading here would likely not be made public without the efforts of professional journalists asking questions, interviewing sources and obtaining documents.
A bill to shield Maine lobstermen from new whale rules through 2035 is in doubt after Gov. Janet Mills’ administration told U.S. senators it is no longer essential.
The Maine Department of Marine Resources told a U.S. Senate panel in a letter last week obtained by the Bangor Daily News that the Northeast Lobsterman Protection Act was no longer seen as essential by the agency and a handful of groups representing lobstermen. It cited the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s pledge to examine its standards.
The move leaves the bill’s fate hanging in the final weeks of a lame-duck session. Two of its leading champions, outgoing Democratic U.S. Rep. Jared Golden and U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her reelection bid this month, will leave Congress in January. Democrats seen as less friendly to the industry could take over key committee positions.
Without the bill, the current pause expires at the end of 2028, weeks before the next president takes office. Multiple sources Monday said lawmakers in Washington were caught off guard by the department’s stance on the legislation. It had passed the House in September with the backing of the White House and was poised to move in the Senate.
Collins and independent U.S. Sen. Angus King in September asked Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, to advance the bill through the panel, which he said he’d do just days before the election that Maine’s Republican senator lost to Democrat Troy Jackson. But the bill is not scheduled for a hearing.
Golden, who introduced the bill with U.S. Rep. Mike Lawler, R-New York, is breaking with the state and pressing the industry to keep backing it. In his own letter circulating among industry leaders and Maine’s congressional delegation and also obtained by the BDN, he wrote that the move “by DMR and others effectively kills all momentum in the Senate.”
“In response to a single whale entanglement, a new administration in control of NOAA after the 2028 election could easily reverse course and fall back into their old pattern of dismissing lobstermen’s concerns and expertise and pushing unworkable new regulations that could put you out of business,” he wrote.
NOAA is poised to craft new whale protection regulations soon. Earlier this month, it said new models suggest whale deaths and serious injuries tied to U.S. commercial fixed gear fisheries will be substantially lower than previous estimates, falling within range of the federal standard for protecting endangered North Atlantic right whales.
The shift followed the Maine Lobstermen’s Association’s 2023 victory in court, joined by DMR, over the National Marine Fisheries Service, whose “reliance on worst-case assumptions in assessing the lobster fishery’s impact” on whales jeopardized the industry, according to the association.
Lobstermen’s groups are split. Virginia Olsen of the Maine Lobstering Union Local 207 called NOAA’s new estimates “good news.” But “we are still supporting this bill,” she said, noting peer-reviewed research on the industry’s impacts to whales remains ongoing and won’t be complete until next spring. She said she’s reached out to the state, the delegation, and Republican and Democratic staffers on Cruz’s committee.
Jason Joyce, a spokesman for the New England Fishermen’s Stewardship Association, said the recent announcement from NOAA was encouraging. But he noted his group’s significant work in support of the pause and said it still supports the legislation despite being mentioned by state officials among groups no longer viewing it as crucial to protect the industry.
The department referred to its letter to the Commerce Committee, noting state officials and several groups no longer view the bill as essential “based on recent announcements outlining NOAA Fisheries’ commitment to developing durable solutions, along with improved scientific data and updated models.”
A day after NOAA’s announcement, the department brought together leadership from Maine Lobstermen’s Association, NEFSA, other groups and a stakeholder group to discuss impacts on the fishery, the agency said. The department and industry members met with congressional staff three days later and provided its statement on NOAA’s updates and the pause.
The Maine Lobstermen’s Association did not respond to requests for comment by deadline, nor did Cruz’s office and committee spokespeople, Collins’ office, Jackson’s transition team and the office of Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington, the top Commerce Democrat, who pledged her support for the bill in Maine last month.
The Maine delegation backed Golden’s bill and generally works in tandem with industry and state officials. U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, a Democrat from the 1st District, said after the announcement from NOAA, her office has been in conversation with lobstermen, industry representatives and state officials “about how best to give the lobster industry the predictability it needs to plan ahead.”
King has been working for months to extend the pause, spokesperson Matthew Felling said.
“In the past week, he has heard from the state and representatives of the lobster industry about their shift in stance and continues to seek the most durable ways to put the lobster fishery in the strongest long-term position possible,” he said.

title: Belfast’s Colonial Theatre to be sold to former operator
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Colonial Theatre in downtown Belfast is slated to be sold to a film industry pro who has held many roles with the historic movie house.
Kyle Walton is under contract to buy the theater in December, owner Hawthorne Arts Collaborative announced on Tuesday.
The nonprofit bought the High Street theater with the Art Deco facade and elephant sculpture on the roof in 2023 from longtime owners Mike Hurley and Therese Bagnardi, who had closed it the previous year after a two-decade run as a for-profit business. The theater first opened in 1912.
The theater reopened in late 2023 offering a mix of new releases, one-time screenings, special events and live performances.
Walton, an executive producer in film and television with strong connections to Maine films, was part of the Hawthorne leadership team and served as the theater’s executive director and then program director.
He previously held multiple roles at the Colonial, working as a general staffer and later operations manager under Hurley and Bagnardi. Prior to Tuesday’s announcement, he had been away from the theater for about a year.
Speaking on Tuesday night, Walton said the theater will continue to run blockbusters and niche films, but the key is going to be diversifying to avoid leaning too heavily on one source of revenue. One of the smaller theaters in the three-screen venue is capable of being used as a black-box theater, he said.
“You know, there’s just so much more that theater can be,” he said.
Hawthorne Arts completed some major infrastructure projects during its three-year tenure, including fire safety and HVAC improvements. Walton said the business will need to be “shored up, from an operational perspective” so it can fulfill the big dreams of the community.
“It will continue to be a place where you can see things that are extremely niche and specialty to, you know, big blockbusters,” he said, noting the upcoming releases of “Dune: Part Three” and “Avengers: Doomsday” in December.
In Tuesday’s announcement, the Hawthorne Arts Collaborative said it has struggled, particularly in the past six months, to find ways to make the theater financially sustainable.
Facing high costs of presenting new films, inflation and major repairs to the building, the group’s board of directors said it was relieved to be approached by Walton as an interested buyer.
Walton described the financing behind the purchase and ongoing enterprise as similar to any business, including help from a local lender.
“The Colonial isn’t different,” he said. “It operates on really tight margins, but that doesn’t make it a risky investment. There’s just a scenario where the sweat equity and the involvement from the ownership helps make those margins a little bit more secure, and I have never really struggled to do that.”
The only thing he asks of Greater Waldo County is to show up when the Colonial has something that they’re interested in. The theater will also continue to offer annual memberships and honor existing members.

title: Aroostook Leader Joins Pingree Transition Team
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) - Governor‑elect Hannah Pingree has put together a transition committee that includes leaders from across the state. The committee will help guide her first term and staff Maine’s agencies before her inauguration. Governor‑elect Hannah Pingree’s 22-member transition committee is recruiting and recommending candidates for 15 cabinet positions and an appointment to the Workers’ Compensation Board.
The only member of the committee from Aroostook County is Jason Parent, CEO of Avec Community Action and he says the committee has already been hard at work. “That’s been rapid fire. It’s been wonderful. There’s a lot to do in a relatively short period of time. Governor elect Pingree is hoping to have all of her commissioners named by her inauguration on January 6. So, we’ve rolled up our sleeves, and we’ve gotten right to work.”
Parent says it’s wonderful to have people from all over the state involved. “I think that’s a very positive sign is that there are those of us from Aroostook clear down to York County involved. So, it’s a very inclusive group of people with a very diverse set of backgrounds and we’re working to essentially help to vet and to review candidates who are applying to be commissioners for the various departments of state government.”
Parent says it’s been an honor to be chosen as a representative for Aroostook County. “I feel honored and privileged to be a voice for Aroostook County in this effort. I think my background and my experience across Aroostook County with my roots being in the St. John Valley and the diverse work that I’ve done both in higher education, and healthcare, and now in community action, and economic development. I think that that brings a diverse set of experience, a diverse set of skills, and really the perspectives of the people of this vast geographic county.”
Parent says leaders from across Maine have already been reaching out with interest in a cabinet position or to be on the Workers’ Compensation Board. “I’ve had folks reach out to me and other members of the transition team have had other folks reach out to them as well. We’re certainly encouraging anybody who wants to be considered for roles in the administration who might feel that they have the qualifications to certainly do so by connecting with the governor elect’s transition website. You can upload an application right onto that site. What the governor elect has told us is she really does want the best and brightest right here in the state of Maine to lead these important and critical roles moving forward and I’m happy to do whatever I can to support that effort to ensure that those people are in place in her administration.”
Governor-elect Hannah Pingree will be inaugurated as Maine’s 76th Governor on January 6, 2027. If you’re interested in serving Maine as part of the Governor’s Office or her Cabinet, you can apply by visiting hannahpingreetransition.com.

title: Hot meals and hospitality are tradition for the Maine family behind Taj restaurant
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SOUTH PORTLAND – “Hot food is in here.”
A sign taped to the bright red door of the heated metal food locker that sits outside Taj Indian Cuisine in South Portland invites people to help themselves to a meal, no questions asked.
“If we ran out, please go inside and they will make you one,” the sign reads.
On a drizzly recent Thursday afternoon, the locker was empty, except for a few scattered grains of rice.
Sai Guntaka, the owner of Taj and its sister restaurants, has given out thousands of free meals to community members in need for years, going back to the beginning of the COVID pandemic. Each day, people pick up an average of 200 meals from the box in the entryway to the restaurant’s Clarks Pond location, he said.
Rasa Indian Cuisine, Guntaka’s restaurant on Exchange Street in Bangor, will also start providing daily free meals this winter, too, he said.
“It feels good to give back,” he said.
When asked about his family’s outreach, Guntaka is reluctant to say much about himself, or his family’s and employees’ charitable efforts. But the restaurant’s generosity has been noted, and not just by locals.
In 2025, Taj was nominated as a James Beard Foundation finalist in the Outstanding Hospitality category. The restaurant has also been recognized for its outreach, both by the Maine Public Health Association and by the city of South Portland.
The family business – with Sai Guntaka’s mother, Hemalatha, at the helm in the kitchen and his father, Sudarsana, hand-picking spices on trips back to India – draws upon and continues the family’s tradition of taking care of people in need.
AN ONGOING COMMITMENT
Guntaka started passing out free meals in 2020 during the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic.
“We made lots of food that first week,” he said, and he didn’t want it to go to waste. The restaurant delivered meals to healthcare workers, first responders and homeless shelters.
Meal delivery continued through the holidays, because Guntaka saw online that people were losing their jobs and struggling to make ends meet. A warm, worry-free meal goes a long way, he thought.
Taj has offered free meals on Thanksgiving for years, providing thousands of appetizers (like their samosas) and entrees (like their curries). This Thanksgiving, they expect to deliver about 9,000 free meals, in addition to their typical business operation, he said.
Employee Jim Baldi, who described his title as “worker bee,” has been with the Guntakas through a couple of Thanksgivings. Employees report and start cooking at 4 a.m. – even many who worked the night before. There’s always fresh chai. “We need that extra caffeine,” Baldi said.
Hemalatha, Sai’s mother, cooks an elaborate breakfast spread for the staff, including punugulu, a fritter served with coconut chutney that’s Baldi’s favorite.
“It sets us up for the morning,” Baldi said.
The silver serving platters are removed from the buffet room and the space is converted into a staging area. Staff and volunteers buzz in and out all day.
Thanksgiving is one of their busiest days, though it’s not the only time they provide free food.
Last fall, when the federal government cut Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program benefits, the restaurant set up a warming cabinet in its entryway to provide prepared meals – including chicken curry, butter chicken, mixed vegetable curry and chana masala – to those who needed it, according to Guntaka. The food locker became a permanent feature earlier this year.
“Why don’t we just do this every day?” he said.
The food in the cabinet is, the same food that’s being served in the more than 20 silver buffet dishes at lunchtime, like saag paneer and tikka masala. The sauces are all simmered in the same vats of fragrant spices on the large, industrial stoves.
“We’re eating the food as well,” Guntaka said. “We want to serve the food that we want to eat.”
The restaurant doesn’t solicit donations to fund its charitable efforts. When asked about the extra expense, Guntaka says he doesn’t know how much it costs his company to give out free meals. He said he just orders more ingredients.
Even without direct donations, it’s safe to assume the community’s steady support helps fuel the restaurant’s efforts.
Business is booming. Taj moved into a larger space last summer with a 62-seat dining room and 11-seat bar, opened a sister restaurant in the Old Port in the spring and launched a brunch cafe, Cobblestone Coffee & Co., in Taj’s original location. The coffees and pastries sold there subsidize the free meals.
A FAMILY EFFORT
Giving back is woven into the Guntaka family’s DNA.
Guntaka’s paternal grandfather built a reputation for his charitable kindness in Ramachandrapurah, a town in the state of Andhra Pradesh in southern India, Guntaka said.
He had a lot of land and money, and shared most of it before he died. More than 20,000 people attended his funeral, Guntaka said, an indication of his impact on his community.
Guntaka was only 8 years old when his family moved from India to the U.S., but he remembers there were always 15 or 20 people sharing meals at his grandfather’s house. “People couldn’t leave without eating,” he said.
Guntaka remembers his grandfather’s kindness, and the soda and candy that he bought from street vendors with the money his grandfather gave him.
The Guntaka family still maintains close ties to their community in India.
Guntaka and his father support an orphanage near Ramachandrapurah, providing backpacks and food to the 20 children living there. His grandfather assisted the same organization.
And Sudarsana Guntaka, Sai’s father, recently built a Hindu temple, Shivadattasai Mandir, in his hometown, a lifelong dream.
More than 16,000 people attended the 2025 opening of the gathering space decorated with hand-crafted details. Sai Guntaka recalls stirring large pots of curries and sauces over an open fire, and family and friends passing out meals beneath vibrantly colored tents. It was a celebration of community and of the possibilities of the new space, which hosts religious services and weddings.
The Guntakas keep their connections to home close, even though they live thousands of miles away. Baldi estimates that about one third of the nearly 100 staff members are family members or family friends – which, to Guntaka, are synonymous. Guntaka’s wife helps out at Cobblestone Coffee, and his brother-in-law manages front-of-house operations for Taj.
Sidhu Myneni, a server at Taj, grew up about 20 minutes from the Guntakas in India. His father is a friend of Sai’s father.
On a recent chilly Thursday afternoon, Myneni greeted and seated customers during the restaurant’s lunch rush. When things slowed down, he set empty tables, placing silverware wrapped in jade-colored napkins on plates.
He’s been working at Taj for about a year and a half, and has become friends with the other servers. He said moving to Maine from India wasn’t scary because he knew the Guntakas would take good care of him.
“I got to come into a new family,” he said.

title: 2 teens stranded on capsized boat rescued without injury by deputies in Florida
text:
2 teens stranded on capsized boat rescued without injury by deputies in Florida
With cold, windy weather moving into Florida's Gulf Coast, two teens ended up stranded on a capsized boat near the Sanibel Causeway Saturday morning before a Lee County Sheriff's Office Marine Unit pulled them to safety.
LCSO said the teens were found sitting on top of the boat, and the marine unit brought them to safety without any injuries.
The sheriff's office advised boaters to use extra caution when cooler temperatures and windy conditions hit Florida's Gulf Coast, as larger waves can cause vessels to take on water and increase the chances of capsizing. LCSO also said boaters should check marine forecasts before heading out, wear a life jacket, and remain vigilant of changing weather conditions.

title: The Kerch Bridge is crucial to Russia’s war effort and for asserting Moscow’s control of Crimea
text:
The Kerch Bridge is crucial to Russia’s war effort and for asserting Moscow’s control of Crimea
There is perhaps no more potent symbol of Moscow's illegal annexation of Crimea than the bridge connecting the peninsula with Russia over the Kerch Strait — and it has come under repeated Ukrainian attacks since the nearly 5-year-old war began.
The Kerch Bridge is a key artery for military and civilian supplies to Crimea, which was seized in defiance of international law by Russia in 2014. The span serves as a concrete and steel assertion of that Kremlin control.
The latest attacks came on Monday and Tuesday. The Ukrainian General Staff said an arch and a span of the bridge’s road section collapsed into the water, severing the link for vehicular traffic, while the railway line was still standing but with a damaged arch.
Related video: Who's meeting with President Trump for this week's historic nuclear summit in Asia?
“The symbol of the occupation has cracked,” the Ukrainian General Staff said in a statement.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the bridge was struck with a combination of drones and missiles, part of a complex operation in the works for weeks. This way, Kyiv was “reminding Russia that war will always return to where it began,” he said.
Crimea extends south of Ukraine's mainland
The Crimean Peninsula extends south from Ukraine’s mainland, with road connections on two isthmuses, one of which is less than 2 kilometers (1 mile) wide, and by a bridge from a narrow spit. Those links to Ukraine go into territory that is occupied by Russian forces that come under attack from the Ukrainian military.
The bridge, which connects Crimea’s eastern extremity with Russia’s Krasnodar region, provides the only fixed link that steers clear of Russian-held land.
The 19-kilometer (12-mile) bridge over the Kerch Strait that links the Black and Azov seas carries road and rail traffic on separate sections and is vital to sustaining Russia’s military operations. It also carries supplies to Crimean cities such as Sevastopol, Simferopol and Yalta.
The bridge is a symbol of Russian pride
The bridge is the longest in Europe and the object of considerable pride for Russia. Construction began in 2016, despite strong objections from Ukraine, and was completed in little over two years. The pace of construction was impressive but led some critics to question whether it was hastily designed and built.
President Vladimir Putin drove across the bridge at its formal opening on May 15, 2018. Putin is closely connected to construction tycoon Arkady Rotenberg, whose company got the $3.5 billion contract for the bridge.
For Ukrainians, the bridge is the most visible and persistent reminder of Russia’s claim over Crimea.
The bridge has come under several Ukrainian attacks since Russia’s full-scale invasion of its neighbor in 2022. The first was in October of that year from what Moscow said was a truck bomb, temporarily halting rail and vehicular traffic. Putin drove over it in December 2022 after repairs.
In July 2023, two maritime drones struck the bridge, killing two people on the span, according to Russia’s Investigative Committee.
Zelenskyy says the latest attacks were weeks in the making
The attacks on Monday and Tuesday were the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes in several stages, Zelenskyy said on social media.
Ukrainian forces knocked out defense systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment and other designated targets before launching Monday night’s final attack, he said.
Domestically developed long-range drones struck the bridge’s road section during the night while Ukraine’s Neptune missiles and other drones aimed at the rail section, he said, adding that the final blow came from precision-guided Flamingo missiles.
Russia’s Investigative Committee said the bridge was attacked by drones on both days and sustained damage. It did not elaborate on the extent of the damage.
Russian-installed officials in Crimea said bridge traffic has been halted, and they urged travelers to avoid it. Train traffic on the span later resumed, they said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said “there is no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than it was before.”
Monday's attack halted vehicular traffic on the bridge for hours and delayed several trains. Peskov described the damage from that attack as “insignificant.”

title: Melbourne Cup horse So You Are found dead in a waste facility, sparking an inquiry
text:
SYDNEY (AP) — The body of Melbourne Cup horse So You Are was found in a waste facility in Sydney less than two weeks after competing in the most prestigious event in Australian horse racing.
The Sydney Morning Herald newspaper reported Tuesday that racing stewards were investigating after a construction worker saw a dead horse in a dumpster at a licensed waste center and posted a video on Facebook.
Trainer Bjorn Baker had released a statement Monday saying So You Are died following a severe bout of colic. The 5-year-old gelding was rushed to a specialist equine hospital for emergency veterinary treatment but couldn’t be saved.
Baker posted an update Tuesday after discovering So You Are hadn’t been properly buried.
“Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are’s remains,” Baker said in a statement. “He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death.”
So You Are placed eighth in the Melbourne Cup on Nov. 3, with Point of Law winning the 166th running of the 2-mile classic.
REC Equine Specialists managing partner Dr. Jonathan Lumsden issued a statement saying So You Are had been “humanely euthanized under anesthesia” after receiving emergency treatment.
“After his death, So You Are was collected by our contracted service provider and taken to a licensed landfill. He should have been promptly and respectfully buried,” Lumsden said. “What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone who cared for him. We are deeply sorry.”
Lumsden said he was working with the service provider and the state’s horse racing authority, Racing NSW, to establish what went wrong and to put in processes to ensure it never happens again.
“So You Are was in our care. We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that,” he said. “We should have known exactly how horses were handled after leaving our hospital, and we did not. That process is not good enough, and it must change.
“No owner should have to go through what So You Are’s connections have experienced this week.”
Racing NSW said So You Are was being held temporarily, awaiting burial, when the video was recorded.
“These images are distressing for all involved and for all of us who care deeply about our horses,” Racing NSW said in a statement. “The way in which So You Are’s body was left is distressing and completely unacceptable. So You Are deserved to be treated with dignity and respect.”
The state’s racing regulator said under industry guidelines — now under review — a licensed landfill was the preferred option for animals which have been euthanized because of the chemicals involved in the process.
“That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner,” the statement continued. “If through the course of our ongoing investigation any wrongdoing is found, Racing NSW will not hesitate to take appropriate action.”

title: Do school phone bans help students learn? So far, gains are 'modest'
text:
The argument for school cellphone bans is simple: Phones offer endless distraction. Take them away and students can focus on classwork, engage with peers and, ultimately, learn more.
But the reality is more complicated, as emerging research shows. Schools can lock phones away in pouches or banish them to backpacks, but they can’t shut out the digital world.
In the past few years, more than 40 U.S. states have passed laws that restrict cellphones at schools, according to the Phone Free Schools State Report Card, which tracks state phone legislation. But those laws vary widely and often let schools design their own policies, resulting in a patchwork of rules and enforcement across the country.
A large-scale study published Tuesday found strict cellphone restrictions — ones that require students to put phones in locked pouches for the entire school day — result in small academic gains. But, the researchers said, the gains can add up if schools continue banning phones.
Phone bans appear to help, to a point
The study, led by Harvard’s Center for Education Policy Research, found the schools with strict phone restrictions saw “modest” improvements in academic growth, compared with students in similar schools without those restrictions. The study, which analyzed test scores of 3.3 million students at 4,600 schools nationally, estimates the academic gains were equivalent to about an additional week or two of learning over a school year.
Student achievement has been falling globally since 2013, which is roughly when social media-enabled smartphones took off. The researchers sought to determine if the decline is being reversed now that schools have started taking phones away, said Harvard professor Thomas Kane, one of the study’s authors.
“Our answer is yes, phone bans do have a positive effect on growth. But it’s not a panacea,” Kane said. Learning loss was gradual over a decade, he notes, and it’s not surprising that gains would also be gradual. The study used math and reading test data for grades four through 10 from the past five academic years.
“While schools should not expect large boosts in achievement immediately, storing students’ phones seems to be a cost-effective way to add 1-2 weeks of instruction each year, which could add up over time, just as the initial declines did,” the study says.
The boost is equal to about half the annual decline in test scores since smartphones became mainstream, the study said.
Academic gains are overall ‘disappointing,’ one researcher says
Still, the connection between phones and learning is not clear-cut.
A different study published in May concluded strict school phone bans had “close to zero” effect on test scores. It compared schools with bans with tens of thousands of other schools.
The National Bureau of Economic Research study looked at a different set of standardized test scores than Harvard’s study, as well as GPS phone activity, teacher surveys and data from Yondr, the leading provider of lockable phone pouches, at 4,600 schools that use the pouches.
The study had found “modest positive effects” in high school test scores over three years, particularly in math. But the report’s authors, researchers at Stanford, the University of Michigan, Duke and the University of Pennsylvania, were hesitant to conclude overall learning benefits from the bans.
Both studies point to a similar conclusion, said Stanford education economist Thomas Dee, an author of the NBER study. “The early results from school phone bans are largely disappointing and raise unresolved questions,” Dee said.
Noting that the Harvard study showed learning gains may accumulate over time, Dee said: “I hope they’re right. However, I’m not comfortable making that extrapolation from estimates that are small, sensitive and based on just a few years of phone bans.”
The reasons, Dee said, could be that students are still distracted on other devices at school. Or, he said, “it may be that we see these disappointing results because out-of-school phone use is harming child development.”
Phones aren’t the only tech distracting teens
Just because schools or states have phone bans does not mean they’re being enforced, said Jean Twenge, a psychologist at San Diego State University and author of “10 Rules for Raising Kids in a High-Tech World.”
Ask any teacher — or teenager — and they’ll tell you that some phone bans are largely cosmetic. Teens come up with creative workarounds, including stowing burner phones or even phone-shaped rocks in their locked pouches. At schools that rely on students to keep phones in backpacks, adherence to the ban can be spotty.
“It happens pretty often that there’s a policy of no phones during the school day, bell-to-bell, and you go into the school and phones are everywhere,” Twenge said.
Even without phones, “Do they have laptops at school? Are they just doing social media on laptops instead?” Twenge said.
Phone use outside of school affects academics too, Twenge said. “If they have that phone available when they’re studying, how much are they really taking in?”
Kane, of the Harvard study, agrees the effect of cellphone use outside of school is “the big question.” But researchers have not been able to investigate parents and educators’ suspicions that late-night binges on YouTube and other platforms are costly for students.
“I find it astonishing that social media companies know how much time kids spend on their platforms, but that data has never been linked to student outcomes,” Kane said. “We can’t provide answers until the social media companies share data.”

title: Brunswick library hires new director
text:
Following the retirement of its longtime leader, Brunswick’s Curtis Memorial Library has hired a new executive director.
Kevin King will join the Curtis Library in December following a regional and nationwide search, the library announced Tuesday.
King’s experience includes more than 20 years leading public libraries in Michigan.
He’ll succeed Liz Doucett, who retired in the summer after two decades and recently oversaw the renovation of the library’s lobby.
“It is an honor to have been chosen to build upon the incredible work of such a passionate, creative, and dedicated staff,” King said in a news release. “Over the next few months, I look forward to getting out into the Brunswick and Harpswell communities, meeting as many people as possible and learning what it means to become a Mainer.”
King spent much of his career at Kalamazoo Public Library in Michigan, which serves more than 120,000 residents. Curtis Library serves 25,000 residents of Brunswick and Harpswell with roughly 1,000 visitors per day.
At the Kalamazoo Library, King launched a peer navigator program to support patrons in need of social services and resources, according to the news release.
He also directed the East Lansing Public Library in Michigan, where he developed long-term plans and secured government funds for library programs.
“Kevin is a dynamic and experienced professional with an impressive track record of public library leadership,” said Curtis library board Chair Tahnthawan Coffin. “He brings a breadth of experience managing large teams and budgets, a passion for community engagement, a dedicated history of collaborating with local nonprofits, municipal departments and academic institutions, and dedicated involvement in library advocacy and innovation at the national level.”
King begins at Curtis on Dec. 1. In his first week, the community is invited to grab free coffee from the library at 23 Pleasant St. on Friday and Saturday mornings, and join the Brunswick Public Library Association’s annual meeting on Wednesday, Dec. 2, in the Morrell Meeting Room.

title: Belfast temporarily caps rent increases on mobile home lots
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Belfast city councilors on Tuesday approved a temporary 3% cap on rent increases for mobile home lots.
The cap will last 180 days, allowing temporary relief for tenants while the city’s Housing and Property Development Committee comes up with policy recommendations.
It applies to arrangements in which a resident owns their home but rents the land it sits on, and at least three mobile homes are on the same parcel. It does not apply to landlord-owned mobile homes or mobile home parks that are collectively owned by the residents.
Landlords who violate the cap will be fined $200 and required to refund any money collected in excess of the 3% increase.
Landlords are not required to report rent increases to the city. As a result, the city will use reports from tenants to identify violations.
“We are relying on people hopefully being aware of the moratorium,” city attorney Kristin Collins said.
Belfast has five mobile home parks, ranging in size from four to 70 homes.
Because residents own the building but not the land, mobile homes have unique affordability challenges, Collins said.
“It’s such a peculiar housing type,” she said. “You can’t just go anywhere to put your mobile home. You can’t just leave. You’re sort of captive. And also, a lot of landlords have the practice of jacking up the rent on a vacant lot … which means it might be harder to sell your mobile home in place.”
The average mobile home lot rent in Waldo County is $602 a month, higher than in any other Maine county, according to the Maine Office of Community Affairs. The statewide average is $479 a month.
The lot rent increases have taken place alongside a surge in out-of-state private equity firms buying mobile home parks.
City Manager Erin Herbig said the topic was first brought to the City Council by someone who lived in a local mobile home park and was struggling with rising mobile home law rent rates.
Anecdotal data suggests that rents have increased sharply in the past three years, Deputy Economic Development Director Joellyn Warren said. While the cap is in place, the Belfast Housing and Property Development Committee will more systematically collect data about mobile home lot rent. That may include knocking on residents’ doors and sending out mailers.
“We’re going to hit the ground running,” Warren said. “The framework of the data collection and process will have to be decided fairly quickly, possibly on Monday, so that we can get this out as quickly as possible.”

title: In defense of farmed salmon
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I’m writing because I’m seeing television ads on streaming services with rather alarming depictions of the salmon farming industry, suggesting that we not purchase their products.
People should be aware of where these ads are coming from and not be swayed by their self-serving claims.
While there are some valid concerns about salmon farming in Chile, that is certainly not the case with our neighbors in Canada and the Bay of Fundy, and also the Gulf of Maine. The extreme tides are ideal for salmon farming, and the industry is a good fit with lobstering as well. Salmon farming here is well regulated and is very important to the lives of many people.
It is irresponsible to allow these ads to air without some serious fact-checking. Please continue to purchase farmed salmon. It is reasonably priced, and very good for us.
Philip Miller
Kennebunk

title: Z107.3 annual ‘Free the Z’ Turkey Drive now underway
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BREWER, Maine (WABI) - Z107.3 annual Free the Z Turkey Drive got underway Tuesday morning at the Hannaford parking lot in Brewer.
Last year they collected 3,200 turkeys before wrapping things up at the Brewer Hannaford.
This is the first leg of a joint effort with Penquis and WABI.
On Thursday, Nov. 19 from 4 p.m. to 6:30 p.m., during WABI newscasts, members of the WABI team, the Penquis team and other volunteers will be waiting by the phones to take donations. Every $15 donation provides one turkey.
Local partners
A network of more than 40 local food pantries and nonprofit organizations are partners in the effort, making it possible to distribute turkeys to so many families throughout Penquis’ service area.
“Thanksgiving is a time to come together with family and friends, share traditions, and create lasting memories,” said Renae Muscatell, Community Relations Manager at Penquis. “Every turkey and every financial contribution helps make it possible for families to enjoy a holiday meal together. Donating a turkey or its cash equivalent is an easy and manageable way to support those in our community. The generosity we see year after year is a powerful reminder of how neighbors continue to support one another.”
How to donate outside the events
Those wanting to help outside of these events can donate online at turkey.penquis.org or Text TURKEY to 44321 to make a donation.

title: Somali American Uber driver strangled and run over by a passenger, authorities say
text:
Somali American Uber driver strangled and run over by a passenger, authorities say
A Somali American Uber driver was in critical condition, and a passenger was charged with attempted murder Tuesday after a weekend attack in which authorities say the driver was strangled with a seatbelt, run over by his own car, and left in a ditch.
Mohamed Yusuf, fighting for his life, has broken ribs, a broken leg, spinal injuries, collapsed lungs and significant internal bleeding from the attack, which occurred after the passenger allegedly told Yusuf he didn’t like the name Mohamed.
Samit Apurva Patel, 25, was charged with attempted second-degree murder and carjacking, but there wasn’t enough evidence to prove the attack was motivated by bias, said Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty. She said that decision “does not diminish the pain that the family and the Somali community is feeling right now.”
An attorney listed for Patel did not immediately return a message Tuesday. A person who answered a phone number associated with Patel’s address said, “No comment,” before hanging up.
The violence early Saturday in the Minneapolis suburb of Hopkins has increased fear among the Somali community after years of racist rhetoric, including from President Donald Trump. Minnesota has the largest Somali population in the U.S., with many concentrated in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area. The overwhelming majority are American citizens.
According to court documents, Yusuf was on the phone with his brother, who is also an Uber driver, when Yusuf picked up the passenger near a Minneapolis bar just before 1 a.m. Saturday. The drop-off location was in the nearby suburb of Hopkins.
Yusuf's brother says he heard the passenger tell Yusuf he didn’t like the name Mohamed, the court documents say. He later heard Yusuf screaming in Somali that he was being choked with a belt and run over by the car, according to the filings.
Moriarty said the motive remains unknown but said, “There were some serious issues going on with this gentleman at the time he went home that so alarmed his parents that they called 911.”
She said she did not believe there was a recording of the call between Yusuf and his brother, and there was a camera in Yusuf’s car but it was not on.
Patel's parents called for a wellness check after Patel arrived home appearing intoxicated and “exhibiting signs of emotional distress and belligerent behavior,” according to the court filings. When officers arrived, they found Yusuf's car in the driveway with the exterior and driver's seatbelt damaged, according to the filings. Dirt, burs and a shoe were found in the driver's side interior, and the phone call with Yusuf's brother was still active through the car's system, court records show.
Officers said Patel told them he had been drinking and “admitted he took an Uber home, but he claimed not to know where his Uber driver was," the filing says.
Officers found Yusuf in a patch of burs in a ditch off the side of the road using location data from his smartwatch and a drone with thermal imaging.
Uber said in a statement that it was horrified by the attack, has been in touch with the driver’s family and has banned the rider from the platform.
Jaylani Hussein, executive director of the Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, said dozens of community members have been stopping by the hospital to show support for Yusuf.
“We feel as a community we’re under threat, constantly,” Hussein said. “Our community has, unfortunately, been feeling the brunt end of a disinformation and demonization campaign that has been going on now, and it’s coming from every corner.”
The Trump administration's largest immigration enforcement operation, Operation Metro Surge, targeted the Twin Cities. Leading up to that operation, Trump said immigrants from the war-torn East African country have “caused a lot of trouble,” and he wants them to leave. He also referred to Somali immigrants in the U.S. as “garbage.”
Muhiyadin Yusuf, who knows Mohamed Yusuf but is not related to him, has been driving for ride-hailing apps in the Twin Cities for more than a decade. He said he's felt unsafe in general because of comments from Trump and other politicians targeting Somalis. But since Saturday, he's reduced his nighttime driving hours and added a third camera to his car. Some friends of his have stopped driving altogether.
“As a Muslim, as an immigrant, as a driver and as a Somali community, it affects me,” he said. “I'm scared now, more than before.”

title: Maine beats many US metros to the plug with first hybrid ferry
text:
As high-profile green transit projects in New York and Seattle stall over missing dockside power, Maine has quietly outpaced the rest of the country by plugging in its first hybrid commuter ferry on Day 1.
The Capt. Almer Dinsmore, which can hold up to 250 passengers and 23 vehicles, launched last week. It runs on electric power while docked and switches to hybrid or diesel during its 15-mile runs between Rockland and Vinalhaven, according to the Maine State Ferry Service.
“It’s a significant step forward in modernizing our fleet,” said EJ Dupont, director of the ferry service.
The price tag? About $22.2 million. The state paid $15.3 million. Federal funds covered the rest.
Other states have bought hybrid ferries. A few short-distance river ferries or tourist vessels are even in service. But most of the highly touted clean ferries lack the dockside stations needed to charge the lithium ion battery packs that store their onboard electricity.
New York City’s $33 million hybrid ferry has yet to reach its projected fuel and emissions savings because federal grant holdups have stalled construction of its shoreside charging station, according to Sarah Krautheim, chief of staff for The Trust for Governors Island, which operates the route.
Washington State runs a diesel-electric ferry that cannot connect to shoreside power until 2029 due to utility grid coordination delays. A Seattle suburb docked its hybrid ferry last month when a battery system failed — after scrapping plans to build another due to federal funding concerns.
State-run ferry services in Texas and Louisiana have proven that diesel-hybrid propulsion works for short hops. The Esperanza Andrade and the Holly Beach use batteries to traverse Gulf Coast channels no more than 3 miles wide, while the Dinsmore travels 15 miles each way.
Maine’s ferry service — which operates a fleet of seven vessels in the Midcoast and Down East regions — is launching the Dinsmore a year ahead of the schedule laid out in the state’s climate action plan. It plans to build a second hybrid ferry to serve Islesboro.
Casco Bay Lines also is adding a hybrid ferry. The Battery Steele, which will carry passengers and vehicles between Portland and Peaks Island, was due to launch this fall but has run into engineering delays.
Unlike New York and Washington State, Maine considered power delivery a prerequisite for its electrification goals rather than an afterthought. It nailed down its shoreside charging capability two years before the Dinsmore even touched the water.
Dupont said that Maine’s biggest advantage, though, is that instead of waiting for the complex multimegawatt fast chargers, the state built a shore power system that allows the ferry to plug in overnight, charging its battery bank gradually, while also keeping the ferry warm for morning passengers.
Central Maine Power Co. spent months upgrading the wiring in Rockland, installing heavier duty electrical wires, a bigger transformer and upgraded breakers to essentially double the dockside charging capacity, Dupont said.
Hybrid ferries present an opportunity to reduce emissions from greenhouse gases, which are created by the burning of fossil fuels and create a planetary blanket that lets sunlight in, but doesn’t let the heat out.
The Maine Department of Transportation estimates the Dinsmore will use 35,000 fewer gallons of diesel fuel a year than a traditionally powered ferry of the same size. That could save the state more than $165,000 on fuel, and 785,506 pounds of carbon dioxide emissions annually, based on standard federal conversion rates.
That CO2 reduction is the equivalent of taking 75 gas-powered vehicles off the road for one year. That’s especially important in Maine, where transportation accounts for 49% of greenhouse gas emissions and consumer range fears have slowed electric vehicle adoption.
The ferry relies on battery power while idling during passenger loading, which eliminates the diesel fumes and heavy engine noise that are a hallmark of almost any working waterfront.
“While in port under battery power, the vessel operates with a substantial reduction in noise associated with traditional diesel engines, creating a noticeably quieter experience for the passengers, crew and our waterfront communities,” Dupont said.
Battery power can supplement the diesel engines during periods of higher demand, and power the vessel during lower-demand operations, like entering or departing from the terminal. That allows the engines to operate more efficiently, which also helps save fuel.
Once in open water, the captain simply flips a switch in the pilot house to transfer from electric to hybrid power. The 75-minute voyage is made in hybrid mode so the 154-foot vessel maintains the speed necessary to stay on schedule.
Maine’s maritime electrification campaign is gathering momentum beyond Rockland Harbor.
Early next year, Casco Bay Lines plans to launch Battery Steele. The boat is due to arrive in Portland this month, according to the company’s website. The ferry will need two months of crew training and charger interface testing before it can seek Coast Guard certification, with a hope that it can begin passenger service in the first quarter of 2027.
The Battery Steele is expected to eliminate up to 1.8 million pounds of carbon emissions annually.
The Casco Bay Lines hybrid yields greater carbon reductions because its high-frequency, short-run commuter service replaces significantly more daily diesel engine hours during Peaks Island voyages than the lower-frequency, long-distance Rockland-to-Vinalhaven route.

title: How ‘human infrastructure’ connects public and private working waterfront
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s working waterfronts face threats from development, extreme storms and sea level rise, aging infrastructure and the high cost of maintenance and repair.
The Maine Working Waterfront Conference, held Nov. 12-13 in Bar Harbor, sought to address these issues. The conference brought together fishermen, sea farmers, wharf owners, municipal officials, industry representatives, researchers, engineers, nonprofit leaders, students and others to consider the sector’s future.
A key consideration is the “human infrastructure” that characterizes the larger picture of how diverse interests collaborate to support working waterfront, said Linda Nelson, the economic and community development director for the town of Stonington, Maine’s largest lobster fishing community.
“Our piers can be as sustainable to sea level rise as we want them to be,” she said. “But if there’s no one fishing them or using them, it doesn’t matter.”
Nelson said the challenges are exacerbated by a political view that polarizes public and private infrastructure. The two sides can’t work without each other and the idea of human infrastructure recognizes that connection, she said.
Nelson works on the public side through her work with the town of Stonington, which often leads the state in value and volume of lobster landings and manages three separate harbors, including a municipally-owned commercial fish pier. She also co-chairs the Governor’s Commission on Infrastructure Rebuilding & Resilience.
From the public perspective, Nelson said she advocates for better state planning to support the private-sector fisheries and the blue economy.
“The private sector has access to the markets that the public sector doesn’t have,” she said. “We have to work together.”
Changing markets
From the business perspective, the ability to be nimble in responding to market changes is critical, said Curt Brown, co-owner of Prospect Harbor seafood processing plant Bold Coast Seafood, a marine biologist and a commercial lobsterman.
“Our role is to do the product justice,” he said.
Harvesters and growers have been great stewards of the resources off the coast of Maine, allowing for the expansion of markets domestically and globally, he said.
But the private sector depends on public infrastructure.
“If we don’t have the public infrastructure to get it over the causeway that’s at risk from storms, then our business is at risk,” he said. “So we need public infrastructure locally and beyond to get our amazing products to the rest of the world.
Often, he said, owners are focused on their own businesses. Instead, public-private collaboration is key, he said. Growing those partnerships, and being good stewards and good community members, are key responsibilities of private industry, he said.
Schools and plumbers
Brown said that one of his biggest concerns is whether the younger generation will join the seafood economy.
“I’m not sure if I see that same spark today,” he said. “Without harvesters on the water, none of what we do in the private sectors works — it just doesn’t exist. How do you draw the next generation in? That would be my top concern.”
Nelson agreed, but added that, for those who want to work on the water, the decline of affordable housing, schools, professional services and community services in coastal communities makes it difficult.
“The human infrastructure can’t survive with what’s happening to our property values right now,” Nelson said.
“It’s not just people who work on the boats. They need schools for their kids, and carpenters, electricians, plumbers. We’ve got fishermen living over an hour away from their boats.”
A primary goal of the Working Waterfront Advisory Council is to identify and seek solutions to challenges facing working waterfronts and to submit annual recommendations to the Legislature on potential policy changes and support for addressing those identified challenges.
The council is housed within the Maine Office of Community Affairs and staffed by the Maine Coastal Program.

title: Classified communications network at the National Security Agency goes down, defense official says
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — An internal network the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline Tuesday after what the agency described as “routine maintenance.”
A defense official said that the problem affected NSANet, a classified internal network used by employees of the agency. A different U.S. official said that the NSA “experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.”
The official added, “while some internal systems were affected, mission/critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues.”
Another person familiar with the matter said the issue occurred during routine patching. The three individuals spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss non-public information.
The NSA episode is the latest in a series of cyber-related disruptions to critical government and private sector functions in the last week, including one Friday that resulted in a ground stop of air traffic in the United States because of a system overload, a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase on Monday that caused ripple effects throughout the financial system and an internal systems outage at United Airlines that delayed departing flights.

title: Aging Untold: Prostate health and symptoms men should not ignore
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we examine prostate health, highlighting early warning signs like frequent nighttime bathroom trips and explaining when men should get screened.
Then, we explore the financial, legal and family considerations of tying the knot later in life.
Finally, we meet a Navy veteran and former first responder providing free mental health resources and lifelines of support to struggling heroes.
The prostate is a small gland that slowly enlarges with age, and it can have a big impact on a man’s health.
Dr. Rhea Rogers said an enlarged prostate can be a sign of prostate cancer, which often has no symptoms.
Trouble urinating, frequent nighttime bathroom trips, back pressure and frequent urinary tract infections should not be treated as normal.
Don’t ignore urinary changes, the Aging Untold experts said. Talk to a doctor.
Getting married as an older adult means making a legal and financial decision as much as an emotional one, Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said older couples who are thinking about marriage should start with practical questions, including about money, caregiving and children.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose also recommends working with an estate planning attorney.
High school football coach Shannon Jones was diagnosed with colon cancer that had spread to his liver. His chances for survival were low.
Then, he sought a second opinion at Mayo Clinic from Dr. Denise Harnois, a liver transplant specialist. After months of testing, Jones was approved for a liver transplant.
Advances in chemotherapy and other treatments now prevent colon cancer cells from migrating around the body. Mayo Clinic and a few other centers now perform liver transplants for highly selected colon cancer patients.
(Editor’s note: This story discusses suicide. If you or a loved one needs help, call or text the Suicide Prevention Hotline at 988.)
Navy veteran Billy Bowering was packing for a weekend camping trip with his wife in 2022 when he felt what he said was “this incredible sense of loss and worthlessness.” Then he called his wife to say goodbye.
The call she made changed Bowering’s life.
Within two minutes, Bowering’s friend from church, a Vietnam veteran, knocked at his door. It was in that moment that Bowering realized “that it was time to be one of those interrupters.”
He has created the Day One, Week One nonprofit, which provides mental health resources, financial services and couples counseling for veterans and first responders, all for free.

title: Wisdom Boys End 43-Year Regional Championship Drought
text:
The Fall Five and Five No. 4: Wisdom Boys Kept Finding a Way
Some postseason runs are memorable because a team dominates from start to finish. Wisdom's wasn't like that, and that's part of what made this one so much fun to follow.
The Pioneers finished the regular season 11-3 and entered the Eight-Player North tournament as the No. 3 seed. By the time their season was over, they had survived penalty kicks, played one of the wildest regional championship games of the fall and ended a championship drought that stretched back more than four decades.
Wisdom opened tournament play with a 5-0 win over Lee Academy, but things got much more difficult in the semifinal against Calais. James Desjardins scored Wisdom's goal in regulation, and neither team could find enough separation to finish things before penalty kicks.
Preston Lavoie, Sam Paradis, Zeek Cyr and Cayden Hargrove all converted their attempts, and goalkeeper Bentley Nadeau came up with the save Wisdom needed most, stopping Calais' final kick and sending the Pioneers to the Northern Maine championship.
That alone would have made for a pretty memorable tournament game. What happened next somehow topped it.
Wisdom faced an unbeaten PCHS team in the regional final and trailed 1-0 at halftime. Then Hargrove took over.
He scored four times in the second half, helping Wisdom turn that one-goal deficit into a 4-1 lead. For a while, it looked like the Pioneers had finally created enough separation to put the game away.
PCHS wasn't finished.
Three unanswered goals tied the game at 4-4 with 6:29 remaining, and as the final minutes ticked away, it looked like another Wisdom tournament game was headed for overtime.
Then came one more chance.
With just 13 seconds remaining, Hargrove helped create an opportunity for Cyr, who put it away.
Wisdom 5, PCHS 4.
For the first time in 43 years, the Wisdom boys were Northern Maine champions.
The program's previous regional championship came in 1983, when the Pioneers went on to play for a state title. Four decades later, another Wisdom team had finally earned its own chance to play for a Gold Ball.
And the way they got there made it even more memorable.
Four second-half goals from Hargrove. A three-goal lead that disappeared. A tied championship game in the final minute. Then Cyr's winner with 13 seconds left.
The regional title sent Wisdom to the Eight-Player state championship in Presque Isle, giving the Pioneers an opportunity to play for a Gold Ball close to home. Telstar ultimately came away with a 4-1 victory, leaving Wisdom one win short of the finish it wanted.
But that loss doesn't erase what happened along the way.
Wisdom won three very different tournament games. The Pioneers opened with a shutout, survived a penalty-kick semifinal and then ended a 43-year regional championship drought with one of the most dramatic finishes of the fall.
When I look back on their season, that's what stands out.
They kept getting tested, and when it looked like their run might finally be over, they kept finding another way to extend it.
Forty-three years after the last one, Wisdom boys soccer was finally Northern Maine champion again.
That's why the Pioneers are No. 4 in my five moments that defined the fall of 2026.
Tomorrow, the Countdown continues with Number 3!

title: David Beckham sues for $41 million after his fragrance is sold in gas stations and discount stores
text:
LONDON (AP) — A dispute over the sale of David Beckham perfumes has struck a sour note with the soccer star turned style icon.
Beckham’s commercial company is suing a beauty firm after his “luxury” fragrances were allegedly found for sale in discount stores and a gas station bargain bin.
DB Ventures has filed a claim in the New York Supreme Court against German beauty group Coty, which makes and distributes a range of Beckham-branded fragrances and toiletries. They include the Classic and Instinct lines and the eaux de toilette Intimately and Exquisite Leather.
The claim argues that Beckham’s “world-renowned global brand is synonymous with excellence and refinement,” and “David Beckham products are a symbol of everyday luxury.”
“Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station,” the legal document says. “How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”
Lawyers for DB Ventures allege that Beckham-branded products “ended up in the bargain bin inside a gas station” and at British budget retailer Poundland, “allowing the product to be sold for dollar store prices and associating the David Beckham brand with cheap, discount products.”
DB Ventures is seeking at least $41 million in damages for breach of its licensing agreement.
Coty has asked a judge to dismiss the lawsuit, which was filed in April. The company argues that New York courts have no jurisdiction in the case, and says DB Ventures is using the claim to “manufacture its early exit” from its licensing deal and hand over the Beckham contracts to another firm, Interparfums.
The company told The Associated Press on Tuesday that “Coty strongly disputes the claims and has asked the court to dismiss them. As this is an ongoing legal matter, we will not comment further.”
DB Ventures’ parent company, U.S. entertainment and lifestyles firm Authentic Brands, declined to comment.
Beckham, who played for a number of clubs including Manchester United and Real Madrid and captained the England men’s national team, parlayed success on the pitch into a lucrative business career that includes co-ownership of soccer team Inter Miami. He was knighted last year by King Charles III, becoming Sir David.
He also has had a very public persona as a fashion model, “Bend It Like Beckham” movie muse and husband of Spice Girl-turned-fashion designer Victoria “Posh Spice” Beckham. The couple have four children.
The Sunday Times Rich List earlier this year estimated the Beckhams’ wealth at almost 1.2 billion pounds ($1.58 billion).

title: Mullin defends use of government plane to go to college football game after ground stop
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday defended his use of a government plane to fly to a college football game the day after a nationwide ground stop which caused massive travel disruptions and left people stranded across the country.
Mullin, speaking on CNBC, acknowledged earlier reporting in the New York Post that he flew to the LSU-Texas college football game a day after all planes were grounded.
Asked whether he is required to fly on government planes and whether he paid for the trip personally, Mullin said yes.
“We would have never went if the airways weren’t completely open,” he said on CNBC. “They’d been completely open for 21 hours.”
He added: “We would have never taken airspace if airspace wasn’t open. And we still gotta live our lives at the same time.”
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the flight.
The day before his flight, Mullin was at the White House alongside Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy giving updates on the ground stop.
The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from U.S. airports.
President Donald Trump’s administration has said last week’s air traffic snarls were caused by a router issue in the aging air traffic control system. Trump on Monday got defensive during a lengthy — sometimes testy — exchange with reporters as he left the White House for his trip to Asia.
He faulted old technology and Democrats for the incident that caused upheaval at the country’s airports — especially his predecessor, President Joe Biden.
“I don’t take any responsibility” for Friday’s ground stop, Trump said,
“What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,” the president said. He later noted: “Incredibly, everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt. No crashes, no nothing.”
Trump was silent on the chaos until Sunday, when he posted on social media blasting his Democratic predecessor and asking Congress for more money to cover the cost of system improvements.

title: Minimum wage increase needs to be on Congress’ to-do list
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Orlando Delogu is an emeritus professor at the University of Maine School of Law.
A recent opinion piece in the New York Times listed “8 Bold Ideas for the Next Democratic Congress,” i.e., build housing, lower prices, stop giving AI a free pass, end the Iran war, stop Musk’s political contributions, pass Medicare for all (especially children), legalize undocumented aliens and expand the Supreme Court.
All seem worth doing. Some seem too narrowly focused. Most will take time before the lives of ordinary citizens are benefited.
In this writer’s view a glaring omission from this listing of things to do is raising the minimum wage. In 1938, Congress passed the Fair Labor Standards Act. It contained provisions establishing a federal minimum wage of 25 cents per hour. Subsequent congressional enactments raised the minimum wage.
Most recently, in 2009, the minimum wage was raised to $7.25 per hour, pursuant to a congressional enactment. Federal data indicates that inflation (year-to-year price increases) has risen 57% from 2009-2026, but the federal minimum wage has not been increased in 17 years.
It’s important that we not be misled by the term “federal minimum wage.” The FLSA applies nationally. Federal minimum wage provisions apply to all federal, state and local government employees and to almost all private sector employees in all 50 states (with limited exceptions for “tipped wage,” part-time and some agricultural workers).
It should also be noted that the FLSA allows states to pass legislation that raises the minimum wage above the federal level. Thirty states and the District of Columbia have taken advantage of these provisions. Eighteen of these states and the District of Columbia have minimum wage rates of $15 or more. Maine’s current rate is $15.10. It follows that 12 states have minimum wage rates below $15 but above the federal rate, and that 20 states have nothing more than the poverty- inducing federal minimum wage rate of $7.25 per hour.
Given these statistical realities three things seem clear. First, raising the current federal minimum wage rate is long overdue. Second, wage-based employees (millions of people) in the 20 states adhering to the federal minimum wage would immediately benefit by establishing a more realistic federal wage rate. Ideally this rate would be tied (as are Social Security benefits) to ongoing inflation rates.
Third, and most important, raising the federal minimum wage can be done immediately. It would be an immensely popular enactment in all parts of the country — an enactment made possible by the recent elections that have given congressional Democrats overwhelming legislative power. On Jan. 3, 2027, they will have the votes in both the House and Senate to pass this legislation without Republican support.
That said, prudence dictates that Democrats actively seek the support of congressional
Republicans in passing this legislation. 
The two parties need to relearn the art of working together. Moreover, this is an easy piece of legislation for Republicans in Congress to support. In the past more than a few of them have supported raising the federal minimum wage, and large numbers of Republican voters in all parts of the country have long supported raising the minimum wage.
Finally, jointly supported legislation raising the federal minimum wage reduces the likelihood of a presidential veto, and if an obdurate president does veto such legislation, the likelihood the veto will be overturned is high. That’s my view.

title: Trump didn’t just lose the midterms
text:
It seems that Trump was caught in the headlights of adulation during “The Apprentice” and figured it would last forever, not reckoning that more moderate Christian, Jewish and Muslim folks — of many different denominations and sects — take their religion to heart and wish to follow the tenets of morality therein.
Trump backs having the 10 Commandments posted in schools, but ignores them in backing plans that eradicate equal opportunities in school admissions; in backing plans that eradicate equal opportunities in school admissions; when it comes to loving neighbors, be they red, Black, white, yellow, brown. Trump has not separated the “worst of the worst” from those trying their best to be good enough folks to become citizens. In fact, he has backed killing citizens without cause, killing schoolchildren in Iran, etc.
The president has manipulated the markets, the oil business, the weapons manufacturers and the tariffs so that his buddies make more money. And in Stephen Miller, he has promoted a man who espouses war, separating families and deporting folks who work at jobs most Americans don’t want to do, just to make a quota.
No, Trump didn’t just lose the election, he was hung by his own petard. Perhaps his latest choice will be another major blunder.
