Harpswell

title: Do-it-yourself marketing brings new activity to Auburn Mall, just in time for the holidays
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUBURN — What a difference a few months can make.
The Auburn Mall is in a period of renaissance entering the most important time of the year for retail: the holiday season.
In July, more than half of the mall’s storefronts were empty, frequented mainly by regulars who walk the mall, some loyal customers, and the curious.
Now, there are new store owners, a third restaurant has just opened, and a half-dozen unique kiosks and carts have been added to the indoor mall.
Jan Tillson, of Sabattus, opened her kiosk called Little Daffodil last week, selling baked goods and maple products made by her family.
Tillson is a regular mall walker and figured she’d take a chance. She’s open Monday, Wednesday and Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. for now, but is optimistic.
Of the original 50 stores from the Auburn Mall’s opening in 1979, Thatcher’s Restaurant, JCPenney, and Spencer’s remain. Spencer’s parent company also owns Spirit Halloween, the seasonal pop-up that just ended its 2026 run at the mall.
New businesses fill previously empty spaces, selling an array of goods from clothes, furniture, toys and collectibles to the paranormal. There’s even a mini museum at Beyond the Boards, where co-owner Jeff Witham sells horror-themed paranormal gifts and collectibles.
Foot traffic is anecdotally up; the best evidence can be seen on weekends.
Kevin Boillard is the founder of Kaydenz Kitchen and Alter LA, Lewiston’s only low-barrier homeless shelter. He opened Alter 207 — a retail and thrift store at the mall — in October, and says he’s happy with the decision.
The store is well lit, orderly, and all proceeds help his nonprofits be self-sustaining.
“Traffic has been great and this is a great model for the mall,” he said. “There’s a new energy in the building.”
At least nine businesses have signed leases at the mall in the past few months. Varro, a new cafe and bakery, opened this past weekend. Mary Ann Chandler, the mall’s administrative assistant, hopes to have seven kiosks up and running by Black Friday.
That leaves just four empty stores available for rent, according to Chandler, ranging in size from 1,600 to 6,550 square feet, plus the anchor tenant spot that previously housed TD Bank’s calling center, which covers more than 60,000 square feet.
A collective effort to attract new business to the mall began with one of the mall’s existing tenants, Jeff Mitchell. He and his wife own Family Time Dine and Play as well as Fluff Me, and have leased space at the mall for 13 years.
Earlier this summer, with permission from mall management, Mitchell began a series of posts to social media that were directed at local businesses. The posts invited them to explore and consider the Auburn Mall — touting the low-cost, location, abundant parking and provided maintenance. The posts were widely shared.
“I feel that it has been successful,” Mitchell said. “The negative comments online have slowed, and (I) have seen a flip. … The mindset is shifting. This positive new outlook from the community is only going to benefit the renewal.”
Miller Fitness at Auburn Mall is one of the gym’s busiest locations, bringing hundreds of people to the building every day. Thatcher’s and JCPenney have loyal followings as well. Newcomer 7 Jam Kitchen is establishing a following and Toys R Us recently signed a lease and moved in.
CM Collective is run by a stay-at-home mother who started her boutique online through TikTok. Owner Callie Libby started looking for a storefront in the Augusta area, but says she found that “everything is priced crazily high.”
The Auburn Mall’s low rent attracted Angie Bisson too. She ran a thrift store in South Paris and now operates Angie’s Attic. “Rent prices were cheap” she said, which matched her policy of “buy cheap, sell cheap” with an eye on volume to make it a good financial decision.
The mall is now a mix of businesses from shoe stores, clothing, entertainment, eye care, thrift stores and more. If you ask people what kind of stores they want to see in the mall, they’ll tell you a movie theater, more food, a sports store or exchange, and even antiques.
“I often get a lot of comments that people want this store or that store,” Mitchell said. “My suggestion to the community is to take the wheel like I did and reach out to those businesses. Major retailers listen to the masses more than they listen to some random person offering affordable rent.”

title: Another wipeout hits Wall Street as Nvidia, other jittery AI stocks swing lower
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The U.S. stock market shook again Tuesday as Nvidia and other jittery stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry led widespread losses on Wall Street.
The S&P 500 sank 1% and at one point was on track for its first back-to-back losses of at least 1.5% since March. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 848 points, or 1.6%, and the Nasdaq composite fell 0.7%.
The center of the action was again Nvidia, which resumed its whipsaw moves. After flipping between modest gains and losses in the morning, it veered lower and dropped as much as 3.7% before trimming the loss down to 0.4%.
The swings came ahead of the chip company’s latest earnings report, which arrived after trading ended for the day and once again came in above analysts’ expectations. It was Nvidia’s first earnings report since interim CEO Colette Kress took over for Jensen Huang, the leather-jacketed star who became one of the most famous faces of the AI boom.
The pressure is on Kress and Nvidia to show whether the company’s tremendous growth can continue following the stunning resignation of one of AI’s strongest influencers. Nvidia is creating a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance following revelations that Huang had a relationship with an alleged spy for China.
Huang said on the X social-media network Tuesday that he would come back as CEO if “the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America.”
Other AI stocks also swung sharply. Advanced Micro Devices went from an early gain of 1.6% to a drop of 4.7% before trimming its fall to 0.2%. CoreWeave initially climbed 1.8%, flipped to a loss of 6.1% and then finished nearly unchanged.
AI-related stocks have been shaky for months because of a rolling chain of worries. At first, it was concerns that AI stock prices had broadly shot too high in their frenzy. Then it was worries that high interest rates would mean less borrowed money to fund further growth. More recently, it was concerns that Democratic victories in this month’s U.S. midterm elections could mean tougher regulations and restrictions on AI data centers.
Such stocks can almost single-handedly set the U.S. market’s course because they’ve grown into some of Wall Street’s most valuable and most influential.
Most of Wall Street was weak Tuesday, as 17 out of every 20 stocks within the index fell,
Home Depot sank 2.4% even though it reported profit for the latest quarter that edged past analysts’ expectations.
The retailer has been hampered by a housing market chilled by expensive mortgage rates, which have climbed with Treasury yields because of high oil prices, high inflation and other factors.
The 10-year Treasury yield climbed toward 5.15% Tuesday morning from 5.12% late Monday before later pulling back to 5.10%. It erased its gain after the sharp drops for AI stocks pushed investors to herd into investments seen as safer bets.
In the morning, yields got support from a report showing better growth in an underlying measure of spending at U.S. retailers than economists expected. Such spending, along with big investments in AI, has helped the U.S. economy continue to grow despite frustration with high inflation.
Elsewhere on Wall Street, stocks of banks fell amid concerns about how much pain the broad U.S. economy will feel from any pullback in AI-related spending.
JPMorgan Chase fell 2.4%. A day before, a technical issue at the bank had slowed transactions for customers trying to use the Zelle payment system.
Apple and Marriott had only modest moves following outages in their systems. Apple slipped 0.2%, and Marriott International fell 0.7%.
United Airlines had its own operational struggles, as a system outage forced the carrier to delay departing flights Monday. That came just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop.
United’s stock lost 4%, but it was also hurt by a rise in oil prices.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 0.8% to $93.14. It’s been yo-yoing amid uncertainty about what will happen in the war with Iran.
The downward momentum on Wall Street was strong enough to erase early gains for The Walt Disney Co. and pull it down 1.5%, even though it reported stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 76.06 points to 7,340.53. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 848.75 to 50,759.42, and the Nasdaq composite sank 181.37 to 24,328.38.
Stock prices generally tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term, depending on how interest rates behave. The big businesses across the S&P 500 index are on track to deliver earnings per share for the summer that are nearly 32% higher than a year earlier, according to FactSet.
In stock markets abroad, indexes sank across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi fell 2.6% and dropped to its lowest closing level since February.
___
AP Writers Elaine Lai and Matt Ott contributed to this report.

title: BDN promotes 3 editors, hires sports editor as it expands coverage
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Bangor Daily News has promoted three editors and hired a fourth, including two in newly created roles as the BDN bolsters its newsroom leadership.
The new roles will focus on expanding coverage into more parts of Maine and setting the newsroom’s coverage priorities as the BDN continues to invest in independent local journalism.
“Our mission is to tell stories that would otherwise stay hidden and to connect Maine communities with the information they need,” BDN Executive Editor Dan MacLeod said. “These changes will strengthen our accountability reporting and help us tell exclusive stories in more places.”
Lindsay Putnam is becoming managing editor, a role the BDN hasn’t had in recent years. She will manage day-to-day operations across the newsroom, set coverage priorities and guide digital work, including video and newsletters.
Putnam has been with the BDN for nearly a decade in several editing roles, most recently as chief news editor overseeing the Bangor desk. She is from York Beach, graduated from Colby College and lives in Bangor.
“Lindsay is a great leader who knows how to support our talented staff in their mission of serving our Maine audiences,” MacLeod said. “She’s the perfect person to lead the day-to-day operations of our newsroom.”
Paul Koenig, previously chief digital editor, is becoming chief state editor, a new role leading the BDN’s regional journalism and expansion into new parts of Maine. He will oversee reporting in coastal Maine and Aroostook County, as well as The County and the Piscataquis Observer, and work to develop new beats and partnerships.
“Paul has stellar news judgment and a strong sense of what makes a BDN story. I’m really excited to see him launch new beats and improve our already strong statewide coverage,” MacLeod said.
Koenig joined the BDN in 2022 after working at Maine Magazine, Old Port magazine, Mainebiz and the Kennebec Journal.
Sawyer Loftus is taking over Putnam’s previous role leading the city desk, overseeing coverage of Greater Bangor, including the housing and criminal justice beats.
Loftus joined the BDN five years ago and most recently was an investigative reporter on the Maine Focus team. He was named Maine Journalist of the Year in 2024 and was a 2024-25 fellow in ProPublica’s Local Reporting Network.
“Sawyer’s record of landing scoops and reporting fearless investigations makes him an ideal person to build on watchdog coverage of our hometown,” MacLeod said.
Trey Stewart is the BDN’s new sports editor.
Stewart, who is no relation to the Maine state senator of the same name, comes from South Carolina, where he most recently was regional editor at GreerNews.com. He previously was sports editor at The Greer Citizen and, after that paper closed, founded Greer Sports Star, a digital outlet covering high school sports.
“Trey has already hit the ground running,” MacLeod said. “He has an enterprising spirit and a great eye for what makes a great Maine sports story.”

title: Angus King strikes out with support for Chuck Schumer
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Barbara Hausman-Smith of Belfast had a long career as a legal aid lawyer and guardian ad litem. More than 40 years after she argued a case before the court, she protested at the U.S. Supreme Court in 2024 because she believes it protects corporate interests, not the interests of the American people.
Sen. Angus King went on record before he had to and committed to Chuck Schumer’s leadership in the U.S. Senate. He says Schumer collected more money for Democrats than Elon Musk. Musk? Why remind us?
The voters’ message was clear: dumping cash doesn’t win elections, particularly when it’s linked to AIPAC, who created “dummy” PACs to hide their contributions. I think Maine demonstrated a greater concern about money in politics than the national average.
Schumer was late to support Scott Colom in Mississippi. Secondly, King gives Schumer credit for recruiting candidates who would flip the Senate, like Roy Cooper in North Carolina and Sherrod Brown in Ohio. Yet I believe that was before Democrats found their voice. Let’s not mention the others he threw money at, for example the loser Janet Mills and the turncoat Haley Stevens in Michigan.
And then the soundbite: “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” Most obvious is the bad politics of giving Schumer credit for the 55-seat or larger Senate majority, when it was the people who they should answer to. Now they take credit for the hard work of the voters themselves who put new Democrats in office.
Did anyone else react to King’s soundbite like me? I thought it was an answer a parent tells a child when they don’t want to explain themselves or the complexities of the question.
What I believe too few have mentioned about Schumer or the 2026 midterms and can no longer be avoided is the billions taxpayers are giving to Israel because AIPAC appears to control so many politicians. When so many voters complain that Schumer is old guard or out of touch, many are saying they are sick of politicians allowing policy or laws that the people do not want because our representatives are beholden to the money they get from special interests.
And because I believe Israel has proved itself to the world that they are bad players, the majority of people want that blood money to be slowed or to stop. All the soundbites and self-serving statements cannot compensate for the reality they create, which is that our country can’t afford to spend taxpayer money on healthcare, childcare, natural disasters, or saving the planet.
Schumer and King are smart people. Does going to Washington remove all sense? Does compromise negate their initial motivation to do the right thing? What does it take for them to recognize the old ways have been firmly rejected?
They can’t do everything but they have to pivot or the people will throw them out also.

title: Cause of death revealed for Gypsy-Rose Blanchard’s ex-fiancé Ken Urker
text:
(Gray News) - Gypsy-Rose Blanchard’s ex-fiancé’s cause of death has been revealed.
Ken Urker died of an accidental drug overdose, according to the Lafourche Parish Coroner’s Office.
The autopsy and toxicology testing determined Urker’s cause of death was “accidental polysubstance drug toxicity.”
The coroner’s office said the case is now complete.
Urker was found unresponsive on Oct. 1, which was his 34th birthday. A family member found him at a home, according to People.
The Lafourche Parish Sheriff’s Department said Urker was found “dead upon arrival.”
After his death, Blanchard told People that she believed Urker died of an accidental overdose, but did not know if it was “intentional,” adding that “he was not in a good state of mind lately.”
“I’m in disbelief. I can’t think. I’ve screamed until my throat burns,” Blanchard told People.
Blanchard and Urker share a daughter, Aurora, who was born in December 2024.

title: A 2-month lull ends with Iran’s third strike on US targets in Bahrain
text:
A 2-month lull ends with Iran’s third strike on US targets in Bahrain
Iran fired drones across the Persian Gulf on Tuesday at a U.S. radar facility in Bahrain, its third attack in recent days on American military targets in the tiny island kingdom as Tehran resumed strikes on its Arab neighbors after a roughly two-month lull.
After issuing an alert about the incoming fire, Bahrain said that its air defense systems had successfully intercepted the “treacherous Iranian aerial attacks.”
The attacks on American infrastructure in Bahrain are part of an evolution in Iran's strategy from waiting for an attack and then retaliating to targeting the operational capability of bases, Tehran-based security analyst Mostafa Najafi said.
Related video: Is a potential government shutdown worth it to end the Iran war?
“Tehran has shifted toward a more active, preemptive strategy — one focused on countering threats during their very formative stages,” he told The Associated Press.
Tuesday's attack came after the U.S. military's Central Command confirmed that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group had arrived in the region. The move adds a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the American presence as U.S. President Donald Trump keeps his options open for his next move in the war, which began nearly nine months ago.
The combined U.S. naval assets in the Gulf, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean now exceed the force deployed when the U.S. and Israel conducted joint strikes on Iran to launch the war on Feb. 28 — the presence provides greater offensive firepower and missile interception capacity, according to a new analysis by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.
The Roosevelt joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller U.S. Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain a blockade of Iranian shipping. U.S. Central Command wouldn't comment on whether it plans to keep all three carrier strike groups in the region or replace the Washington, which had been redeployed from the Asia-Pacific region to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln amid concerns of its lengthy deployment.
The Washington itself has now been deployed for around six months.
Iran says it's responding to U.S. attacks
Iran's attack on Bahrain on Tuesday came after it targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in the country on Friday, and on Sunday fired at a radar system at an American helicopter base there. Despite claims of success, there appeared to be little or no damage done.
The attacks followed U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers and ongoing drone surveillance operations, and Iran said that they were done in retaliation.
“Continued aggression against the country's airspace, as well as the use of regional military bases and facilities for hostile acts against Iran will not go unanswered,” Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement.
The U.S. military didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the recent attacks.
With negotiations stagnating on bringing an end to the war, despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar, the latest military developments have further complicated prospects for a negotiated settlement, said Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, in an analysis posted to X.
As the U.S. mulls whether to resume all-out military attacks on Iran or to intensify its blockade to further sap strength from Iran's economy, Iranian leaders will also now be weighing whether “breaking the blockade through escalation is less costly than accepting its continuation,” Azizi wrote.
“In other words, the risk of renewed war no longer depends solely on whether Trump decides to attack Iran again,” he said. “It also depends on whether Tehran concludes that the costs of continued restraint have become greater than the risks of escalation.”
Iran may be losing patience as conflict drags on
The attacks on the American facilities in Bahrain are a sign that Tehran is growing impatient with the waiting game as its economic woes mount, said Sascha Bruchmann, a Bahrain-based defense analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
“Shooting at ships causes fear, but is not effective enough to change the strategic equation,” Bruchmann told the AP. “Tehran knows it needs to do something, but I wouldn’t overestimate what we saw against Bahrain this week. This is not it — yet.”
Iranian officials have termed the current situation “no war, no peace” and vowed that it must be brought to an end.
Tehran has said that it's open to a negotiated deal, but also signaled a readiness to escalate the conflict in the face of tightening sanctions and the blockade that are throttling Iran’s economy.
Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran’s influential parliamentary chief, posted on social media on Monday that leaders view U.S. economic pressure as an effort to create a domestic “security crisis.” He said that the strikes on Bahrain were meant “to prevent the gradual expansion of enemy operations and to impose costs on its military infrastructure.”
2 critical shipping lanes threatened by Iran and its proxies
Iran has also continued to attack ships seeking to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which leads from the Persian Gulf toward the open seas.
Before the war, ships had freely passed through the key waterway, carrying about a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas. Since then, Iran has held a tight grip on the strait and only a fraction of the peacetime shipping traffic has been able to pass through, despite U.S. efforts to provide escorts.
On Tuesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization said that a tanker was reportedly attacked twice north of Oman, and that the second strike caused a fire on board.
Iran's Fars news agency also reported that two ships were struck by mines in the strait, causing them to catch fire. It wasn't immediately clear whether one was the incident reported by the British military's UKMTO.
In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi rebels now have solidified their control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another critical shipping route, which connects the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea, after a group allied with the Saudi-backed Yemeni government retreated on the weekend in a setback to the anti-Houthi coalition.
Those government-allied forces are now fortifying their defenses in areas leading to the southern city of Aden, which serves as an interim capital of the internationally recognized government, two Yemeni military officials said.
Their efforts are focused on deploying more troops and equipment in and around the district of Tur al-Baha in the southern province of Lahij, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to brief the media.
___
Rising reported from Bangkok. Sam Metz in Jerusalem and Ahmed al-Haj in Aden, Yemen, contributed to this report.

title: Several people injured after severe turbulence on flight headed to Florida, officials say
text:
Several people injured after severe turbulence on flight headed to Florida, officials say
Several JetBlue passengers and crew members suffered injuries Tuesday morning after their flight encountered severe turbulence en route to Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport in Florida, officials said.
Related video above: How the Trump administration is trying to prevent future travel disruptions after ground stop?
At about 6:25 a.m. on Tuesday, the fire and rescue unit of the Broward County Sheriff’s Office responded to reports of injuries from JetBlue Flight 1717, which was arriving from Ponce, Puerto Rico, the unit said in a release to CNN.
“The aircraft landed safely at approximately 6:58 a.m. and proceeded to Terminal 3, where Broward Sheriff Fire Rescue personnel were standing by to evaluate those reporting injuries,” the unit said. “Fire rescue personnel identified five individuals reporting injuries or requiring evaluation.”
The injured passengers and crew members declined transportation to area hospitals, the unit said. There were no reports of structural damage to the aircraft.

title: Bangor overnight warming shelter reopens as need grows, church faces financial worries
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - An overnight warming shelter is back open in Bangor as organizers say the need is even greater this year.
The Brick Church, located on the corner of Main Street and Union Street, is open seven nights a week for those who need a warm place to sleep.
The overnight warming center opens at 6 p.m. and guests can stay until 7 a.m., or 8:30 a.m. if they would like to attend the Alcoholics Anonymous meeting held there every morning.
The shelter opened Sunday night. Pastor Leon Licata says need has increased this year.
At this time last year, about 11 people were staying overnight. Already this year, he says that number was up to almost 40 Monday night.
While guests are at the Brick Church, they can take advantage of the showers, food and other resources available, including doctors, detox, case management and more.
With cameras throughout the property and a separation of guests and belongings, organizers say not only does the Brick Church give people a place to stay warm, but a safe one.
“Being out on the street is not always safe, and they’re looking for a secure place to go, someplace where they can actually just go and relax and just get a good night’s sleep. And it’s very vital,” Licata described. “It’s good for your mental health. It’s good for your physical health to get a good night’s sleep. And that’s what we offer. We offer that security here.“
Licata says this season is bringing deep financial worries to the church.
They need to raise $176,000 by Dec. 31 to cover the building’s lease, due to a donor backing out.

Why are web systems going down nationwide? Trump administration warns of more outages
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Why are web systems going down nationwide? Trump administration warns of more outages
The FBI and Google warn that artificial intelligence is accelerating cyberattacks.
Why are web systems going down nationwide? Trump administration warns of more outages
The FBI and Google warn that artificial intelligence is accelerating cyberattacks.
The Trump administration is suggesting new technology may be overwhelming aging computer systems as a string of outages disrupts everything from banking and air travel to national security networks. But cybersecurity experts say that may not explain all the disruptions.
Meanwhile, new warnings from the FBI and Google reveal how artificial intelligence is making cyberattacks faster and more sophisticated.
"I believe we're going to see more of this as new technology rolls out," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Tuesday on CNBC's "Squawk Box."
"They're pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems, and it just seems to overwhelm the system a little bit, and it's not able to catch up. But it has nothing to do with cyberattacks," he added.
Gregory Falco, a Cornell University assistant professor of aerospace and systems engineering, said Mullin's explanation is possible but questioned whether it accounts for all the recent outages.
"That doesn't happen for all of these systems overnight. So I think it has to be something a little deeper than that," Falco said.
Falco cautioned that he could only speculate about the cause of the disruptions but raised the possibility of Iranian cyberattacks.
"Iran has gotten really good at getting in some deep network somewhere. I think we shouldn't discount that," Falco said.
Falco also suggested software updates involving AI could be causing cascading failures. There is no confirmed evidence linking Iran or other malicious actors to the recent outages.
Congressional Democrats are demanding the Trump administration brief lawmakers on the disruptions.
"It's unclear if it's all infrastructure related or whether there's some malignant activity," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Tuesday.
Widespread disruptions
The Federal Aviation Administration announced Tuesday it had paused the installation of routers linked to Friday's nationwide ground stop, which disrupted air travel across the country. The agency is still investigating what caused the ground stop.
A technical issue at JPMorgan Chase also caused online banking delays, while a Microsoft outage disrupted email services.
Meanwhile, the National Security Agency said in a statement to Hearst Television that some of its internal systems were affected during scheduled maintenance.
"The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance. While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues," an NSA spokesperson said.
The agency added that its infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.
An evolving cyber threat
On Monday, a separate cyberattack affected 178 organizations, including IKEA, Zoom and Equifax, potentially exposing website visitors' credit card information and putting vulnerable iPhones and iPads at risk.
Cybersecurity researchers traced the attack to Optimizely, a service companies use to test and update their websites. The breach did not mean the organizations' internal computer systems were compromised.
Meanwhile, the FBI is warning that hackers are using an AI-powered tool capable of gaining privileged access to computer systems in less than three hours.
In a report released Monday, Google researchers said they had, for the first time, identified hackers using AI to fully automate the discovery and exploitation of security vulnerabilities without human intervention.
Researchers found hackers could use AI to analyze software updates, identify the security flaws those updates fix and target organizations that have not yet installed them.
Despite the recent disruptions, Falco expressed confidence in the ability of critical systems to withstand failures, but like Mullin, also predicted there could be more outages.
"So I think that we have enough of these resilient and redundant systems to enable our society to continue," Falco said. "But it's going to be hard and it's going to be a little bit painful along the way."
Scammers exploiting outages
Microsoft has also warned that scammers are taking advantage of recent technology disruptions by sending fake emails claiming users lost messages during last week's outage and asking them to click a link to recover them.
The goal is to steal users' login information. Rather than clicking those links, users should go directly to their email provider's website.

title: Warmer temperatures will bring back the feel of October
text:
Warmer temperatures will bring back the feel of October
High pressure will keep our weather dry and unusually mild through the rest of the week and into the weekend. Afternoon temperatures will climb into the 50s and even lower 60s in many areas, well above normal for mid-November.
Despite the mild afternoons, clear skies and light winds will allow temperatures to drop quickly at night. Some clouds tonight should keep temperatures from falling quite as low as last night.
The dry stretch looks to continue through most of the weekend, with our next chance of rain arriving late Sunday or, more likely, Monday. While the timing is still uncertain, there's growing confidence that a wetter pattern may return for early next week.
Get your latest Maine’s Total Weather video forecast from Meteorologist Roger Griswold.

title: 11 Things To Love About November In Maine, Beyond The Turkey
text:
Most people list the reasons to dislike November in Maine, like the cold and the end of summer, but I wanted to take a more positive approach.
November in Maine is Filled With Negatives Like the Numbers on the Thermometer
Are you one of those people who hates November because it signals the end of Maine's best season?
Me too.
READ MORE: Maine is the Third Best State to Raise a Family
The Earth is gray and cold and waiting for winter.
You can almost feel Mother Nature bracing for what comes next.
But that's the pessimist's way to look at November in Maine when, in reality, there are a lot of wonderful reasons to look forward to this time of year.
November in Maine Can Be Great for More Than Just Turkey
I'm not going to lie; I needed help coming up with some of these because, as I said, November is not my favorite time of year.
It always reminds me of my years at the University of Maine, living on the Orono campus.
This is when I had to start piling on extra layers to walk across campus for class.
Then I'd spend the first few minutes of class unwinding myself from scarves, hats, and heavy jackets.
The room would be impossibly warm, and I'd feel overheated until it was time to layer up again and go back into the chill.
Surviving a Maine Winter is All About Attitude and Layers
But I digress. This post is about the positive aspects of November in Maine.
For one, I'm not a college student anymore, and I don't have to do that ever again.
So, here we go:11 positive things about November in Maine, other than the Thanksgiving turkey.
Grab a hot cup of coffee, a warm blanket, and see if this helps your mood.

title: Man accessed US military plane at Ireland airport and destroyed it, DOJ says
text:
Man accessed US military plane at Ireland airport and destroyed it, DOJ says
A grand jury in New York has indicted an Irish national who allegedly destroyed a US military aircraft by gaining access to the plane at an airport in Ireland, cutting wires, placing ball bearings inside fuel tanks, and pouring corrosive substances that could have resulted in an explosion.
Law enforcement alleges Daithi O’Corrain meticulously plotted the attack to cause significant damage. The indictment includes images of smashed gauges and ax marks on the plane’s exterior — some of the extraordinary destruction inside and outside the plane — which prosecutors say caused at least $60 million in damage.
See more images in the video player above
O’Corrain, 48, allegedly spent months planning the attack, which was the fourth time since May 2025 that people gained unauthorized access to the Shannon airport in County Clare, prosecutors say.
CNN attempted to reach O’Corrain’s lawyer for comment.
Authorities allege that just after 4:30 a.m. on April 11, O’Corrain snuck onto the taxiway at the airport and broke into the U.S. C-130 Hercules aircraft, barricading himself inside. Prosecutors say, while inside, O’Corrain cut wires and hydraulic lines, crimped a liquid oxygen line, and destroyed every gauge in the cockpit, according to the indictment.
O’Corrain also brought onboard capsules of gallium — a corrosive material that can rapidly eat through aluminum and damage steel. The plane wasn’t salvageable after the attack and had to be destroyed, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in Manhattan.
“This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism. The defendant allegedly spent months researching the aircraft, acquiring tools and materials, and preparing to maximize the destruction he could inflict,” said James C. Barnacle, FBI Assistant Director in Charge of the New York field office.
O’Corrain was indicted on one charge of destroying US government property. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison. He was arrested by Irish authorities in April and is not in US custody at this time.
There is no indication of a motive in the court documents.
Prosecutors allege O’Corrain carefully planned the attack by searching for information about the aircraft’s construction and the security perimeter around Shannon Airport. He ordered gallium online and tools that he used in the attack and signed up for flight alerts to track flight paths, including those of U.S. military aircraft. He also attempted to contact a person involved in a previous attack at the airport, the indictment alleges.
Members of the aircraft’s flight crew discovered O’Corrain around 9:40 a.m. when they returned to the aircraft to depart. O’Corrain escaped out a hatch in the roof and hit the plane’s exterior with an axe, according to the indictment. He also allegedly poured ball bearings into the plane’s fuel tanks. The flight crew contacted security and Irish police arrested O’Corrain and took him into custody.
Law enforcement alleges O’Corrain was sophisticated in his attack, researching which lines he could cut without injuring himself. According to the indictment, “O’Corrain cut, rather than crimped, the Aircraft’s liquid oxygen line, as he had its wire bundles; there would have been a high chance of a massive explosion within the Aircraft.”
In May 2025, three people were arrested by Irish authorities for driving a van through a perimeter fence. Two weeks later, three people entered the runway and spray-painted a U.S. military aircraft. In November 2025, three individuals in a van breached the security perimeter and drove to a restricted area where a US military aircraft was parked, where they were detained by security.

title: This sculptor uses art to rise from grief
text:
RANDOLPH, Vt. (InvestigateTV) - In the hills of central Vermont, where the ocean is nowhere in sight, two massive mammals rise from the earth. Visitors who stumble upon them are often stopped in their tracks.
“You come up here and you think you’re up in the mountains, you’re out in the wilderness, and all of a sudden you see two whale tails,” said Court Perkins, a visitor from Connecticut.
Whale Dance is the creation of local artist Jim Sardonis. “I mainly love nature in all its forms.”
The Randolph sculpture, installed in 2019, has an older sibling, Reverence, which migrated from Randolph to South Burlington in 1999, and is seen by thousands each day as they head up Interstate 89.
“Surprising how many people know about them when I go to Boston, or some place, people mentioned them,” Sardonis said.
People like the Perkins family from Connecticut, who every summer take selfies with friends and family at the whales, and who on this day got a special treat, meeting the sculptor himself.
“We always wondered who designed them and why,” Perkins said.
In Brookfield, Sardonis’ first piece is set in stone. It’s near the historic floating bridge in the village — two hippos called Father and Son.
“I did it shortly after my father died and my son was born,” Sardonis said. At the time, he was teaching and thought it would be a good summer project. “It’s given a lot of fun to kids over the years.”
The whales came later, in a dream. “I had been standing on a beach looking at the water, and these two tails came up at the same time.”
But Sardonis’ most poignant work wasn’t born from a dream. It was born of a broken heart. He and his wife, Dianne, lost an unborn daughter to anencephaly.
“The brain doesn’t develop for some unknown reason,” Sardonis said. “So, they knew she wouldn’t live when she was born. So, we had a tough weekend, knowing on Monday we would deliver her and spent an hour with her.”
Her name was Leah. Through the grief, Sardonis decided to make a sculpture to honor her and the care workers at nearby Gifford Hospital. It’s called Vermont Family.
“Spending the year working on the sculpture was, yeah, just what I needed,” he said. “We didn’t realize until the sculpture was done that we would have a baby girl.”
“Well, you seem very honest about what you’ve gone through and what this means to you,” reporter Joe Carroll said.
“We certainly have had a lot more joy in our lives than sorrow,” Sardonis responded.
Proof that even in the deepest valley of grief, art prevails.

title: Spicy cat rescued from precarious perch over NH highway
text:
Cats will never be accused of possessing a surfeit of gratitude.
Judging by some photos circulating online Monday, a cat rescued from a precarious perch over Interstate 293 in New Hampshire this weekend showed no love for its heroes.
In fact, he seemed ready to throw down claws with the law.
The cat was stuck on a highway sign over I-293, near Second Street and Queen City Avenue in Manchester, according to the Manchester Police Department.
Animal Control Officer Sophia Landrey (left) holds a stray cat that was rescued over the weekend from a sign hanging over Interstate 293 (right) in Manchester, New Hampshire. Credit: Courtesy of the Manchester Police Department
Firefighters and the animal control officer used a ladder truck to bring the spicy fluff to safety.
The cat, believed to be a stray, was taken to an emergency veterinary clinic for treatment of a tail injury.
“Otherwise, this little adventurer seems to be doing just fine!” Manchester police said.
By all appearances, the cat begged to differ.

title: Wisdom Boys End 43-Year Regional Championship Drought
text:
The Fall Five and Five No. 4: Wisdom Boys Kept Finding a Way
Some postseason runs are memorable because a team dominates from start to finish. Wisdom's wasn't like that, and that's part of what made this one so much fun to follow.
The Pioneers finished the regular season 11-3 and entered the Eight-Player North tournament as the No. 3 seed. By the time their season was over, they had survived penalty kicks, played one of the wildest regional championship games of the fall and ended a championship drought that stretched back more than four decades.
Wisdom opened tournament play with a 5-0 win over Lee Academy, but things got much more difficult in the semifinal against Calais. James Desjardins scored Wisdom's goal in regulation, and neither team could find enough separation to finish things before penalty kicks.
Preston Lavoie, Sam Paradis, Zeek Cyr and Cayden Hargrove all converted their attempts, and goalkeeper Bentley Nadeau came up with the save Wisdom needed most, stopping Calais' final kick and sending the Pioneers to the Northern Maine championship.
That alone would have made for a pretty memorable tournament game. What happened next somehow topped it.
Wisdom faced an unbeaten PCHS team in the regional final and trailed 1-0 at halftime. Then Hargrove took over.
He scored four times in the second half, helping Wisdom turn that one-goal deficit into a 4-1 lead. For a while, it looked like the Pioneers had finally created enough separation to put the game away.
PCHS wasn't finished.
Three unanswered goals tied the game at 4-4 with 6:29 remaining, and as the final minutes ticked away, it looked like another Wisdom tournament game was headed for overtime.
Then came one more chance.
With just 13 seconds remaining, Hargrove helped create an opportunity for Cyr, who put it away.
Wisdom 5, PCHS 4.
For the first time in 43 years, the Wisdom boys were Northern Maine champions.
The program's previous regional championship came in 1983, when the Pioneers went on to play for a state title. Four decades later, another Wisdom team had finally earned its own chance to play for a Gold Ball.
And the way they got there made it even more memorable.
Four second-half goals from Hargrove. A three-goal lead that disappeared. A tied championship game in the final minute. Then Cyr's winner with 13 seconds left.
The regional title sent Wisdom to the Eight-Player state championship in Presque Isle, giving the Pioneers an opportunity to play for a Gold Ball close to home. Telstar ultimately came away with a 4-1 victory, leaving Wisdom one win short of the finish it wanted.
But that loss doesn't erase what happened along the way.
Wisdom won three very different tournament games. The Pioneers opened with a shutout, survived a penalty-kick semifinal and then ended a 43-year regional championship drought with one of the most dramatic finishes of the fall.
When I look back on their season, that's what stands out.
They kept getting tested, and when it looked like their run might finally be over, they kept finding another way to extend it.
Forty-three years after the last one, Wisdom boys soccer was finally Northern Maine champion again.
That's why the Pioneers are No. 4 in my five moments that defined the fall of 2026.
Tomorrow, the Countdown continues with Number 3!

title: Maine state representative charged with domestic violence resigns
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - Maine State Rep. Lucas Lanigan (R-Sanford) has submitted his resignation to the clerk of the House, according to a statement from Maine House Speaker Ryan Fecteau. Lanigan is charged in an ongoing trial, accused of strangling his wife during a domestic dispute.
Lanigan turned himself in to authorities on Oct. 28, 2024, after a warrant was issued for his arrest on one count of domestic violence aggravated assault. He made his first court appearance two days later. In March 2025, he pleaded not guilty to domestic violence charges.
According to the initial police report, Lanigan’s wife claimed he strangled her during a domestic dispute. But during Lanigan’s court appearance, his wife claimed the incident was a misunderstanding.
“Representative Lucas Lanigan should have resigned more than two years ago — days after he allegedly attempted to strangle his wife. He was charged with felony aggravated domestic violence in October of 2024, one of Maine’s most serious domestic violence charges,” Maine House Speaker Ryan Fecteau said in a statement. ”His case continues to be litigated in court. His refusal to step down – despite the extremely serious charges against him – was a disservice to the legislature and a profound disservice to every person in House District 141. Maine people expect and deserve far better from their elected officials.”
Lanigan is a Republican representing portions of Newfield, Shapleigh and Sanford in the Maine House.

title: InvestigateTV+: Firing college coaches can cost millions
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Firing college football coaches can cost millions of dollars, and InvestigateTV+ has uncovered how, in some cases, students are helping to foot the bill.
Then, one woman shares how she was forced to marry as a teenager and is now using her past to help protect young lives.
Plus, a grandfather says he’s counting his blessings after surviving a rattlesnake bite, and we talk to wildlife experts about where to tread carefully.
Billion Dollar Blitz
Across America, big-time college athletics is a $12 billion industry, in most cases, living beyond its means.
Ticket sales, TV deals, sponsorships and other revenue sources don’t bring in enough money to cover the bills.
So, universities are filling sometimes massive gaps from their general funds and charging students millions of dollars in mandatory fees to support athletics.
Ending children marriages
Protecting children from forced marriages in recent years, several states have taken action to stop what some call abuse.
Before 2017, every state allowed marriage under 18, according to the nonprofit Unchained At Last. Since then, a growing number of states have outlawed child marriage with no exceptions, not even parental consent.
Ohio is the latest considering a change. In 2019, the state raised the minimum age to 17. But advocates and some lawmakers believe the age should be 18 with no exceptions.
How to watch out for snakes
Wildlife experts say when the weather heats up, rattlesnakes can pop up anywhere — not just on hiking trails.
“Yesterday I removed a snake from a neighborhood garage, so it is possible for them to enter your home, backyard, all different kinds of areas. It’s really anywhere,” Clark said.

title: Gloria Steinem’s famed talking circles are still going strong. This one had a twist: Men only
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — For more than half a century, Gloria Steinem welcomed guests into her inviting, art-filled Manhattan living room, gathering women from all walks of life to discuss issues of vital importance in health, education, business, politics and beyond.
It was her long-held dream that these “talking circles” continue after she was gone — and, two months after her death, they’re indeed going strong. Last week, though, marked a first that close associates say would have particularly delighted the feminist trailblazer: a men-only circle, focused on male well-being.
“I know Gloria would have loved this,” exclaimed Jill Heller of Gloria’s Foundation, which is working on preserving the home as a permanent center, as she welcomed the men. “Wherever she is, I hope she’s tap-dancing,” she added — a wry reference to one of Steinem’s lesser-known talents.
Then the circle’s facilitator, Janna Meyrowitz Turner, explained the genesis of the idea to bring the 12 guests — advocates, academics and others working with men and boys — into one room.
“If she were here, Gloria would tell you that men’s liberation and men’s well-being have always been a part of feminism,” said Meyrowitz Turner, CEO of Antenna Up, a media and events platform that aims to build trust between men and women. “She would say that healthier men means healthier women.”
The circle, she noted, had been planned with Steinem’s enthusiastic support before her death in September at age 92. Originally scheduled for the summer, the event had been postponed due to travel schedules.
“We’ll forgive her for not getting to this one,” Meyrowitz Turner said, to chuckles. “Gloria owes us nothing.”
One man was thanked for ‘bringing your tears’ into the room
When Brendan Kwiatkowski-Hartman’s turn came to speak, he soon found he was overcome. The sociologist, who specializes in the emotional life of teen boys, was describing his journey away from a religious childhood in which he was taught to believe that feminism was “anti-Christianity.”
“I knew nothing about Gloria Steinem other than as a bogeyman,” he said.
In college, he met a professor who was a Christian feminist, and his views began to shift. Now, seated in the home of Steinem herself, he said: “Feminism has given me a mirror to see myself better.”
He began to choke up as he said it, drawing thanks from another circle member for “bringing tears into this space.”
“You’ve done one of the bravest things in this conversation,” said Johnny Cole, an advocate who also works with men and boys. One thing young men really need, he said, is “to see more men crying, and willing to do it in front of men.”
Like many in the room, Cole’s work focuses on the importance of self-esteem. “You can’t enact change … if you don’t have self-esteem,” he said. “The model that most young men have today is a man devoid of self-esteem.”
Educator and author Jackson Katz urged those assembled to remember that “We wouldn’t be here without women’s leadership.” Katz had written in Ms. Magazine, upon Steinem’s death, about how she had changed men’s lives, too.
“This didn’t come out of nowhere,” he told the group about their conversation. “The driving energy is women’s leadership.”
Steinem first moved into her home in the late ’60s, with a roommate
Steinem first made her home in the Upper East Side brownstone in 1967, Heller explained to the room. Then, it was a one-floor rental; she and her roommate fashioned a loft bed space in the living room, which remains.
“That’s the OG bed,” said Heller, pointing upward; whichever roommate came home first got the bed. Two decades later, Steinem bought the floor below, where the foundation now works. It also has space on the third floor, and the hope is that eventually the foundation can occupy the entire building.
Ms. Magazine, co-founded by Steinem in the early ’70s, had its early meetings in the living room, where many groups and initiatives were also born. The talking circles began almost from the start, and still usually take place a few times a week. Exactly one week after Steinem died, women gathered to discuss leadership and style in a circle hosted by the Argent fashion label.
Steinem explained the circles’ meaning in an interview with this reporter earlier this year, six months before her death.
“There’s a continuing series of meetings going on in my living room, sometimes initiated by me, sometimes initiated by other people,” she said, adding that she also usually had a guest or two staying in the spare bedroom.
“We are communal animals, you know,” Steinem said. “We don’t generate the famous oxytocin, the chemical that allows us to empathize with each other, unless we’re physically together. It’s why solitary confinement is the worst punishment everywhere in the world. We do need to be together.”
The home, including Steinem’s own bedroom down the hall from the living room and past a small kitchen, is filled with mementos from her constant travels. Every surface seems to contain an expression of her personality. Her fireplace bears a banner that says “Hope.” On the mantel above sits a colorful matchbox emblazoned with the words “Wonder Woman” — a character Steinem had particular fondness for and even placed on Ms. Magazine’s cover.
The men were urged to be a support system for each other
As the speakers took turns last Tuesday, each man recounted why he was there and what he hoped to accomplish.
Nate Glasser, an internist and pediatrician at the University of Chicago, told of how, during his residency, “the curriculum was telling us almost explicitly not to pay attention to the interior lives of men.”
His own colleagues, he said, “miss that boys have interior lives. That is what brings me here.”
CJ Goulding spoke about his work with a group called Boyz N The Wood, providing healing spaces in nature. “We are a part of something bigger when we’re in nature,” he said.
Rawle Andrews Jr., executive director of the American Psychiatric Association Foundation, injected a note of humor when he quipped that some women on his team had asked him: “Why do YOU get to go to Gloria’s house? Take us!”
There were more laughs when two of the men, sitting on a small piece of furniture, thought they’d broken it. “The first time we get men in the room!!” joked Meyrowitz Turner, in mock horror. Heller assured everyone the damage had been there previously.
Meyrowitz Turner closed out the session by urging the men to serve as a support system for each other — as women more often do. “This work can be really lonely,” she said. The men, in turn, thanked her for “nudging” them to answer her emails.
Heller returned at the end with a tearful note of thanks.
“This is just what Gloria envisioned for this space,” she said, noting that Steinem had hoped she could “just go to sleep, and the work would go on.”
And she invited them all back.
“Consider it your living room, too,” she said.

title: Veteran turns depression struggle into free lifeline for first responders
text:
(Editor’s note: This story discusses suicide. If you or a loved one needs help, call or text the Suicide Prevention Hotline at 988.)
MYRTLE BEACH, S.C. (Aging Untold) — A Navy veteran and former first responder outside Myrtle Beach is sharing his struggle with depression to help break the stigma around mental health challenges that first responders, including firefighters, paramedics and police, face.
Billy Bowering started Day One, Week One in June 2023. The nonprofit provides mental health resources, financial services and couples counseling for first responders and veterans, all for free.
“I understand the traumas. I understand some of the dark days,” he said. “I wanted to do something different. I didn’t want to just talk about, ‘Hey, let’s have awareness.’”
Nonprofit and podcast aim to reach first responders and veterans
Day One, Week One also has a podcast where first responders and veterans can share what keeps them up at night.
“The concept behind it is we really want to be able to reach that person that may not look for counseling,” Bowering said.
Former paramedic shares her story
Parker McBryde, a former paramedic, listened to the podcast and decided to take part in an episode. She spoke about battling PTSD and depression.
McBryde also faced losing her eyesight after learning she could not afford cataract surgery.
A few days later, Bowering called back with the message, “I’ve secured it. We’re going to help you,” McBryde said.
“It was such a huge relief to know that my eyesight was finally going to at least be restored, or at least to a level where I’d have glasses or something that I could at least see,” McBryde said. “So I’m very thankful for Day One.”
The faith-based organization also helped seven others by paying off almost $4,000 in bills last year.
“You wonder sometimes if things are tangible, if you’re making a difference and there’s a tangible difference,” Bowering said.
Name comes from boot camp
Bowering said the name Day One, Week One came from his company commander in boot camp.
“He’s like, ‘All right, boys, today is Day One, Week One. This is the first day of the rest of your life, and it kind of stuck with me,’” Bowering said. “And he said, ‘My voice will stay in your head the rest of your life, and it did.’”
A day in 2022
The phrase is also a reminder of Bowering’s own Day One, Week One story.
In 2022, while packing for a weekend camping trip with his wife, Bowering said he felt “this incredible sense of loss and worthlessness” and had made a decision.
“I can’t do this anymore,” he said.
He called his wife to say goodbye. She then called his friend from church, a Vietnam veteran.
Bowering said that within about two minutes, there was a knock on the door. His friend was there.
“I realized in that moment that it was time to be one of those interrupters,” Bowering said.
Sharing stories to break the stigma
Bowering now shares stories and helps others pay it forward.
“I think the more that we share them, I think it does help to break that stigma,” McBryde said.
“Whenever someone is struggling, we’re going to try to be that source of strength and that hope for tomorrow,” Bowering said.

title: Murder case in death of Tasia Fortune, found hanging from tree, sent back to police
text:
JACKSON, Miss. (WLBT/Gray News) - The case against a man charged with murder in the death of Tasia Fortune is being sent back to police for further investigation.
During a preliminary hearing Tuesday for 25-year-old Earnest Lloyd, the judge agreed there was not enough evidence against him.
The case was sent back to the Jackson Police Department.
Fortune’s mother questions investigation
Fortune’s mother, Christy Spivey, attended the hearing. She said she does not think Fortune will ever get justice.
“No, no. I think it was handled sloppily, and I’ve also come to realize that they’re so thin,” Spivey said.
Spivey said she spoke with Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney about the case. She said she had a “meeting with the chief” and does not think the department has the necessary resources.
“I just think they’re so thin that how do you even have time to investigate a case? There are only eight detectives, is what the chief told me, and 93 murders. Who does what?” Spivey said.
Spivey said she does not know how her daughter died.
“It’s hard. I don’t even know how she died. Her death certificate says homicide by unspecified means, and I can’t even see the autopsy. I don’t know. I don’t even know how she died,” Spivey said.
Spivey said she is working on a petition to sue the Jackson Police Department over how the case was handled.
Case background
Lloyd was arrested Sept. 22 and charged with murder for his alleged role in Fortune’s death. He was denied bond shortly after.
Three suspects have been arrested in connection with the investigation.
Fortune, 29, was found hanging from a tree behind a vacant house in the 500 block of Road of Remembrance in Jackson on Aug. 3.
Investigators have not publicly disclosed her exact cause of death.
The case has drawn national and local attention. Community leaders and activists have called for answers about the circumstances of Fortune’s death.

title: David Beckham sues for $41 million after his fragrance is sold in gas stations and discount stores
text:
LONDON (AP) — A dispute over the sale of David Beckham perfumes has struck a sour note with the soccer star turned style icon.
Beckham’s commercial company is suing a beauty firm after his “luxury” fragrances were allegedly found for sale in discount stores and a gas station bargain bin.
DB Ventures has filed a claim in the New York Supreme Court against German beauty group Coty, which makes and distributes a range of Beckham-branded fragrances and toiletries. They include the Classic and Instinct lines and the eaux de toilette Intimately and Exquisite Leather.
The claim argues that Beckham’s “world-renowned global brand is synonymous with excellence and refinement,” and “David Beckham products are a symbol of everyday luxury.”
“Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station,” the legal document says. “How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”
Lawyers for DB Ventures allege that Beckham-branded products “ended up in the bargain bin inside a gas station” and at British budget retailer Poundland, “allowing the product to be sold for dollar store prices and associating the David Beckham brand with cheap, discount products.”
DB Ventures is seeking at least $41 million in damages for breach of its licensing agreement.
Coty has asked a judge to dismiss the lawsuit, which was filed in April. The company argues that New York courts have no jurisdiction in the case, and says DB Ventures is using the claim to “manufacture its early exit” from its licensing deal and hand over the Beckham contracts to another firm, Interparfums.
The company told The Associated Press on Tuesday that “Coty strongly disputes the claims and has asked the court to dismiss them. As this is an ongoing legal matter, we will not comment further.”
DB Ventures’ parent company, U.S. entertainment and lifestyles firm Authentic Brands, declined to comment.
Beckham, who played for a number of clubs including Manchester United and Real Madrid and captained the England men’s national team, parlayed success on the pitch into a lucrative business career that includes co-ownership of soccer team Inter Miami. He was knighted last year by King Charles III, becoming Sir David.
He also has had a very public persona as a fashion model, “Bend It Like Beckham” movie muse and husband of Spice Girl-turned-fashion designer Victoria “Posh Spice” Beckham. The couple have four children.
The Sunday Times Rich List earlier this year estimated the Beckhams’ wealth at almost 1.2 billion pounds ($1.58 billion).

title: Doctors sound the alarm about US babies born with measles for the first time in decades
text:
(AP) - For the first time in decades, U.S. doctors are sounding the alarm about babies coming into the world with measles.
Congenital measles happens when a pregnant woman passes the virus to her fetus in the womb. It can lead to serious complications or even be deadly for newborns.
From the start of 2025 through the end of this September, 13 congenital measles cases were reported to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention during large measles outbreaks, according to preliminary figures published in a medical journal on Monday.
“This is a brand new phenomenon,” said Michael Osterholm, who directs the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy.
The condition’s emergence is driven by declining vaccination rates, which have fueled the virus’s spread so much that the Pan American Health Organization is expected to officially announce Tuesday that the U.S. has lost the measles-free status it’s had since 2000. In the past two years, according to the CDC, there have been more than 7,500 measles cases.
“We’re now seeing levels of measles that we haven’t seen in 30 years,” said Dr. Adam Ratner, a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics’ infectious diseases committee. “When you have measles under control,” congenital measles doesn’t happen.
The preliminary case figures were released in a public health alert published by NEJM Evidence in partnership with the center Osterholm directs. The alert also said there were 112 cases of confirmed measles during pregnancy — almost all among women who didn’t get vaccinated against measles beforehand or whose vaccination status was unknown. The alert said getting vaccinated before pregnancy and having high vaccination rates in the community “are important to prevent measles and related complications.” CDC scientists authored the alert.
Guidance on congenital measles from the pediatrics academy is already reaching doctors. And Pennsylvania’s health department published an advisory last month for healthcare providers, schools, childcare centers and others in the state, which currently has the largest measles outbreak in the nation.
A new reality allows congenital measles to emerge
People gain immunity to measles by getting the disease or the vaccine. Before the shots existed, lots of people were infected by the extremely contagious virus in childhood. Later, high vaccination rates protected everyone. But a new and historic reality — shaped both by the success of the vaccine and recent skepticism about it — has triggered congenital measles.
“What’s happening is we have so many women of childbearing age who were not vaccinated in the last 25 years, nor have they ever had exposure to measles because for the last 25 years we have beaten it back,” Osterholm said. “Now, this group is highly susceptible to measles.”
Doctors say the best way to prevent the disease is for women to get the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, before pregnancy. This protects the fetus too because antibodies pass from mother to baby through the placenta. Protection can last a few months after birth.
MMR can’t be given during pregnancy. Unvaccinated women who have never had measles and are exposed while pregnant can get a solution containing antibodies within six days to reduce the risk of infection and complications.
Congenital measles can seriously harm babies
If a woman gets measles toward the end of pregnancy, there’s a good chance she will pass it along. An estimated 25% to 30% of babies born to someone who gets measles shortly before delivery may become infected, the pediatrics group says.
Babies are considered to have congenital measles if they were exposed in the uterus and doctors find evidence of measles very soon after birth. Common symptoms include fever, jaundice and a measles rash. Severe complications include pneumonia, encephalitis and a rare condition known as SSPE, a brain disorder that generally develops many years after a measles infection and is almost always fatal.
Ratner, who wrote a book about measles, said there are indications that kids with congenital measles are at higher risk for SSPE and may develop it sooner after having measles than other children. “That’s something that sadly we’re learning more about,” he said.
Doctors worry things may get worse if vaccination rates keep dropping. Outbreaks are considered unlikely if a community has a 95% MMR rate, but rates in many communities have dipped below that threshold. Nationally, the CDC said, 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners in 2025-26 received required MMR shots.
This puts many vulnerable people at risk, including infants too young to be vaccinated. The first MMR dose is routinely given at 12 to 15 months old, and the earliest babies can get the shots is 6 months in outbreak areas.
“We need to get back to the point where everybody who can get vaccinated is getting vaccinated, and that’s gonna take some doing,” Ratner said. “It’s going to be a lot of work on the part of pediatricians and public health institutions and lots of others. But it’s an important thing for us to do.”
___
AP Medical Writer Mike Stobbe contributed from New York.

title: 78-year-old dies after trying to help woman break up a dogfight, authorities say
text:
WARRENVILLE, S.C. (WRDW/Gray News) - A 78-year-old man died after trying to help a woman break up a dogfight at a South Carolina home, according to authorities.
Aiken County Coroner Darryl Ables said the incident happened at a home and was reported shortly before 1:30 p.m.
Investigators said a woman suffered severe injuries to her arm while trying to break up a fight between two dogs inside the home.
The man stepped in to help and fell, hitting the back of his head on the floor. He was pronounced dead at the scene.
The woman was taken to a hospital for treatment.
An autopsy will be performed to determine the man’s cause of death.
The sheriff’s office and coroner’s office are investigating.

title: Pilot killed in Sweden, Maine, plane crash identified by authorities
text:
Pilot killed in Sweden, Maine, plane crash identified by Oxford County Sheriff's Office
The pilot who died in Monday's plane crash in the Oxford County town of Sweden lived in a neighboring western Maine community.
William Connelly, 65, of Lovell, has been identified as the victim of the plane crash, which happened at about 3:55 p.m. in the area of 201 Smarts Hill Road, according to the Oxford County Sheriff's Office.
Officials said the Cessna 182 that Connelly was flying took off from Fryeburg Airport.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) are investigating the plane crash.
A preliminary report from the FAA states that the single-engine plane crashed under unknown circumstances.
The FAA Aircraft Registry shows that Connelly was the registered owner of the Cessna 182 that crashed.
The FAA said the NTSB will be in charge of the crash investigation and provide additional updates.

title: Parents arrested after 6-year-old child found unresponsive and dies at hospital
text:
NASH COUNTY, N.C. (WITN/Gray News) - Two parents have been arrested and charged after the death of their 6-year-old child in North Carolina.
According to the Nash County Sheriff’s Office, deputies responded to a call about an unresponsive child on Monday at a residence in the area.
First responders said they attempted lifesaving measures on the child and took them to UNC Nash Hospital, but the 6-year-old did not survive.
The child’s parents, identified as 29-year-old Jacob McNinch and 30-year-old Danielle Stanton, were arrested and charged in connection with the death.
McNinch was charged with assault on a female and child abuse/neglect, serious bodily injury. Stanton’s charges included child abuse/neglect and serious bodily injury.
McNinch was being held without bond while Stanton received a $50,000 secured bond.
Both were scheduled to appear in court on Tuesday.
The sheriff’s office said the investigation remains ongoing and no further information was immediately released regarding the family or the child.

title: Puppy wanders into car dealership after being abandoned and finds her forever home
text:
WICHITA FALLS, Texas (KAUZ/Gray News) - For an abandoned 6-month-old puppy, wandering into a Texas car dealership turned out to be the beginning of a second chance.
Nova, a 6-month-old Great Pyrenees, wandered into the Always Auto showroom in Wichita Falls after being abandoned. Instead of turning her away, the employees welcomed her with food, water and plenty of love.
“She ran right into the dealership, ran right up to me, and I just kind of knew it was meant to be,” Roman Letsis said. “I can’t believe somebody dumped her, too. It’s pretty sad. So, we took her under our care and just fell in love with her.”
However, just as Nova was settling in, her health took a frightening turn. She stopped eating and moving, showing signs of parvovirus, a potentially deadly disease in puppies.
Her new family knew they had to act fast. After struggling to find an available veterinarian nearby, they decided to make the drive more than 100 miles to Denton to get her the care she needed.
Josh Letsis, the dealership’s owner, said there was never any question about getting Nova help.
“There wasn’t even a thought. It was like, ‘Let’s just find somebody that can get her in tonight. It doesn’t matter if we have to go to Fort Worth or Dallas or whatever...’ So, it just wasn’t even a question. My son jumped in the truck with me, and we took her right in,” Josh Letsis said.
Roman Letsis said the trip was worth it, knowing Nova might not have survived without treatment.
“It was worth it taking her in, and we’re glad we did because she might have not made it another day,” he said.
Nova spent the next week in the hospital fighting for her life. Her family initially expected her treatment to last only a couple of days, but her condition remained uncertain.
Josh Letsis said there were two days when the family wasn’t sure whether Nova would pull through. She eventually began receiving food through a feeding tube and slowly started showing signs of improvement.
After a difficult week, Nova finally made it through. Roman Letsis said seeing her recover after everything she had been through was an incredible feeling.
“Seeing her pull through after that full week was amazing,” he said.
Now, Nova is continuing her recovery and has found a forever home with the Always Auto family. Roman Letsis said he plans to make Nova his own dog, and she will become a permanent fixture at the dealership.
“Yeah, I’m gonna make her my dog,” he said. “So, I’m glad she found me, and she found us. She’s gonna be a little dealership dog.”
After everything Nova has experienced, her family hopes her story encourages others to help animals in need. They recommend fostering puppies or donating to local animal shelters to give more animals a chance at finding their forever homes.
