title: Forensic expert says Epstein was likely killed, but NYC medical examiner stands by suicide ruling
text:
Forensic expert says Epstein was likely killed, but NYC medical examiner stands by suicide ruling
A forensics expert on Monday announced findings that he says points to Jeffrey Epstein having been killed while in custody, contradicting the New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner’s ruling that the disgraced financier died by suicide.
Michael Freeman, a scholar and consultant in forensic medicine epidemiology, teamed up with Anders Eriksson, a forensic pathologist and professor of forensic medicine at Umea University in Sweden, and Itiel Dror, a cognitive neuroscientist and researcher, as part of his investigation into Epstein’s death — presenting their research Monday in London which said there is no evidence a hanging took place.
Additionally, “there were no non-hanging-related bruises or other injuries anywhere on the body,” which was “pretty much pristine,” the presentation said.
After reviewing the entire autopsy file and completing a reconstruction using autopsy photos, the writers claim they found Epstein’s injuries were consistent with an assault and struggle, and he was killed.
“The ligature marks are most consistent with homicidal strangulation from behind, most likely using a narrow knotted fabric ligature,” said the presentation given to Middle Temple, a London legal society.
In a statement Monday to CNN, the New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner said it “stands by its determination” that Epstein died by suicide and the manner was hanging.
Epstein’s body was found hanging in a cell in the New York City Metropolitan Correctional Center on Aug. 10, 2019. There were reportedly no photographs taken of Epstein hanging in his cell or his body positioned at the scene.
He was on suicide watch in the weeks prior to his death, but had been taken off it on July 24, weeks before his death.
After the initial determination was made a week after the convicted sex offender’s death, Epstein’s lawyers said they were not satisfied with the conclusions and urged more scrutiny of the jail.
Both the FBI and the Justice Department’s Inspector General investigated the circumstances around the accused sex trafficker’s death, and released millions of documents relating to Epstein that shed new light into his final hours - but which did little to dispel conspiracy theories about the nature of Epstein’s death.
Security cameras positioned near Epstein’s cell that night in the Special Housing Unit failed to record, the result of a long-term problem with the facility’s cameras, detailed in a 2023 DOJ report.
It was also unclear regarding the incident which placed Epstein on suicide watch. Epstein stated, “I have no interest in killing myself” on July 24, the day after his reported suicide attempt, according to the psychologist report.
In 2019, Epstein was charged with having operated a sex trafficking ring in which he sexually abused dozens of underage girls.
He was accused of running a trafficking enterprise between 2002 and 2005, allegedly paying hundreds of dollars in cash to girls as young as 14 to have sex with him at his Upper East Side home and his estate in Palm Beach.
While the documents failed to confirm some Epstein-related conspiracy theories, such as whether he had a client list of men he blackmailed, they have caused headaches for powerful people around the world, shedding light on multiple awkward relationships Epstein had with business titans, billionaires, royals, government officials — in the US and abroad — and media figures.
In an interview with The New York Times, Freeman, a forensic scientist who analyzes homicides, said he has no idea who might have killed Epstein and he doesn’t care. He said he was focused on what he called oversights in the investigation into the death and the autopsy report.
“All I’m interested in is, how did this get so sideways?” he told the newspaper.
According to the Times, Freeman was shared Epstein’s autopsy file by Epstein’s brother, Mark Epstein, one of few people with access to it. The findings have yet to be peer reviewed.

title: Nonpartisan primaries would be good for Maine, America
text:
Jack Brogan’s recent op-ed, from a writer just 18 years old, was amazing (“Growing up in Maine exposes the folly of party politics,” Oct. 18).
Indeed, Maine’s not a leader among the states. Its semi-closed primary runs contrary to the first three words of the U.S. Constitution: We The People. Maine’s in the middle of the pack. Both California and Alaska have true primary systems, nonpartisan, where the parties can’t limit candidate choice for the voter.
Brogan mentioned Sen. Rick Bennett as an independent. Does he realize Bennett supports nonpartisan primaries? Is he aware Sen. Joe Baldacci bravely sponsored a nonpartisan primary bill in 2025? Unfortunately, he and Sen. Bennett are termed out in 2027. Other legislators must step up to revive this proposal in 2027.
Maine once led the nation in election reform. Today, our Legislature is failing us by retaining a partisan primary system. If a nonpartisan bill passes in 2027, Maine’s Legislature will honor “we the people” over “we the party.” Maine will help save the parties from statistically dwindling further.
May the Maine State Legislature co-sponsor the nonpartisan primary bill that Sen. Baldacci submitted in 2025. May Bennett join with him, and citizens urge all members of our Legislature to do the same. May Jack Brogan and all Mainers demand a true nonpartisan primary become reality.
Joe Pickering Jr.
Bangor

title: McDonald’s Unveils ‘Home Alone’ Meal With Pizza Fries and Sauce
text:
McDonald’s Unveils ‘Home Alone’ Meal With Pizza-Flavored Fries and Sauce
[Macaulay Culkin screaming face]
Continuing a tradition of recent years, McDonald’s is doing a holiday season meal tied to a beloved piece of Christmas IP. This year it’s Home Alone — with original franchise star Macaulay Culkin reprising his role as Kevin McAllister in a new McDonald’s ad.
The Home Alone meal includes the entree of your choice plus limited-time items inspired by Kevin’s preferred foods from the film. That includes “Little Nero’s Pizza McShaker Fries,” which McDonald’s describes as their regular fries seasoned with “notes of tangy tomato, savory garlic, Italian herbs and rich cheese.” There’s also a “Lovely Cheese Pizza Dipping Sauce,” which is supposedly a “creamy sauce blending rich tomato flavor, warm aged Parmesan cheese, garden herbs and a whisper of garlic” that’s intended for chicken McNugget dipping.
Each meal also comes with one of four pairs of socks, featuring old school McDonald’s characters like the Hamburglar or Kevin McAllister screaming, possibly because his contract included a clause allowing McDonald’s to put his likeness on footwear.
READ MORE: A Brief History of Movie Tie-In Food
McDonald’s will also offer a “Everything Sundae McFlurry,” with “creamy vanilla soft serve and swirls in hot fudge, crunchy pieces of Oreo cookies and colorful M&M’s. I’m not sure what that has to do with Home Alone but what child left alone by his terrible parents doesn’t enjoy eating all the ice cream in the freezer?
The Home Alone meal at McDonald’s is something of a sequel to the Grinch meal the fast-food giant did last year around the holiday season. That one came with pickle-flavored fries and socks — because if there is anything that makes people hungry it’s the odors of pickles and socks.
(What do pickles and the Grinch have in common? Well pickles, like the Grinch, can be a little sour. Also they’re green. The Grinch is kind of a living hairy pickle when you think about it.)
The Home Alone meal will be available at McDonald’s starting on December 1. The secondary market on those Kevin socks is gonna be fierce.

title: Letter: Permitting reform bill should not be rushed
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
We should all contact our senators’ offices today to urge them to oppose the “permitting bill” — the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA; S. 5653) — that is set to be considered on the floor this week.
According to experts ranging from a former Federal Energy Regulatory Commission chairman (nominated by President Donald Trump) to Earthjustice, the BAAJA would hand the Trump administration and subsequent administrations virtually unlimited power to permit and subsidize projects in a way that would cost electric rate payers billions of dollars and would, in some cases irreversibly, harm the clean water and wildlife people have spent years restoring.
The non-partisan Congressional Research Service describes the havoc the bill would wreak on our fundamental environmental laws and citizens’ ability to participate in decisions and to challenge illegal, harmful agency actions in court.
Maine is downwind of America’s air pollution and much ocean water pollution, and we create pollution of our own. Maine’s own Sen. Edmund Muskie co-authored the Clean Air Act and the Clean Water Act, and shepherded the National Environmental Policy Act through the Senate.
Maine’s Sen. George Mitchell served on the Environment and Public Works Committee for years. He enhanced those laws. In recent years environmental impact statements were subjected to limits in time and length, but Maine’s senators did not fundamentally weaken these laws when some of their colleagues attempted to do so.
Let’s ask this Congress to wait until January to calmly take the best of the bill and leave the rest.
John Fitzgerald
Sedgwick

title: Supreme Court declines Trump push to cut research grants related to DEI
text:
Supreme Court declines Trump push to cut research grants related to DEI
The Supreme Court declined on Monday to take up an appeal from the Trump administration defending its decision to cancel tens of millions of dollars in grants to University of California researchers because their work touched on diversity, equity and inclusion — allowing the money to flow to the school.
At stake was about $150 million in National Science Foundation and National Endowment for the Humanities grants that President Donald Trump attempted to cancel shortly after taking office, part of the administration’s broader campaign to attack any initiative focused on diversity. Billions of dollars in research grants to other entities have also been caught up in litigation that could eventually reach the Supreme Court.
Related video above: Trump administration sues Penn State over in-state tuition for students in the US illegally
The San Francisco-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals concluded that canceling the grants likely violated the First Amendment, and the Trump administration appealed to the high court in August. By declining to take the appeal, the Supreme Court left in place a ruling that requires the administration to fund the grants related to DEI and allowed these cases to proceed in federal district courts (rather than the specialized federal claims court).
“The government can point to no case where this court, or any court, has held that the president and federal agencies may terminate grants awarded through a merit-driven competitive process based on the perceived viewpoint of the research,” the California researchers told the high court.
Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration’s top appellate attorney, framed the debate as a shift in priorities for federal funding that he said did not implicate the First Amendment.
The First Amendment, the Justice Department argued in its appeal, “does not prohibit the government from declining to award competitive grants that fund research projects that promote DEI.”
“In addition to leaving intact the lower courts’ ruling for the researchers, the denial is also significant in at least tacitly endorsing the lower courts’ conclusion that these kinds of disputes properly belong in federal district courts, rather than the specialized federal claims court,” said Steve Vladeck, CNN Supreme Court analyst and professor at Georgetown University Law Center.
“That may seem like an incredibly technical distinction, but the claims court can only issue narrow, limited relief against the government at the end of the case, whereas district courts, as in this case, can move much faster and much more coercively to restore funds that were wrongly cut off.”
As is usually the case, the Supreme Court did not explain its decision to deny the appeal. There were no dissents.

title: Trump faces criticism as allies press the White House for answers on tech problems
text:
President Donald Trump faced a groundswell of criticism Tuesday as friends and foes alike said the White House must answer for a cascade of service outages that snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications.
Even staunch Trump allies accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause of the disruptions. In recent days, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected.
Each outage has been blamed on internal technical problems, with the companies and government agencies involved denying that they were the result of cyberattacks or rogue artificial intelligence systems. Trump was nonchalant after arriving in Asia on Tuesday, declaring that “things like that happen,” a response that did little to calm the country.
Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s former press secretary, offered advice for her old colleagues in the administration.
“What I would say to the White House is transparency is key,” Leavitt said on Fox News. She said the president or someone else at the White House should explain what they know after Trump returns from Asia “to really calm the temperature.”
She later praised the White House for having Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton address the outages in an interview on Fox Business Network. “Looking very diligently across the landscape, we are not seeing this as a cyber attack incident,” Clayton said in a clip that Leavitt shared on X. He said the U.S. government believes the incidents are caused by organizations making security upgrades that are taking longer than planned and encountering unexpected hiccups.
Tricia McLaughlin, a former spokesperson for Trump’s Department of Homeland Security, was skeptical about the lack of information coming out of the federal government.
“Americans aren’t stupid,” she posted on social media. “We want and deserve to know what’s really going on.”
Meghan McCain, who is sometimes at odds with Trump and his allies, had similar advice.
“Someone high in the administration needs to get on tv and tell the American people NOW what is going on,” McCain wrote on X. “No one who lived through Covid is believing this is all a coincidence.”
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
Some prominent figures in Trump’s Make America Great Again movement expressed alarm.
“Our leaders are lying to us. This is very clearly a coordinated cyber attack,” Laura Loomer wrote on social media. “President Trump should come back to the United States.” She did not present any evidence of an attack.
The series of outages began on Thursday, when Microsoft’s email and other tools went down, paralyzing millions of workers who rely on them. Microsoft traced the issue to “an earlier network capacity upgrade.”
Flights across the country were grounded the next day in the longest so-called ground stop since 9/11. The Federal Aviation Administration blamed a router upgrade.
By Monday, the banks were in the spotlight, as customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major financial institutions and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said it was caused by “a software bug” and was “not cyber-related.”
The same day, United Airlines said that it had resolved an internal system outage that delayed departing flights.
And on Tuesday, an internal network that the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what the agency described as “routine maintenance.”
Trump was dismissive when asked whether he was concerned about the Chase outage.
“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine,” Trump said in Manila, Philippines, where he began a three-day Asian trip on Tuesday.
Trump’s nonchalance was not shared by those already distrustful of the government and big institutions. And for Americans across the political spectrum, the drip-drip-drip of alarming and frustrating outages is an unsettling reminder of perils posed by interconnected tech networks.
“Where is the transparency? Where is the accountability?” conservative commentator Kylie Jane Kremer wrote on X. “And why does it feel like we’re being told everything is fine while the very systems our country depends on are experiencing serious failures?”

title: Trump arrives in Philippines to kick off Asia trip with economic deals and talks with allies
text:
MANILA, Philippines (AP) — President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he met with regional partners, sought to formalize a trade deal and get a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.
Manila, the Philippine capital, is Trump’s first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea’s leader Kim Jong Un.
The visit marks Trump’s first travel abroad since his party suffered deep losses in midterm elections. The White House and stock market alike have been rattled by the departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved.
But Trump could not escape all the controversies still swirling in the U.S. Reporters asked him about the recent service outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration and online banking with JPMorgan Chase. The president played down the problems that caused mass flight cancellations and disrupted workdays.
“It’s life,” Trump said. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”
The president was also asked about a CNN report that Iran was putting together plans to attack Washington with a dirty bomb or chemical weapons.
“Well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before,” Trump said, adding, “I hope it’s not. But we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy.”
Trump to be feted at the annual ASEAN summit
Trump’s first hours in the Philippines included all the reassuring optics from Washington’s oldest treaty ally in Asia, such as a cocktail reception and dinner with other world leaders, an intermission from some of the thorniest issues at home. He’s being feted Tuesday night at a gala as the “guest of honor” at the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
The ASEAN leaders have been working on a non-aggression pact with China in the contested waters of the South China Sea, a key global trade route. Confrontations have escalated in recent years, particularly between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals.
After landing in Manila, Trump met with the leaders of the Quad nations, comprising the U.S., Australia, India, and Japan, that have aimed to counter China’s influence in the Asia Pacific, for the first time since he returned to the White House last year.
“We’re all friends,” Trump said. ”It’s a lot easier that way.”
The president announced that the Quad would conduct an exercise featuring maritime patrol aircraft and launch an accelerator to speed the development of artificial intelligence.
Trump signed a trade statement with Thailand, the type of agreement he has relished striking since launching a trade war last year buttressed by steep tariff threats. The president said that he was looking forward “to finalizing the details of our formal agreement in the coming weeks.”
The joint statement included details that were posted more than a year ago by the U.S. government. Thailand would remove tariffs on most American goods, as well as barriers for importing American autos, food products and pharmaceutical drugs. Trump said Tuesday that Thailand would buy $2.6 billion in U.S. agricultural products.
As part of the gala dinner Tuesday night, Trump participated in what was billed as a “special summit” with the ASEAN leaders. They finalized a set of principles to tackle online scams, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said.
Leaders at the dinner were also expected to discuss efforts to deepen trade and security ties as well as the region’s longstanding conflicts, including yearslong violence in Myanmar and escalating disputes in the South China Sea, which Beijing claims virtually in its entirety.
Washington has rejected China’s expansive claim to the waterway, and has repeatedly stated that it’s obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces come under an armed attack.
Anti-Trump protesters are gathered in Manila
About 1,500 left-wing protesters held a noisy rally in a downtown Manila square ahead of Trump’s arrival, calling on Philippine leaders not to take their foreign policy cues from the U.S.
They waved red flags and held up a large streamer that read, “Resist U.S. war and plunder!” They planned to burn an effigy of Trump. Riot police with shields and wooden truncheons stood nearby.
“The Philippine government should not deal with such a loser so our call to the Marcos administration is to stop being a puppet of Donald Trump and to uphold an independent foreign policy for the Philippines,” protest leader Teddy Casiño told The Associated Press.
Nearly 23,000 police personnel and other law enforcers, including SWAT teams, were deployed to secure the ASEAN summit.
Planned meetings with the Philippine president — and possibly an old friend
On Wednesday, Trump is set to receive a red-carpet welcome and full military honors from Marcos Jr., followed by a state banquet as part of his visit to the Malacanang presidential palace. Trump and Marcos are expected to affirm their commitment to their countries’ longstanding treaty alliance.
Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion in Malacanang with an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she’s well enough and gets her doctors’ nod.
Now 97 and using a wheelchair, the former jet set Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a strongman leader, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 “People Power” public uprising.
But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: “How’s Imelda?” Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press.
“Personal connections are very important to him,” Romualdez said.
When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. “President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, ‘please say hello to your mother,’” according to Romualdez.
Trump is also expected to announce a series of commercial deals and investments in the aviation, defense, energy, and technology sectors, before heading to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
___
Boak reported from Shenzhen, China.

title: Maine bowhunters can extend deer season at this coastal wildlife refuge
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
Hunters looking to extend their deer season have another option along Maine’s southern coast. Rachel Carson National Wildlife Refuge offers thousands of acres of habitat where bowhunters can pursue deer during the expanded archery season, which remains open through Dec. 12.
The expanded archery season offers an opportunity to put more venison in the freezer and enjoy a few more days in the deer woods before the long wait for another season. With the appropriate expanded archery permits, hunters can take one buck and multiple antlerless deer.
The expanded archery season was established in 1997 to provide additional hunting opportunities in select areas with high deer populations that could withstand more hunting pressure. At the time, the designated areas were primarily densely populated residential and urban communities. They remain that way today.
Since the program began, boundaries have been updated and new zones added. Most recently, in 2026, the new South Coastal Zone replaced and combined five former zones into one. Maine now has 10 expanded archery zones, including areas surrounding some of the state’s largest cities, such as Augusta, Bangor and Waterville.
Most of the land within expanded archery zones is privately owned. I have lived near one of these zones for nearly 30 years, and it took me years to find landowners willing to allow me to hunt their properties. Many do not.
Certain public lands, including sanctuaries, are also closed to hunting. Municipal ordinances in places such as Hallowell, Waterville and Portland may also restrict or prohibit the discharge of archery equipment.
Unless a hunter lives within an expanded archery zone and owns huntable land, or knows someone who does and has access to it, finding a place to hunt can be daunting and time-consuming.
I have found this especially true in the new South Coastal Zone, which includes Wildlife Management District 24. Stretching roughly from Bath south along the immediate coast to Kittery, it is one of the most densely developed and populated areas of the state. It is also rich in deer. Some towns within the district produce some of Maine’s highest deer harvests each year, but finding private or public land to hunt can be difficult, particularly south of Portland.
For archers looking for a place to finish the season, one option is Rachel Carson National Wildlife Refuge.
The refuge covers 5,600 acres across 11 divisions along 50 miles of coastline between Kittery and Cape Elizabeth. Nine of the 11 divisions, covering approximately 2,500 acres, are open to big-game hunting, including deer hunting during the expanded archery season. All are located within the South Coastal Zone.
In addition to a state archery license and the appropriate expanded archery antlerless or either-sex permits, hunters must obtain a $10 refuge big-game permit. The permit must be carried at all times while hunting on the refuge. Permits are available online only.
Portable tree stands are allowed but must be removed each day. State archery hunting regulations apply, although individual divisions may have additional rules. Hunters should check the regulations for the specific division they plan to hunt.
It is also important to know the refuge boundaries, which are marked with the familiar flying-goose refuge signs. In many areas, the boundary follows local and state roads. In others, property lines follow creeks and other natural features, veering away from roads.
Each division also has areas closed to hunting and some designated as youth hunting areas or archery-only areas, regardless of the hunting season. The Timber Point area in the Little River Division, for example, is one of my favorite places and is open to archery hunting only. Areas closed to hunting are generally posted.
Each division is a patchwork of refuge land, varying in size and often interspersed with private property. It’s important to know which land belongs to the refuge and which areas are open to hunting. Despite the complicated boundaries, I have never found the posted signs to be an issue.
Even though I have lived relatively close to some refuge divisions for decades, I still make a point of revisiting areas I like and planning where to hunt. Hunters who have never hunted the refuge or are unfamiliar with its divisions should do the same, particularly to identify parking areas and access points to land open to hunting.
Maps outlining the open hunting areas, division-specific regulations and other details are available on the refuge’s hunting webpage.
Another reason to visit before hunting is to scout potential locations. Because of its proximity to the coast, the refuge offers a mix of habitats, including upland woodlands, coastal meadows, salt marshes and barrier beaches.
Some divisions consist mostly of salt marsh and coastal meadows, while others offer more upland habitat. Deer can be found in most of these environments, but I have found some areas offer better hunting potential. Spending time scouting to identify them can pay off.
The expanded archery season and Rachel Carson National Wildlife Refuge offer bowhunters another opportunity to pursue deer before the season ends. Taking advantage of it requires some advance planning, but based on my experience, the effort can be well worth it.

title: As more parents refuse vitamin K shots, bleeding in infants has risen, new data shows
text:
As more parents refuse vitamin K shots, bleeding in infants has risen, new data shows
Giving newborns a single shot of vitamin K after birth can prevent dangerous internal bleeding. But in recent years, more parents have declined to give it to their babies. Doctors worried that cases of potentially fatal vitamin K deficiency bleeding would increase as a result, but didn’t have much data to consider.
Until now.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
A study published Nov. 5 in the Journal of the American Medical Association reviewed the medical records of over 11 million babies up to 6 months old born in the U.S. from 2017 through 2025. It found:
- More parents declined shots. During the study timeframe, the percentage of babies receiving a vitamin K shot decreased from 97.7% to 95%.
- Vitamin K deficiency bleeding, or VKDB, went up. During that same period, cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding increased by 347.1%. Rates went from 24 babies per 100,000 to 107 babies per 100,000.
- Rates of vitamin K deficiency also rose by 215.7%. These babies may not have active bleeding but could be at risk for bleeding in the future.
- Eighty percent of the babies who developed vitamin K deficiency bleeding had not gotten the shot.
- Some infants developed brain bleeds. Among the babies diagnosed with vitamin K deficiency, almost 7% also had a diagnosed brain bleed. For babies with VKDB, 2.4% had a brain bleed.
Dr. Elizabeth R. Wolf, the study’s author and a Virginia Commonwealth University pediatrician, told Well Informed she knew vitamin K refusals had been rising, but “we were surprised by the magnitude of increase that we observed.”
Another study published Nov. 5 looked at a cohort of 5.2 million infants during the same time period, with very similar results. More parents refused shots, and rates of dangerous bleeding in infants increased. This study included more than just babies diagnosed with vitamin K deficiency bleeding and also included other kinds of internal bleeding.
“Diagnosing vitamin K deficiency bleeding requires that a clinician both recognizes and documents that bleeding was related to vitamin K deficiency,” Dr. Kristan Scott, a neonatologist at Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta and author of this second study. “We wanted to avoid missing bleeding events that may have not been specifically recorded as related to vitamin K deficiency.”
The second study found that infants who did not get a vitamin K shot had a significantly higher risk of bleeding before 6 months of age than infants who received the shot. Infants without the shot were also at significantly higher risk of a brain bleed.
Dr. Jaspreet Loyal, a Yale University pediatrician, said she hopes this research helps underscore that “serious bleeding in the absence of vitamin K prophylaxis in the United States is real, relevant, dangerous and preventable.”
Why is vitamin K so important?
Vitamin K is essential for human blood to clot, which helps the body stop bleeding if it’s injured. Adults get the vitamin largely from food, but babies are born with very little. It doesn’t pass easily from mother to child during pregnancy or through breastfeeding. Babies who are fed formula can get a small amount of vitamin K, but not enough.
Low levels of vitamin K put babies at risk for potentially fatal internal bleeding called vitamin K deficiency bleeding. Depending on when the bleeding occurs, it can be hard to detect until a baby has suffered a permanent disability or died.
“As more newborns do not receive vitamin K, the population of infants vulnerable to potentially serious bleeding continues to grow,” said Scott.
Because of the danger, since the 1960s, the American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended babies get an intramuscular injection of vitamin K shortly after birth.
The academy currently recommends giving the shot within the first six hours of life for babies weighing at least 3.3 pounds.
It works remarkably well at preventing vitamin K deficiency bleeding, and is “safe and effective,” Wolf said.
Research shows an early dose of vitamin K is sufficient protection against the bleeding until a child starts eating solid food around four to six months and can absorb the vitamin themselves.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

- Email interview with Dr. Elizabeth R. Wolf, pediatrician at Virginia Commonwealth University, Nov. 15, 2026
- Email interview with Dr. Jaspreet Loyal, pediatrician at Yale University, Nov. 16, 2026
- JAMA Pediatrics, Vitamin K Deficiency and Associated Bleeding in Infants, Nov. 5, 2026
- PolitiFact, Facts on the vitamin K shot for newborns, March 24, 2026

title: Analysis: UMaine football seeking to salvage forgettable season with win over rival UNH
text:
The beauty of a rivalry game is that it often exists as a separate entity.
It means something special to both teams involved. It’s especially important if both participants have endured underwhelming seasons.
That will be exactly the scenario on Saturday at 1 p.m. when UMaine football hosts arch-rival New Hampshire in the annual battle for the Brice-Cowell Musket.
UNH came into the season under first-year head coach Sean Goldrich picked fourth among 13 teams in the CAA preseason coaches poll. UNH was coming off back-to-back 8-5 seasons and FCS playoff berths.
The Wildcats have had a late resurgence, with back-to-back home wins over Rhode Island and Stony Brook, but they still come to Orono with an overall record of just 4-7 and a league mark of 3-4.
Even with a win over UMaine, it will be UNH’s fewest wins in a season since 2021, when it went 3-8. That was also the last time UMaine beat UNH. The Brice-Cowell Musket has been on display at UNH for the past four seasons and for 13 of the last 15 years. The Wildcats have owned the rivalry in recent years.
Maine enters Saturday’s contest riding a nine-game losing streak and in danger of setting the school record for losses in a season, dating back to 1892. The Black Bears are 1-6 in the conference.
They were 6-6 a year ago and were chosen seventh in this year’s CAA preseason poll.
The team’s primary problem has been its anemic offense.
There are 124 FCS schools. Of those schools, UMaine is ranked 115th or worse in five offensive categories: 123rd in points per game (12.3); 120th in red zone offense (63.6 percent conversion but just nine touchdowns in 22 chances and five field goals); 118th in fourth down conversions (31%); 117th in total yards per game (276.2 yards); and 115th in third down conversions (29.9%).
The Black Bears are 107th in rushing yards (106.1) and 102nd in passing yards (170.1).
In addition, the Black Bears have had seven kicks blocked this season, good for second-worst in the entire FCS.
UMaine fifth-year head coach Jordan Stevens replaced offensive coordinator/quarterbacks coach Mikahael Waters six games into the season with first-year assistant Sean Green, the running backs coach.
The Black Bears have averaged 15 more yards over the last four games under Green but have scored 5.5 fewer points.
Even if you don’t feel the Black Bears have been creative enough on offense with either coordinator, it still falls on the players to block, run, throw, and catch. Those have been real challenges.
During the CAA coaches’ weekly Zoom call with the media, Stevens said there are no excuses for the team’s offensive woes, but he also said he firmly believes there is talent on the offensive side of the ball.
However, he noted that many of the skill-position players are true freshmen.
“We have such a young team on offense,” said Stevens. “A true freshman tight end, four true freshmen wide receivers and another one who is a back-up running back.”
The Black Bears have also been victimized by subpar quarterback play from three inexperienced signal-callers: Caden Drezek, Eddie Buehler, and Mike McMaugh.
All have shown glimpses of promise, but Stevens will need to search the transfer portal after the season and bring in someone with experience and a good track record, much like he did with Carter Peevy from Mercer University, who lifted the program from back-to-back 2-9 seasons to 5-7 and 6-6 campaigns during his two seasons in Orono.
Stevens noted this week’s game gives the Black Bears a chance to end a dismal year on a high note.
“This is such an important game for us. It’s something we talk about all year long,” said Stevens. “We still have a program goal we can meet. It’s an opportunity to leave the jersey better than where we found it. Through all the adversity we’ve had this season, here is an opportunity to finish in a positive way.”
Something will have to give on Saturday, as UMaine is 0-4 at home and UNH is 0-5 on the road.

title: Mount Desert Selectboard hears from County Budget Advisory Committee
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MOUNT DESERT — The Mount Desert Selectboard heard a report from the Hancock County Budget Advisory Committee at its regular meeting Monday night.
The county BAC reviews budgets line by line to give recommendations on what should be cut or included in the proposed budget. There are 10 committee members, three from each district, plus a member of the Hancock County legislative delegation.
County Commissioners have the final say on approving the budget and can override recommendations made by the BAC as they function in an advisory capacity.
Littlefield shared her experience serving on the BAC for the first time and highlighted some figures from the proposed county budget.
“I have finished with my month of budget advisory meetings,” said Littlefield. “These meetings were very interesting, and I am happy that I was able to serve on the committee and represent the Town of Mount Desert.”
The Town of Mount Desert has the highest valuation in the county, meaning the town also contributes the largest sum of property taxes. In 2026, Mount Desert had a state valuation of $3,395,500,000, and the town’s tax liability was $1,591,624. The second-highest state valuation in Hancock County belonged to Bar Harbor at $2,990,400,000 with a tax liability of $1,401,735.36.
Littlefield made note of the cost to run the Hancock County Jail, a topic that garnered lengthy conversation at the BAC meeting in October.
The Hancock County Jail costs approximately $4.2 million to run with an average of 30 inmates.
The proposed expenditures for all of county government starting Jan. 1, 2027, are $13,921,292, a 13.1% increase. Revenues ring in at $3,008,468 and come from various fees for county operations, such as the Registries of Probate and Deeds and boarding inmates from other jails.
According to Littlefield, the BAC recommended a budget that included a 4% increase across the board in salaries. The proposed budget included raises from a recent salary survey that had varying increases. Littlefield explained the BAC did not approve those raises and instead opted for the 4% increase because the BAC did not have access to the salary survey initially.
Members of the Selectboard expressed thanks to Littlefield for participating in the committee and sharing her updates.
“I think we need really, as the towns on the island, band together, make sure we have a really strong showing,” said Kimball. “And then also making sure that our county commissioners understand that we’re paying attention to the process.”
In other business, the Selectboard members looked over the schedule for this year’s budget timeline.
They discussed whether agencies applying for a Memorandum of Understanding with the town to receive budget funds must complete an in-person presentation to the Selectboard and Warrant Committee every year. They agreed that if an agency is applying for the same amount of funds as last year, they still need to complete the application process but do not need to present
Town Manager Alex Kimball used the example of The Neighborhood House, an organization that applies for the same amount of funds each year.
Members of the Selectboard emphasized that every agency must still complete the application. Reducing the number of presentations was suggested as a means of streamlining the budgetary process.

title: Owls Head says South Thomaston's discharge of firefighting foam 'boggles the mind'
text:
OWLS HEAD, Maine — Town officials said they cannot understand why South Thomaston came to Owls Head and discharged toxic firefighting foam one night earlier this month.
“It just boggles my mind with all the attention of what happened with the Brunswick discharge,” Owls Head Town Administrator Rodney Mason told the Select Board at its Monday meeting.
On Aug. 19, 2024, approximately 1,450 gallons of aqueous film-forming foam concentrate mixed with approximately 50,000 gallons of water was released at the Brunswick Executive Airport. The release made its way out of a hangar into an oil/water separator and into nearby stormwater ponds.
The Owls Head discharge occurred the night of Nov. 2 at the intersection of Ash Point and North Shore drives. Mason noticed a fire truck using a hydrant at that location and spraying water. He thought it was an Owls Head truck and called the chief to ask what was going on, and was told it was not an Owls Head truck.
Mason said he then returned and videotaped what the South Thomaston truck and crew were doing because he noticed they were washing away gravel and loam he had put down at the former Grange Hall property that he and his wife had purchased.
Owls Head’s fire chief then called Mason back to say he had spoken to the South Thomaston chief who said someone had accidentally turned on a switch and filled its tanker with firefighting foam. The department took the truck to the hydrant in Owls Head to flush out the foam.
The town, including the fire department, was not notified that South Thomaston would be coming to their town, Mason said.
Mason said the foam was being discharged into a culvert and with the water from the fire hydrant at the intersection, it spread the chemical across his property and across North Shore Drive. Some of the homes in that area get their water from wells.
The town administrator said the foam was clearly visible the following day.
The town administrator notified the Maine Department of Environmental Protection and someone came down and did some soil testing the next day.
“The DEP is aware of the discharge and has taken a soil sample from the area as well as samples directly from the fire truck which consisted of mixtures of foam and water. DEP is evaluating next steps and determining whether any private drinking water wells in the area may be at risk,” DEP Deputy Commissioner David Madore said Monday.
The amount of foam discharged has not yet been determined.
The foam is used for chemical fires by covering fuel and depriving it of oxygen which prevents the fuel from igniting. The foam, however, has per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, also known as PFAS, which are a family of toxic chemicals linked to contamination of soil and water sources. PFAs are known as “forever chemicals” because they aren’t easily broken down in the environment or in living things.
Mason suggested the Select Board write a letter to the South Thomaston Select Board.
“The chemical is not good for eating, drinking, or living,” Mason said.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: NSA internal systems experienced outage following routine maintenance, US official confirms
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — An internal network the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline Tuesday after what the agency described as “routine maintenance.”
The problem disrupted the operations of NSANet, a classified internal network used by employees of the agency, according to a defense official who was not authorized to discuss the matter by name and spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity.
“The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the NSA said in a statement. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”
EN ESPAÑOL | Red de comunicaciones de seguridad de EE.UU., altamente clasificada, sufre caída, reporta CNN
The intelligence agency did not provide any additional details on the cause of the outage or the scope of the disruption.
The outage was first reported by CNN.
The NSA episode is among a series of cyber-related disruptions to critical government and private sector functions in the last week, including a system overload Friday that resulted in a ground stop of air traffic in the United States, a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase on Monday that caused ripple effects in the financial system and an internal systems outage at United Airlines that delayed departing flights.
On Tuesday , Apple acknowledged on its system status page that its Apple Music, App Store and AppleCare services suffered full outages after an internal update.
Top Trump administration national security officials said there was no indication that the events are related or attributable to a cyberattack or hostile activity.
“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation-state, with a malign actor of any kind,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters while traveling with the president in Asia.
Rubio acknowledged that it was “unsettling to see these reports day after day of some technical failures” and that while the government is always vigilant, each of the recent events “are distinct, and they’re different in their causation — in some cases, highly technical.”
Jay Clayton, the Trump administration’s director of national intelligence, attributed the problem to government institutions and private companies pushing through upgrades of their computer systems around the same time, resulting in periodic technological hiccups.
“Many people are patching their systems,” Clayton said in a CNBC interview Tuesday about the spate of disruptions. ”They know that their legacy systems have vulnerabilities. They’re outdated, they don’t work well with new systems. It is time for an upgrade across our digital infrastructure. And as you patch and upgrade your systems — taking them down and bringing them back up — there are things like this that happen.”
Sen. Mark Warner, the Democratic vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, echoed that assessment.
“AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” Warner said in a statement. “While we still need to get to the bottom of these incidents, the evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity.”

title: Pizza Hut co-founder Dan Carney dies at 95
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH/Gray News) - Dan Carney, who founded Pizza Hut with his brother, Frank, on Wichita State University’s campus in 1958, has died at 95.
Wichita State University announced the death.
Wichita State graduate
Dan Carney graduated from Wichita State University in 1953. He earned a Master of Business Administration 51 years later.
Pizza Hut’s start
Dan and Frank Carney opened the first Pizza Hut to cater to students. The business expanded to various Kansas locations and then became a national chain.
The business started with a $600 loan from their mother. The original location still stands on Wichita State University’s campus.
University statement
Wichita State University said Dan Carney’s legacy extended beyond his business success.
“For more than seven decades, Dan was deeply committed to Wichita State, sharing his time, leadership and generosity in ways that strengthened the university and created opportunities with countless students,” the university said in a statement on Facebook.
Dan Carney served as chair and a member of both the Wichita State University Foundation Board of Directors and the Wichita State University Board of Trustees.
Dan Carney is survived by his wife, Gayla, and numerous friends and family.

title: State approves higher standard offer rates for CMP and Versant’s Aroostook district
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Customers of the state’s two largest electrical utilities will pay a little more in 2027.
The Maine Public Utilities Commission on Tuesday accepted final standard offer bids for Central Maine Power and Versant Power’s Aroostook County district.
The new rates will increase the monthly bill of the average residential CMP customer by about $4.99 a month, according to the PUC. That’s based on monthly use of roughly 550 kWh.
The average residential customer of Versant’s Maine Public District (Aroostook County) will see an increase of about $2.30 a month.
The commission is planning to accept bids for Versant’s Bangor Hydro District (Penobscot, Hancock and Washington counties) on Wednesday.
The new rates take effect Jan. 1, 2027.
MPUC Acting Commission Chair Patrick Scully said electricity supply prices in Maine and New England are largely driven by the price of natural gas which has gone up because of limited pipeline capacity to New England, and the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
“While no price increase is ideal, especially when consumers are experiencing high energy costs across the board, we believe these are the best prices available through the competitive bidding process,” Scully said.
The changes approved Tuesday apply only to customers who don’t choose a supplier for their electricity and instead receive the Standard Offer Supply by default.
